column1: CLOUD-01 | A new approval extension needs immediate document validation and an external supplier portal. Would you put everything on-stack or on BTP?
column2:
Short answer
Keep the document check where it can reject the document before saving, using a supported local extension point. The supplier portal can be a separate BTP app if its users and release cycle justify that. Connect them through released remote interfaces. Make pending and failed steps visible. Choose based on timing, APIs, permissions, and recovery rather than putting everything in one place.

Reasoning and example
Suppose every internal posting waits for a live response from the supplier portal. A network outage can now stop all postings, even when the core document itself is valid. If the business permits it, save a valid submission locally and let the portal interaction happen afterward through a reliable integration process.

The user then needs to see whether the request is waiting, accepted, or failed. Track retries with a stable request identity and decide what withdrawal means after submission. Some rules must still reject the local document immediately, so keep those at a suitable supported local point. A separate application does not make remote work part of the same database transaction.

Avoid
Deploying side-by-side does not make synchronous cross-system validation atomic or automatically clean-core compliant.
Extension placement decision

Start from the business need and transaction boundary before choosing an extension location.
Explain it: When would local transactional consistency favor an on-stack extension?
Limit: Placement does not establish Clean Core level or availability in a specific edition.
Local and remote transaction boundaries

The remote commit belongs to another system, so local failure needs an explicit recovery strategy.
Explain it: What should happen if the remote side succeeds but the response is lost?
Limit: This explains distributed consistency, not a particular messaging product guarantee.
Remote commit and uncertain local outcome

The local application durably records intent before separately owned delivery. The remote payment commits, but its reply is lost; recovery must identify the existing effect through REQ-42.
Explain it: How do you distinguish an unprocessed request from a committed payment whose response never arrived?
Limit: The delivery and idempotency mechanisms are design requirements, not automatic guarantees from HTTP or RAP. This example does not claim distributed atomicity.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which business rule must be checked before the core document is committed?
  • How does the user recover when the portal accepts a request but the core system is unavailable?
Strong answer criteria
  • Explains which business steps run in which system
  • Compares response time and independent release needs
  • Explains recovery when only part of the process succeeds
Verification evidence
An architecture decision record, target API availability checks, and a failure-sequence test showing pending, retry, and withdrawal outcomes.

column1: CLOUD-02 | A stakeholder says ABAP Cloud means moving the existing application to SAP BTP ABAP environment. How would you correct the proposal?
column2:
Short answer
ABAP Cloud is a development model, not just a place to run code. It uses restricted language versions, released APIs, and models such as RAP on supported S/4HANA systems and SAP BTP ABAP environment. Moving to BTP is a separate decision. Check the data, business APIs, connectivity, and operational responsibilities available there before promising that an existing app will move unchanged.

Reasoning and example
A class currently reads sales data through a local S/4HANA interface. In a BTP ABAP system, the same business data and local interface may not exist. The new application might need a remote service, a supported replication design, or a different owner for that information. Valid ABAP syntax alone does not solve that difference.

List the application's dependencies and map each to an available target capability. Try the most important integration with realistic input before estimating the move. This separates two questions: can the code follow ABAP Cloud's rules, and is the proposed runtime the right place for the application? Both need evidence, even though they are often discussed together.

Avoid
Cloud-compatible syntax does not establish identical application content, API availability, or deployment portability.
BTP account and runtime map

Read the nesting as an organizational example, then distinguish the application, service instance and credentials.
Explain it: How is a service instance different from a binding or service key?
Limit: Schematic Cloud Foundry route; other BTP environments have different runtime structures.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which dependencies become remote after the move?
  • What target-system evidence would you require before estimating migration?
Strong answer criteria
  • Distinguishes model from runtime
  • Identifies lost data locality
  • Checks product-specific capabilities
Verification evidence
A list of target-system capabilities mapping each dependency to a supported local or remote replacement, plus a tested integration example.

Read and verify
  • SAP ABAP Cloud development model
    Use the documented rules to check the design choice. Confirm that the required option exists on the target product.

column1: CLOUD-03 | A developer proposes dynamic calls to an unreleased SAP class because static ABAP Cloud checks reject it. What do you do?
column2:
Short answer
Do not hide an unsupported dependency behind a dynamic call. Check the object's actual release state and look for a released alternative, supported extension point, or remote API on the target version. Revisit standard functionality if needed. An allowed classic boundary may be an option in a suitable private-edition landscape. It must be explicit and governed, not disguised as ABAP Cloud compliance.

Reasoning and example
A dynamically named class call may escape a superficial scan but still fail after an upgrade. The language or runtime may also reject it. Demonstrating that the call worked once does not prove that SAP supports the dependency or will keep its behavior stable.

Write down the exact capability that is missing and test supported alternatives with representative input. Where a classic exception is permitted, isolate it, identify its risk and owner, and keep the implementation within the product's actual rules. Public-edition restrictions do not disappear because another landscape allows classic development. An ATC suppression changes what is reported; it does not create a release contract for the object.

Avoid
An ATC suppression or dynamic name does not create a supported API contract.
Clean Core wrapper dependency

Trace dependencies across the wrapper instead of classifying the solution from its visible surface alone.
Explain it: What evidence would let you accept a classic SAP dependency responsibly?
Limit: A governance review must consider technology restrictions, classifications and lifecycle risk.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What options remain in Public Edition when no released extension exists?
  • How would you track an API gap without blocking unrelated delivery?
Strong answer criteria
  • Rejects hidden dependency bypass
  • Verifies target-specific alternatives
  • Separates private-edition exceptions from public-cloud rules
Verification evidence
ADT API-state evidence, a documented capability gap, and a decision record showing supported alternatives and any approved bounded exception.

    Use the documented rules to check the design choice. Confirm that the required option exists on the target product.

column1: CLOUD-04 | Two teams want independent releases but share pricing helpers and persistence types. How would you structure packages and software components?
column2:
Short answer
Give shared code a clear owner and a small, stable interface. Packages organize code and access; software components also affect delivery and lifecycle dependencies. Keep private database types with their owning component. Avoid circular dependencies and define delivery order. Supported component relations can allow targeted access, but access permission alone does not promise that an interface will stay compatible.

Reasoning and example
Two teams say they can release independently, but each uses the other's database row types. A field change can then require both components to activate together. Replacing those types with a narrow pricing request and result reduces the number of changes that callers must follow. The shared pricing capability also needs an owner and compatibility tests.

If that interface is still changing frequently, coordinated releases may be the honest choice for now. Creating more components does not itself remove the dependency. Document the direction of calls, permitted component access, and import order. Check that a provider change still supports previously delivered consumers before describing the components as independently releasable.

Avoid
More software components do not create independent lifecycles when their dependencies still require lockstep delivery.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • When would you choose a component relation instead of a C1 API?
  • How would an incompatible dependency removal be detected?
Strong answer criteria
  • Shows which component depends on which
  • Distinguishes permission to call an interface from a promise of compatibility
  • Matches component boundaries to how releases actually work
Verification evidence
A dependency graph without cycles, explicit component relations, a transport/import sequence, and compatibility checks against the prior delivered API snapshot.

  • SAP software component organization and lifecycle boundaries

column1: CLOUD-05 | The same business capability is exposed through a local released API and a remote service. Which should an on-stack application consume?
column2:
Short answer
Compare what the two APIs actually do. A suitable local API avoids network calls and may fit the supported local transaction. A remote API has its own identity, failures, and transaction boundary. They may expose different operations despite similar names. Choose the contract that fits permissions, timing, and saving; do not assume local and remote access are interchangeable.

Reasoning and example
Calling the same SAP system through HTTP from a save routine can open another session. That session may compete for locks or commit separately, which makes a simple-looking self-call difficult to reason about. Check whether a suitable released local operation can be used in the required RAP phase instead.

On the other hand, a local read interface does not replace a remote command just because both concern purchase orders. Compare the operation, authorization, and failure behavior, then test concurrent use. A C1 local-use contract and a C2 remote-use contract authorize different kinds of consumption. If the caller may later move to BTP, keep that future network boundary in mind without pretending it already has local transaction guarantees.

Avoid
C1 local consumption and C2 remote consumption are different purposes; one release contract does not authorize the other.
Local and remote transaction boundaries

The remote commit belongs to another system, so local failure needs an explicit recovery strategy.
Explain it: What should happen if the remote side succeeds but the response is lost?
Limit: This explains distributed consistency, not a particular messaging product guarantee.
Release contracts versus Clean Core levels

The two tables are separate classification axes. C1 identifies a local-use contract, while Level C identifies internal-object exposure in the Clean Core assessment context.
Explain it: What else must you verify after finding a C1 release flag, and why does a wrapper not erase the underlying exposure?
Limit: These are the three contracts requested for this comparison, not the complete release-contract catalogue. Exact object classification, extension technology, target edition, and ATC scope remain decisive.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Can the chosen local command participate in this RAP save phase?
  • What changes if the consumer moves to BTP next year?
Strong answer criteria
  • Compares full contracts
  • Recognizes self-call transaction risks
  • Plans a replaceable consumption boundary
Verification evidence
Documented local and remote API contracts plus a transaction and authorization test for the chosen consumption path.

Read and verify

    Use the documented rules to check the design choice. Confirm that the required option exists on the target product.

column1: CLOUD-06 | A CDS object compiles in the development system but fails after delivery to an older supported release. How would you prevent recurrence?
column2:
Short answer
Define the products and releases the application supports before choosing features. Check CDS syntax, provider contracts, bindings, language rules, and released APIs on those targets. Test the lowest supported release. When a feature is unavailable, choose a compatible design, raise the minimum supported version explicitly, or maintain a separate variant. Activation on the development system proves only that system works.

Reasoning and example
A developer copies a projection example from current documentation. It activates locally, but an older delivery target does not support its provider contract. The transport fails before anyone can test the screen. Checking only the ABAP class would not have caught the CDS and service dependency.

Build a small compatibility test containing the related CDS, behavior, and service artifacts and execute a representative request on the lowest target. Record which features and API releases are available there. Keep broadly reusable business contracts separate from newer delivery features where that helps. Do not silently change the supported release promise after development; the design and support policy need to agree.

Avoid
An object being active in development does not prove compatibility with every product edition or supported transport target.
RAP release and consumption gates

Review eligibility, behavior and delivery as separate evidence gates.
Explain it: Which gate would catch an API-compatible change that breaks deployment configuration?
Limit: A teaching checklist; exact release contracts, component visibility and delivery tools depend on the product.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Where would you document the minimum feature level?
  • Which differences justify a versioned implementation rather than a shared code path?
Strong answer criteria
  • Sets a concrete support matrix
  • Tests the lowest supported release
  • Includes dependent repository artifacts
Verification evidence
A versioned compatibility matrix, target activation evidence, and service tests tied to the exact supported release and delivery revision.

  • SAP released APIs, contracts, visibility, and states

column1: CLOUD-07 | Should a request, its approval history, and an external purchase order be one RAP business object?
column2:
Short answer
Put data in one RAP business object when it has shared ownership, lifecycle, and rules that must hold in one transaction. Request items may belong to their request. Approval history may need separate retention rules. An external purchase order has another owner and transaction, so usually reference it through an API. Screen layout alone should not decide the composition tree.

Reasoning and example
Deleting a request should not accidentally remove approval evidence that the business must retain. It also cannot safely cascade a database deletion into another system's purchase order as if both were local rows. Define cancellation, retention, and external failure outcomes before drawing the composition hierarchy.

The opposite mistake is separating request lines that must be checked and locked together. That can make a simple total rule difficult to enforce consistently. Write down which facts must always agree at save time and who owns each piece of data. Keep tightly related local data together where appropriate, and use an explicit workflow or reconciliation process for relationships that cross system boundaries.

Avoid
A composition relationship is not a convenient visual grouping and cannot provide atomicity across an external system.
CDS links and ownership

Items belong to the order BO; a partner reference crosses to an independently managed object.
Explain it: What breaks if a declared to-one relationship actually returns two partners?
Limit: Composition semantics and generated operations still require the corresponding RAP model.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which business rule requires the changes to commit together?
  • How do retention and cancellation rules affect which entities belong in the composition?
Strong answer criteria
  • Starts with the business rules that must always hold
  • Identifies data ownership and retention needs
  • Explains how separate systems stay consistent
Verification evidence
A list of business rules, allowed states and transitions, and reasons for the composition design, with deletion, cancellation, and remote-posting failure tests.

Read and verify
  • SAP extension architecture guidance
    Use the documented rules to check the design choice. Confirm that the required option exists on the target product.

column1: CLOUD-08 | A partner wants one ABAP solution to serve several customers. What isolation questions must be answered before calling it multitenant?
column2:
Short answer
First verify the runtime's supported multitenancy model. Separate each customer's data and access across storage, configuration, caches, jobs, logs, and outbound connections. Automatic client handling covers only part of this. Define onboarding, upgrades, and offboarding too. Prove the boundary with tests where one tenant tries to read or affect another; a tenant column alone is not enough.

Reasoning and example
Two customers both have document number 100. If a shared cache uses only that number as its key, it may return the wrong customer's result where the runtime scope allows reuse. Database queries can be correctly restricted while the cache still leaks information. An outbound connection selected from the wrong tenant context can cause a similar problem.

Use the supported tenant context throughout the design and separate provider administration from customer permissions. Test background jobs and resources that live longer than one request. During offboarding, confirm that access and the intended data are removed without affecting another customer. Calling the solution multitenant requires this broader isolation evidence, not only a successful two-client database query.

Avoid
Adding a tenant field or relying on automatic client filtering alone does not establish complete multitenancy isolation.
BTP account and runtime map

Read the nesting as an organizational example, then distinguish the application, service instance and credentials.
Explain it: How is a service instance different from a binding or service key?
Limit: Schematic Cloud Foundry route; other BTP environments have different runtime structures.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which caches or jobs outlive one request?
  • How do you prove offboarding removes access without damaging another tenant?
Strong answer criteria
  • Covers non-database isolation paths
  • Uses supported tenant context
  • Includes tenant lifecycle operations
Verification evidence
A tenant-boundary threat model, two-tenant negative integration tests, and an onboarding/offboarding runbook validated in the target runtime.

Read and verify
  • SAP ABAP development and multitenancy guidance
    Use the documented rules to check the design choice. Confirm that the required option exists on the target product.

column1: CLOUD-09 | A business team requests a new field, a rule, and a custom app. How do you decide between configuration, key-user, and developer extensibility?
column2:
Short answer
Break the request into the field, rule, and application needs. Check standard configuration first, then supported key-user options. Use developer extensibility for requirements those options cannot meet safely. Verify where the field must appear and when the rule must run. Keep meaning, permissions, transport, and ownership consistent across the chosen mechanisms instead of rebuilding everything in custom code.

Reasoning and example
The new field must appear in a standard form, an API, and analytics. A supported key-user business context may already provide those publication paths. Creating a field in a separate custom table does not automatically connect it to them. Try the exact propagation on the target system before choosing the implementation.

The rule may fit a supported key-user hook if its data and execution limits match. Complex orchestration might need developer code instead. Assign an owner for changes to business-maintained rules and test their permissions and transport behavior. The right choice follows the requirement; key-user tooling is not inherently less serious, and developer tooling is not a reason to duplicate existing configuration.

Avoid
Key-user extensibility is not inherently less serious engineering, and developer extensibility is not a reason to duplicate standard configuration.
Extension placement decision

Start from the business need and transaction boundary before choosing an extension location.
Explain it: When would local transactional consistency favor an on-stack extension?
Limit: Placement does not establish Clean Core level or availability in a specific edition.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Who owns a rule that business users can change?
  • How will the field reach the required integration and output artifacts?
Strong answer criteria
  • Checks standard options for each part of the requirement
  • Checks where the field appears and what the extension hook allows
  • Names who maintains and delivers each extension
Verification evidence
A requirement-to-extension matrix and a target-system demonstration of field propagation, rule authorization, and transport behavior.

column1: CLOUD-10 | Can you expose the same RAP projection to a Fiori UI and long-lived external consumers?
column2:
Short answer
Reuse the business model where it makes sense, but protect external consumers from routine UI changes. A Fiori UI may need draft and feature controls; an integration needs a stable API, paging, retry rules, and communication setup. Separate projections or services can support those different needs. Check the available binding features and test both consumers against the same business rules.

Reasoning and example
A UI team removes a property it no longer displays. If a nightly integration uses the same uncontrolled service contract, that harmless screen change can break the job. A draft-based editing process may also be a poor fit for an external command that expects a final posting result.

Define which fields and operations each consumer can rely on, and keep shared business checks in the common implementation where appropriate. Record service metadata and run compatibility tests before changes. For a breaking external change, provide an explicit version or migration path and deprecation policy. Generating an OData endpoint for a UI is not the same as committing to a durable external API contract.

Avoid
An OData endpoint generated for a UI is not automatically a released, durable integration contract for external systems.
RAP contract stack

Read from the client down to storage, then explain what each artifact contributes.
Explain it: Where would you restrict the exposed operation set?
Limit: Conceptual layers; the exact artifact set depends on the scenario and release.
RAP release and consumption gates

Review eligibility, behavior and delivery as separate evidence gates.
Explain it: Which gate would catch an API-compatible change that breaks deployment configuration?
Limit: A teaching checklist; exact release contracts, component visibility and delivery tools depend on the product.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which behavior should be shared and which should be projected differently?
  • How would you introduce a breaking external-contract change?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates consumer contracts
  • Preserves shared business rules
  • Addresses external API lifecycle
Verification evidence
Service metadata baselines, UI and integration contract tests, and documented compatibility and deprecation rules.

Read and verify

    Use the documented rules to check the design choice. Confirm that the required option exists on the target product.

column1: CLOUD-11 | A released CDS view contains all required fields. Why might it still be unsuitable for implementing a business command?
column2:
Short answer
A released read view lets you read data; it does not automatically let you change that business object. Find the supported command API and check its permissions, locks, validation, and save rules. Do not update underlying tables because their fields are visible in a query. If no suitable command exists, revisit the process or record an API gap.

Reasoning and example
A view exposes a purchase order's approval status. Updating that status directly in the database may appear to approve the order, while skipping change history, outputs, follow-on checks, or related state. The field is part of a larger business operation, not simply a value that any reader may change.

Use a supported command and test both acceptance and rejection. Also consider a change made after your initial read: the command needs the correct concurrency handling rather than trusting an earlier status forever. If the released interface does not provide the required command, document that limitation. A useful read model cannot grant write ownership over its provider's persistence.

Avoid
A released read API does not release its underlying tables for mutation or guarantee that its fields form a write contract.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How would you handle a query result that becomes stale before the command?
  • What evidence distinguishes a supported command from a database shortcut?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates query and command semantics
  • Preserves provider ownership
  • Handles stale reads and concurrency
Verification evidence
The command API's release and behavior documentation, plus concurrent-change and validation-failure tests.

column1: CLOUD-12 | A large classic application cannot be replaced in one release. How would you introduce ABAP Cloud without creating two inconsistent applications?
column2:
Short answer
Move one clear business capability at a time and keep one authoritative owner for each business state. Define how old and new callers are routed, how identifiers stay consistent, and how results are reconciled. A governed classic boundary may support coexistence in a suitable landscape. Avoid uncontrolled writes from both paths. Give the temporary bridge explicit retirement criteria.

Reasoning and example
The old report and the new RAP app both update the same document through different rules. Users can now reach states that one application accepts and the other rejects. A safer first step may change the screen or read path while both versions still use the same approved posting owner.

Plan when write ownership changes, how traffic is routed, and how you can reverse the cutover if needed. Compare results and reconcile records before retiring the old path. Set a measurable condition for removing the temporary adapter so it does not become an ownerless permanent platform. A RAP screen alone does not prove that the legacy posting transaction behind it now follows ABAP Cloud rules.

Avoid
Using RAP for the new UI does not by itself modernize or validate the legacy posting transaction behind it.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which system owns writes during each transition phase?
  • What objective condition lets you remove the bridge?
Strong answer criteria
  • Defines one authoritative writer
  • Plans coexistence and cutover
  • Sets retirement criteria
Verification evidence
A phased ownership map, routing and rollback plan, reconciliation results, and an explicit bridge-removal milestone.

Read and verify
  • SAP extension architecture guidance
    Use the documented rules to check the design choice. Confirm that the required option exists on the target product.

column1: CLOUD-13 | A shared custom API is widely used but has no named owner. What would you change before accepting another dependency on it?
column2:
Short answer
Name an owner before adding more consumers. That owner must maintain the API's meaning, compatibility, security, operations, and support policy. Find existing callers and record current behavior. Choose an appropriate release or component-access mechanism and explain the limits to users of the API. A technically callable object is not a reliable shared service without those responsibilities.

Reasoning and example
A shared pricing helper changes its rounding rule without changing a parameter. Every caller still compiles, but invoice totals now differ. The API owner needs to treat that as a behavior change and assess it with consumers, not declare compatibility because the ABAP signature stayed the same.

Capture examples for amounts, units, exceptions, and transaction assumptions, then use them as regression checks. Inventory remote or external consumers too; a local where-used list may not show them all. Set a change-notification and support process. If no team can sustain that responsibility, do not advertise the helper as independently reusable infrastructure merely by making it public or setting a release flag.

Avoid
Public visibility or a C1 release flag does not replace accountable ownership and semantic compatibility testing.
RAP release and consumption gates

Review eligibility, behavior and delivery as separate evidence gates.
Explain it: Which gate would catch an API-compatible change that breaks deployment configuration?
Limit: A teaching checklist; exact release contracts, component visibility and delivery tools depend on the product.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Who approves a behavioral change without a signature change?
  • How do you discover consumers outside the local where-used list?
Strong answer criteria
  • Names who maintains the API promise
  • Tests behavior as well as signatures
  • Finds the real consumers
Verification evidence
An API owner record, consumer inventory, support policy, and executable consumer-contract examples tied to a released baseline.

column1: CLOUD-14 | A released BAdI exists, but it runs after the point where the requirement must reject a transaction. Is it still the right extension?
column2:
Short answer
A released extension point can still run at the wrong time for your rule. Check when it executes, what data it sees, what it may change, and how it can reject work. If the rule must prevent saving, use a supported point that can do that. Otherwise revise the process; reporting an error after commit cannot undo the document.

Reasoning and example
The business says that an invalid approval reference must prevent document creation. You find a released notification BAdI that runs after saving. Raising a message there cannot turn the already committed creation into a rejected save. A later reversal is a separate business operation, with its own history and possible downstream effects.

Map the actual transaction phases and inspect the extension contract before choosing the hook. Test invalid input, rollback, and update failure on the target system. If no suitable preventive hook exists, discuss another supported design with the business. A familiar method name or released status proves neither the required timing nor permission to change the transaction's outcome.

Avoid
A released extension point can still be the wrong place for a particular business rule.
Extension placement decision

Start from the business need and transaction boundary before choosing an extension location.
Explain it: When would local transactional consistency favor an on-stack extension?
Limit: Placement does not establish Clean Core level or availability in a specific edition.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What data and modifications does the BAdI contract actually permit?
  • Would compensating after save meet the same business requirement?
Strong answer criteria
  • Checks hook timing and permissions
  • Distinguishes prevention from compensation
  • Validates behavior with failures
Verification evidence
A transaction-phase map, the extension-point contract, and a target-system test proving when rejection or follow-up occurs.

Read and verify

    Use the documented rules to check the design choice. Confirm that the required option exists on the target product.

column1: CLOUD-15 | Your domain classes depend on Gateway messages, SQL row types, and HTTP clients. How would you improve the architecture without a wholesale rewrite?
column2:
Short answer
Extract one business decision behind a small, clear input and result. Keep HTTP, database, and framework-specific mapping in adapters around it. Preserve existing callers and transaction ownership while making the change. This lets you test the rule without rebuilding the whole application. Adding wrapper classes helps only if the business logic actually stops depending on infrastructure details.

Reasoning and example
An eligibility calculation currently reads an HTTP request and creates Gateway messages directly. Let it instead receive the needed business values and return an eligibility decision with a clear reason. An adapter can translate that result into RAP messages or an integration response. Persistence and communication remain separate collaborators rather than hidden work inside the rule.

Before extracting it, capture cases for rounding, missing data, and failures so existing behavior stays protected. Move one responsibility at a time and rerun the real integration acceptance tests. Do not move commits or change the caller's transaction expectations accidentally. A new class per framework object adds little value if every supposedly reusable method still exposes framework types.

Avoid
Wrapping every framework call in another class adds layers without isolating business policy if framework types still dominate the contract.
OO interfaces and dependency injection

The service depends on a repository contract. Production and test implementations fit the same socket; the composition boundary supplies the appropriate collaborator.
Explain it: Which object chooses the implementation, and what does a double-based test fail to prove?
Limit: The plug is a design metaphor, not a SAP connector or code signature. Injection does not itself guarantee a good abstraction or production integration.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which extraction has the lowest transaction risk?
  • What should remain in the RAP behavior implementation?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates one clear business responsibility
  • Preserves callers and transaction ownership
  • Tests observable behavior before and after the change
Verification evidence
A bounded before/after dependency map and passing business-policy tests plus unchanged integration acceptance results.

Read and verify
  • SAP extension architecture guidance
    Use the documented rules to check the design choice. Confirm that the required option exists on the target product.

column1: CLOUD-16 | A side-by-side service needs to act for users and also run scheduled reconciliation. Would you use one technical identity for both?
column2:
Short answer
Treat user requests and unattended jobs as different access needs. Choose supported communication scenarios, authentication, and permissions for each. Use separate identities or scopes when required by those needs. Record who initiated a business action and plan credential rotation and tenant selection. One broad technical identity can give interactive users more access than they should have.

Reasoning and example
A reconciliation job may legitimately read documents across many business areas. A person using the portal should see only their permitted documents. If the portal forwards every request using the job's broad identity without the required authorization design, the UI can accidentally expose that wider access to every user.

Using a person's short-lived credentials for a nightly job creates a different problem: the job may stop when those credentials expire. Define the supported user-delegation and machine-to-machine flows separately. Test denied access, audit attribution, rotation, and tenant offboarding. Successful authentication proves which identity connected; it does not prove that the requested operation or tenant is allowed for that identity.

Avoid
Authentication success proves identity, not permission for the requested business operation or tenant.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Where is the initiating user recorded when a technical identity performs the command?
  • What happens during credential rotation or tenant offboarding?
Strong answer criteria

column1: CLOUD-17 | A released dependency is deprecated but still works. How do you decide when and how to replace it?
column2:
Short answer
Deprecated means an API should be replaced according to its lifecycle guidance, not necessarily that it has already stopped working. Check the successor, support limits, affected callers, and supported target releases. Compare behavior as well as names and parameters. Plan tests, rollout, and monitoring before switching. Avoid adding unnecessary new dependencies on an API already scheduled for replacement.

Reasoning and example
A successor serves the same business purpose but returns different keys and uses another paging model. A mechanical method-name replacement may miss records or duplicate work. It might also change permissions or return a pending result where the old API completed synchronously. Test those differences with representative consumers and failure cases.

Check whether the successor exists on the lowest supported release. If not, the transition may require a deliberate compatibility path or a support-policy decision. Roll out with clear success measures and a supported way to reverse the change if needed. Keep old and new behavior visible until migration is complete, then remove the old dependency and its maintenance burden.

Avoid
A release contract does not mean an API never evolves, and deprecation is different from decommissioning.

column1: CLOUD-18 | What would you require before approving a senior team's ABAP Cloud architecture for production?
column2:
Short answer
Require evidence that the main business rules, permissions, transaction boundaries, and recovery paths work on the intended runtime. Check released dependencies, realistic workload, monitoring, retention, and deployment order. Give important assumptions an owner and a test result. Distinguish a prototype from a production-tested solution. Remaining risk can be accepted deliberately, with practical controls and clear responsibility.

Reasoning and example
A Fiori demo using mocked data looks convincing, but it cannot prove real RAP locking or permissions. Walk through a concurrent update, a dependency outage, a failed deployment, and a recovery exercise on the relevant environment. Link each result to the actual release candidate so old evidence is not mistaken for proof of new code.

Focus effort on failures that would harm the business rather than collecting diagrams alone. Confirm who monitors failures, who can retry safely, and how data remains consistent during recovery. A green syntax check or ATC run supports the review but cannot replace these checks. Production approval should state what was demonstrated and which controlled risks remain.

column1: RAP-01 | What are the building blocks of a RAP application?
column2:
Short answer
A RAP app has a data model, business rules, and a service. Tables store the data, and CDS describes what that data means. The behavior definition says what users can do; ABAP handlers add your business logic. Projections choose what a particular app exposes. The service definition and binding make those entities available through a chosen protocol.

Reasoning and example
Imagine a purchase-request app with a Submit button. CDS describes the request and its items. The behavior definition declares Submit, and its handler checks or changes the request as the operation requires. The transaction first holds those changes in memory. The RAP save sequence then writes valid changes to the database.

The projection exposes the fields and operations this app needs. The service definition selects the entities, while the binding chooses, for example, an OData service type. Read-access rules and UI annotations handle other concerns. Keeping these jobs separate makes it easier to find where a missing field, failed operation, or incorrect screen comes from.

The behavior definition (BDEF) is the operation contract. The behavior pool is its ABAP implementation container; generated local handler methods implement custom rules and operations. Managed RAP already supplies standard CRUD handling. strict(2) checks modeling requirements, not whether every referenced API is released or every permission is correct.

Avoid
Behavior is not implemented by the service definition, and a binding alone does not make the endpoint production-ready.

column1: RAP-02 | How do you choose managed versus unmanaged RAP?
column2:
Short answer
Use managed RAP when the framework can handle your object's changes and database writes. Use unmanaged RAP when your implementation must handle those jobs, often because an existing business API already owns them. Managed RAP with unmanaged save is a middle option: RAP handles changes, and your code handles persistence. In every option, RAP still controls the transaction.

Reasoning and example
For a new travel-request app with your own tables, managed RAP usually avoids writing basic create, update, and delete handling yourself. You can focus on rules such as checking travel dates. For an existing application, a business API may already update several related tables correctly. Reusing it may justify unmanaged save or a fully unmanaged implementation.

Before choosing, check whether that API commits by itself, uses update tasks, or requires its own locks. A commit inside local RAP processing violates its runtime rules and may be rejected. Moving the call to a separate transaction creates another problem: it can save independently, and a later local rollback cannot undo it. Choose based on the API's behavior, not the application's age.

Avoid
Unmanaged does not permit arbitrary COMMIT WORK or database changes anywhere in a handler.

column1: RAP-03 | What is the transactional buffer?
column2:
Short answer
The transactional buffer is the transaction's working copy of a business object. It includes changes that have not yet been saved. EML can read this current state through the business object. A direct database SELECT may still see the old saved values. Managed RAP supplies buffer handling; an unmanaged implementation must provide the required handling.

Reasoning and example
Suppose an order item has quantity 2 in the database. The user changes it to 5, and RAP must recalculate the order total before saving. Reading the item through the business object lets the calculation use the pending quantity of 5. Reading only the database can give 2 and produce an outdated total.

After a successful save, the database contains the new state. Until then, the buffer belongs to this transaction. It is not a place to keep unfinished work across unrelated HTTP requests. Draft provides separate persistent storage for that use case. This distinction helps explain why a correct database query can still be wrong inside a business rule.

Avoid
The buffer is not a durable draft store and does not survive arbitrary stateless HTTP requests.

column1: RAP-04 | Where may COMMIT ENTITIES be called?
column2:
Short answer
Call COMMIT ENTITIES from an external ABAP program that owns an EML transaction. Inside a RAP handler or saver, let the framework finish the transaction. Do not call COMMIT ENTITIES or COMMIT WORK there. This rule also applies to actions, validations, and determinations. The OData request framework owns the save boundary for its requests.

Reasoning and example
A standalone ABAP program creates a request and its items with EML. It checks the modification responses, then calls COMMIT ENTITIES at the point where the complete business change should be saved. It must also check the save responses, because accepting a modification does not prove that saving succeeded.

Now put the same creation logic inside a RAP action. The action may make permitted changes, but it must not commit them itself. The framework still has other rules and changes to process. An early commit could split what should be one transaction, and violating the RAP contract can cause a runtime error. Moving the commit into a saver method does not fix that.

Avoid
Moving the commit from validation into SAVE or CANCEL does not make it valid.

column1: RAP-05 | What are the steps of the RAP save sequence, and where is the point of no return?
column2:
Short answer
RAP saves changes in this order: FINALIZE finishes calculations, CHECK_BEFORE_SAVE checks the data, ADJUST_NUMBERS assigns final keys when late numbering is used, SAVE writes the data, and CLEANUP clears the buffer. The point of no return comes after CHECK_BEFORE_SAVE has passed for every involved business object. Remember it as: calculate, check, number, write, clear.

Reasoning and example
1. FINALIZE - finish the data. For an order, calculate the total from its items. In a managed BO, relevant on-save determinations do this work; in an unmanaged BO, use the corresponding saver method. This is the last phase for permitted changes to the transactional buffer. Ordinary EML MODIFY requests after FINALIZE cause runtime errors; the ban does not start at the beginning of FINALIZE.

2. CHECK_BEFORE_SAVE - make the final business checks. For example, reject an order whose delivery date is invalid. Managed BOs use validations; unmanaged BOs implement the corresponding saver check. Only when every involved BO passes do we cross the point of no return. A failed check stops the save before late numbering and persistence.

3. ADJUST_NUMBERS - assign final keys for late numbering. Our new order now receives document number 4711. Early numbering has already assigned the key, so it does not need this late assignment. Receiving a number does not yet prove that the database commit succeeded.

4. SAVE - write the changes. With normal managed save, RAP writes the BO data. With additional save, RAP still writes it, and your save_modified method adds work such as an audit row. With managed interaction plus with unmanaged save, your save_modified method replaces managed persistence. A fully unmanaged BO instead implements save in its local saver class. SAVE is the phase name; it does not mean every scenario uses a method named save.

5. CLEANUP - clear transaction-local buffers when the LUW finishes, including after rollback. This prevents old working data from leaking into the next transaction. CLEANUP_FINALIZE is a separate early-failure hook when FINALIZE or CHECK_BEFORE_SAVE fails in an involved BO; it can undo work done during finalization. It is not the last step of a successful save, and you should not assume every rejected save automatically discards all user input.

Example: two order items cost 40 and 60. FINALIZE calculates 100. CHECK_BEFORE_SAVE detects a bad delivery date, so the save stops: no late document number and no persisted order. With a valid date, late numbering can assign 4711 and persistence writes the order and items. The transaction owner completes the commit; cleanup then removes the working data. A handler or saver must not issue its own commit.

Senior detail: the point of no return means ordinary business checks must already have passed. It does not mean a database outage is impossible. SAP also documents a special failure-capable saver, CL_ABAP_BEHAVIOR_SAVER_FAILED, for supported cases such as BAPI integration. Check the exact scenario and release rather than treating that exception as permission to move normal validation into late save.

Avoid
Do not ban all EML changes inside FINALIZE, put normal validation after the point of no return, or confuse save_modified in a managed BO with the save method of a fully unmanaged BO. CLEANUP_FINALIZE belongs to the early-failure path.

Follow one order from total calculation to buffer cleanup. The orange branch stops a rejected save before late numbering and persistence.

Compare four persistence choices. Both save extensions of managed BOs use save_modified; a fully unmanaged BO uses save.

column1: RAP-06 | Determination validation action or precheck?
column2:
Short answer
Use a determination to fill or calculate values automatically. Use a validation to check whether data is acceptable for saving. Use an action for an operation a caller explicitly requests, such as Submit. Use a precheck to reject an incoming change before it enters the buffer. Choose by what must happen and when, rather than putting every rule in one handler.

Reasoning and example
In a request app, a determination can fill the default currency. A validation can reject an end date that is before the start date. Submit is an action because the user deliberately asks for a business step. A suitable precheck can reject a proposed field value before the update is accepted into the transaction.

A validation should report a problem, not silently repair the data. Also check the implementation type: in unmanaged RAP, declared determinations and validations apply to draft instances. For active instances, the appropriate unmanaged operation handlers and save checks must enforce consistency. Copying a managed example without that distinction can leave invalid active data unchecked.

Avoid
An action is not simply another name for a CRUD event, and validations should not modify business data.

column1: RAP-07 | How do FAILED REPORTED and MAPPED differ?
column2:
Short answer
FAILED says which instance or operation was rejected. REPORTED carries messages, including their severity and the field or instance they concern. MAPPED links a caller's creation identifier to the created object's identity where the operation supports it. These structures do different jobs. An error message in REPORTED alone does not necessarily make an operation fail.

Reasoning and example
A user saves two requests, and one has an invalid delivery date. A validation must identify the rejected request in FAILED and explain the problem in REPORTED. Adding a field reference lets the UI point to the date the user should fix. Reporting only an error-looking message is not a reliable way to reject the save.

For a successful create, the caller may have used a content ID before a final identity was available. MAPPED allows the caller to connect that input to the new object. Always use the response parameters actually provided by the handler contract. For example, a determination does not provide FAILED, so it is not a substitute for a rejecting validation.

Avoid
Error severity in REPORTED is not a substitute for FAILED; determinations do not expose FAILED.

column1: RAP-08 | What is EML and when do you use it instead of SQL?
column2:
Short answer
EML lets ABAP code work with a RAP business object through its operations. READ ENTITIES reads its transactional state; MODIFY ENTITIES requests changes or actions. SQL reads or changes database data directly. It does not run the object's business behavior. Use EML when you need the business operation, and choose a suitable query interface when you only need database results.

Reasoning and example
Suppose a background program must submit an expense request. Updating its status column with SQL may skip checks, locks, and authorization handling that belong to Submit. Calling the exposed action through EML uses the business object's defined behavior and returns operation responses that the program must inspect.

The program also needs to handle the eventual save result. A successful action response is not proof of a completed commit. For a read-only report, a suitable CDS or SQL query may be the clearer and faster choice. EML is useful because it follows business behavior, not because every EML read is automatically faster than SQL.

An EML read normally starts from known entity keys or an association. It is not the managed list query with $filter, $orderby and paging that an OData consumer uses to find orders. Use a suitable query to find the records, then the BO operations to work with their transactional state.

Avoid
EML does not mean that every read is automatically the best performance choice; use the correct semantic interface.

column1: RAP-09 | What does IN LOCAL MODE mean?
column2:
Short answer
IN LOCAL MODE is for a business object's own internal EML calls. Depending on the operation, it skips checks such as authorization, feature control, and prechecks so internal logic can maintain the object. It does not create a separate transaction or allow forbidden save behavior. It is not a general way for external callers to turn off another object's security.

Reasoning and example
A request total is readonly to users because the application calculates it. A determination inside that business object may need to update the total after an item changes. An internal EML update in local mode allows this kind of controlled maintenance even though a normal external update of the field is restricted.

The public operation still needs its proper permission checks and business rules. Review what the internal code changes and why it is trusted. A call to a different business object needs its own supported access contract; do not treat local mode as a reusable security bypass. The changes still belong to RAP's transaction and must follow its save rules.

Avoid
It is not a general-purpose option for external callers to disable security on any BO.

column1: RAP-10 | What do %cid %cid_ref %tky and %pid mean?
column2:
Short answer
These fields identify objects at different stages of a RAP request. %cid labels a new instance, and %cid_ref refers to that creation, for example when adding its items. %tky is the transactional key, including relevant context such as draft state. %pid is a preliminary identifier for late numbering. None of these names means they are interchangeable.

Reasoning and example
Create a header and one item in one request. The header may not yet have its final document number. Give its creation a content ID, then refer to that ID when creating the item by association. RAP can connect them without requiring the caller to guess a final key.

Inside handlers, use the supplied transactional identity when returning results or messages. Rebuilding a key from only the document number can lose draft context. For late numbering, ADJUST_NUMBERS maps the preliminary identification in %pre to the final %key. A content ID belongs to request correlation; it is not a business number to store and show forever.

Avoid
%tky means transactional key, not temporary key; %cid is not a persisted business document number.

column1: RAP-11 | Early numbering versus late numbering?
column2:
Short answer
Early numbering gives an instance its final key during interaction. Late numbering keeps a preliminary identity and assigns the final key late in saving. A technical UUID and a business document number can be separate fields with different rules. Late numbering can avoid consuming numbers for some rejected changes. It does not, by itself, promise a gap-free business sequence.

Reasoning and example
A new request can receive a UUID immediately so its items have a stable technical parent. The business may want the visible approval number only when the request is accepted. That number can follow a separate supported numbering design rather than being used as the only technical identity.

Now consider two users saving at the same time. Reading the highest number and adding one can give both users the same result. Use suitable number-range and transaction handling instead. If the business requires no gaps, also examine failed saves, cancellations, and the exact numbering guarantees. Choosing late numbering is only one part of that design, not proof that every possible gap has disappeared.

Start by separating identity from the label a person sees. OrderUUID can be a stable technical key generated immediately, while OrderNumber is a later business number. Late numbering is needed when the actual entity key must be assigned late; a later display number alone does not automatically require it.

Avoid
Late numbering alone does not guarantee a gap-free sequence, and SELECT MAX plus one is unsafe under concurrency.

column1: RAP-12 | What problem does draft solve?
column2:
Short answer
Draft saves unfinished editing work separately from active business data. It lets a user continue across HTTP requests or return after an interruption. RAP provides operations such as Edit, Resume, Activate, and Discard; Prepare can run selected checks and calculations. Activation moves valid draft changes into active processing. The request still needs its save sequence to finish.

Reasoning and example
Maya edits order 4703 from 80 EUR to 120 EUR and closes the browser. The draft keeps her unfinished 120 EUR edit, while active business data stays at 80 EUR. When she returns, activation rejects 120 EUR because this example permits at most 100 EUR. She corrects the draft to 90 EUR; only successful activation and save make 90 EUR the active value.

When the user activates it, required checks can reject missing or invalid data. Successful activation is part of the processing that produces active data; it does not authorize a custom handler to commit on its own. Keep draft and active identities clear in reads, messages, and actions. A custom Submit action may represent a separate business step and is not automatically the same as draft activation.

column1: RAP-13 | Can you rely on determination and validation order?
column2:
Short answer
Do not make one independent determination depend on another running first unless the framework contract guarantees it. Calculate related values together or make their dependency explicit. Derivations should give a consistent result when repeated. RAP does have defined processing phases. That does not mean every handler inside a phase has an order you may rely on.

Reasoning and example
Suppose one determination converts an amount into the display currency and another calculates the total. If the total assumes conversion has already run, a later change may leave an incorrect result. A clearer design calculates both from the same current source values, or puts the dependent steps into one suitable operation.

Test more than the first create. Change the quantity twice, change the currency, and repeat the same update. The final total should remain correct and the handlers should not keep triggering each other unnecessarily. The issue is not that all RAP ordering is random. The issue is relying on an execution order that the documented contract never promised.

column1: RAP-14 | How does persistent field mapping work?
column2:
Short answer
Field mapping tells RAP which persistence field belongs to a CDS element when their names differ. For example, RequestUUID can map to the table field request_uuid. The mapping connects names for the selected persistence implementation. It does not calculate new values or join tables. Business calculations and conversions need their own supported logic.

Reasoning and example
Your table uses request_uuid, but the CDS model exposes the clearer element name RequestUUID. The behavior mapping connects those names so persistence handling can read and write the intended field. Check every relevant field rather than assuming similarly named elements map themselves in every scenario.

Now imagine the screen shows amounts in another currency. Mapping Amount to a table column will not perform the currency conversion. That belongs in appropriate calculation or query logic. Projections and generated EML types also have their own names and identity fields, so use the correct type at each boundary. A field-name mapping does not remove those distinctions.

Mapping is not a database join or a universal value-conversion mechanism.

column1: RAP-15 | Can you call a BAPI from RAP, and what happens if it executes COMMIT?
column2:
Short answer
Some BAPIs can be used in RAP; some cannot. A BAPI does not always execute its own COMMIT. Check the specific API. A local COMMIT WORK or BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT inside RAP handler or saver code breaks RAP transaction ownership and can cause a runtime error. Moving that call to unmanaged save or save_modified does not make the COMMIT legal.

Reasoning and example
First inspect what the BAPI actually does: validation, authorization, locks, direct database writes, update tasks and internal COMMIT. Also check whether the API is permitted in the target ABAP language version. A released API is not automatically usable in every RAP phase.

For a compatible legacy API, an action can collect the intent in the transactional buffer. The documented save integration performs the actual write later. In a managed BO with unmanaged save, save_modified replaces managed persistence; with additional save it supplements managed persistence. A fully unmanaged BO normally uses its saver save method. These are different options, not permission to end the LUW yourself. RAP owns the final commit.

Example: an action requests an update through a suitable BAPI. Validate predictable errors before the point of no return, retain the request in the buffer, call the API in the documented late-save exit, map its responses correctly, and let RAP finish the transaction. For supported create scenarios with late numbering, SAP documents BAPI use in ADJUST_NUMBERS; check the exact release and failure-handling contract.

If the BAPI inevitably commits internally, do not paste it into save_modified or hide it behind a wrapper. Look for a suitable API or redesign the process around an explicit asynchronous boundary. That changes when the business operation completes and needs visible pending/failed states. BRFplus is a rules engine, not a transaction workaround; see RAP-17. Keep the real permission check at the supported authorization boundary and use the documented authorization-context pattern where needed.

Avoid
Unmanaged means you implement more of the behavior or persistence. It does not mean unrestricted COMMIT. A wrapper, BRFplus call or RFC destination cannot magically preserve one atomic LUW.
RAP transaction and workflow boundary

Separate the local transaction from event delivery and the later workflow callback.
Explain it: What is lost if a handler calls a committing legacy API?
Limit: Exact RAP save methods and supported event infrastructure depend on scenario and release.
RAP buffer with a concrete value change

During modification, the transactional view can show 120 EUR while saved data still shows 100 EUR.
Explain it: Why can a direct SQL read be the wrong way to read the BO during modification?
Limit: Simplified single-record example, not a promise about a particular SQL isolation level.
Local and remote transaction boundaries

The remote commit belongs to another system, so local failure needs an explicit recovery strategy.
Explain it: What should happen if the remote side succeeds but the response is lost?
Limit: This explains distributed consistency, not a particular messaging product guarantee.

column1: RAP-16 | How do you group a multi-select Fiori action into one changeset with InvocationGrouping?
column2:
Short answer
For a supported Fiori elements action, set invocationGrouping: #CHANGE_SET on its @UI.lineItem action annotation. The default #ISOLATED allows separate changesets for the selected instances. Both can still travel inside one HTTP $batch request. $batch is the envelope; a changeset is the atomic group inside it. Check the generated metadata and the actual network request.

Reasoning and example
Imagine selecting orders A, B and C and pressing Approve. B is invalid. With separate changesets, A and C may succeed while B fails. With one shared changeset, the intended result is all-or-nothing: B failing prevents A and C from being committed in that group.

Put the annotation on the action entry in a CDS metadata extension. Keep type: #FOR_ACTION and the correct dataAction name. In OData metadata, verify UI.InvocationGrouping uses UI.OperationGroupingType/ChangeSet. Then inspect the browser Network tab: seeing /$batch alone is not proof that there is one shared changeset. Test one deliberately invalid selected order and check persisted data.

This configures how the supporting UI invokes the action; it does not combine arbitrary requests from every client or promise one ABAP handler call. The handler must accept multiple keys correctly. A freestyle SAPUI5 client also needs the appropriate OData model group/submission configuration. Remote side effects that already committed cannot be undone by a local changeset rollback.

Avoid
Do not equate #ISOLATED with no $batch, or #CHANGE_SET with automatic atomicity across remote systems. Verify the Fiori elements/OData version and service behavior.

Read and verify
  • SAP: UI.lineItem.invocationGrouping
    Annotation values, default and intended multi-instance grouping.
  • SAPUI5: action invocation grouping
    Distinguish a batch request from the changesets carried inside it.

column1: RAP-17 | Do BRFplus, bgPF or bgRFC make an internally committing BAPI safe in RAP?
column2:
Short answer
BRFplus evaluates business rules; it does not fix a BAPI commit problem. bgPF is a background framework. Where supported, its uncontrolled operation variant can run logic that needs its own COMMIT. That work runs separately from the original RAP save, so it is not one immediate all-or-nothing transaction. Choose this only if the business process can accept a later result, retries and possible failure. An ordinary bgRFC unit still forbids COMMIT inside it.

Reasoning and example
Example: saving an order should start slow follow-up processing. With a supported bgPF integration, register the background work at the allowed point in RAP save so it becomes eligible after the initiating transaction succeeds. The user can see Pending, then Completed or Failed. Design retries, duplicate protection, monitoring and recovery. If the later work fails, the already committed order is not automatically rolled back.

Distinguish ordinary bgRFC units from the explicit bgPF uncontrolled operation contract. SAP provides IF_BGMC_OP_SINGLE_TX_UNCONTR and set_operation_tx_uncontrolled for the latter; its sample names COMMIT WORK as a use case. Check availability and restrictions in your target system. This does not allow COMMIT in the original RAP handler or saver. Intermediate commits in later processing can leave partial results, so retrying must not create duplicates.

BRFplus might decide which approval rule applies. It does not schedule background work or repair RAP transaction consistency. If someone says use BRF+ for the BAPI commit problem, clarify whether they meant bgPF or bgRFC, then review that design on its own merits.

Avoid
Do not confuse BRFplus with bgPF, or a bgPF uncontrolled operation with an ordinary bgRFC unit. A supported background COMMIT does not make it atomic with the original RAP save.

    BRFplus defines and evaluates business rules.
  • SAP: Background Processing Framework
    bgPF supports reliable asynchronous processing on top of bgRFC.
  • SAP: CALL FUNCTION IN BACKGROUND UNIT
    Read transaction restrictions inside a bgRFC unit.
  • SAP: Controlled SAP LUW
    RAP uses the controlled transaction model. Check the chosen bgPF operation variant separately.

    The trace documentation lists both operation interfaces; use the target release documentation for their full contracts.

    The sample distinguishes the operation interfaces and illustrates registration with set_operation_tx_uncontrolled. Verify the target release and error/retry contract.

column1: RAP-18 | How do you enable and use create, update, and delete in managed RAP?
column2:
Short answer
Declare create, update, and delete in the base behavior definition. Managed RAP supplies their standard implementation. A consumer calls those operations through EML or a service; RAP first changes the transactional buffer. Accepted changes are not yet saved. The transaction owner must complete the save successfully.

Reasoning and example
Imagine a small Order with OrderUUID and Comment. RAP generates the UUID on create. An external ABAP program creates an order with Comment = Draft, checks FAILED and REPORTED, and uses MAPPED to find the new UUID. It can then read or update that same order before saving. A pending delete removes an instance from transactional state; it is not a completed database deletion yet.

An external EML transaction owner uses COMMIT ENTITIES and checks the separate save response. A service request leaves transaction handling to the framework. A behavior handler must not issue its own COMMIT. On a rejected standalone operation, preserve the failure/messages and roll back the pending transaction; do not print a success message merely because MODIFY returned. For a service, also expose the permitted operations through the projection and implement the required permissions and business validations.

Avoid
Managed CRUD avoids handwritten basic persistence, not authorization, validation, or checking save errors.

Read and verify

    Follow the linked lesson and verify the feature set in your target ABAP release.

column1: RAP-19 | How do an order and its items form one managed RAP business object?
column2:
Short answer
The order is the root; its items are composition children in the same BO. Define behavior for both entities. Create items through the parent association, and declare their supported update and delete operations. Children normally depend on the root for locking and authorization. A shared BO boundary lets RAP save their changes together.

Reasoning and example
For Order A, create two items through Order._Items. The parent connection tells RAP which order owns them. In the ordinary managed composition model, deleting the root also deletes its composition children. An associated Customer is different: it is a separately owned record and must not disappear when the order is deleted.

The CDS composition and association-to-parent must agree with the behavior aliases and dependencies. Expose the child and redirected associations in the service projection as needed. For a new parent and new children in one request, use the %cid/%cid_ref correlation described in RAP-10; do not guess a parent key that numbering has not supplied.

Avoid
A normal association to a customer does not make the customer part of the order lifecycle.

    Follow the linked lesson and verify the feature set in your target ABAP release.

column1: RAP-20 | Create or an action exists in the BO but is missing in the service. What do you check?
column2:
Short answer
Follow the capability from the base behavior to the projection and then to the service actually called. A base operation is not automatically exposed by every projection. Check use create or use action, the projected entity, and the active binding metadata. Then distinguish a missing operation from one disabled by features, denied by authorization, or simply not shown by the UI.

Reasoning and example
Suppose the base Order declares create and action Submit. An app projection reuses update only. Calling a different endpoint or adding a button cannot expose the missing operations: first reuse the intended capability in the correct projection.

If metadata already contains the action, inspect operation availability, permissions, UI annotations and request responses. A disabled Submit button may be correct for an approved order. A 403 is a permissions issue, not proof that use action is absent. Refresh cached metadata only after confirming which service version the client uses.

Avoid
Do not fix missing service behavior by adding a UI button or bypassing authorization.

Read and verify

    Follow the linked lesson and verify the feature set in your target ABAP release.

column1: RAP-21 | How do you read an order's items with EML, and what do RESULT and LINK contain?
column2:
Short answer
Use READ ENTITIES with BY association and the source order keys. RESULT contains the item data you requested. LINK connects each source order identity to a target item identity. It is useful when reading children of several parents. Check FAILED and REPORTED instead of assuming every input produced children.

Reasoning and example
Order A has items A1 and A2; order B has B1. RESULT gives three item rows. LINK says A -> A1, A -> A2 and B -> B1. Use those links when grouping the response by its source, especially when target fields alone are not enough to identify the path. An order with no items has no child result; a failed order read must be diagnosed separately.

Inside the BO, this read can include pending child changes from the transaction. Keep the generated %tky identity, including draft state where present. Reading the database directly can miss an item just created in the buffer. RBA follows the declared association; it is not an arbitrary SQL join or a replacement for list-query filtering.

Avoid
RESULT is entity data; LINK is the source-to-target relationship, not a second copy of those data fields.

Read and verify

    Follow the linked lesson and verify the feature set in your target ABAP release.

column1: RAP-22 | Why does EML need derived types and %control instead of a database-table row?
column2:
Short answer
An EML request describes an operation, not just stored fields. Derived types come from the CDS and behavior contract and include the identities and flags that operation needs. %control says which fields were supplied. An initial value can therefore mean either leave unchanged or deliberately clear the field, depending on its flag.

Reasoning and example
The stored Comment is Rush. An update sends Comment = an empty string. With %control-Comment = if_abap_behv=>mk-on, it asks to clear Comment. With the flag off, that field is not part of the update. The FIELDS addition can set these flags for listed fields.

Use TYPE TABLE FOR UPDATE for update input and TYPE TABLE FOR READ RESULT for read data. Carry %tky from the generated input or result so draft identity is not lost. %cid correlates a newly requested instance before its final identity is available; it is not a persistent business key. A table row copied from SQL does not express all these operation-specific details.

Avoid
Use if_abap_behv=>mk-on for behavior flags. abap_true is not the same flag type.

Read and verify

    Follow the linked lesson and verify the feature set in your target ABAP release.

column1: RAP-23 | What must change when a managed RAP BO becomes draft-enabled?
column2:
Short answer
Draft needs coordinated changes across the model, behavior, persistence and projection. Enable draft in the base behavior, provide compatible draft tables and administrative fields, and define the required draft actions. Configure entity ETags and the root total ETag with the correct lock dependencies. Reuse draft in the projection and expose the required associations and operations.

Reasoning and example
An order draft must survive closing the browser. Its draft persistence stores unfinished input separately from the active business record. For a composition, include the child entities and draft-aware associations too. Generate or adjust the draft tables from the actual definitions; do not copy an unrelated table layout.

Prepare should include the relevant validations so the consumer can receive state messages. Activation must transfer a valid state to active persistence. Test create, edit, reopen, discard and activate, plus a competing active change and expired draft lock. Verify both active and draft identities in EML. RAP-12 explains the lifecycle; ADV-01 explains why the total ETag and normal entity ETag protect different situations.

Avoid
Adding with draft alone is not a complete draft implementation, and saving a draft is not activating a business record.

Read and verify
  • SAP Learning: draft behavior implementation
    Follow the linked lesson and verify the feature set in your target ABAP release.

column1: RAP-24 | What is a determine action, and how does it differ from a determination or ordinary action?
column2:
Short answer
A determination is a rule that derives data when its trigger applies. A normal action implements a requested business operation, such as Submit. A determine action groups existing determinations and validations so a consumer can request their evaluation. In managed RAP it reuses those rule implementations rather than adding an ordinary action handler.

Reasoning and example
After a delivery date changes, a supported consumer can request a determine action that evaluates the related date validation. This can show feedback before the user chooses final save. Draft Prepare is a draft-specific determine action used in the activation flow.

Assigned rules still follow their trigger and optimization contracts unless an applicable always setting changes that. Listing rules is not a promise that each one runs every time or in the written order. Determinations run before validations; do not build dependencies on arbitrary order within either group. Expose the capability through the supported projection and consumer configuration. Evaluation alone does not mean COMMIT or successful persistence.

Avoid
A determine action is not a place to write arbitrary action logic, and it does not replace save-time consistency checks.

Read and verify
