    Follow the linked lesson and verify the feature set in your target ABAP release.

column1: SRAP-01 | A new approval app has custom persistence, while its posting step must reuse an existing transactional API. Which RAP implementation type would you choose?
column2:
Short answer
Start with managed RAP for the new approval tables. If an eligible API must perform the actual writes while RAP can manage the pending changes, consider managed RAP with unmanaged save. Use fully unmanaged RAP when existing logic must also handle interaction. Check the API's locks, permissions, numbering, buffering, and commits. Calling it a BAPI does not prove it fits.

Reasoning and example
Follow one successful approval and one rejected approval through the proposed design. Identify who holds pending changes and who writes each document. Additional save adds work alongside managed database writes; it is not a way to replace the owner of those writes. Make that choice explicit before implementing the handlers.

If posting happens in another system, it has a separate transaction. A managed approval object with a pending-posting state and reliable asynchronous processing may fit better than a synchronous action that promises everything commits together. Test what happens when approval saves but posting is unavailable, and how a retry avoids creating a second document. Complexity alone is not a reason to choose unmanaged RAP.

Avoid
Choosing unmanaged merely because the application is complex, or assuming managed with unmanaged save removes RAP transaction rules.
RAP buffer with a concrete value change

During modification, the transactional view can show 120 EUR while saved data still shows 100 EUR.
Explain it: Why can a direct SQL read be the wrong way to read the BO during modification?
Limit: Simplified single-record example, not a promise about a particular SQL isolation level.

Explain it: Which part stays managed when only the save implementation is replaced?
Limit: Conceptual comparison; specific saver variants and failure support depend on release and scenario.

  • Which implementation responsibilities would your choice leave with the framework?

  • Checks what the API actually does
  • Separates remote processing from one local transaction

column1: SRAP-02 | An audit record must be saved with every managed order change. Should you use a determination, additional save, or unmanaged save?
column2:
Short answer
For an audit that must be saved with a managed order change, additional save may fit. RAP still writes the order, and the supported save extension writes the audit without committing separately. A determination is for deriving object data, not recording an already completed save. Distinguish this business audit from technical logs that may need to survive a rejected transaction.

Reasoning and example
An audit record may need the user, operation, changed values, and an identifier linking it to the order change. Check which data the save extension actually receives. Changed-field input is not necessarily a complete before-and-after image; use the documented data options and obtain any required previous values correctly. Explicitly cleared fields matter too.

Test order creation, update, deletion, and a rejected save. The business audit should match the actual saved outcome, rather than claiming a change happened when it rolled back. Technical diagnostics for the failure may have a separate purpose and lifecycle. Do not switch all order persistence to unmanaged save merely to add logging, or directly rewrite managed order tables from additional save.

For a managed BO, with additional save keeps the framework's order persistence and adds save_modified for extra work. With unmanaged save replaces that persistence with your implementation of save_modified. A fully unmanaged BO has its own saver contract, commonly save. Neither variant allows your code to execute COMMIT WORK or BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT. BRFplus does not change these rules. For a BAPI integration, review RAP-15 rather than assuming that any API is safe in the audit save hook.

Avoid
Writing the audit in another LUW and claiming it is guaranteed to match the order, or updating managed order tables directly from additional save.
Save options: who writes the data and which method runs?

Compare four persistence choices. Both save extensions of managed BOs use save_modified; a fully unmanaged BO uses save.
Explain it: Why is with unmanaged save not the same implementation as a fully unmanaged BO?
Limit: Conceptual ownership comparison. The complete BDEF, change-image options and saver signatures depend on the scenario and release.
RAP transaction and workflow boundary

Separate the local transaction from event delivery and the later workflow callback.
Explain it: What is lost if a handler calls a committing legacy API?
Limit: Exact RAP save methods and supported event infrastructure depend on scenario and release.
RAP hook responsibilities

Read each card as a separate design question; this is not an execution sequence.
Explain it: Where would you derive a total, reject an invalid input and implement Submit?
Limit: Check scenario and release support; do not rely on an undocumented ordering of independent hooks.
RAP implementation ownership matrix

Trace the same request through three implementation choices and name the owner of each responsibility.
Explain it: Which part stays managed when only the save implementation is replaced?
Limit: Conceptual comparison; specific saver variants and failure support depend on release and scenario.
Augmentation versus additional save

Locate the input transformation and persistence supplement on the same conceptual timeline.
Explain it: Why would writing an audit row not make augmentation the right save hook?
Limit: The arrow is conceptual; availability, supported fields and trigger details depend on the target RAP release.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How do you obtain a trustworthy before-image?
  • Should an audit failure reject the transaction, and in which phase can you detect predictable errors?
Strong answer criteria
  • Distinguishes business audit from diagnostics
  • Preserves managed persistence and commit ownership
  • Checks available change-image semantics
Verification evidence

column1: SRAP-03 | A developer puts ordinary business validation in SAVE because the final data is available there. What would you change?
column2:
Short answer
Move predictable business checks to the supported early save checks, after needed calculations and before late saving. Late save normally writes data that has already passed those checks. An error message is not a general rollback mechanism there. SAP does document special failure-capable saver options for some BAPI integrations. Verify that exact option and release instead of assuming all late failures work alike.

Reasoning and example
An approval amount exceeds the permitted limit. Detect that before database writes and return a message linked to the failing instance. The user can then correct the amount. Waiting until SAVE just because the final values are convenient there puts an ordinary business check at the wrong stage.

A database outage is a different technical failure and needs its supported recovery behavior. If a BAPI integration genuinely needs a documented failure-capable saver, inspect its generated signature and target-release guidance. That exception is not a reason to postpone checks that can run earlier, and it does not allow independently committed side effects. Avoid both absolutes: routine errors cannot all be returned from SAVE, but supported special cases do exist.

Avoid
Saying either 'all errors can be returned from SAVE' or 'no supported late-save failure mechanism exists anywhere'.
RAP save sequence and early failure path

Follow one order from total calculation to buffer cleanup. The orange branch stops a rejected save before late numbering and persistence.
Explain it: Where is the last buffer-change phase, and when is the point of no return reached?
Limit: Simplified phase flow, not a trace of every runtime call. Managed and unmanaged implementation hooks differ; special late-failure support is scenario- and release-dependent.
RAP transaction and workflow boundary

Separate the local transaction from event delivery and the later workflow callback.
Explain it: What is lost if a handler calls a committing legacy API?
Limit: Exact RAP save methods and supported event infrastructure depend on scenario and release.
RAP hook responsibilities

Read each card as a separate design question; this is not an execution sequence.
Explain it: Where would you derive a total, reject an invalid input and implement Submit?
Limit: Check scenario and release support; do not rely on an undocumented ordering of independent hooks.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Where do final derivations belong relative to final consistency checks?
  • What evidence would justify using a failure-capable saver here?
Strong answer criteria
  • Rejects predictable business errors before late save
  • Distinguishes invalid business data from technical failures
  • Explains the documented BAPI exception and its limits
Verification evidence

column1: SRAP-04 | One action updates two local RAP BOs and then calls a remote payment service. Can the whole action be atomic?
column2:
Short answer
Compatible local RAP objects can take part in the same RAP-controlled SAP transaction. A normal HTTP payment call cannot join that database transaction. If payment succeeds and local saving fails, local rollback will not undo payment. Model pending work and reliable delivery, or an explicit compensating process. Define timeout, retry, and reconciliation behavior instead of promising one atomic action.

Reasoning and example
Update the two local objects through supported behavior interfaces and check the permitted cross-object operations for the phase. Do not commit each object separately. Their shared local transaction can coordinate those compatible changes, but a remote payment has its own outcome and owner.

Store a stable business reference for the payment request. If the remote response times out, payment may still have completed; treat the result as unknown until a status check or reconciliation establishes it. A blind retry can charge twice. Show users an honest pending or recovery status, and test failures before and after both local save and remote response so every saved state has a recovery path.

Avoid
Assuming that calling HTTP inside an action enrolls the remote system in the SAP database transaction.
Local and remote transaction boundaries

The remote commit belongs to another system, so local failure needs an explicit recovery strategy.
Explain it: What should happen if the remote side succeeds but the response is lost?
Limit: This explains distributed consistency, not a particular messaging product guarantee.
Remote commit and uncertain local outcome

The local application durably records intent before separately owned delivery. The remote payment commits, but its reply is lost; recovery must identify the existing effect through REQ-42.
Explain it: How do you distinguish an unprocessed request from a committed payment whose response never arrived?
Limit: The delivery and idempotency mechanisms are design requirements, not automatic guarantees from HTTP or RAP. This example does not claim distributed atomicity.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What happens after a payment timeout followed by a retry?
  • How would you recover after local commit succeeds but event delivery is delayed?
Strong answer criteria
  • Draws the local transaction boundary
  • Models uncertain remote outcomes
  • Designs idempotency and reconciliation
Verification evidence
Fault-inject before and after each local save and remote response boundary; verify that every persisted state has a documented recovery path.

Read and verify

    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-05 | A bulk EML update contains 200 instances, including missing keys and unauthorized changes. How do you report and process the result?
column2:
Short answer
Handle all 200 inputs and keep each response linked to the right instance. FAILED identifies rejected work; REPORTED carries messages, including non-errors. MAPPED is for supported identity mappings, not a list of every success. Combine nested-call responses without losing earlier failures. The caller must still apply its commit policy and inspect the later save result.

Reasoning and example
Read the required current object state in suitable bulk operations instead of running a separate query for each row. Some keys may be missing, some updates may be unauthorized, and others may be valid. Every input needs an accountable outcome; unprocessed rows must not accidentally look successful because no error was added for them.

The consumer then decides whether the intended business unit permits eligible updates to continue or requires rejection of the whole unit. That decision depends on the supported operation and transaction boundary. Test several different failures in one input set and reconcile counts, identities, messages, and final database state. MODIFY ENTITIES accepting a change is not proof it has been committed.

Avoid
Checking only the first input row, treating every REPORTED entry as failure, or declaring the operation committed after MODIFY ENTITIES.
FAILED, REPORTED, and MAPPED in a worked create

Three input identities produce separate rejection, message, and key-correlation information. A message on C3 does not itself reject that input, and assigned keys do not prove durable persistence.
Explain it: What must the consumer inspect after this interaction, and what happens if the later save fails?
Limit: Conceptual response contents, not executable EML. Available fields and correlation depend on the operation and BO; save and atomicity semantics must be tested separately.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How would you associate a child error with its root request?
  • What do you check again after the external consumer issues COMMIT ENTITIES?
Strong answer criteria
  • Handles all inputs and aggregates responses
  • Separates response roles and transaction phases
  • Avoids row-by-row dependency access
Verification evidence
Run a mixed-input EML test with multiple distinct failures; assert key/message correlation, processed counts and final database state.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Entity Manipulation Language
    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-06 | An API consumer sends an empty comment to clear it, but the previous text remains. What do you investigate?
column2:
Short answer
Check whether the caller supplied an empty value or omitted the field. In EML, the field list or %control says which fields should change. An empty value without that update instruction can correctly leave the old value alone. Trace payload conversion, adapter change flags, and defaulting logic. Do not mark every field supplied just to fix one cleared comment.

Reasoning and example
The caller sends only Comment with an empty value because it wants to remove the text. Amount and Currency are omitted and must remain unchanged. Verify that the service-to-EML mapping marks Comment for update, then check whether a determination fills the old default again. If a legacy API is called, map the corresponding change indicator too.

Test three cases separately: omitted comment, explicitly empty comment, and new nonempty text. Apply the same distinction to zero or false values where the field's business rules permit them. IS INITIAL alone cannot tell you whether the caller intended a change. Setting all control flags can fix the comment while accidentally clearing unrelated fields.

Avoid
Using IS INITIAL to mean 'not provided' for every update field, or blindly setting all control flags on.
EML update intent: absent versus clear

The first two requests carry the same initial ABAP value but differ in update intent. The field control decides whether the old comment is preserved or explicitly cleared.
Explain it: How would you preserve Amount while clearing Comment, and how could an adapter lose that distinction?
Limit: This is a worked mapping example. Actual generated EML types, UPDATE FIELDS syntax, protocol nullability, and business validation remain authoritative.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How would you represent 'leave unchanged' versus 'set to zero'?
  • Where can a defaulting determination accidentally undo the requested clear?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates presence from value
  • Preserves partial-update semantics
  • Traces control mapping through adapters
Verification evidence
Test omitted Comment, explicit empty Comment and nonempty Comment while asserting that all untouched fields remain unchanged.

column1: SRAP-07 | You must create three new orders with items in one EML request before final order numbers exist. How do you correlate the tree?
column2:
Short answer
Give each new order a unique content ID for this request. Use %cid_ref to connect item creation to the correct newly created parent. Keep child identities and creation mappings too. Use the generated behavior types and read mappings by identifier, not row position. These content IDs link work within a request; they are not final document numbers or durable retry keys.

Reasoning and example
Create three orders, each with several items, before final order numbers are assigned. One item under the second order is invalid. Its message must still point to the correct child and parent, even if inputs are reordered or one creation is rejected. Guessing database keys or matching response-table positions makes this fragile.

Use the supported create-by-association correlation and retain draft or preliminary-key context where applicable. When final keys are assigned, the original parent-child relationships must remain correct. Check MAPPED rather than assuming its order matches the input. Finally, let the external transaction owner apply the intended all-or-nothing policy; correct creation mapping does not by itself decide whether the three orders must save together.

Avoid
Assigning a fake database key to a new parent, correlating by row index, or confusing %cid with %pid.
EML identity tags

Content IDs connect entries within a request. Transactional and preliminary identities address other lifecycle needs.
Explain it: How can a new item refer to a newly created order before the final order number exists?
Limit: Generated EML types and available components are authoritative for the specific BO.
FAILED, REPORTED, and MAPPED in a worked create

Three input identities produce separate rejection, message, and key-correlation information. A message on C3 does not itself reject that input, and assigned keys do not prove durable persistence.
Explain it: What must the consumer inspect after this interaction, and what happens if the later save fails?
Limit: Conceptual response contents, not executable EML. Available fields and correlation depend on the operation and BO; save and atomicity semantics must be tested separately.
RAP identity and numbering timeline

Compare when the identity becomes final and when persistence is confirmed.
Explain it: What must an external EML consumer inspect after MODIFY and after COMMIT?
Limit: Illustrative numbering paths; exact %pid/%pre mapping and conversion syntax are release/scenario-specific.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What changes if the BO uses draft and late numbering?
  • How do you correlate an error when the final parent key is still unavailable?
Strong answer criteria
  • Connects new parents and children using content IDs
  • Keeps the full transactional identity
  • Tests errors in requests with several parents and children
Verification evidence
Execute a reordered multi-parent deep-create case with one failed child and verify associations, mappings and error paths before and after save.

Read and verify

    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-08 | A posting API returns the final document number only when called. How would you integrate numbering without publishing incorrect keys?
column2:
Short answer
Keep preliminary identities until the supported save process assigns final document keys. Map %pre to the final %key during number adjustment. SAP documents a BAPI pattern that calls creation in ADJUST_NUMBERS with a suitable failure-capable saver. Check its availability, API release status, and error rules on the target system. Do not present an earlier identifier as a committed document number.

Reasoning and example
Create several documents concurrently and include a rejected API call. Verify that items and returned mappings still identify the right final documents. Do not publish a number in an email or external event before the business change is durably saved. Late numbering alone also does not guarantee a gap-free sequence; number-range and posting-API behavior still matter.

In the documented failure-capable late-save scenario, a late-save failure makes COMMIT ENTITIES return sy-subrc 8. An external EML consumer must issue ROLLBACK ENTITIES before continuing. Verify support for that exact pattern. This rule does not allow commit or rollback statements inside a behavior implementation, and ordinary ADJUST_NUMBERS must not be assumed to offer the special failure response.

Avoid
Do not use SELECT MAX plus one, lose the preliminary-to-final key mapping, or assume ordinary ADJUST_NUMBERS supports recoverable failures without the documented special saver.
EML identity tags

Content IDs connect entries within a request. Transactional and preliminary identities address other lifecycle needs.
Explain it: How can a new item refer to a newly created order before the final order number exists?
Limit: Generated EML types and available components are authoritative for the specific BO.
RAP identity and numbering timeline

Compare when the identity becomes final and when persistence is confirmed.
Explain it: What must an external EML consumer inspect after MODIFY and after COMMIT?
Limit: Illustrative numbering paths; exact %pid/%pre mapping and conversion syntax are release/scenario-specific.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How does the external EML consumer obtain the final key?
  • What must be demonstrated if the business insists on gap-free numbering?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates preliminary and final identities
  • Qualifies the BAPI saver exception
  • Does not promise gap-free numbers from RAP alone
Verification evidence
Create several documents concurrently, include a failing API call, and verify final key conversion, associations and number-allocation behavior.

Read and verify

    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-09 | A user saves a draft, closes the browser, returns, and presses Activate. What state transitions and failures would you explain?
column2:
Short answer
A saved draft is unfinished work, separate from active data. Activating a new draft creates active data; activating an edit draft applies changes to its active instance. Assigned Prepare checks, activation, and final saving must succeed. Discarding an edit draft leaves the existing active object intact. A business Submit action is a separate operation unless explicitly designed otherwise.

Reasoning and example
Ask what the user means by Save. A draft update can store unfinished editing data without completing the business document. The user can close the browser and later continue from that stored draft. If activation finds missing required data, the user should be able to correct the draft rather than lose the work.

Test both new and edit drafts through the intended UI or service. Discard a new draft and confirm it creates no active object; discard an edit draft and confirm the previous active object remains. Reopen in a fresh browser session and check messages as well as data. Other consumers that write active instances directly still need the appropriate checks; a draft-only flow cannot protect every write automatically.

Avoid
Treating draft persistence as a final business commit or implementing Submit by directly updating draft tables.
Draft lifecycle

Follow edit, activate and discard for an existing active object, then explain how a new-object draft differs.
Explain it: What remains after discarding an edit draft? What if activation fails?
Limit: Schematic state transitions; draft actions and supported flows depend on the BO and consumer.
Three storage lifetimes: an illustrated analogy

The desk represents the current transactional buffer; the draft cabinet represents persistent work across requests; the shared archive represents saved active data.
Explain it: Which of the three can survive several HTTP requests without becoming active business data?
Limit: An analogy, not literal SAP storage architecture or a mandatory three-stage pipeline. A new draft may have no active instance. Active business records may still be updated.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which checks must still protect an API that writes active instances directly?
  • What remains after discarding an edit draft versus a new draft?
Strong answer criteria
  • Distinguishes draft, activation and business status
  • Explains both new and edit drafts
  • Preserves a recoverable validation experience
Verification evidence
Test new/edit draft creation, browser reopen, failed Prepare, successful activation and both discard variants; inspect active and draft results.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Draft runtime
    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-10 | A draft lock expires, another process changes an active child, and the first user resumes editing. How do you prevent silent loss of the child change?
column2:
Short answer
Check the total ETag for the whole relevant active object, including child changes. After an exclusive draft lock expires, resume uses that version to detect changes made to active data. A normal entity ETag has a different request-level job. If a child update does not advance the required total version, an old draft may overwrite newer work unnoticed.

Reasoning and example
A user starts editing an order draft and leaves it open until the exclusive lock expires. Another process changes only an active item. When the first user resumes, the application should detect that the active object changed and offer the supported conflict recovery, rather than treating the old draft as current.

Test this exact child-only case with two sessions. Check all active update paths, including APIs outside the UI. In unmanaged RAP, inspect the implemented lock and version maintenance rather than assuming it is provided automatically. Direct table writes can bypass it entirely. Renewing a lock is not proof that a stored draft still matches active data; the total-ETag check supplies that missing comparison.

Avoid
Checking only the root's own business fields or assuming an expired lock means the stored draft is automatically current.
Draft lifecycle

Follow edit, activate and discard for an existing active object, then explain how a new-object draft differs.
Explain it: What remains after discarding an edit draft? What if activation fails?
Limit: Schematic state transitions; draft actions and supported flows depend on the BO and consumer.
Two ETag boundaries

The left side tests a conditional entity update; the right tests the active-state basis of a resumed draft.
Explain it: Why does testing one entity ETag not prove the draft total-ETag implementation?
Limit: ETags are opaque. Verify lock expiry, relevant child changes and generated behavior on the actual system.
Two editors and one version: an illustrated story

Alice and Ben read version 7. Alice updates successfully, producing version 8. Ben must not overwrite that newer state using the stale version 7 precondition.
Explain it: Why should the client refresh and resolve the conflict instead of blindly retrying its old payload?
Limit: Version numbers are illustrative. Real ETags are opaque validators; a failed If-Match precondition commonly returns HTTP 412. This is optimistic concurrency, not a pessimistic lock.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which timestamp should change after a child-only modification?
  • How do you distinguish stale If-Match handling from draft resume protection?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates ordinary and total ETags
  • Includes child and alternative update paths
  • Defines a stale-draft recovery experience
Verification evidence
Use two sessions, expire the draft lock, change only an active child, then resume and verify the conflict and unchanged active data.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP total ETag
    Check how the total ETag protects draft resume after a lock expires. Distinguish it from the ETag used for a normal entity update.

column1: SRAP-11 | Two determinations calculate discount and total. Production results depend on which one executes first. How would you redesign them?
column2:
Short answer
Calculate discount and total from the current source values without relying on an unspecified handler order. Repeating the calculation with the same input must give the same result. Cover every input that can affect it and avoid trigger loops. A shared calculation routine can help. For unmanaged active instances, first confirm that the chosen determination mechanism is actually supported.

Reasoning and example
If a rule subtracts a discount from an amount already discounted by a previous run, repeating it keeps lowering the total. Calculate from base price, quantity, and the intended discount instead. Changing Quantity and Discount together should produce the same final total as changing them separately. Update only the derived values that need changing.

Test repeated execution, combined edits, draft activation, and rules that trigger each other. Make sure they settle on a consistent result rather than loop or create extra children. Keep notifications and remote side effects out of repeatable calculations. A session flag saying run once can hide the symptom while leaving later valid changes uncalculated, so it is not a reliable replacement for correct derivation logic.

Avoid
Depending on declaration order, using a session flag to run once, or sending a notification each time the determination runs.
RAP hook responsibilities

Read each card as a separate design question; this is not an execution sequence.
Explain it: Where would you derive a total, reject an invalid input and implement Submit?
Limit: Check scenario and release support; do not rely on an undocumented ordering of independent hooks.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What happens when activation reuses already executed consistency work?
  • How would you detect and prevent a determination-trigger cycle?
Strong answer criteria
  • Repeating a calculation gives the same result
  • Does not rely on an unsupported handler order
  • Checks triggers and what the implementation type supports
Verification evidence
Test combined and separate field changes, repeated evaluation, draft activation and create-then-delete in one transaction; compare final values.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Determinations
    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-12 | A request changes CompanyCode to an unauthorized value and also makes its dates inconsistent. Would you use prechecks or validations?
column2:
Short answer
Use a supported precheck to reject a disallowed incoming company-code change before it enters the buffer. Use the appropriate validation to reject inconsistent final dates. Keep the complete RAP authorization design as well; neither mechanism replaces it. For partial updates, combine supplied fields with the existing values needed for the check. Do not assume the request contains every field.

Reasoning and example
A user may be allowed to edit a request in company 1000 but not move it to company 2000. Check the proposed target context at the allowed operation boundary, including any permissions needed for the original context. The precheck must not accidentally accept an unauthorized change because it only examines the old company.

Separately, check the resulting date range. If only the end date is supplied, read the current start date needed for comparison. Test through both EML and the service so the rule is not just a UI convenience. For unmanaged active instances, implement consistency in the suitable handler or save checks; declared draft validations do not automatically protect active database writes.

Avoid
Treating prechecks as a global security bypass or believing a UI mandatory marker enforces all backend invariants.
RAP hook responsibilities

Read each card as a separate design question; this is not an execution sequence.
Explain it: Where would you derive a total, reject an invalid input and implement Submit?
Limit: Check scenario and release support; do not rely on an undocumented ordering of independent hooks.
EML update intent: absent versus clear

The first two requests carry the same initial ABAP value but differ in update intent. The field control decides whether the old comment is preserved or explicitly cleared.
Explain it: How would you preserve Amount while clearing Comment, and how could an adapter lose that distinction?
Limit: This is a worked mapping example. Actual generated EML types, UPDATE FIELDS syntax, protocol nullability, and business validation remain authoritative.
Existing and proposed state authorization

Editing the current A instance and moving it into B are different authorization decisions. Partial input must be interpreted with existing state without treating omitted fields as explicit clears.
Explain it: Which state does each check inspect, and what happens if a determination changes the target scope?
Limit: A policy example, not a universal company-code rule. Implement through the target RAP scenario's supported hooks; prechecks do not replace the complete authorization model.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which state does the precheck see before the update is applied?
  • How would the rule behave for a partial update that omits both dates?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates incoming intent from final state
  • Keeps authorization explicit
  • Accounts for partial updates and unmanaged restrictions
Verification evidence
Verify that a denied target context is rejected by the precheck before entering the transactional buffer. Separately verify that inconsistent dates are rejected by validation and cannot be persisted; test correction and successful retry through EML and the service.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP operation prechecks
    Check that prechecks inspect proposed changes before they enter the buffer. Validations reject invalid final data at their supported point in processing.

column1: SRAP-13 | A CopyOrder action creates an order, but the UI stays on the source and the consumer cannot identify the copy. How do you review the action contract?
column2:
Short answer
Decide whether CopyOrder should be a factory action that creates a new instance. Its MAPPED response links the caller's content ID to that creation; it is not an ordinary action-result parameter. A normal action with a declared result must fill that result correctly instead. Check supported cardinality and UI navigation on the target release. Returning $self does not automatically mean create a copy.

Reasoning and example
Define what copying means before debugging navigation. Generate a new identity, reset approval status, omit source audit ownership, and decide which children should be copied. Assigning the whole source structure can incorrectly copy permissions or business state even when the new key is returned correctly.

Then call the action with several inputs through EML and the UI. Verify that each created object maps to the right source request and that the UI navigates according to the supported action behavior. If one source must create several targets, check the allowed cardinality for this release and consumer. A hard-coded UI redirect can hide a broken action response instead of fixing its identification rules.

Avoid
Assuming all factory-action cardinalities are identical on every release or solving wrong result mapping with a hard-coded UI redirect.
EML identity tags

Content IDs connect entries within a request. Transactional and preliminary identities address other lifecycle needs.
Explain it: How can a new item refer to a newly created order before the final order number exists?
Limit: Generated EML types and available components are authoritative for the specific BO.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What changes if one source must create several target objects?
  • Which source fields and children must never be copied automatically?
Strong answer criteria
  • Chooses factory versus ordinary action deliberately
  • Preserves request-to-created-instance mapping
  • Defines copy semantics and release-dependent consumer behavior
Verification evidence
Call the action through EML and the UI with multiple inputs; verify mappings, new identities, reset fields and navigation to the correct instance.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Action definition
    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-14 | A projection accepts a convenience field that must enrich an underlying create. Why might augmentation fit, and what are its boundaries?
column2:
Short answer
Augmentation can add or translate input for supported operations at a RAP projection. Preserve values the caller already supplied and link generated work back to its original request. Check the permitted operations, control flags, and response behavior on the target release. It is not a general save hook. The base object's business rules must still protect every consumer.

Reasoning and example
A specialized projection accepts a display language when creating a request. Supported augmentation may add a related text creation so the underlying object receives both pieces of input. If the caller already supplied that text or a conflicting value, handle the conflict deliberately rather than overwriting it without explanation.

Use unique content IDs and the supported correlation mechanism so an error in generated child work can be traced to the original create. Test multiple instances, omitted convenience input, and generated-operation failures. Augmenting EML does not behave like an unrestricted normal modify call with arbitrary immediate results. Keep permanent consistency checks in the base behavior so another projection cannot bypass them by omitting the augmentation.

Avoid
Using augmentation to bypass base validations or expecting an unrestricted local result from an augmenting operation.
Augmentation versus additional save

Locate the input transformation and persistence supplement on the same conceptual timeline.
Explain it: Why would writing an audit row not make augmentation the right save hook?
Limit: The arrow is conceptual; availability, supported fields and trigger details depend on the target RAP release.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What if the caller already supplied the field your augmentation wants to set?
  • How is a generated child operation related back to the original request?
Strong answer criteria
  • Uses augmentation to adapt projection input
  • Preserves supplied-field flags and request correlation
  • Keeps shared business checks in the base object
Verification evidence
Test absent/present convenience fields, conflicting underlying input, multi-instance requests and generated-operation failures with the supported augmentation API.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Operation augmentation
    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-15 | A legacy function module issues COMMIT WORK internally. Can you make it safe by wrapping it in a RAP action?
column2:
Short answer
No. The wrapper still executes the function module's commit, which conflicts with RAP owning the transaction. Moving that call into a saver does not remove the problem. Look for a supported API with compatible buffering and saving, or design a separate asynchronous transaction explicitly. Check the entire call chain, language permissions, API release state, and authorization rules before integrating it.

Reasoning and example
Calling a function module that commits inside local RAP processing violates the runtime rules and may cause a runtime error. Do not assume the commit will simply succeed and RAP will continue normally. Trace the full call chain to find explicit or implicit commits before selecting the integration approach.

Moving the call to RFC or HTTP in a separate transaction does not restore atomicity. That remote operation can commit while local RAP saving later fails, leaving a real document behind despite the local rejection. If separate processing is necessary, define pending states, safe retry, and reconciliation. Test where durable effects occur. Do not hide the committing call or disable checks while promising that RAP can roll everything back.

Avoid
Do not hide a commit inside a wrapper or disable runtime checks. Moving it to another task does not make the separate transactions one LUW.
RAP transaction and workflow boundary

Separate the local transaction from event delivery and the later workflow callback.
Explain it: What is lost if a handler calls a committing legacy API?
Limit: Exact RAP save methods and supported event infrastructure depend on scenario and release.
Local and remote transaction boundaries

The remote commit belongs to another system, so local failure needs an explicit recovery strategy.
Explain it: What should happen if the remote side succeeds but the response is lost?
Limit: This explains distributed consistency, not a particular messaging product guarantee.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How would you discover an implicit commit several calls below the adapter?
  • What business states would an asynchronous replacement expose?
Strong answer criteria
  • Preserves RAP transaction ownership
  • Audits nested and implicit transaction effects
  • Offers a viable alternative integration boundary
Verification evidence
Review the dependency call graph and trace successful and rejected requests; document the first durable effect and the actual transaction owner.

Read and verify

    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.
  • SAP: BAPI consumption, late numbering and save sequence
    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-16 | An older RAP BO works without strict mode. The team wants to release it for cloud consumption by adding strict(2). Is that sufficient?
column2:
Short answer
No. strict(2) adds modeling and implementation checks; it does not release the object as an API. Review base and projection behavior together, including locks, permissions, ETags, and composition relationships. Check derived-type changes and eligible dependencies. A released API also needs a stable supported interface and lifecycle plan. Syntax success alone proves neither compatibility nor secure operation.

Reasoning and example
Capture the existing service metadata and representative EML and OData calls before enabling strict mode. Previously implicit behavior may need to be declared explicitly, and changes can affect what existing callers may do. Activate and test the whole dependent model on the target release, not just the base behavior definition.

Decide what the future released interface promises and which implementation details remain private. Check consumption and extension permissions separately, and define how incompatible changes will be handled. Documentation for a newer product version may describe features unavailable on this target. Run appropriate ATC checks and real consumer regressions, but do not treat strict mode as a Clean Core grade or an automatic API-release switch.

Avoid
Treating strict(2) as a clean-core grade or API-release switch, or enabling it only on one layer and ignoring resulting contract changes.
RAP contract stack

Read from the client down to storage, then explain what each artifact contributes.
Explain it: Where would you restrict the exposed operation set?
Limit: Conceptual layers; the exact artifact set depends on the scenario and release.
RAP release and consumption gates

Review eligibility, behavior and delivery as separate evidence gates.
Explain it: Which gate would catch an API-compatible change that breaks deployment configuration?
Limit: A teaching checklist; exact release contracts, component visibility and delivery tools depend on the product.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which implicit behavior could disappear when strict mode is enabled?
  • What would you freeze in a released BO interface rather than in the base implementation?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates strict checks from API release
  • Reviews all affected layers
  • Plans compatibility and consumer regression evidence
Verification evidence
Record before/after metadata, activate the full dependency set, run ATC and execute representative old consumer calls on the target release.

Read and verify

    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-17 | An unmanaged BO passes isolated tests but a second request reads leftovers after an earlier save rejection. Where do you look?
column2:
Short answer
Inspect the custom buffer's lifetime and every cleanup path, including early save rejection and external rollback. Reads must show this transaction's changes, not leftovers from an earlier one. CLEANUP and CLEANUP_FINALIZE have different jobs. After an early rejection, remove the appropriate finalize-derived work while retaining the state needed for valid continued interaction. Do not clear all data blindly.

Reasoning and example
An unmanaged implementation stores pending rows in a static internal table. Tests pass when each starts in a fresh session, but a failed transaction leaves entries that the next transaction reads. The problem can affect deleted rows, preliminary keys, counters, and dependency data as well as ordinary updates. A static table is not automatically a safe cache.

Run failure-then-success and rollback-then-read sequences in a reused session. Also test correcting data after an early save rejection. Identify which values came from user interaction and which were added during FINALIZE, then apply the documented cleanup behavior for each phase. Cleaning only after successful saves leaks state; erasing every user change after rejection can break the intended retry behavior.

Avoid
Implementing cleanup only after success or deleting all user changes after an early-save rejection without understanding the retry contract.
RAP buffer with a concrete value change

During modification, the transactional view can show 120 EUR while saved data still shows 100 EUR.
Explain it: Why can a direct SQL read be the wrong way to read the BO during modification?
Limit: Simplified single-record example, not a promise about a particular SQL isolation level.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which data was created during FINALIZE rather than during user interaction?
  • How would an in-transaction READ differ from a direct SELECT after an unsaved update?
Strong answer criteria
  • Keeps pending state inside its intended transaction
  • Distinguishes the cleanup phases
  • Reads current pending changes and preserves correct retry behavior
Verification evidence
Run failure-then-success, rollback-then-read and repeated-save sequences within a reused session; assert no stale buffer entries or leaked temporary identifiers.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Cleanup after early save failure
    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-18 | An Approved event should trigger an external workflow. Why is calling its HTTP endpoint from an on-save determination unreliable?
column2:
Short answer
An on-save determination can run before commit and can run again. Its remote HTTP call cannot be undone by a local rollback. Use supported transactional event publication or another deliberately designed delivery mechanism. The event should describe a committed business change. Delivery and processing can still be retried, so the consumer must prevent duplicate effects and support recovery.

Reasoning and example
An order is approved locally, but saving later fails. If a determination already called the workflow endpoint, a workflow may exist for an approval that never became permanent. Publish through the supported transaction-aware path so that rejected local work does not create that false business fact.

Give the event a stable identity and enough version or transition information for the consumer to recognize duplicates and stale work. A repeated event must not create a second workflow, and a delayed event may need checking against a later cancellation. Monitor the local change, publication, delivery attempts, and consumer outcome separately. A successful HTTP response or in-process event is not proof of exactly-once business completion.

Avoid
Equating a successful HTTP response or a raised in-process event with durable, exactly-once end-to-end workflow execution.
RAP transaction and workflow boundary

Separate the local transaction from event delivery and the later workflow callback.
Explain it: What is lost if a handler calls a committing legacy API?
Limit: Exact RAP save methods and supported event infrastructure depend on scenario and release.
Duplicate events and stale approvals

The event identity and current business state decide whether to apply, ignore or reject the request.
Explain it: Two consumers process the same event simultaneously: what prevents a double effect?
Limit: Exact transactional deduplication mechanisms depend on the chosen infrastructure.
Remote commit and uncertain local outcome

The local application durably records intent before separately owned delivery. The remote payment commits, but its reply is lost; recovery must identify the existing effect through REQ-42.
Explain it: How do you distinguish an unprocessed request from a committed payment whose response never arrived?
Limit: The delivery and idempotency mechanisms are design requirements, not automatic guarantees from HTTP or RAP. This example does not claim distributed atomicity.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How would you recover an event that is delivered after the order is cancelled?
  • What identifier prevents duplicate workflow creation?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates local commit from remote effects
  • Handles duplicate and stale events safely
  • Monitors publication separately from consumer processing
Verification evidence
Test rejected save, publisher outage, duplicate delivery and stale delivery; verify no workflow for rejected data and one effective workflow per transition.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Business events
    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-19 | A credit-limit check runs successfully on a draft, but active data is later saved through another consumer with an invalid amount. What is missing?
column2:
Short answer
Protect the credit rule on every supported write path, including direct active updates. Check validation triggers, Prepare, and the implementation type. Managed save validation and fully unmanaged active consistency handling are different mechanisms. Also consider concurrent credit use. Passing a check earlier does not reserve credit or guarantee that the same amount is still available when saving.

Reasoning and example
A draft passes the credit check at 10:00. Before activation, another order uses part of the same customer's limit. The old check now describes an earlier situation. An API that writes active data directly can also miss a rule implemented only for a draft screen or draft-specific check.

Test both draft activation and direct active writes. Then run two transactions whose individual amounts fit the limit but whose combined amount exceeds it. Depending on the credit service, you may need an authoritative reservation, suitable locking, or a process that permits later rejection. Adding the same simple read twice does not eliminate the race between checking available credit and consuming it.

Avoid
Duplicating the check only in the UI or assuming validation alone eliminates a cross-transaction race.
RAP buffer with a concrete value change

During modification, the transactional view can show 120 EUR while saved data still shows 100 EUR.
Explain it: Why can a direct SQL read be the wrong way to read the BO during modification?
Limit: Simplified single-record example, not a promise about a particular SQL isolation level.
RAP hook responsibilities

Read each card as a separate design question; this is not an execution sequence.
Explain it: Where would you derive a total, reject an invalid input and implement Submit?
Limit: Check scenario and release support; do not rely on an undocumented ordering of independent hooks.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What prevents two parallel orders from consuming the same available credit?
  • Which direct active-instance consumer tests would you add?
Strong answer criteria
  • Protects the credit rule for all supported callers
  • Handles unmanaged active writes correctly
  • Recognizes that data can change between checking and using it
Verification evidence
Exercise draft activation and direct active writes, then run two competing transactions whose combined amount exceeds the limit.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Validations
    Check when validation runs, its draft Prepare assignment, and managed versus unmanaged behavior. The proposed credit reservation and concurrency design is an example; validation alone does not guarantee it.

column1: SRAP-20 | In a mass approval request, one instance fails. Must all other approvals be rolled back?
column2:
Short answer
It depends on the business unit of work and the actual transaction boundary. An EML operation, a SAP LUW, an OData atomicity group, and a whole batch are not the same scope. One FAILED entry alone does not define the outcome for every other input. The transaction owner must inspect responses and apply the required save or rollback policy.

Reasoning and example
If the business approves a package only when every request qualifies, model that package's all-or-nothing requirement explicitly and test the save boundary. If approvals are independent, split work into appropriate independent units and show each result clearly. Neither policy should happen accidentally because of how a loop or HTTP envelope was written.

Run a mixed-success case through the actual EML consumer and OData request structure. Check the final database state after the chosen commit or rollback path. A successful interaction response is not proof of persistence, and an OData batch can contain separate atomicity groups. Align the technical boundary with the business expectation rather than claiming every batch succeeds or fails as one transaction.

Avoid
Claiming that any FAILED entry universally rolls back every request, or that every OData batch is one atomic transaction.
OData batch envelope and atomic groups

The outer envelope reduces HTTP packaging overhead; it does not establish one universal database transaction.
Explain it: If a later independent group fails, must an earlier successful group be rolled back?
Limit: Conceptual grouping, not an exact multipart or JSON batch payload.
FAILED, REPORTED, and MAPPED in a worked create

Three input identities produce separate rejection, message, and key-correlation information. A message on C3 does not itself reject that input, and assigned keys do not prove durable persistence.
Explain it: What must the consumer inspect after this interaction, and what happens if the later save fails?
Limit: Conceptual response contents, not executable EML. Available fields and correlation depend on the operation and BO; save and atomicity semantics must be tested separately.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How does your answer change for separate atomicity groups?
  • What must an external EML consumer do after a partial interaction failure?
Strong answer criteria
  • Identifies which changes must succeed together
  • Distinguishes accepted changes from a successful save
  • Matches transaction handling to the business requirement
Verification evidence
Test a mixed-success action via EML and the actual OData request shape; inspect persisted state after both intended commit and rollback paths.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Entity Manipulation Language
    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-21 | After a quantity change, the backend total is correct but the Fiori page displays the old value. Is this a transaction bug?
column2:
Short answer
First check whether the backend value is correct in the relevant draft or active state. If it is, inspect action results, side-effect metadata, and the UI's actual refresh requests. Side effects tell supported consumers what to reread; they do not calculate totals or commit data. Fix the refresh rule when that is the problem, rather than adding a commit.

Reasoning and example
Change an item quantity, then read the object through the service or EML in the same relevant state. If the total is already correct there, compare the browser's requests and response values. A missing refresh after a child change can explain why the screen shows the old total even though the calculation worked.

Verify that the metadata asks the supported client to refresh the needed total and action availability, and confirm those requests really occur. Reloading the entire page may hide the issue while losing edit context and fetching unnecessary data. If the total only becomes correct after activation, investigate the backend trigger timing too. Keep backend calculation and client display evidence separate throughout diagnosis.

Avoid
Adding COMMIT WORK to make the UI update or treating a side-effect declaration as a substitute for a backend determination.
Side effects and stale UI diagnosis

Use the observed backend value to choose the next debugging branch.
Explain it: What request proves that the consumer refreshed the calculated total?
Limit: Consumer and metadata support are release-dependent; a valid backend side effect is not proof that every client processes it.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What if the total is correct only after activation?
  • Which refresh targets and requests would you expect after an item quantity change?
Strong answer criteria
  • Diagnoses backend state and client state separately
  • Preserves transaction ownership
  • Validates metadata against real consumer behavior
Verification evidence
Compare EML/service values with browser requests before and after the change; verify draft context, refreshed totals and request volume.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP side effects
    Check which field change or action triggers a refresh and what should be reread. Verify that the actual UI supports it.

column1: SRAP-22 | Your team finds a useful SAP RAP base BO in ADT, but only a narrower BO interface is released. Which layer should your application consume?
column2:
Short answer
Use the released BO interface and only the fields and operations it exposes for your allowed use. Visible source in ADT is not permission to consume the underlying base object. The interface lets the provider change internals while supporting callers. If an operation is missing, find another released API, request it, or revise the process. Do not bypass the interface with table writes.

Reasoning and example
Check whether the released interface includes the actions, fields, associations, and draft operations your application needs. A RAP BO interface exposes a supported subset of a business object; it is not simply an ordinary OO interface where you invent a handler. Target-release and cross-component visibility rules still apply.

Build the consumer using only that exposed subset and test its permissions and failure responses. If the base implementation has a useful extra operation, resist calling it merely because it activates today. C1 permission to consume the interface also does not imply permission to extend every underlying object. Record the actual capability gap so the design decision is explicit rather than hidden in an unsupported call.

Avoid
Calling the base BO because it activates today, or equating C1 consumption permission with permission to extend every underlying artifact.
RAP contract stack

Read from the client down to storage, then explain what each artifact contributes.
Explain it: Where would you restrict the exposed operation set?
Limit: Conceptual layers; the exact artifact set depends on the scenario and release.
RAP release and consumption gates

Review eligibility, behavior and delivery as separate evidence gates.
Explain it: Which gate would catch an API-compatible change that breaks deployment configuration?
Limit: A teaching checklist; exact release contracts, component visibility and delivery tools depend on the product.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What does the interface protect when the provider changes its persistence model?
  • How would you handle a required operation absent from the released interface?
Strong answer criteria
  • Calls the released interface
  • Separates permission to use from permission to extend
  • Checks missing capabilities before implementing
Verification evidence
Record API state and visibility in the target system; compile and test the consumer using only exposed fields, associations and operations.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Business object interface
    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-23 | Two requests execute Submit for the same order, and one client retries after a timeout. How do you prevent duplicate business effects?
column2:
Short answer
Protect Submit as a business-state change using the appropriate locks and version checks. Then define what a retry means once submission has already succeeded. Return the original effective result or reject the repeat consistently. Use durable correlation for downstream work so retries do not duplicate it. A disabled button or request-local content ID cannot provide that protection across requests.

Reasoning and example
Two requests both read status Open before either has protected the transition. Without the right concurrency handling, both may start submission. Coordinate the transition and its durable follow-up intent so only the intended business effect is created. Test simultaneous calls as well as a later retry after the response to a successful commit was lost.

If callers provide an idempotency key, scope it to the operation and relevant business context. Detect reuse with incompatible parameters and decide how long the result is retained and found. A timeout should not force the caller to guess whether another Submit is safe. A singleton flag, browser debounce, or %cid does not store the cross-request business history needed for this decision.

Avoid
Relying on a singleton flag, browser debounce, or request-local %cid as a durable cross-request idempotency key.
Duplicate events and stale approvals

The event identity and current business state decide whether to apply, ignore or reject the request.
Explain it: Two consumers process the same event simultaneously: what prevents a double effect?
Limit: Exact transactional deduplication mechanisms depend on the chosen infrastructure.
Remote commit and uncertain local outcome

The local application durably records intent before separately owned delivery. The remote payment commits, but its reply is lost; recovery must identify the existing effect through REQ-42.
Explain it: How do you distinguish an unprocessed request from a committed payment whose response never arrived?
Limit: The delivery and idempotency mechanisms are design requirements, not automatic guarantees from HTTP or RAP. This example does not claim distributed atomicity.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What response should the retry receive if the first call committed but its response was lost?
  • How do you handle the same idempotency key with different parameters?
Strong answer criteria
  • Coordinates state transition and concurrency
  • Defines retry outcomes explicitly
  • Prevents duplicate downstream effects durably
Verification evidence
Run simultaneous Submit calls and replay after a simulated lost response; verify one effective transition and one intended downstream operation.

Read and verify
  • SAP: General RAP BO implementation contract
    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.
  • SAP: Business events
    Read what this operation is allowed to do in this RAP phase, and check support on the target release.

column1: SRAP-24 | A validation reports the right error once, but the message remains after correction or appears on the wrong child. How would you debug it?
column2:
Short answer
Check the message's transactional key, field markers, parent path, and state area. A state message must be removed or replaced when its condition is checked again. Confirm that correction triggers the right validation and uses the right draft instance. Add FAILED where rejection is required. Correct text alone cannot fix a message attached to the wrong child or stale state.

Reasoning and example
Two items have different delivery dates, and only the second is invalid. The message must identify that item and its parent path correctly. After the user fixes its date, revalidate the affected state area and clear the obsolete result using the supported pattern. Do not simply append another copy of the same message on every call.

Test invalid-to-valid-to-invalid edits, deletion of the failing child, and draft activation. Preserve unrelated errors from other checks rather than clearing all messages globally. Compare state messages that describe current invalid data with transition messages that describe one operation. Finally, verify the actual save rejection: REPORTED alone is not a substitute for the required FAILED response.

Avoid
Appending error text on every call without resetting its state area, or assuming REPORTED alone rejects a save.
RAP message lifecycle and correction

Follow the same child through an error and correction instead of treating a message as timeless text.
Explain it: Which identity and state area would you inspect when the old error remains?
Limit: Message lifetime and permitted state-message scenarios depend on active/draft and the supported operation contract.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which message should survive a round trip and which should not?
  • How would you preserve an unrelated validation's error while clearing this one?
Strong answer criteria
  • Correlates messages to transactional identity and fields
  • Manages state areas without erasing unrelated state
  • Separates messaging from operation rejection
Verification evidence
Test invalid-to-valid-to-invalid edits on two children, child deletion and activation; assert message paths, stale-message removal and correct save rejection.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP state messages
    Compare messages about the current object state with messages about one operation. Check which instance each message belongs to and how old state messages are cleared.

column1: CDS-01 | What does ABAP CDS add to a SQL query?
column2:
Short answer
CDS turns a database query into a reusable ABAP data model. It can describe fields, relationships, currency meanings, annotations, and read-access rules. Several apps can use that model instead of rebuilding the same query. SQL still produces the database result. If users must create or change business objects, RAP behavior supplies those operations separately.

Reasoning and example
A sales-order list needs an order number, customer, and amount. A CDS model can expose these fields, connect the customer data, and identify the amount's currency. Appropriate access control can restrict which orders the caller reads. Another application can reuse this model instead of copying all the joins and rules.

That reuse also means the exposed fields and meanings matter to callers. Changing a field's meaning can break an app even when the query still runs. And a readable order model does not automatically support creating an order. For that, define the supported business operations and their behavior rather than treating a CDS SELECT as a complete transaction implementation.

Avoid
A CDS definition does not automatically implement create, update and delete operations.

Read and verify
  • SAP Learning on CDS concepts
    Check which CDS entity type is used, what its provider contract allows, and what the target release supports.

column1: CDS-02 | What is the difference between a classic CDS view and a CDS view entity?
column2:
Short answer
A classic CDS view creates both a CDS entity and a separately named DDIC SQL view. A CDS view entity does not create that separate SQL-view object. For new development, prefer view entities where the target release and consumers support them. Migration needs care because existing programs may call the old SQL-view name directly.

Reasoning and example
Suppose a classic view declares a SQL-view name that several reports use in SELECT statements. Replacing the CDS definition with a view entity changes more than the source syntax: those reports still expect the separately named object. Find the consumers and plan how they will use the replacement.

Check release support and the requirements of tools that consume the view before converting it. Test representative reads after changing the callers, including their fields and result identity. Do not copy AbapCatalog.sqlViewName into the view entity, because it belongs to the classic pattern. The useful interview distinction is which repository objects exist and who depends on them, rather than simply calling one syntax old and the other new.

Avoid
Do not copy AbapCatalog.sqlViewName into a view entity or assume all older systems support view entities.

Read and verify
  • SAP Learning on CDS concepts
    Check which CDS entity type is used, what its provider contract allows, and what the target release supports.

column1: CDS-03 | Association or join and how do you select cardinality?
column2:
Short answer
A join combines sources in the current query. An association defines a relationship that a consumer can follow, often producing a join when used. Cardinality describes how many related rows can really match the ON condition. It must match the data. Declaring a relationship to-one when several rows can match can lead to incorrect results.

Reasoning and example
Order 4710 has amount 100 EUR and a status with English and German texts. Joining only on Status finds both texts, so the order appears twice and a sum can incorrectly show 200 EUR. Match Status and the requested Language. If the text source is truly unique for that pair, a to-one target cardinality may be correct. Test missing texts and unexpected duplicates too.

The order's own key is a separate issue. Declaring OrderUUID as a key does not remove rows duplicated by an incomplete join. Likewise, writing a to-one cardinality does not enforce uniqueness in the text source; the ON condition and actual target data must support it. Also measure performance where needed. An association is useful for modeling relationships, but is not automatically faster than writing a join.

Avoid
Associations are not automatically faster than joins and do not enforce referential integrity.
CDS links and ownership

Items belong to the order BO; a partner reference crosses to an independently managed object.
Explain it: What breaks if a declared to-one relationship actually returns two partners?
Limit: Composition semantics and generated operations still require the corresponding RAP model.

Read and verify

    Check which CDS entity type is used, what its provider contract allows, and what the target release supports.

column1: CDS-04 | Association versus composition in RAP?
column2:
Short answer
Use an association for a relationship between entities. Use a composition when a child belongs to a parent within one RAP business object, such as an order item belonging to its order. That ownership affects the object's lifecycle and modeled lock and authorization dependencies. When exposing projections, redirect these relationships to the matching projected entities.

Reasoning and example
An order item has its own table row, but it normally exists as part of an order. A composition expresses that ownership and supports operations such as creating items through their parent. Review the modeled delete behavior and how children depend on the root for locking and authorization. Those choices must match the business object's lifecycle.

A customer linked to the order is different: deleting the order should not normally delete the customer. That relationship belongs as an association rather than a composition. In the app's projections, make sure navigation points to the projected order and item entities. A foreign key alone does not decide whether the target is an owned child.

Avoid
Not every foreign key should become a composition; lifecycle ownership is the deciding factor.
CDS links and ownership

Items belong to the order BO; a partner reference crosses to an independently managed object.
Explain it: What breaks if a declared to-one relationship actually returns two partners?
Limit: Composition semantics and generated operations still require the corresponding RAP model.

Read and verify
  • SAP Learning on compositions
    Check which CDS entity type is used, what its provider contract allows, and what the target release supports.

column1: CDS-05 | What do interface composite consumption and projection mean?
column2:
Short answer
These names describe different modeling jobs. Interface views aim at reuse, and consumption views serve particular consumers. VDM basic, composite, and consumption annotations describe a modeling convention. A RAP projection exposes a supported view of one underlying entity for a use case. Its provider contract limits what it can do. None of these labels publishes a service by itself.

Reasoning and example
Two apps may share the same request model but need different fields and operations. Keep common meanings in the reusable model. Give each app an appropriate projection, and redirect its relationships consistently so navigation reaches the intended projected entities. This avoids copying core business definitions for every screen.

Do not add an extra CDS layer just to satisfy a naming diagram if it adds no useful responsibility. Likewise, labeling a view composite does not make it eligible for every projection feature or create a service binding. Check the provider contract before adding joins or expressions. The key explanation is what each layer does for a consumer and what changes it protects that consumer from.

Avoid
A VDM composite annotation is neither a prerequisite for service binding nor permission to perform arbitrary joins in a RAP projection.
RAP contract stack

Read from the client down to storage, then explain what each artifact contributes.
Explain it: Where would you restrict the exposed operation set?
Limit: Conceptual layers; the exact artifact set depends on the scenario and release.

Read and verify
  • SAP Learning on CDS concepts
    Check which CDS entity type is used, what its provider contract allows, and what the target release supports.

column1: CDS-06 | What are CDS abstract and custom entities?
column2:
Short answer
An abstract entity defines a structured type, for example the input of an action. It does not produce a database query result. A custom entity defines query data that an ABAP provider supplies instead of generated SQL. Neither means an abstract ABAP superclass. Choose according to whether you need a data shape or an implemented query.

Reasoning and example
A Submit action might need a comment and requested approval date. An abstract entity can describe that input shape; the action is still declared in the behavior definition. There is no table of action parameters to read merely because this type exists.

For a supplier search backed by a remote service, a custom entity can describe the result fields while an ABAP query provider fetches the data. That provider must respect the requested filters, ordering, paging, count, and permissions as applicable. Returning the remote service's first page without honoring the caller's request can make the list misleading. The custom entity supplies the model, not an automatic implementation of those query rules.

Avoid
Do not describe an abstract entity as a BO that other CDS entities inherit and persist.

Read and verify

    Check which CDS entity type is used, what its provider contract allows, and what the target release supports.

column1: CDS-07 | Does DCL on a base view automatically protect every higher view?
column2:
Short answer
No. Access control on a lower CDS view does not automatically protect every view built on it. Design the read rules for the entity that callers actually access. Supported DCL inheritance can reuse conditions with the required mappings. The #CHECK annotation alone creates no rule. RAP permissions for changing objects are a separate check.

Reasoning and example
Assume the base order model restricts Lea to sales organization A, and a service exposes a higher consumption view. Test that exposed view through its actual read path. If order B1 from organization B appears alongside A1, the protected base view has not proved the service is protected. Check the customer value help separately so it does not reveal B-Customer either.

Inspect the effective DCL on the accessed entity and any inherited conditions and field mappings. Include users with different permissions and realistic filters in the test. Then test update or approval permission separately in RAP. A correct read filter limits visible rows; it does not automatically decide whether the user may execute every action on those rows.

Avoid
DCL on one layer does not automatically secure an arbitrary view-on-view stack.
CDS security boundaries

Review security where consumers enter the model, rather than assuming that lower layers protect every upper view.
Explain it: Which two tests prove that an exposed service rejects unauthorized access?
Limit: Authorization behavior depends on the access path and supported DCL inheritance mechanisms.
