column1: CDS-08 | Where do UI annotations and value helps belong?
column2:
Short answer
Put supported UI and value-help annotations in metadata extensions when the model allows it. Keep data meanings, such as the link between an amount and its currency, in the data model. Check which annotations and extension layers the release supports. A value help makes input easier, but the backend must still check submitted values and permissions.

Reasoning and example
A Fiori elements list shows a request amount and offers a cost-center value help. A metadata extension can describe the list columns and the supported value-help setup. The CDS data model still needs to say which currency belongs to the amount so consumers interpret the value correctly.

Now call the service directly and submit a cost center that the value help would never offer. The backend must reject it when it violates a business rule or permission. Hiding a field or narrowing a picker is not enough. Also check annotation layer precedence: a customer or partner extension may interact with existing metadata, so moving every annotation mechanically can change the resulting UI.

Avoid
UI.hidden and a value help are not security or data-integrity controls.
RAP contract stack

Read from the client down to storage, then explain what each artifact contributes.
Explain it: Where would you restrict the exposed operation set?
Limit: Conceptual layers; the exact artifact set depends on the scenario and release.

column1: CDS-09 | What is a virtual element and what are its limits?
column2:
Short answer
A virtual element is calculated in ABAP for a supported query scenario, often through a SADL calculation exit. It is not a stored database column. That matters when callers want to filter or sort by it. Those operations need explicit supported handling, and support varies by service and release. Use database-side modeling when efficient database filtering is essential.

Reasoning and example
A list might display a status description calculated from data that is not stored in its main table. A virtual element can be suitable if the supported query flow calls the calculation and supplies the needed input fields. Request only the inputs required rather than fetching unrelated data for every row.

Now suppose users need to sort thousands of rows by that value before paging. A calculation performed after reading a page cannot automatically produce the correct global order. Check supported sorting or filtering handling, or choose a different model. A UI requestAtLeast hint can help a particular UI request fields, but it is not a guarantee for every possible consumer.

Avoid
requestAtLeast is a UI request hint, not a universal guarantee that every consumer calculates a virtual element.
Calculation placement and query semantics

Use the requirement to decide where a value must exist before filtering, ordering or aggregation.
Explain it: Why can a correct calculation still yield a wrong page of results?
Limit: Architecture alternatives, not a promise that all listed options are supported by each projection/custom provider.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP: implementing sorting of virtual elements
    Explains supported ways to translate sorting by a virtual element before reading the data. Check support for the projection, protocol, released interface, and actual client on the target release.

column1: CDS-10 | How do analytical CDS models differ from transactional models?
column2:
Short answer
An analytical model answers questions such as totals by month or company. It organizes measures, dimensions, and supported aggregation rules. A transactional RAP model identifies individual objects and exposes operations such as Create or Approve. A model designed for one job is not automatically correct for the other. Always account for currencies, units, and the actual query engine.

Reasoning and example
An order app may display individual orders and allow approval. A spending report instead groups values by supplier and month. If some orders are in EUR and others in USD, adding the raw amounts gives a number without a valid common currency. Group them appropriately or use the intended conversion before interpreting a total.

Check what the selected analytical engine, service protocol, and client actually support. A cube or analytical query has responsibilities that an ordinary transactional list does not. Merely adding a VDM annotation or sending $apply does not prove that grouping, conversion, and aggregation have the intended meaning. Test a small dataset with known mixed currencies before trusting the totals.

Avoid
A VDM annotation or an OData $apply request alone does not guarantee correct analytical semantics.

Read and verify
  • SAP analytical projection views
    Check which CDS entity type is used, what its provider contract allows, and what the target release supports.

column1: CDS-11 | How do CDS keys and database keys relate?
column2:
Short answer
A CDS key tells consumers which fields identify a row. It does not force the query result to be unique. A database key enforces uniqueness in a table, but joins and grouping can change the result. RAP and OData need a stable, truly unique identity. Check the complete result, not just the key declarations.

Reasoning and example
Imagine flight rows identified by carrier, connection, and flight date. If a CDS entity marks only carrier and connection as keys, two flights on different dates appear to have the same identity to the client. A list may confuse them or address the wrong row even though the database has two valid records.

Include the fields needed to identify one result row and check what joins do to that uniqueness. Joining a flight to several related rows can multiply the result again. Marking another field as key does not remove duplicates or repair the underlying query. Test with realistic repeated business values, not just sample data where every connection happens to appear once.

Avoid
Marking an element key does not remove duplicate rows.
CDS links and ownership

Items belong to the order BO; a partner reference crosses to an independently managed object.
Explain it: What breaks if a declared to-one relationship actually returns two partners?
Limit: Composition semantics and generated operations still require the corresponding RAP model.

column1: CDS-12 | Is a maintenance view a RAP view and how are defaults supplied?
column2:
Short answer
A classic maintenance view belongs to DDIC table or view maintenance, often used through SM30. A RAP app uses a CDS model and behavior to provide a different kind of maintenance application. In RAP, determinations or supported defaulting functions can supply defaults. The chosen UI and metadata control presentation. First clarify which maintenance approach the question means.

Reasoning and example
A team asks for a small configuration maintenance screen. If it means an existing SM30 dialog, examine its maintenance events and supported classic setup. If it means a Fiori RAP app, design the CDS entities and behavior, including who may change entries and how default values are supplied. The word maintenance does not make these the same technology.

For example, a RAP determination may fill an initial currency while backend checks still reject invalid input. UI annotations can help present the fields, but they do not replace that behavior. Do not invent generic Metadata.ignore or Metadata.defaultValue annotations as a shortcut: verify the actual supported defaulting and visibility mechanisms for the chosen app.

Avoid
Metadata.ignore and Metadata.defaultValue are not generic annotations that implement maintenance behavior.

Read and verify

    Check which CDS entity type is used, what its provider contract allows, and what the target release supports.
  • SAP Learning on DCL inheritance
    Check which CDS entity type is used, what its provider contract allows, and what the target release supports.

column1: MODEL-01 | A new consumption entity exposes orders outside the user's sales organization. The base CDS has DCL. What do you investigate?
column2:
Short answer
Trace the entity that the service actually reads and its access rules. DCL on the base view does not automatically protect every higher view or navigation path. Define the required restrictions, using supported inheritance and mappings where appropriate. Test both allowed and denied data. A UI filter or #CHECK annotation alone cannot create the missing security rule.

Reasoning and example
Create similar orders in sales organizations A and B, then use an identity allowed only for A. Compare direct base reads, the exposed projection, and association navigation. This reveals where the intended restriction stops being applied, rather than assuming the layer with DCL secures all later layers.

Include counts, value helps, and alternative service paths. A hidden organization's key or count can still disclose information even when its rows are absent from the main list. Preserve legitimate access and any deliberate documented exceptions while fixing the rule. Keep RAP update and action permissions separate: proving which rows a user can read does not prove which operations that user may perform.

Avoid
Do not add #CHECK and assume it creates a missing rule.
CDS security boundaries

Review security where consumers enter the model, rather than assuming that lower layers protect every upper view.
Explain it: Which two tests prove that an exposed service rejects unauthorized access?
Limit: Authorization behavior depends on the access path and supported DCL inheritance mechanisms.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which entry point actually evaluated DCL?
  • How would a field rename affect inherited restrictions?
Strong answer criteria
  • Traces the exposed read path
  • Defines restrictions at the correct boundary
  • Tests negative and positive identities
Verification evidence
Capture the real service responses for two organizational scopes, including navigation and counts.

Read and verify
  • SAP Learning: authority checks and DCL
    Test the entity and service callers actually use. Include denied users, filters, and attempts to cross the allowed access boundary.

column1: MODEL-02 | An approver may update organization A. Can an update move an order from A to B using only existing-instance authorization?
column2:
Short answer
Permission to update an order in A does not automatically allow moving it into B. Check both the current object and the proposed target values at the appropriate operation boundary. Supported prechecks can help reject disallowed input before it enters the buffer. Cover creates, updates, and derived changes. Keep the complete authorization and business validation design, not just the existing-instance check.

Reasoning and example
An approver can edit an order in organization A, so the check against its current state succeeds. The update payload changes Organization to B, which the user is not allowed to choose. Without a target-value check, permission for A becomes an unintended route into B.

Test A-to-A changes, denied A-to-B changes, initial values, and several inputs in one request. If a determination derives the organization, that result must also remain within the intended rules. Internal local-mode updates should sit behind a properly checked public operation, not provide an indirect way to submit forbidden values. Creation needs its own checks because there is no existing instance whose authorization settles the question.

Avoid
Do not equate authorization for the current object with authorization for any future object state.
Identity, authorization and feature control

Treat identity, business permission and contextual availability as separate checks.
Explain it: If Submit is disabled in Fiori, what happens when someone calls the service directly?
Limit: Static operation characteristics differ from dynamic instance/global feature checks.
Existing and proposed state authorization

Editing the current A instance and moving it into B are different authorization decisions. Partial input must be interpreted with existing state without treating omitted fields as explicit clears.

column1: MODEL-03 | A custom query returns only authorized rows but an unrestricted total count. Is it secure?
column2:
Short answer
No. The count must describe the same authorized, filtered result as the returned rows, before paging. A custom provider cannot assume remote or manually assembled data is protected automatically by database access control. Apply the same restrictions to data, count, and supported aggregates. If an operation cannot be answered securely and correctly, reject it clearly instead of returning misleading information.

Reasoning and example
A user can see five permitted orders, but the service returns a total count of 900 including hidden orders. The list has filtered the rows, yet the count still reveals information. Use one consistent definition of the permitted result before calculating its count or selecting a page. Do not simply fetch everything remotely and hide only the displayed rows.

Test a user with no access, a count-only request, filters, ordering, and any navigation or aggregation the service supports. A count-only request must still apply permissions even when no rows are requested. If the remote source cannot support the required secure selection, choose a suitable safe implementation or explicitly reject the unsupported request.

Avoid
Filtering only the displayed page leaves count, aggregates and existence checks exposed.
Filtering, paging and total count

Count and paging answer different questions. Stable ordering matters when the client requests successive pages.
Explain it: For this example, what count belongs beside a page of five records?
Limit: Provider-side execution order may be optimized while preserving request semantics.
Secure custom-query filtering, count, and page

The same authorized logical set contains IDs 2, 4, and 6. Counting it returns three; skipping one and taking two returns IDs 4 and 6 without revealing hidden B rows.
Explain it: What should a count-only request return, and what should happen if the filter cannot be represented safely?
Limit: The drawing specifies semantics, not a mandatory physical execution plan. A remote/custom provider must preserve equivalent authorization, filtering, count, and ordering behavior.

  • Protects count and aggregates
  • Rejects unsupported semantics explicitly
Verification evidence

column1: MODEL-04 | A query-provider filter cannot be converted to simple ranges. A developer catches the exception and returns everything. What is the correction?
column2:
Short answer
Do not turn a filter-conversion failure into an unrestricted read. Preserve the original AND/OR grouping using a supported expression representation or another safe translation. If the provider cannot support the filter, reject it clearly. Keep mandatory authorization restrictions separate from user filters so neither disappears on an error. Handle dynamic field names and values through supported safe APIs.

Reasoning and example
The filter means either region A with amount above 100, or region B with Urgent true. Converting that into separate region and amount ranges can change which records match. A request that should return selected urgent B records may instead return too much or hide legitimate matches.

Create test rows that distinguish the original grouped expression from the simplified one. Include an unsupported function and verify that its failure returns the documented error rather than all records. Authorization restrictions must remain in force regardless of filter parsing. If the backend cannot express the requested condition faithfully, an explicit unsupported-request response is safer and more useful than a successful-looking incorrect dataset.

Avoid
A swallowed filter exception must not become an unrestricted selection.

column1: MODEL-05 | A paged custom entity repeats some rows after an insertion. How would you make the contract predictable?
column2:
Short answer

Stable ordering does not freeze the data: an insertion can still shift offset-based pages. Use a supported continuation or snapshot approach where required, or document the weaker behavior of a live list. A complete export needs stronger planning than ordinary UI browsing.

Reasoning and example
Twenty orders share the same creation date. Sorting only by that date leaves their relative order unclear, so add an appropriate unique key as a tie-breaker. Now insert an order between page requests: even with that stable order, an offset can move and cause a repeated or missed row. These are two different problems.

Clarify whether the screen should show a changing current list or the caller needs a reproducible extraction. Test equal sort values, descending order, insertions, deletions, empty pages, and changing counts. Choose a supported mechanism that meets the requirement and state its limits. Adding ORDER BY fixes ambiguous ordering, but cannot alone promise a frozen dataset across separate requests.

Avoid
Adding ORDER BY alone does not guarantee a frozen dataset across requests.

column1: MODEL-06 | Adding a language-dependent text association doubles order totals. Would DISTINCT be a good fix?
column2:
Short answer
Find out what one result row should represent and why the join produces more than one matching text. Check language, validity dates, and any other condition needed for uniqueness. Fix that relationship or aggregate at the correct level. DISTINCT may hide rows without fixing totals. Declaring to-one cardinality does not make duplicate matches disappear.

Reasoning and example
An order for 100 EUR joins to two language texts. The resulting query now contains two copies of the order amount, so a later sum becomes 200 EUR. The problem is the relationship's actual multiplicity, not simply the appearance of repeated labels. A false to-one declaration can also mislead query optimization.

Use fixtures with two languages, missing texts, and overlapping validity periods. Decide which text should apply and express the supported condition, or separate text retrieval from aggregation where appropriate. Check both detailed rows and the consuming total. DISTINCT can discard legitimate detail or leave the incorrect aggregate in place, so demonstrate the intended row identity and amount after the real fix.

Avoid
Do not fix an incorrect join by simply declaring a to-one cardinality.
SQL join multiplication

Joining two order headers to three items repeats order 10's total, inflating a naive sum from EUR 180 to EUR 280. For outer joins, matching conditions in ON can preserve unmatched left rows, while right-side conditions in WHERE can remove them.
Explain it: What is one row of this result supposed to represent? Where should a language filter go for optional text?
Limit: This is an inner-join example. WHERE and ON placement must follow intended semantics; neither DISTINCT nor SUM(DISTINCT amount) repairs every incorrect join or aggregation.
CDS links and ownership

Items belong to the order BO; a partner reference crosses to an independently managed object.
Explain it: What breaks if a declared to-one relationship actually returns two partners?

column1: MODEL-07 | A CDS report sums 100 EUR and 100 USD into 200. What should the model and service do?
column2:
Short answer
Do not add amounts in different currencies as though they were the same unit. Group totals by currency or perform an agreed conversion first. Define the target currency, rate type, date, and rounding rule with the business. Preserve the currency and unit links in the model. An annotation describes those links; it does not automatically perform conversion.

Reasoning and example
A report contains 100 EUR and 100 USD. Showing 200 without a currency policy gives a misleading total. The business may want separate currency totals, or a total in EUR using a specified exchange-rate date. Those are different valid requirements and should be chosen deliberately.

Test mixed currencies, a missing rate, and values that require rounding. Check whether rounding happens per item or after aggregation, because totals can differ. Keep original values where reconciliation needs them and inspect how the real analytical or transactional consumer interprets the fields. The same principle applies to quantities with different units. A correctly annotated amount still needs correctly designed calculation behavior.

Avoid
Do not confuse semantic annotations with conversion logic.

column1: MODEL-08 | A transactional projection needs a calculated field that its provider contract does not permit. How do you redesign it?
column2:
Short answer
Check what the projection's provider contract allows on the target release. Put the calculation in a suitable underlying model, a separate read model, or a supported virtual element if its limits fit. Preserve stable identity, permissions, and update behavior. Do not force arbitrary joins into a transactional projection just for display. Test filtering and sorting as well as reading the field.

Reasoning and example
The UI asks for a calculated risk band and wants to filter orders by it. An ABAP-calculated display value might look correct for the current page but not support the required server-side filter. Decide where that value belongs: stored business state, a database expression, or a read-only enrichment with clearly limited query support.

Identify who recalculates it when source data changes. Then test read, filter, order, and update through the intended binding on the actual release. The transactional entity must still identify the right object and preserve behavior mapping and authorization. A field appearing in a preview proves display in that path, not a complete supported query-and-update design for every consumer.

column1: MODEL-09 | The business wants to sort a million-row list by a virtual element computed through a remote call. What would you propose?
column2:
Short answer
Do not calculate a million remote scores row by row just to sort a list. A virtual element does not automatically support efficient database sorting or filtering. Consider a suitable stored read model with refresh rules, a supported database calculation, or limited enrichment without global sorting. Agree how fresh results must be and how failures appear. Measure with realistic data.

Reasoning and example
A remote provider supplies each customer's risk score. Sorting all orders by that score may require far more work than displaying scores for one small page. Ten demo rows hide the cost of remote calls, data transfer, and rebuilding the result before paging. Virtual-element logic does not automatically move to HANA.

Ask whether scores can be stored and refreshed under an agreed policy, or whether users can work with a bounded result instead. Define what happens when the provider is unavailable and how stale values are marked or reconciled. Measure latency, calls, and transferred rows for both data and count requests. Choose a design that makes the sort correct at the required scale, not merely visually convincing.

Do not claim that adding a virtual element automatically pushes its logic to HANA.

column1: MODEL-10 | Two rows in a service share the declared CDS key after a join. Why is this more than a display issue?
column2:
Short answer

An order-item entity exposes only OrderId as its key. Two items in the same order therefore look like the same resource to the client. The list may show rows, but opening or updating one can target the wrong item. Client-side deduplication hides the symptom while losing legitimate data.

Test multiple items with read-by-key, navigation, stable URLs, and update targeting. Repeat reads in different orders to expose cache or selection confusion. Determine whether one row should represent an item or an aggregate, then choose the matching identity and query. If callers already rely on the incorrect public key, coordinate a migration instead of silently changing what an existing URL means.

Do not hide duplicate-key rows with client-side deduplication.

column1: MODEL-11 | A value help reveals customer names that the order list hides. Where should the fix live?
column2:
Short answer
Protect the value-help entity and its text and navigation paths as read entry points in their own right. Linking it from a protected order list does not automatically restrict it. Test direct service access with the actual user context. Also validate selected values when writing an order. Clients can submit a customer key without ever opening the picker.

Reasoning and example
A restricted user cannot see another organization's orders but can search its customer names in the value help. The auxiliary search is leaking information even though the main list looks correct. Check its access rules, text associations, search results, and counts using the same restricted identity. Hiding the picker does not protect direct requests.

Then send an update containing a forbidden customer key directly to the service. The write path must reject it under the required business and permission rules even if the search now hides it correctly. Read restrictions stop disclosure; write checks stop an invalid or unauthorized reference being saved. Both are necessary because the UI is only one possible consumer.

Avoid
Hiding the value-help control is not a backend security fix.

Review security where consumers enter the model, rather than assuming that lower layers protect every upper view.

column1: MODEL-12 | A batch job asks to use privileged EML because normal authorization rejects it. How do you evaluate the request?
column2:
Short answer
First check the job's legitimate scope and whether normal permissions can represent it. Privileged EML requires a provider-supported privilege design; it is not a generic fix for rejected calls. Verify exactly which checks it bypasses and which trusted callers may reach it. Keep business checks and auditability. PRIVILEGED, IN LOCAL MODE, and a technical user are different mechanisms.

Reasoning and example
A repair job is authorized to reconcile one organization. Giving it a broadly callable privileged helper could accidentally let normal consumers perform unrestricted posting. Review the provider's authorization contexts and enabled privileged entry points, then expose only the narrow operation the job actually needs.

Test the approved repair and a denied attempt from an ordinary caller. Record who requested the repair and which business records it affected. If ordinary scoped authorization can meet the requirement, prefer that simpler model. If privilege is justified, document the precise bypass behavior on this provider and release. The fact that a background identity is technical does not by itself explain or authorize every bypass.

Avoid
Do not assume PRIVILEGED, IN LOCAL MODE and a technical user are equivalent.

column1: MODEL-13 | A developer uses IN LOCAL MODE in a helper to avoid feature checks. What makes the helper safe or unsafe?
column2:
Short answer

Test those action inputs and examine which controls the specific local-mode operation bypasses. column1: MODEL-14 | A CDS unit test passes, but the same entity leaks data for a restricted user. What may the test be missing?
column2:
Short answer

Use supported access-control test setup with meaningful permission data where available. Add real service tests with restricted identities. Keep query correctness and deployed authorization evidence separate.

A unit test proves that a join returns three expected rows from fixture data. That is useful, but it says nothing about whether a user should see all three. Add cases for no access and two different organizational scopes, and inspect the test configuration to confirm that DCL is enabled and exercised.

Finally call the real service with restricted users. That checks the consumed entity, binding, and identity propagation that the isolated test may not cover. Capture positive cases too, so a fix does not simply block everyone. A green double-based test and a passing restricted-user service test prove different things; neither result should be inferred from the other.

column1: MODEL-15 | An integration user can access all tenants or clients through a custom read provider. What boundaries must be reviewed?
column2:
Short answer

Do not trust an unrestricted tenant selector from request input. Use the environment's supported tenant-aware configuration and check the identity seen downstream. The correct isolation model depends on the actual runtime.

The caller supplies a tenant or company parameter, and a custom provider forwards it through a remote connection with broad privileges. The remote response may contain another customer's records even if the local CDS model appears restricted. Inspect who controls that selector and how it is checked before building the remote request.

Test two scopes that share the same document numbers. Verify request construction, remote identity, and returned data so matching business IDs do not hide a cross-scope leak. column1: MODEL-17 | A released entity gains a new field that is expensive and sensitive. Is an additive change automatically safe?
column2:
Short answer
An added field can still change security, cost, or behavior for existing consumers. Check default reads, broad selections, serialization, metadata-driven clients, and permissions. A sensitive or expensive field may belong in a more restricted interface. Verify the release contract's evolution rules and test unchanged callers. Old code still compiling is not enough to prove the addition is safe.

Reasoning and example
A new personal-data field appears automatically in a broad select or export. No caller changed, yet users now receive information that needs a different access decision. Another added field calculates remotely for every returned row, making an existing list much slower. Both are compatibility concerns beyond the ABAP signature.

Compare old and new payloads, permission results, and latency for representative requests. Test explicit field selection, default selection, and UIs that build screens from metadata. Decide whether the field should be exposed separately, selected only when needed, or protected differently under supported mechanisms. Keep existing consumers' expectations in view before describing an additive change as harmless.

Avoid
Do not assess compatibility using only whether old source code still compiles.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Does an existing broad select expose it?
  • How does it affect authorization and request cost?
Strong answer criteria
  • Checks changes in meaning, access, and runtime cost
  • Controls what existing reads expose by default
  • Tests existing callers without changing them
Verification evidence
Compare old/new payloads, access results and latency for representative existing requests.

Read and verify
  • SAP BO interfaces
    Test the entity and service callers actually use. Include denied users, filters, and attempts to cross the allowed access boundary.

column1: MODEL-18 | An analytical requirement is added to a transactional BO. Would you put every aggregate into its projection?
column2:
Short answer
Choose an analytical read model that represents the required totals and groups. Do not distort an editable object's identity to fit every aggregate. Reuse reliable data meanings where possible, but define aggregation, currency, permissions, and freshness explicitly. Keep changes on the transactional object's supported operations. A separate read model needs ownership and consistency rules, not duplicated business logic nobody maintains.

Reasoning and example
An approval app edits individual items, while management wants monthly spend by organization. One monthly total is not the same kind of entity as one editable item. Treating both as a single transactional projection can make keys, permissions, and behavior confusing. Build a read model that clearly represents the monthly grouping instead.

Reconcile its totals with authorized transactional fixtures, including mixed currencies and late changes. Decide whether a live query meets response-time needs or whether a refreshed read model needs a defined delay and reconciliation process. Keep shared rules owned and consistent across the models. The fact that an aggregate comes from writable business data does not make the aggregate itself a sensible writable object.

Avoid
Do not make an aggregate writable merely because its source is a transactional BO.
SQL join multiplication

Joining two order headers to three items repeats order 10's total, inflating a naive sum from EUR 180 to EUR 280. For outer joins, matching conditions in ON can preserve unmatched left rows, while right-side conditions in WHERE can remove them.
Explain it: What is one row of this result supposed to represent? Where should a language filter go for optional text?
Limit: This is an inner-join example. WHERE and ON placement must follow intended semantics; neither DISTINCT nor SUM(DISTINCT amount) repairs every incorrect join or aggregation.
Calculation placement and query semantics

Use the requirement to decide where a value must exist before filtering, ordering or aggregation.
Explain it: Why can a correct calculation still yield a wrong page of results?
Limit: Architecture alternatives, not a promise that all listed options are supported by each projection/custom provider.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What should one aggregate row represent?
  • How do both models preserve permissions and currency meaning?
Strong answer criteria
  • Distinguishes editable objects from grouped results
  • Reuses data meanings deliberately
  • Defines freshness and reconciliation
Verification evidence
Reconcile grouped totals to authorized transactional fixtures and validate the intended analytical consumer.

Read and verify
  • SAP analytical projection modeling
    Test the entity and service callers actually use. Include denied users, filters, and attempts to cross the allowed access boundary.

column1: ADV-01 | How do pessimistic locks and ETags complement each other?
column2:
Short answer
A lock stops conflicting processing while it is held. An ETag lets a write request check whether the data has changed since the client read it. They solve different problems and are often needed together. RAP declares the relevant lock and version handling in behavior. Draft scenarios also need total-ETag handling for relevant changes to active data.

Reasoning and example
Ana and Ben read order 4704 at quantity 2 with ETag V1. Ana saves quantity 3, producing ETag V2. Ben tries to save quantity 4 with his older V1. The If-Match check rejects that stale update, leaving quantity 3 intact. Ben must refresh and decide whether quantity 4 is still the change he wants. The ETag did not reserve the order while he was reading it.

A pessimistic lock addresses conflicting processing during the period it is held. Draft editing and changes to active data require the matching draft lock and total-ETag design. Test stale updates and draft resume behavior separately. A lock is temporary coordination; an ETag is a version check, and neither is an audit log.

Avoid
Locking and logging are different concepts; an ETag is not a log and does not reserve the object.
Draft lifecycle

Follow edit, activate and discard for an existing active object, then explain how a new-object draft differs.
Explain it: What remains after discarding an edit draft? What if activation fails?
Limit: Schematic state transitions; draft actions and supported flows depend on the BO and consumer.
Two ETag boundaries

The left side tests a conditional entity update; the right tests the active-state basis of a resumed draft.
Explain it: Why does testing one entity ETag not prove the draft total-ETag implementation?
Limit: ETags are opaque. Verify lock expiry, relevant child changes and generated behavior on the actual system.
Two editors and one version: an illustrated story

Alice and Ben read version 7. Alice updates successfully, producing version 8. Ben must not overwrite that newer state using the stale version 7 precondition.
Explain it: Why should the client refresh and resolve the conflict instead of blindly retrying its old payload?
Limit: Version numbers are illustrative. Real ETags are opaque validators; a failed If-Match precondition commonly returns HTTP 412. This is optimistic concurrency, not a pessimistic lock.

Read and verify
  • SAP draft concept
    Check which RAP behavior is supported by the target release and the client that calls it.

column1: ADV-02 | What is the difference between global and instance authorization in RAP, and where do DCL and prechecks fit?
column2:
Short answer
Global authorization asks: may this user perform Update in general? Instance authorization asks: may this user update this particular record? Here, instance means a business-object record, not an ABAP class instance. DCL controls which rows a read returns. A precheck can reject incoming values before they enter the transactional buffer.

Reasoning and example
A user may change projects in Company Code 1000, but not 2000. The global check permits Update as an operation. The instance check permits project A in 1000 and rejects project B in 2000. A global pass is not permission to change every project.

The BDEF can declare authorization master ( global, instance ). get_global_authorizations receives requested_authorizations without record keys. get_instance_authorizations also receives keys and returns decisions identified by %tky. AUTHORITY-CHECK with BUKRS DUMMY ignores that field; the instance check instead supplies the existing project's CompanyCode.

Instance authorization checks existing data, not the new values submitted by the current request. For Create, or an Update that changes CompanyCode, check the proposed value in a precheck when that boundary needs protection. Otherwise, being allowed to edit a project in 1000 could be mistaken for permission to move it to 2000. CDS DCL remains responsible for read filtering.

Feature control has another job: availability under business rules. A closed project may be uneditable even for an authorized user. Test both an unauthorized user on an editable project and an authorized user on a closed project through the service, not only through disabled buttons.

Avoid
Global authorization, instance authorization, DCL, prechecks and feature control solve different problems. A global pass or disabled button does not secure every record or incoming value.
CDS security boundaries

Review security where consumers enter the model, rather than assuming that lower layers protect every upper view.
Explain it: Which two tests prove that an exposed service rejects unauthorized access?
Limit: Authorization behavior depends on the access path and supported DCL inheritance mechanisms.
Identity, authorization and feature control

Treat identity, business permission and contextual availability as separate checks.
Explain it: If Submit is disabled in Fiori, what happens when someone calls the service directly?
Limit: Static operation characteristics differ from dynamic instance/global feature checks.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Authorization definition and prechecks
    Global checks are independent of an instance; instance checks use existing instance data; prechecks inspect incoming values.
  • SAP Learning: implementing authority checks
    Use CDS access control for reads and RAP authorization for operations. Instance checks do not replace a check of new input values.

column1: ADV-03 | What does authorization none on an action mean?
column2:
Short answer
Where the behavior syntax supports it, authorization: none exempts that action from its RAP authorization checks. It does not make the whole service anonymous. Service authentication and checks inside called APIs can still apply. Use this only when the action's security design justifies the exemption. Do not add it simply to make an authorization error disappear.

Reasoning and example
Consider an action whose result is intentionally available to every authenticated user of that service and needs no object-specific permission. Its design may justify an explicit RAP authorization exemption. Document what data it reads or changes and why access at the service boundary is enough for that action.

If the action calls another API, that API may still check its own permissions and reject the call. Conversely, exempting a sensitive approval action can remove a necessary protection even when login is still required. Test with a user who can access the service but should not perform privileged work. Verify the exact syntax and supported action contract on the target release.

Avoid
Do not propose it as a universal fix for authorization errors or expose a sensitive action by accident.
Identity, authorization and feature control

Treat identity, business permission and contextual availability as separate checks.
Explain it: If Submit is disabled in Fiori, what happens when someone calls the service directly?
Limit: Static operation characteristics differ from dynamic instance/global feature checks.

Read and verify
  • SAP Learning on authorization
    Check which RAP behavior is supported by the target release and the client that calls it.

column1: ADV-04 | Instance static and factory actions?
column2:
Short answer
An instance action works on an existing identified object, such as approving one request. A static action does not need an existing instance as its input target. A factory action creates instances and returns the required creation mapping. Choose the type that matches the business operation. Their input, result, and identity rules are different.

Reasoning and example
Approve needs a request to approve, so it is an instance action. A calculation preview may be a static action when it uses supplied input without needing an existing request. CopyRequest may be a factory action because its purpose is to create a new request and tell the caller which object was created.

Check the generated handler signature and return the result and mappings that the chosen action type requires. Returning $self from an ordinary instance action does not turn it into a factory action. Likewise, static describes how the RAP action is used; it is not permission to ignore the RAP transaction or treat the handler like an unrelated static utility method.

Avoid
Static does not mean a static ABAP method that can ignore RAP identity and response contracts.
RAP hook responsibilities

Read each card as a separate design question; this is not an execution sequence.
Explain it: Where would you derive a total, reject an invalid input and implement Submit?
Limit: Check scenario and release support; do not rely on an undocumented ordering of independent hooks.

Read and verify
  • SAP action definitions
    Check which RAP behavior is supported by the target release and the client that calls it.

column1: ADV-05 | How do action parameters and results work?
column2:
Short answer
An action's behavior definition describes its input and result. A CDS abstract entity can define a structured input such as a comment and date. The generated handler receives that input and must return the declared result and response information. Result cardinality and instance binding matter. A UI can offer a parameter dialog only where the consumer supports it.

Reasoning and example
Suppose Submit accepts an approval comment. Define that parameter shape, declare it on the action, and use the generated handler signature to read it. The abstract entity describes the input fields; it does not itself contain or implement the action. The handler still carries out the business step under RAP's rules.

A different action, CalculatePreview, may return estimated totals without saving a new object. Its result type and cardinality should describe that outcome clearly. Test missing or invalid parameters and inspect what the caller actually receives. Do not assume that defining parameters guarantees the same input dialog in every client; metadata and consumer support determine the user experience.

A handler can receive several requested keys. Process all of them, collect failures and messages, and build the declared result for the successful requests. For an instance action returning [1] $self, the result identifies each successful source instance and places its returned entity data in %param. Updating a row and filling result are separate responsibilities; neither proves that the later save succeeded.

Avoid
Parameters are not defined by putting an action inside an abstract entity.
RAP hook responsibilities

Read each card as a separate design question; this is not an execution sequence.
Explain it: Where would you derive a total, reject an invalid input and implement Submit?
Limit: Check scenario and release support; do not rely on an undocumented ordering of independent hooks.

Read and verify
  • SAP action definitions
    Check which RAP behavior is supported by the target release and the client that calls it.

column1: ADV-06 | What is augmentation and how does it differ from additional save?
column2:
Short answer
Augmentation changes or adds supported input at a RAP projection boundary before the underlying business object handles it. It helps adapt a particular consumer's input. Additional save performs extra persistence-related work in a suitable managed save scenario. These mechanisms run for different reasons. Neither is a general hook for arbitrary work before every save.

Reasoning and example
A specialized projection may accept input that needs to be translated into fields understood by the shared business object. A supported augmentation can make that translation so the underlying behavior receives the right changes. Check the projection's supported modifying operations and keep the core business rules in the appropriate underlying implementation.

Writing an audit record alongside the managed object's persisted changes is a different concern. It may require an additional-save design that follows the transaction rules. Putting it into augmentation just because that code runs during a modification confuses input handling with saving. Similarly, a virtual display field does not become persistent simply because an augmentation exists; design its supported data flow explicitly.

Avoid
Augmentation is not a generic before-save hook for copying every virtual element into a table.
Augmentation versus additional save

Locate the input transformation and persistence supplement on the same conceptual timeline.
Explain it: Why would writing an audit row not make augmentation the right save hook?
Limit: The arrow is conceptual; availability, supported fields and trigger details depend on the target RAP release.

Read and verify
  • SAP operation augmentation
    Check which RAP behavior is supported by the target release and the client that calls it.

column1: ADV-07 | What are side effects in a RAP UI?
column2:
Short answer
Side-effect metadata tells a supported UI what to read again after a change or action. For example, changing quantity may require refreshing the total and available actions. The backend must still calculate the correct values. Side effects only coordinate refreshes. Support depends on the backend release, service metadata, and SAPUI5 consumer.

Reasoning and example
The user changes an item's quantity from 2 to 3 at a unit price of 15 EUR. A backend determination changes the draft total from 30 EUR to 45 EUR, but the screen may still show 30 EUR until it reads that value again. Suitable side-effect metadata tells the UI that the quantity change affects the total and, where supported, related messages or permissions.

Check the actual network requests and displayed result after both field edits and actions, including draft processing. If the backend total is wrong, adding a refresh cannot fix the calculation. If the backend is correct but the UI stays stale, inspect the metadata and client support. A non-UI API caller does not automatically perform these extra reads just because the metadata exists.

Avoid
A side-effect declaration does not implement the calculation or force all non-UI consumers to issue extra reads.
Side effects and stale UI diagnosis

Use the observed backend value to choose the next debugging branch.
Explain it: What request proves that the consumer refreshed the calculated total?
Limit: Consumer and metadata support are release-dependent; a valid backend side effect is not proof that every client processes it.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP side effects
    Check which field change or action triggers a refresh and what should be reread. Verify that the actual UI supports it.

column1: ADV-08 | State messages versus transition messages?
column2:
Short answer
A state message describes a problem in an object's current data, such as a missing required date. In supported draft scenarios it can remain until the state is checked again. A transition message describes the current operation or request. Attach messages to the correct instance, field, and state area. Clear old state messages when they no longer apply.

Reasoning and example
A user saves a draft without a delivery date. A state message can keep the date marked as invalid while the user continues editing. When the date is corrected and the relevant check runs again, handle the state area properly so the old error disappears. Otherwise the screen can show an error for data that is now valid.

A one-time message such as Submission completed belongs to the operation, not to a permanent invalid state. Test repeat edits, correction of errors, and a fresh request to avoid stale messages. Also remember that a message and rejection are different jobs: putting an error in REPORTED does not by itself guarantee that RAP rejects the save.

Avoid
Every error should not be stored as a persistent state message, and REPORTED alone does not block saving.
Draft lifecycle

Follow edit, activate and discard for an existing active object, then explain how a new-object draft differs.
Explain it: What remains after discarding an edit draft? What if activation fails?
Limit: Schematic state transitions; draft actions and supported flows depend on the BO and consumer.
RAP message lifecycle and correction

Follow the same child through an error and correction instead of treating a message as timeless text.
Explain it: Which identity and state area would you inspect when the old error remains?
Limit: Message lifetime and permitted state-message scenarios depend on active/draft and the supported operation contract.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP state messages
    Compare messages about the current object state with messages about one operation. Check which instance each message belongs to and how old state messages are cleared.

column1: ADV-09 | Service definition versus binding and UI versus Web API?
column2:
Short answer
A service definition chooses which entities and names are exposed. A service binding chooses the protocol and service type, such as OData V4 UI or Web API. UI services support relevant UI behavior; Web APIs serve programmatic consumers. Creating these objects is only part of delivery. Authorization, publication, communication setup, and deployment must also be handled.

Reasoning and example
Start with the caller: is it a Fiori elements app or an external integration? Expose the needed entities, choose a suitable binding, then inspect the generated metadata and exercise the actual operations. A service that reads correctly in an ADT preview has not yet proved that the production consumer can authenticate or call it.

Follow the target environment's deployment and communication setup, and test permissions with the intended user or communication identity. Confirm that transported objects and the real endpoint behave as expected. A CDS modeling annotation such as VDM.viewType: #COMPOSITE does not create or activate a binding. Model classification and service delivery are separate responsibilities.

Avoid
VDM.viewType: #COMPOSITE neither creates nor activates a service binding.
RAP contract stack

Read from the client down to storage, then explain what each artifact contributes.
Explain it: Where would you restrict the exposed operation set?
Limit: Conceptual layers; the exact artifact set depends on the scenario and release.

Read and verify
  • SAP service binding documentation
    Check which RAP behavior is supported by the target release and the client that calls it.

column1: ADV-10 | What must a custom query provider implement?
column2:
Short answer
A custom query provider must answer what the caller actually asked for. That includes supported filters, sorting, paging, selected fields, and count, while enforcing permissions. A count request and a data request can arrive independently. Count the authorized, filtered result before paging. Treat zero rows requested differently from PAGE_SIZE_UNLIMITED, and use a stable sort order.

Reasoning and example
Lea asks for open orders in organization A, sorted by CreatedAt, skipping one and taking two. Of 12 source orders, four match both her permission and filter: 101, 104, 108 and 110. Use OrderID to break equal CreatedAt values. The page contains 104 and 108, while the total count remains 4. Keep that ordering stable so rows do not move unpredictably between pages. If a remote source is involved, map errors and account for its paging and consistency limits.

Test a count-only request separately; it must not depend on entering a branch that fetches data. Also test an empty page and a page size of zero. Zero means no rows, not an unrestricted read. Compare it explicitly with IF_RAP_QUERY_PAGING=>PAGE_SIZE_UNLIMITED. Handle unsupported options deliberately instead of silently returning a plausible but incorrect list.

Avoid
Returning any internal table is not a correct implementation of IF_RAP_QUERY_PROVIDER.
Filtering, paging and total count

Count and paging answer different questions. Stable ordering matters when the client requests successive pages.
Explain it: For this example, what count belongs beside a page of five records?
Limit: Provider-side execution order may be optimized while preserving request semantics.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Implementing an Unmanaged Query
    Check which query requests the target release supports. Test bulk reads and caching separately to prove their results are correct and their performance is acceptable.
  • SAP: Requesting and Setting Data or Count
    Handle requests for rows and requests for a count independently. Apply the same permissions and filters to both, and test a request that asks only for the count.
  • SAP: Interface IF_RAP_QUERY_PAGING
    Check offset, zero rows requested, and PAGE_SIZE_UNLIMITED separately. This interface does not by itself freeze the dataset across several requests.

column1: ADV-11 | How do RAP business events differ from ABAP Objects events?
column2:
Short answer
ABAP Objects events use handlers within ABAP execution. RAP business events describe business occurrences using RAP's event rules. Local and remote consumption have their own supported lifecycle. Sending events outside the system also needs configured infrastructure and a publication design tied to the transaction. Consumers should be prepared for retries and duplicate delivery rather than assuming exactly one arrival.

Reasoning and example
A request is submitted successfully, and another system needs to start follow-up work. Publish the business event through the supported transactional mechanism so the external process does not act on a change that later rolls back. A local callback during processing is not proof that the business change has been durably saved.

At the consumer, use the event's business identity and a suitable duplicate-handling design. If the same submission event is delivered again after a retry, it should not create a second approval task. Verify the supported ordering and delivery behavior instead of assuming it. Locally consumed RAP events also should not all be described as ordinary synchronous SET HANDLER callbacks.

Avoid
Do not collapse every locally consumed RAP event into synchronous SET HANDLER semantics or promise universal ordering.
Duplicate events and stale approvals

The event identity and current business state decide whether to apply, ignore or reject the request.
Explain it: Two consumers process the same event simultaneously: what prevents a double effect?
Limit: Exact transactional deduplication mechanisms depend on the chosen infrastructure.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Develop Business Events
    Check how the target release defines, publishes, and consumes RAP events. Verify the messaging infrastructure and its delivery and retry guarantees separately.

column1: ADV-12 | How do you extend an existing RAP BO safely?
column2:
Short answer
First check what the business object officially allows you to extend on your system's release. Then use those supported extension points to add the field or behavior. Follow the change through storage, CDS, projection, service, and any UI metadata. Check permissions and saving too. Being able to see or edit an object's source does not mean SAP supports extending it.

Reasoning and example
Suppose the business wants an Approval Reference field on an existing request. Check the object's extension documentation first: can you add a stored field, expose it through the service, and add any needed rule? If one part is unsupported, adding only a CDS field will not deliver a working feature.

After implementing the supported changes, enter a value, save the request, and reopen it. Confirm the value is stored and returned by the service. Test invalid values, restricted users, and the normal process without the new field. Existing consumers must keep working. Extension support depends on the particular business object and release, so do not copy assumptions from a different RAP example.

Avoid
Being able to create a CDS extension does not prove every BO behavior or API contract is extensible.

Read and verify
  • SAP: RAP Extensibility Enablement
    Check that each layer you need to change is explicitly enabled and released for that kind of extension on the target release.

column1: ADV-13 | How do static and dynamic feature controls differ?
column2:
Short answer
Static restrictions are declared in the behavior definition, such as a readonly field. Dynamic feature controls decide availability from current context, such as making approved requests uneditable. They describe business availability, not who has permission. Check the controls supported for the operation and release. For one operation, choose global or instance feature control; do not declare both.

Reasoning and example
A generated UUID should not be freely edited by the caller, so a static readonly declaration fits. The request description may be editable while the request is open but readonly after approval, which needs a state-dependent rule. Use the applicable generated feature-control handler to express the supported restriction.

Now test an API call as well as the screen. Permission checks must still prevent an unauthorized user from changing an otherwise editable request. Also validate the business data: mandatory field metadata is not a complete substitute for backend consistency rules. Keeping static restrictions, dynamic availability, authorization, and validation separate makes it easier to explain why a request was rejected.

Compare static field controls: readonly prevents consumer writes; readonly:update permits supplying the field on create but prevents later consumer updates; mandatory declares a required input for supporting consumers. Do not rely on a UI required marker alone to reject invalid persistence: implement the necessary backend validation. Dynamic features may make an operation unavailable for the current business state; authorization independently decides whether the caller is allowed.

Avoid
A dynamic UI state does not prove security, and mandatory metadata does not replace all backend business validations.
Identity, authorization and feature control

Treat identity, business permission and contextual availability as separate checks.
Explain it: If Submit is disabled in Fiori, what happens when someone calls the service directly?
Limit: Static operation characteristics differ from dynamic instance/global feature checks.

Read and verify
  • SAP feature control
    Check which RAP behavior is supported by the target release and the client that calls it.

column1: ADV-14 | What is a normal RAP function, and when should you use it instead of an action?
column2:
Short answer
A RAP function returns data or a calculation without changing the business object. Use it to preview an order total, for example. It runs in a FOR READ handler and returns the value in result. It must not update the buffer, save data or trigger a business side effect. Use an action when the operation should change business state.

Reasoning and example
Suppose an order has Quantity 3 and UnitPrice 10. A PreviewTotal function reads the current values through EML and returns Amount 30. The caller sees the calculation, but the order is not changed or saved. If the user changes Quantity to 4 in the same transaction, a new preview can return 40. Read the transactional state rather than assuming the database already contains that edit.

A normal instance function receives the selected instance keys. Its result links each input %tky to the calculated %param. Return a result for each successful input and a FAILED response for a rejected one. A static function is the variant that does not require an existing instance; it uses request correlation such as %cid. Static does not mean background processing.

Declare the function in the BDEF and expose it with use function in the projection when the service needs it. Read-only does not mean public: configure and test the applicable authorization and feature controls. A function must not send an approval email, call a remote posting operation or create new state messages. Check result types, cardinalities, binding and client support on the target release. This RAP function is not an ABAP function module.

Avoid
Do not implement a preview by changing the BO and then trying to undo it. A function returns a result; a determination changes derived BO data, and an action can perform a business change.

Read and verify
  • SAP: RAP function definition
    Read-only behavior, instance versus static, authorization and result support.
  • SAP: FOR READ handler method
    FOR FUNCTION input, result and FAILED/REPORTED response contracts.

column1: ADV-15 | How does a default function suggest values for RAP action parameters?
column2:
Short answer
A default values function proposes initial input for an action dialog. It does not execute the action. For example, opening ApplyDiscount can suggest 10 percent for a large order and 5 percent for a small one. The user can edit the suggestion. When the action is finally called, validate the submitted value again.

Reasoning and example
Attach a default function to the action declaration, for example GetDefaultsForApplyDiscount. Its name follows the GetDefaultsFor convention. RAP derives its input and result types from the operation; generate the handler in ADT rather than inventing a separate parameter contract. For an instance action, preserve each input %tky and fill the suggested parameter fields in %param. If a projection exposes the action, expose the default function there too.

Example: order A totals 1200 EUR and order B totals 200 EUR. A simple teaching rule suggests DiscountPercent 10 for A and 5 for B. The default function reads both orders and returns those suggestions; it does not change either order. A user then enters 80 instead of 10. The action must check its allowed discount range and permissions and reject 80 if the rule forbids it.

The supporting UI requests the default values before execution. A direct API caller can supply different input or skip the default request, so defaults are not an enforcement mechanism. A default can also become outdated before the action runs. Test multiple selected instances, missing keys, a cancelled dialog and invalid submitted values. Check backend release, OData binding and Fiori elements support rather than assuming every client opens the same dialog.

Avoid
Do not confuse an input suggestion with a saved field value, determination or validation. Opening or cancelling the dialog must not perform the action.

Read and verify
  • SAP: defaulting input parameters for operations
    Default function declaration and handler. Check availability in the target release.
  • SAP sample: default values functions for Fiori elements
    Shows BDEF, projection exposure and filling %param.

column1: OPS-01 | How would you test a Submit action without replacing the business object you are supposed to verify?
column2:
Short answer
I run the real Submit action and keep the business rules I want to test. I replace only outside dependencies, such as another service or business object, with suitable test doubles. Then I call the action, often through EML, and check its results, errors and saved state. Mocking Submit itself would not test Submit.

Reasoning and example
A purchase request may be submitted only when every item has an account assignment. I create one valid request and another with an assignment missing. Both tests execute the real Submit implementation. I check that the valid request reaches the intended state and that the invalid one is rejected with the correct message.

If a different business object supplies a spending limit, I can replace that dependency with a supported double and choose its returned limit. That keeps this test focused on Submit. I also verify the saved outcome through the test framework's supported save boundary. A predefined successful response from a fake Submit would prove none of these rules.

Avoid
Do not label a test of a mocked Submit response as a test of Submit.
Testing scope and evidence

The widening base suggests many focused checks, but there is no mandatory numerical ratio.
Explain it: Which risk remains after an ABAP Unit test with doubles passes?
Limit: Conceptual coverage map, not a count of tests actually run in SAP.
Real behavior under test and dependency doubles

Two deliberately different inputs exercise the real Submit rule while a separate limit-provider dependency is controlled. Assertions inspect state and response identity, not only execution coverage.
Explain it: If the account-assignment rejection is removed, which test fails? What evidence remains missing after these tests pass?

column1: OPS-02 | When would SQL doubles, CDS doubles and RAP BO doubles give misleading confidence?
column2:
Short answer
Test doubles replace particular dependencies; they do not prove the whole application works. SQL doubles help isolate database access, CDS doubles help test CDS logic, and RAP BO doubles can replace another object's EML behavior. I choose the double for the rule being tested. Real persistence, permissions and service behavior still need suitable integration checks.

Reasoning and example
A pricing calculation reads a table. A SQL double can supply controlled prices so the test checks the calculation without depending on production data. That test does not prove an external action is still compatible. Likewise, a fake EML error response can test how a consumer handles failure, but it does not test the provider that would produce the real error.

I state what each test actually executes and replaces. A generic BO buffer double does not run arbitrary custom provider logic, and access-control behavior needs explicit checks. Focused integration tests then cover the real save, authorization and service path. A more advanced-looking double does not automatically supply stronger evidence.

Avoid
A more sophisticated double does not automatically provide broader integration evidence.

column1: OPS-03 | A bulk EML action processes ten requests and rejects two. What should its test assert?
column2:
Short answer
I check which specific requests succeeded or failed, using their identities rather than row positions. I verify FAILED entries, message targets and the resulting data. I also test whether the chosen operation should allow partial success or require everything to succeed together. A successful interaction is not enough if saving later rejects the change.

Reasoning and example
I send ten requests with deliberately nonsequential keys. Two have different invalid values. The test checks that exactly those identities appear as failed, that each message points to the right request and that valid requests receive the intended treatment. Reordering inputs helps reveal code that accidentally matches results by row number.

Next, I test a failure during save after the interaction step appeared successful. The consumer must not report that object as permanently completed. I inspect buffered and saved state according to the supported test boundary. The expected all-or-nothing or partial-result rule must be defined first; counting ten messages cannot tell me whether ten operations were handled correctly.

Avoid
Ten messages do not prove ten correct results. Match outcomes to the actual request identities.
FAILED, REPORTED, and MAPPED in a worked create

Three input identities produce separate rejection, message, and key-correlation information. A message on C3 does not itself reject that input, and assigned keys do not prove durable persistence.
Explain it: What must the consumer inspect after this interaction, and what happens if the later save fails?
Limit: Conceptual response contents, not executable EML. Available fields and correlation depend on the operation and BO; save and atomicity semantics must be tested separately.
Real behavior under test and dependency doubles

Two deliberately different inputs exercise the real Submit rule while a separate limit-provider dependency is controlled. Assertions inspect state and response identity, not only execution coverage.
Explain it: If the account-assignment rejection is removed, which test fails? What evidence remains missing after these tests pass?
Limit: The fixture is conceptual and not an executed ABAP Unit result. Framework double support and persistence setup depend on the target release and test boundary.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Must all requests succeed together, or is partial success allowed here?
  • How will the test detect a failure that happens only during save?
Strong answer criteria
  • Matches every result to its input identity
  • Checks interaction results and saved data separately
  • Tests the intended all-or-nothing or partial-success rule
Verification evidence
Show which requests should succeed or fail, where their messages point and which rows remain after each failure case.

column1: OPS-04 | A draft test passes when run alone but fails after another test. What would you inspect?
column2:
Short answer
I look for state left behind by the earlier test. That can include draft or active data, transaction buffers, locks and configured test-double responses. Each test should set up its own state and clean up through supported test mechanisms. I do not add random commits to hide the problem, because that can change what the test proves.

Reasoning and example
Two tests use request 4711. The first leaves a draft or a configured double response behind, while the second assumes a clean active request. Running the second alone works; running the pair fails. I run them in the opposite order and inspect setup and teardown to find the shared state.

Distinct fixture keys can help confirm the cause, but the final fix should still manage the test environment correctly. I check active and draft identities separately, release supported resources and reset doubles as required. A fixture for an active instance is not automatically a valid draft fixture. An order-dependent pass is weak evidence of correct draft behavior.

Avoid
A test that depends on execution order is unreliable evidence for draft behavior.
Draft lifecycle

Follow edit, activate and discard for an existing active object, then explain how a new-object draft differs.
Explain it: What remains after discarding an edit draft? What if activation fails?
Limit: Schematic state transitions; draft actions and supported flows depend on the BO and consumer.
Three storage lifetimes: an illustrated analogy

The desk represents the current transactional buffer; the draft cabinet represents persistent work across requests; the shared archive represents saved active data.
Explain it: Which of the three can survive several HTTP requests without becoming active business data?
Limit: An analogy, not literal SAP storage architecture or a mandatory three-stage pipeline. A new draft may have no active instance. Active business records may still be updated.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Are active and draft transactional keys distinct?
  • Which setup/teardown resource is shared?
Strong answer criteria
  • Distinguishes active and draft identities
  • Resets the test resources correctly
  • Proves tests do not depend on their order
Verification evidence
Run the tests separately, in both orders and in the suite. Keep results showing they behave consistently.

column1: OPS-05 | How do you prove optimistic concurrency rather than merely calling the same update twice?
column2:
Short answer
I use two independent clients that read the same version before either saves. The first update should succeed; the second should be rejected when it sends the old ETag. I check that the first user's data remains intact. Draft locks and the draft total ETag need separate tests because they protect different parts of the editing flow.

Reasoning and example
Alice and Ben both read one entity instance and keep its ETag. Alice changes it and saves. Ben then updates that same instance with his old token. The expected result is a stale-version rejection, not an overwrite. If Ben rereads first, he gets the new token and the test no longer exercises a stale writer.

For draft, I separately test editing while an exclusive lock is valid and resuming after it expires. A child-only change to active data should be considered by the configured draft total ETag check. That is different from the entity-level If-Match test. Two updates inside one shared transaction do not reproduce two users with independent versions.

Avoid
Two updates in one shared transaction are not a realistic two-user concurrency test.
Two ETag boundaries

The left side tests a conditional entity update; the right tests the active-state basis of a resumed draft.
Explain it: Why does testing one entity ETag not prove the draft total-ETag implementation?
Limit: ETags are opaque. Verify lock expiry, relevant child changes and generated behavior on the actual system.
Two editors and one version: an illustrated story

Alice and Ben read version 7. Alice updates successfully, producing version 8. Ben must not overwrite that newer state using the stale version 7 precondition.
Explain it: Why should the client refresh and resolve the conflict instead of blindly retrying its old payload?
Limit: Version numbers are illustrative. Real ETags are opaque validators; a failed If-Match precondition commonly returns HTTP 412. This is optimistic concurrency, not a pessimistic lock.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which token protects this entity update?
  • What separate case should the draft total ETag test cover?
Strong answer criteria
  • Uses independent clients or sessions
  • Sends an intentionally old version token
  • Checks that rejected updates leave data intact
Verification evidence
Record each client version, request, response and final value from the controlled two-user test.

column1: OPS-06 | Fiori still displays an old total after a successful action. How do you separate UI refresh from backend correctness?
column2:
Short answer
I first read the business object again to see whether the server saved the right value. If the value is wrong there, I investigate the backend calculation. If it is right, I check what the UI refreshes after the action. The action result, side effects and deployed metadata must tell the client what changed.

Reasoning and example
An item quantity changes and the server recalculates the order total, but the original Fiori screen still shows the old amount. I compare a direct read, a new UI session and the original session's network requests. If both fresh reads show the correct total, the likely problem is that the original screen did not request the changed field.

I inspect the supported side-effect declaration and action result, then test a targeted refresh with the actual deployed metadata. I do not add a second total calculation in the browser to hide a backend problem. Another commit or a full-page reload may mask the symptom without fixing the missing refresh behavior.

Avoid
A page reload workaround does not explain whether the backend or refresh contract was defective.
Side effects and stale UI diagnosis

Use the observed backend value to choose the next debugging branch.
Explain it: What request proves that the consumer refreshed the calculated total?
Limit: Consumer and metadata support are release-dependent; a valid backend side effect is not proof that every client processes it.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What does a fresh service read return?
  • Which request should refresh the affected property?
Strong answer criteria
  • Checks the value actually held by the backend
  • Inspects metadata and network requests
  • Keeps the business calculation on the server
Verification evidence
Record the action and later reads, showing values before and after in the actual app.

Read and verify
