    Check which field or action triggers a refresh, what gets refreshed and whether the actual UI supports it.

column1: OPS-07 | A RAP list becomes slow after enabling count and expanding children. What do you measure first?
column2:
Short answer
I measure where the request spends its time: selecting rows, counting, loading children or doing extra ABAP and remote work. I use representative data and the affected user's permissions. Then I change the largest proven cost and repeat the same test. I preserve filtering, count correctness and access checks while reducing unnecessary work.

Reasoning and example
A page shows only 20 orders, but its count scans millions of allowed records and its expansion loads many child items. I compare a page-only request, a request with count and one with expansion. Traces show database time, application time, rows and any remote calls, so I can see which addition causes the delay.

I repeat the measurement with a restricted user because authorization filtering can change the database work. If expansion is the issue, the consumer may not need every child on the first screen. If count dominates, changing a small handler calculation will do little. I compare before and after using the same parameters and volume.

Avoid
Do not optimize the shortest visible SELECT before finding the dominant request cost.
Filtering, paging and total count

Count and paging answer different questions. Stable ordering matters when the client requests successive pages.
Explain it: For this example, what count belongs beside a page of five records?
Limit: Provider-side execution order may be optimized while preserving request semantics.
Secure custom-query filtering, count, and page

The same authorized logical set contains IDs 2, 4, and 6. Counting it returns three; skipping one and taking two returns IDs 4 and 6 without revealing hidden B rows.
Explain it: What should a count-only request return, and what should happen if the filter cannot be represented safely?
Limit: The drawing specifies semantics, not a mandatory physical execution plan. A remote/custom provider must preserve equivalent authorization, filtering, count, and ordering behavior.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Is count more expensive than the page?
  • What changes for an authorization-restricted user?
Strong answer criteria
  • Measures the separate parts of the request
  • Uses realistic data and user permissions
  • Keeps correct results and access checks while improving speed
Verification evidence
Keep comparable before-and-after traces showing total time, rows and calls.

column1: OPS-08 | A custom entity calls a remote API once for every returned row. How would you remove the N+1 pattern?
column2:
Short answer
I look for a supported bulk request instead of one remote call per row. I fetch only the references needed for the current result and limit request size. A cache is an option only with clear freshness and access rules. I still handle missing results, throttling and partial failures rather than hide them behind a faster response.

Reasoning and example
A page reads 50 orders and then calls a remote service once for each supplier. Together with the original read, that is 51 calls. A supported bulk endpoint may fetch the needed supplier references in one request. I remove duplicate keys and keep the batch within the service's limits instead of downloading every supplier.

The bulk response may still contain missing references or individual errors. I test those cases and rate limits, not just the reduced call count. If caching is needed, I define how long values remain valid and which user or tenant may reuse them. A shared cache must not expose one customer's data to another.

Avoid
An unbounded cache can trade latency for stale or cross-user data leakage.
Calculation placement and query semantics

Use the requirement to decide where a value must exist before filtering, ordering or aggregation.
Explain it: Why can a correct calculation still yield a wrong page of results?
Limit: Architecture alternatives, not a promise that all listed options are supported by each projection/custom provider.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What is the maximum request size?
  • How are partial remote failures represented?
Strong answer criteria
  • Uses bulk requests with size limits
  • Defines cache freshness and who may reuse data
  • Handles missing results and rate limits
Verification evidence
Measure remote calls and transferred rows, including tests for missing data and rate limits.

Read and verify

    Check the supported request options and target release. Test bulk reads and caching for correct results, access control and speed in your own scenario.

column1: OPS-09 | A service works in development but fails after transport. What evidence should the handoff have included?
column2:
Short answer
A transport moves code, but the service may also need configuration, roles, communication setup and frontend deployment. I verify the active version and dependencies in the target system. The handoff should name these requirements and their owners. A working development preview or successful import does not prove that the real production user can use the service.

Reasoning and example
The RAP behavior activates after import, but an action fails because the destination or communication arrangement is missing. In another system, the endpoint exists but the intended user's role does not grant access. These are different failures from a defect in the business calculation, so I inspect the actual target setup before changing code.

The handoff should list the code and non-code prerequisites, installation order and a small end-to-end check. I verify the imported revision, service exposure, communication settings and consuming identity. Each item needs a responsible person and an observed result. Publishing a binding locally in development does not establish a usable production endpoint.

Avoid
A successful transport import does not prove that the service works for its real users.

column1: OPS-10 | How would you evolve a released RAP service when an action needs a new mandatory input?
column2:
Short answer
A new required parameter can break every existing caller that does not send it. I check whether a valid optional value or default can preserve old behavior. If not, I plan a new operation or version and a controlled migration. The change must meet the real business rule while giving consumers an explicit path to update.

Reasoning and example
An approval action now needs a legal justification. Old clients have no field for it. Supplying an empty default would keep calls running but might violate the new requirement, so technical compatibility alone is not enough. I agree a supported transition that respects when the new business rule must take effect.

That may involve a successor action, an announced retirement date and updates to both UI and integration clients. I test generated clients, metadata-driven screens and direct API consumers separately. I track actual use of the old operation before retiring it where the policy permits a transition. Successful server activation does not prove that existing requests still work.

Avoid
A changed action can activate successfully while still breaking existing callers.

Limit: A teaching checklist; exact release contracts, component visibility and delivery tools depend on the product.

  • How do you know which consumers still use the old contract?

  • Plans a clear migration
  • Tests existing consumers

column1: OPS-11 | A remote approval succeeded, but the RAP caller timed out. How should an operator recover?
column2:
Short answer
A timeout leaves the result unknown until I check it. I use the request's stable reference to find the remote approval before submitting again. If it exists, recovery should reuse that result. If it cannot be determined, the case needs a visible status and an owner. Local rollback cannot erase an approval already committed remotely.

Reasoning and example
The remote workflow creates approval 9001, but its response never reaches the RAP caller. A new creation request could start approval 9002 for the same submission. I query by the original reference or use the service's documented idempotency rule so a retry returns or reuses the first result. The local app records the resolved workflow link.

If the remote outcome cannot be queried, I keep a durable recovery record and use the agreed operator or compensation procedure. I also test a late duplicate callback and a callback for a request version that has since changed. A delayed response must not approve stale local data or repeat an already completed decision.

Avoid
A timeout is not evidence that the other system performed no work.
Local and remote transaction boundaries

The remote commit belongs to another system, so local failure needs an explicit recovery strategy.
Explain it: What should happen if the remote side succeeds but the response is lost?
Limit: This explains distributed consistency, not a particular messaging product guarantee.
Duplicate events and stale approvals

The event identity and current business state decide whether to apply, ignore or reject the request.
Explain it: Two consumers process the same event simultaneously: what prevents a double effect?
Limit: Exact transactional deduplication mechanisms depend on the chosen infrastructure.
Remote commit and uncertain local outcome

The local application durably records intent before separately owned delivery. The remote payment commits, but its reply is lost; recovery must identify the existing effect through REQ-42.
Explain it: How do you distinguish an unprocessed request from a committed payment whose response never arrived?
Limit: The delivery and idempotency mechanisms are design requirements, not automatic guarantees from HTTP or RAP. This example does not claim distributed atomicity.

  • Which stable reference identifies the original request?
  • Who investigates when the remote outcome cannot be queried?
Strong answer criteria
  • Distinguishes unknown from failed
  • Finds the original result before unsafe retry
  • Handles duplicate and outdated callbacks

Simulate a lost response. Verify one intended business effect and a visible status from which recovery is possible.

column1: OPS-12 | A failed save leaves no business record, but support still needs diagnostics. How would you log it safely?
column2:
Short answer
I separate business audit records from technical diagnostics and user messages. A log written inside a rolled-back transaction may disappear too. I use supported monitoring for diagnostics that must survive, rather than add a commit inside RAP behavior code. Logs should identify the failed request without exposing secrets or claiming that a rejected business change succeeded.

Reasoning and example
An order fails validation. FAILED identifies the rejection and REPORTED supplies the relevant message, but no order is saved. Support still needs to connect that user error to the failed request. I use the available service or application monitoring facilities with their documented save and privacy behavior for that diagnostic purpose.

A business audit entry saying 'order submitted' has a different meaning and should accompany a successful business transition, not survive a rejected submission as a false fact. I test success and rollback and inspect which records remain. Adding COMMIT WORK in a handler just to keep a log would break RAP's ownership of transaction completion.

Avoid
Do not add COMMIT WORK inside a handler just to preserve a log entry.

Interviewer follow-ups

  • Does it describe a technical failure or a completed business event?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates business audit from technical diagnostics
  • Lets RAP control transaction completion
  • Keeps sensitive values out of logs
Verification evidence
Test success and rollback, then inspect which supported messages and logs remain.

column1: OPS-13 | A production incident starts after a release. How do you contain it without making the data worse?
column2:
Short answer
I first limit the harmful processing through authorized operational controls and preserve the evidence. Then I identify the affected records and what has already committed. I choose a code fix, rollback or replay only after understanding those effects. Reverting code does not reverse business data, and replaying a backlog can repeat the damage.

Reasoning and example
A new Submit implementation starts duplicate remote approvals. I stop the affected scheduled initiation through the authorized control and record the release, request references and time window. Then I compare local requests with the remote approvals to find what was already created. Simply deploying the old code would not remove those duplicates.

After fixing duplicate handling, I test recovery on a controlled sample and reconcile existing approvals using supported business procedures. Only then do I resume the backlog, watching error counts and the rate of processing. The recovery plan needs a clear condition for resuming and an owner for unresolved records. Replaying everything before the fix could create even more approvals.

Avoid
Do not rerun the whole backlog while the duplicate-creation defect remains active.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which business changes have already been saved?
  • What result proves processing can safely resume?
Strong answer criteria
  • Stops harmful work before replaying it
  • Repairs code and business data separately
  • Defines when processing can safely resume
Verification evidence
Keep an incident timeline, a list of checked affected records and the result of a controlled replay after the fix.

column1: OPS-14 | What belongs in a RAP release gate beyond a passing ATC run?
column2:
Short answer
ATC is one check, not proof that the feature works. I also test the business rules, failures, permissions and integrations affected by the change. Changes involving saves or concurrency need matching rollback and conflict tests. I record the version and environment for each result, and clearly mark anything not run rather than count it as passed.

Reasoning and example
A release changes an action parameter and publishes a new approval event. I test existing callers against the new action, verify the event after a successful save and check duplicate delivery. I also test a user who must not submit. These checks address the risks of this change; they are more useful than repeating an unrelated checklist.

For a label-only adjustment, the required evidence would be much smaller. For this release, I also verify relevant performance, dependency compatibility and target configuration. ATC can find issues covered by its configured checks, but it cannot prove every business rule or external connection. The release record should show executed results, pending checks and their owners.

Choose tests for the failure risks this change creates; a generic checklist alone is not enough.

column1: OPS-15 | A team advertises 95% coverage while never asserting FAILED or persisted state. How would you improve it?
column2:
Short answer
Coverage tells me which statements ran, not whether the results were correct. I add checks that fail when an important business rule is broken. For RAP, that can include rejected identities, messages, saved state and unwanted side effects. I then use coverage to find remaining gaps instead of adding meaningless code or repeating happy-path calls.

Reasoning and example
A test executes a validation for a missing account assignment and reports high coverage. However, it never checks FAILED, the message target or whether the invalid request can be saved. If I temporarily remove the rejection and the test still passes, it does not prove the validation works. I strengthen those assertions and restore the implementation.

I apply the same idea to successful processing: the test must check the expected state and absence of unintended changes. Coverage remains useful for locating paths we never executed, but the percentage is not the acceptance criterion by itself. A smaller set of failure-sensitive tests can provide stronger evidence than many calls without meaningful checks.

High statement coverage can still miss a broken business rule.

column1: OPS-16 | How would you prepare an extension for a platform upgrade?
column2:
Short answer
I list the APIs and extension points the application actually uses, then check what changes in the target release. I prioritize important business flows and known exceptions. Tests run against a representative target system and include affected consumers, permissions and behavior. Released APIs reduce some upgrade risk, but they do not remove the need to test our application.

Reasoning and example
An extension calls a classic dependency through a wrapper and also exposes a released service to another system. I give each dependency an owner and check its target-release status, including any deprecation or successor. A wrapper does not make an underlying upgrade risk disappear. Existing external clients need testing against the upgraded service too.

I then run focused regression tests for the affected metadata, draft behavior, authorization, performance and configuration. If an API must be replaced, the plan includes moving consumers before retiring the old path. Last year's ATC result is not evidence for this year's target release. I retain the tested versions and actual results for the important flows.

Avoid
Do not treat last year's clean ATC report as evidence for the new target release.
Testing scope and evidence

column1: OPS-17 | A cloud job processes 500,000 records and times out. How would you redesign it?
column2:
Short answer
I split the work into limited-size packages that can restart safely. Each package has stable record IDs, a clear commit boundary and recorded progress. I use background or application-job features supported by the target system and limit parallel work. Recovery checks what actually completed, including changes that may have saved just before the job failed.

Reasoning and example
A pricing job finishes 20 packages and crashes during the next. On restart, it should not blindly repeat the completed work. I use recorded progress plus stable business references to distinguish completed, failed, pending and uncertain results. I also check whether a user edited a record after the original calculation so recovery does not overwrite newer data.

A critical test crashes between the business update and checkpoint handling. The design must detect the existing effect or repeat it safely; a checkpoint alone may not prove exactly-once execution. I tune package size and concurrency against database locks and remote limits. Moving one huge loop into a background job does not solve its restart problem.

Moving a job to background avoids a dialog waiting limit; it does not make an unbounded selection or retained internal table use less memory. Reduce the selected population and retained data, or design bounded, restartable processing. See SQL-17 for package lifetime and memory checks.

Avoid
Moving a huge synchronous loop into a background job does not solve its transaction or restart design.
Parallel processing inside a job

A coordinator schedules bounded independent work and collects explicit outcomes; a scheduler does not create parallelism automatically.
Explain it: If worker B fails after A commits, what is safe to retry?
Limit: Conceptual fan-out/fan-in. Worker session and transaction boundaries require explicit design.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What is one package that can recover independently?
  • How does recovery avoid overwriting newer user changes?
Strong answer criteria
  • Limits package size and competing work
  • Defines how to find completed work after a crash
  • Uses supported cloud job features
Verification evidence
Simulate a failure inside a package, then verify restart, resource limits and final business totals.

    Check how supported jobs run, then split the work into limited-size packages with clear restart points.

column1: OPS-18 | How would you communicate senior readiness when you can review code locally but cannot run SAP checks?
column2:
Short answer
I say clearly what I reviewed, what I prepared and what I actually ran. Local review can find defects and produce useful tests, but it cannot prove SAP activation or real runtime behavior. I provide exact target-system steps and expected results. Missing evidence stays pending; I do not replace it with a guessed pass or unrelated performance number.

Reasoning and example
For a RAP approval change, I can review the source and prepare tests for a valid submission, a denied user and a rejected save. I can also provide a two-session concurrency scenario and a service smoke test. The handoff states which source revision to transfer, which roles are needed and what each result should show.

The person with target access then runs syntax and activation checks, ATC and the relevant tests, returning logs tied to that revision and environment. Until then, prepared test code is not an executed result. A UI running against mocks also does not prove integration with RAP. Clear limits make the evidence more useful, not less credible.

Avoid
Do not present prepared test code or a mocked UI as successful SAP integration.
Testing scope and evidence

The widening base suggests many focused checks, but there is no mandatory numerical ratio.

column1: CORE-01 | What is Clean Core in a practical ABAP answer?
column2:
Short answer
Clean Core means extending SAP through supported interfaces so custom changes are easier to keep working during upgrades. First check whether standard configuration already meets the need. When code is needed, choose suitable APIs and extension points, and track any exceptions. Custom code can still exist. Clean Core also covers areas such as business processes, data, and integration.

Reasoning and example
The business needs an extra approval check. First see whether standard configuration supports it. If not, look for a supported extension point at the moment when the check must run. Record which API or extension contract you rely on and test the approval process when the SAP system is upgraded.

In an interview, explain that decision using a real requirement and its outcome. Saying that all custom code should disappear does not explain how the requirement is met. Neither moving the code to BTP nor making its classes neat automatically removes dependence on SAP internals. The useful result is a supported extension whose behavior and upgrade responsibility are clear.

Avoid
Clean Core is not the same as Clean ABAP, zero custom code or moving everything to BTP.

column1: CORE-02 | What are Clean Core levels A B C and D?
column2:
Short answer
The levels describe which SAP dependencies and extension techniques custom code uses. A uses released APIs and extension points under their supported contracts. B uses SAP-designated classic APIs and supported classic options. C uses SAP internals that may change. D uses explicitly non-recommended objects or techniques. Check the actual classification for the product and use involved.

Reasoning and example
Imagine four ways to meet a requirement. A released API that supports the operation is the preferred A path. A designated classic API may provide a justified B path in a landscape where classic development is allowed. Calling an internal object introduces C risk, while an explicitly non-recommended technique belongs to D.

The response should match the risk: prefer A where suitable, assess B, give C a named owner and replacement plan, and prioritize fixing D. Do not classify by familiarity or naming. A function module everyone has used for years is not automatically B, and an unreleased object is not automatically D. Look up the actual dependency and supported operation.

Remember: B is a SAP-designated classic API; C is an internal mechanism without a stability promise; D is an explicitly non-recommended object or technique. SAP describes B as Clean Core, C as conditionally Clean Core, and D as not Clean Core. Reading an internal SAP database table and making an unsupported direct write are different uses and can have different levels. CORE-13 shows where to look up noAPI.

A familiar API is not automatically B, and every unreleased object is not automatically D.

column1: CORE-03 | How do the levels map to ATC messages?
column2:
Short answer
For the configured Clean Core usage checks, A has no corresponding finding. B gives priority 3 information, C gives a priority 2 warning, and D gives a priority 1 error. This mapping applies to those checks. Other ATC checks may use priorities for different problems. A green run is useful only when the right checks and classification data actually ran.

Reasoning and example
A team sees no Clean Core findings after an ATC run and calls the application Level A. Before accepting that, check the variant, check implementation, classification data, and target release. If the relevant usage check was not included, silence says nothing about those dependencies.

When a priority 2 finding appears, inspect the object and the relevant Clean Core classification rather than treating the number as a universal description of every ATC issue. A security finding with the same priority needs its own interpretation. Use the findings to guide dependency review, and test the application separately for correctness and security. Clean Core classification is not a complete application quality certificate.

Look for Usage of APIs in the Clean Core check group. SAP points to SAP Note 3565942 for the relevant checks; availability depends on the ATC system's updates and configuration. Include applicable Allowed SAP enhancement technologies and Critical statements checks: an API catalog alone does not detect every non-recommended technique.

column1: CORE-04 | Why is a classic API Level B rather than Level A?
column2:
Short answer
A classic API can be designated by SAP for supported classic use without being released for ABAP Cloud use. That is why it can be Level B rather than A. The Clean Core classification and the ABAP language version's access rules are related but different. Check the exact object and allowed use; a BAPI name alone proves neither.

Reasoning and example
A private-edition extension needs a function module that SAP designates as a classic API. That designation may make it a reasonable B dependency in an allowed classic implementation. It does not mean an ABAP for Cloud Development class can call it directly, or that public-edition developer extensibility permits the same design.

Check both questions separately: what is the dependency's classification, and what may this consumer use? Inspect the actual API state, classification data, product, and operation. If a permitted wrapper design is needed, account for its underlying dependency too. Calling an interface established or public in conversation is not the same as proving it has the required release contract.

column1: CORE-05 | What does responsible Level C use look like?
column2:
Short answer
Using Level C means accepting a dependency on SAP internals that may change. First explain why a supported alternative does not meet the need. Isolate the dependency, name its owner, test the affected process, and plan its replacement. Recheck it when SAP changes or releases alternatives. Your product restrictions and exception policy still decide whether the use is allowed.

Reasoning and example
Suppose an important report needs information that no suitable supported API currently exposes. In a landscape where the proposed internal read is permitted, keep it behind a small, clear interface so the rest of the app does not depend directly on that internal object. Record why the exception exists and which business process depends on it.

During an upgrade, test that process and inspect changes to the dependency and its classification. If SAP later offers a suitable API, revisit the exception and replace the internal read where feasible. A signed exception does not freeze SAP's implementation or make the risk disappear. C is a managed risk decision, not unrestricted permission to call anything.

C is not an unlimited permission to call anything, nor is it the same risk category as a modification.

column1: CORE-06 | What belongs to Level D and what would you do first?
column2:
Short answer
Level D covers explicitly non-recommended objects or techniques, including problematic modifications and unsupported direct changes to SAP business data. Confirm the exact classification and operation first. Then replace the risky path with a supported business API or extension point. Start with active, high-impact writes and modifications. Use tests and a staged rollout so the replacement preserves the business process.

Reasoning and example
A custom report directly updates an SAP document table and seems to work. The standard business transaction may also update related records, enforce permissions, lock the document, and create change history. The single table update can leave those other parts inconsistent even when the changed field looks correct on screen.

Find the supported API or extension point for the business operation and compare its outcome with the required process. Build regression tests around the full document, not just that one column. Introduce the replacement carefully and monitor the result. Successful execution in a development system is evidence that SQL ran, not evidence that the business transaction is supported or complete.

column1: CORE-07 | Are A through D the same as the old three tiers?
column2:
Short answer
No. The earlier three-tier model described ABAP Cloud development, API enablement through wrappers, and classic extensions. Levels A to D classify the actual dependencies and techniques in more detail. They are especially useful when discussing private-edition and on-premise custom code. A tier number does not translate directly into a Clean Core level.

A classic extension may use a SAP-designated classic API and qualify at B for that dependency. Calling it tier 3 does not automatically make it C. Likewise, a wrapper used to enable an ABAP Cloud consumer can still contain an internal C dependency or a non-recommended D technique.

When reviewing the solution, trace what it really calls and how it extends SAP. Use the applicable current classification instead of converting an old architecture diagram mechanically into grades. You can still explain the three tiers as background for why wrappers exist, but keep placement and dependency assessment distinct. That produces a more useful answer than memorizing tier 1 equals A and so on.

column1: CORE-08 | Does wrapping an unreleased SAP API make it Level A?
column2:
Short answer
No. A released custom wrapper can give its callers a controlled interface where the platform allows that design. The wrapper still calls the underlying SAP object, with that object's classification and upgrade risk. Review the full call chain. Releasing your own interface does not make an internal or non-recommended SAP dependency become Level A.

Reasoning and example
An ABAP Cloud class calls a released custom wrapper, and inspection finds an internal SAP function behind it. The consumer has a clear custom contract, but the internal dependency and its upgrade risk remain. Check the actual release and classification evidence; the wrapper alone cannot support a Level A claim.

The same reasoning applies to a nominated classic B dependency, an internal C dependency or a D technique: hiding it behind one method does not remove it. Record the dependency, owner, and replacement condition. If a suitable released SAP API becomes available, assess moving to it and retiring the wrapper. The wrapper's useful job is to control and isolate access, not to change the facts about the code underneath.

Avoid
A wrapper is not a mechanism for laundering an internal or prohibited dependency into an entirely Level A solution.

column1: CORE-09 | How do public private and on-premise editions change the answer?
column2:
Short answer
Start with the SAP edition and release. Public-edition developer extensibility uses supported ABAP Cloud features and released contracts. Private edition and on-premise can also allow classic development, depending on release. Levels A to D help assess those dependencies. They do not allow forbidden objects or language features in a restricted environment. ABAP Cloud is not limited to BTP.

Reasoning and example
Two teams may ask for the same extra validation but work in different landscapes. One uses public edition; the other has a private-edition system with existing classic extensions. The permitted implementation options can differ even when the business requirement is identical. Check available APIs, extension points, and language-version rules before proposing a solution.

For the private-edition team, a classic option may be available but still need a dependency and risk assessment. For the public-edition team, calling it Level B or an approved exception does not unlock a classic technique the environment forbids. Explain both support and suitability. Where the code runs alone is not enough to identify its development model or its Clean Core level.

column1: CORE-10 | How do you choose key-user on-stack and side-by-side extensibility?
column2:
Short answer
Choose the simplest supported option that meets the business need. Key-user tools fit supported field and process adaptations. On-stack developer extensibility fits logic that needs close access to local business data or the transaction. Side-by-side fits a more independent app or cross-system process. Use supported remote interfaces and plan how separate systems recover when one fails.

Reasoning and example
An extra field may already be supported by a key-user business context, so writing a new application adds little value. A validation that must reject the current document before it saves may fit a released local BAdI. A supplier portal used across several systems may fit a separate BTP application with its own release cycle.

Compare the required timing, users, data, and failure behavior. A remote portal cannot automatically share the local document's database transaction, so define pending and failed states where needed. These are placement choices, not automatic Clean Core grades. Each chosen implementation still needs a review of the APIs and extension technologies it actually uses.

Avoid
These are placement and development choices, not automatic A-D grades or fixed implementation times.

column1: CORE-11 | Why is side-by-side not automatically Clean Core?
column2:
Short answer
Running outside SAP does not remove dependence on SAP. An external app can still use unsupported endpoints, read internal tables, or copy fragile business rules. Clean integration needs supported contracts, security, versioning, monitoring, and clear failure handling. BTP can help separate application lifecycles, but the quality of the integration still decides how safely the systems can change.

Reasoning and example
A portal on BTP reads data through an undocumented endpoint that changes during an SAP upgrade. The portal is outside the ERP system, but its unsupported dependency still breaks it. Moving the code changed its location without making the interface stable. A supported business API provides a clearer contract to build and test against.

If the portal also consumes events, handle retries without creating duplicate business actions and monitor failures. Test changes to the API and business meaning before upgrades. Independent deployment is useful only within the limits of the agreed integration contract. Copying SAP's core business logic into the portal may introduce another source of maintenance and consistency problems.

Moving custom code out of the ERP server does not erase coupling.

column1: CORE-12 | What are release contracts C0 C1 and C2?
column2:
Short answer
C0 is a release contract for extension. C1 is for use within the system, and C2 is for remote use. Check the exact object's release state, contract, and allowed visibility before using it. These contracts say how an object may be consumed. They do not grant business permissions or promise that every operation you need exists.

Reasoning and example
You find a CDS entity that is released for local ABAP use. That can support a local read, but it does not automatically give an external application an HTTP endpoint. A remote API needs the appropriate remote contract and service setup. The reverse also matters: a published remote API does not necessarily release its internal ABAP implementation class for local callers.

For an extension, inspect whether the object actually permits the required kind of extension under the relevant contract. A public class definition or a familiar I_ name is not enough evidence. Then check business authorization separately, because a supported API can still reject a caller who is not allowed to perform the operation.

A public class or an I_ CDS name is not proof of a released API contract.

column1: CORE-13 | Where do you find Classic API, Not Recommended and noAPI classifications, and how do you verify an API choice?
column2:
Short answer
Open the SAP Cloudification Repository Viewer and choose the Classic API Clean Core classification catalog. Search for the exact object; State → No API corresponds to state noAPI in the JSON data. That means Not Recommended, not merely unreleased. Also check the target system's API state and the intended operation, then assess actual usage with maintained ATC checks.

Reasoning and example
Try RFC_READ_TABLE in the linked catalog. The checked SAP data identifies objectType FUNC, objectKey RFC_READ_TABLE and state noAPI. This is evidence of an explicitly non-recommended object; the name being familiar or remote-enabled does not make it a suitable API. Recheck current classification data when assessing another release.

Not Released is not the same as Not Recommended. An object without an ABAP Cloud release can be a designated Classic API (B) or an internal object (C). D also includes non-recommended techniques such as unsupported direct writes to SAP tables; an object lookup alone cannot assess how your code uses it.

For a purchase-document change, verify that the candidate API supports writes, the required fields and your target product. A released read-only CDS entity with a matching name is not a write API. Run ATC Usage of APIs and the relevant enhancement/critical-statement checks on the actual code. CORE-03 explains the scoped priority mapping; a successful syntax check alone does not establish support.

Avoid
Not Released ≠ Not Recommended. Catalog status, allowed language-version access and support for the intended operation are separate checks.

column1: CORE-14 | Can a solution using both A and B dependencies be called entirely A?
column2:

An application has many classes using released interfaces and one wrapper calling a designated classic API. Reporting only the classes in the consumer layer makes the result look cleaner than the actual system. Include the wrapper and explain which business operation depends on it and what maintenance risk remains.

Prioritize by business impact as well as counts. One unsupported write path used for every payment can matter more than many low-impact read findings. Show both the distribution and the critical dependencies, then choose remediation based on exposure, replacement options, and cost. Averaging grades or counting only the top layer does not explain whether the important business process will survive an upgrade.

If an allowed temporary exception remains necessary, record its owner, rejected alternatives, test coverage, and replacement condition. Review it when SAP offers a successor. column1: CORE-16 | What would your Clean Core governance pipeline contain?
column2:
Short answer
Use ATC checks that match the system and include API usage, extension technologies, security, and code quality as appropriate. Review findings instead of hiding them. Give exceptions an owner and a date or condition for review. Track fixes and rerun checks for upgrades. Combine the automated results with architecture review and real business-process regression tests.

A transport contains a new internal API call. The pipeline should identify it with the relevant check and route it for a decision under the team's policy. Some findings may block delivery, while a justified exception may be accepted with a clear owner and follow-up date. Store that decision rather than disabling the whole check.

Before an upgrade, update the relevant check and classification information and rerun the affected process tests. A previously accepted dependency may now have a supported replacement or a changed risk. The priority number helps triage work, but it does not tell you the full business impact. Runtime evidence and responsibility for the exception remain necessary.

column1: CORE-17 | Is Clean ABAP the same thing as Clean Core?
column2:
Short answer
Clean ABAP is about code that people can understand, change, and test. Clean Core is about supported extension choices and dependencies that are easier to maintain across SAP changes. They help each other but measure different things. A well-written class can still depend on SAP internals. Renaming variables does not change that dependency's Clean Core level.

Reasoning and example
Review a custom approval class in two passes. First ask how it connects to SAP: does it use supported APIs and extension points, or directly modify an internal table? That determines the extension and upgrade concern. Then review its responsibilities, naming, interfaces, errors, and tests to judge how maintainable the implementation is.

You might find an easy-to-read class with a dangerous write dependency, or a supported API used through confusing, untested code. Each needs a different improvement. Replacing the unsupported write helps Clean Core; separating responsibilities and adding meaningful tests helps Clean ABAP. A strong interview answer explains both changes and why one does not automatically solve the other.

Avoid
Refactoring variable names does not change the Clean Core level of an unsupported dependency.

column1: CORE-18 | How would you modernize a large custom-code portfolio?
column2:
Short answer
Start by finding which custom code is actually used and valuable. Confirm and retire genuinely unused parts, then classify dependencies in active code. Fix the most important risky paths first and adopt suitable supported APIs step by step. Measure business regressions and upgrade effort. Do not rebuild every classic report in RAP just to make the technology look uniform.

A portfolio contains hundreds of reports, but a small number handle critical daily work. Confirm usage and ownership before deleting anything. Pick one important active dependency, such as an unsupported business-table write, and document the current business outcome. Replace it behind a clear interface and test the entire affected process.

Roll out the change with evidence that users can still complete their work, then repeat for the next priority. Some reports may remain perfectly suitable as reports, while a transactional application may benefit from RAP. The modernization decision should follow business value and risk. An automatic conversion promise hides the need to understand existing behavior, integrations, and exception cases.

column1: GOV-01 | A project claims Level A because its frontend uses RAP. How would you assess the extension?
column2:
Short answer
Check the whole extension, including wrappers and the SAP objects they call. RAP and Fiori do not decide the Clean Core level. A depends on released contracts; B uses classified classic options; C uses internals; D uses non-recommended dependencies or techniques. Record the actual classification for each path on the target system. Do not call a mixed solution entirely Level A.

Reasoning and example
A RAP handler calls a custom wrapper, which then calls an internal SAP class. Looking only at the handler's released custom interface misses the underlying dependency. Assess the consumer and wrapper separately where appropriate, but include both in the delivered solution's dependency record. A customer namespace does not erase the risk.

Link each finding to the business capability it affects and the person responsible for maintaining it. Confirm the applicable API state, classification, and ATC result for the same source version. column1: GOV-02 | An API is released with C1. A team assumes that means Clean Core Level C and permission to expose it remotely. How do you respond?
column2:
Short answer

column1: GOV-03 | A team wraps an internal SAP function module and releases the wrapper. Has the technical debt disappeared?
column2:
Short answer
No. A wrapper can protect callers from some changes, but the underlying SAP dependency still has its original release status and upgrade risk. A useful wrapper hides unstable details; merely renaming the same internal interface adds little protection.

Reasoning and example
If the wrapper exposes the internal function module's structures unchanged, a provider change can still spread to every caller. A smaller request and result designed around the business need can contain more of that change inside the wrapper. Test those promised inputs, outcomes, and failures rather than only checking that the call returns.

A wrapper over a classified classic API can fall within the applicable Level B guidance. Wrapping an internal object does not make it a designated classic API. Keep the target-release assessment visible and define when a released replacement should be adopted. column1: GOV-04 | An urgent release needs an ATC exemption for an internal dependency. What makes the exception governable?
column2:
Short answer

Reasoning and example

Keep security and transaction defects visible as separate decisions; they are not automatically accepted by a Clean Core waiver. State which tests reduce the risk and who will replace the dependency. column1: GOV-05 | A Level B solution works in Private Edition. Can the same approval justify deploying it in Public Edition?
column2:
Short answer

A Private Edition app uses a classic enhancement or SAP GUI-dependent component. It may have a justified role there but no supported equivalent in the proposed Public Edition scope. Separate the parts that can be reused from those needing redesign. Record each missing capability and its effect on the process, then let the business compare alternatives with evidence. column1: GOV-06 | You have thousands of custom objects and a limited upgrade budget. How would you prioritize remediation?
column2:

A year-end report has no executions in a three-month trace. Deleting it based on that trace alone can cause an outage at closing time. An emergency posting tool may run only once a year and still be essential when it is needed. Combine usage evidence with process-owner confirmation and the limits of the observation period.

Then compare target-upgrade changes with business impact and replacement cost. A daily financial dependency that changes in the target release may deserve urgent attention, while an unaffected lower-risk utility can wait. Record why each item has its priority and how success will be tested. A large findings count is not yet a useful remediation plan.

The old approval screen combines several steps that standard applications separate. The real control may be that the requester cannot approve their own request and that every decision is recorded. Rebuilding the exact screen through internal hooks may add upgrade risk without improving either control. Walk through those requirements with the process owner.

Include unusual cases such as withdrawal, delegation, and rejected approvals so standard functionality is not accepted on a happy-path demo alone. Where a real requirement is missing, compare a supported extension or process adjustment with preserving the deviation. column1: GOV-09 | Your team wants to release a custom API used by three other teams. What must be ready before setting its release state?
column2:
Short answer
Before release, define the API's supported inputs, outcomes, errors, transaction behavior, and permissions. Give it an owner willing to maintain compatibility. Keep stable types and behavior public and private storage details private. Capture a delivered baseline and set compatibility, deprecation, and successor rules. If the API is still experimental, coordinated component access may fit better than a premature stability promise.

Reasoning and example
Three teams already call a pricing API. Removing an optional field or changing rounding may look like cleanup to the provider but break one caller's business result. Keep a snapshot of what was delivered and use the applicable compatibility checks for detectable technical changes. Consumer tests cover meanings and outcomes that a signature comparison cannot prove.

Do not replace the old baseline just to silence a genuine incompatibility finding. Plan how current users migrate when a breaking change is needed, and communicate support periods. Supported access permission can enable internal collaboration, but releasing a stable API is a stronger ongoing commitment. Set the release state only when the provider is prepared to meet that commitment.

column2:
Short answer

A custom facade chooses an internal implementation from configuration, so scanning only its direct references misses the actual dependency. A remote service can also change independently of the ABAP transport. Include these paths in the map and assign owners who can explain and test them.

Another upgrade failure may come from data behavior: a query expected one text row, but changed data now gives several and doubles a total. No forbidden direct call is needed for that defect. Rehearse representative configured processes on the target upgrade and document what the checks and tests covered. A green result is meaningful only within that stated scope; it is not proof that all hidden assumptions are safe.

column1: GOV-12 | A vendor upgrade changes an object used by an approved Level C extension. How do you organize the response?

Examples include fewer unsupported write paths, a successful target-upgrade rehearsal, or lower effort to adapt a shared interface. column1: GOV-15 | A required report uses an internal read object with no current replacement. Would you accept Level C, and under what conditions?

column1: ABAP-01 | How do you choose between standard, sorted, and hashed internal tables?
column2:
Short answer
I choose the table by how I will read it. A standard table is useful for processing rows in sequence or by position. A sorted table keeps rows in key order and helps with key ranges. A hashed table is useful for finding one row by its complete unique key. I also consider how often rows change and how much memory the table needs.

Reasoning and example
Imagine importing orders from a file. If I must report errors in file order, I can keep the rows in a standard table. If I repeatedly find one order by its unique ID, a hashed lookup table can avoid searching every row. If I process all orders for one customer together, a sorted key starting with customer is useful.

The important question is which lookup the program actually performs. Searching a hashed table by a different field does not receive the same benefit as using its complete hash key. I test realistic volumes and include the cost of inserting and changing rows, not only reading them.

Avoid
A hashed primary key is unique; that does not mean every field value must be unique or that arbitrary partial-key searches are constant time.
Internal table lookup

A free-key linear search, an ordered lookup, and a complete hashed-key lookup find the same record through different access paths.
Explain it: What changes if I need all rows in a key range, or preserve input order?
Limit: A standard table can use secondary keys; a hash lookup requires a suitable complete key. Hash storage and probe order are schematic, not SAP implementation guarantees.

column1: ABAP-02 | What are primary, secondary, default, and empty internal table keys?
column2:
Short answer
The primary key is the main key in the table definition. A secondary key gives another way to find or order its rows. A default key is chosen from the row type, so it may leave out fields I need. An empty key says that I do not need a primary field-based key for this standard table. Secondary keys cost memory and extra work when data changes.

Reasoning and example
An import table may need to keep file order while also supporting repeated lookups by customer. I can use a standard table with an empty primary key and a sorted secondary key for customer. The rows still have positions in the standard table; an empty key does not remove that index.

When reading by customer, I select the intended secondary key explicitly where required. I check whether faster reads justify maintaining another key during imports and changes. This key belongs to the internal table in ABAP memory. It does not create a database index or make a database query faster.

DELETE ADJACENT DUPLICATES removes only neighboring matches. First SORT by the intended duplicate criteria and any rule for which row to retain, then specify those criteria explicitly with COMPARING. For example, sorting by customer and changed_at descending before COMPARING customer keeps the newest row per customer, provided ties have a defined rule. This deliberately changes the original order.

Avoid
An internal table key is not a database index, and an empty key does not remove the standard table's index.

A free-key linear search, an ordered lookup, and a complete hashed-key lookup find the same record through different access paths.

column1: ABAP-03 | When is BINARY SEARCH correct, and how do table expressions handle missing rows?
column2:
Short answer
BINARY SEARCH works only when a standard table is sorted in ascending order that matches the search fields. Otherwise it can miss an existing row. A normal table expression raises CX_SY_ITAB_LINE_NOT_FOUND when no row matches. I decide whether a missing row is expected and handle it accordingly. For an existence check only, I can use line_exists.

Reasoning and example
Suppose I sort orders by customer and order ID. A binary search must use fields in an order compatible with that sort. Sorting by order ID alone and then searching by customer is not safe. A sorted table can make the intended order harder to break accidentally.

For an optional description, VALUE with OPTIONAL can return an initial value when the row is missing. For a required order, that would hide an error, so I report the missing order instead. When I need the row itself, I normally do one lookup and handle its outcome rather than check existence and repeat the same lookup. line_exists does not set sy-subrc or sy-tabix. Use its boolean result directly; do not inspect those system fields as if READ TABLE had run.

Avoid
Adding BINARY SEARCH to an unsorted table can return incorrect results; modern table-expression syntax does not automatically optimize an unsuitable key.

A free-key linear search, an ordered lookup, and a complete hashed-key lookup find the same record through different access paths.

column1: ABAP-04 | How do a work area, field symbol, and data reference differ?
column2:
Short answer
INTO copies a table row into a work area. Changing that work area alone does not change the table row. ASSIGNING gives a field symbol that points at the row, so changes go straight to it. A data reference stores a reference to a data object that I access explicitly. I check that a field symbol is assigned or a reference is bound before using it.

Reasoning and example
To mark imported orders as checked, I can loop over lt_orders ASSIGNING <ls_order> and change a non-key status field. The change is immediately visible in the internal table. With INTO ls_order, I only change the work area and need a separate table update if that is intended.

I choose the form that makes ownership clear. Copying a row is useful when I need to calculate without changing it yet. Direct access is useful for deliberate updates. I must still respect key restrictions: changing a protected key field through a field symbol can cause an error rather than safely reorganize the table.

Avoid
Do not change protected table-key components through an alias; key restrictions depend on table category and the access in progress.

column1: ABAP-05 | What is the difference between a domain, data element, structure, and table type?
column2:
Short answer
A domain describes technical properties, such as a value type and length. A data element gives a field its business meaning and labels. A structure groups fields into one row. A table type describes an internal table, including its row type and keys. None of these definitions alone creates stored database records.

Reasoning and example
Suppose buyer ID and supplier ID both use the same character length. They may share a domain but use different data elements so the screen labels and documentation explain the correct meaning. A request structure can then combine an ID, amount and currency. A table type describes a list of those request rows.

Creating a variable with that table type gives the program an internal table in memory. Saving rows requires a separate persistence operation against an appropriate database object or business API. Also, domain fixed values describe allowed values in certain contexts; the application must still validate rules that are not automatically enforced by its input path.

Avoid
A DDIC structure is not a database table, and domain fixed values are not a universal substitute for application validation.

column1: ABAP-06 | How do a foreign key, check table, and value table differ in classic DDIC?
column2:
Short answer
A check table contains the values that a field is meant to refer to. A DDIC foreign key describes that relationship and supports applicable input checks. I do not assume it is a database constraint that protects every write. A domain value table is only a proposal when defining the relationship. Setting a value table alone does not complete the check.

Reasoning and example
A country field may refer to a country customizing table. Defining the foreign key tells Dictionary-based tools how the fields belong together and can support input validation. That helps a user choose a valid country in supported screens, but a different program can still write invalid data if it bypasses the required application checks.

I therefore inspect the actual write path before relying on the relationship. A service should reject an unknown country according to its business rules. I also keep the terms separate: the foreign key describes a relationship; a database index helps find rows. One does not automatically provide the function of the other.

column1: ABAP-07 | How do you explain an SAP LUW versus a database LUW?
column2:
Short answer
A database LUW is one database transaction, ending with commit or rollback. An SAP LUW is the whole business change that the application treats as one unit. In classic dialog processing, it can span several database LUWs. SAP locks and the save process help keep that business change consistent. The application or framework that owns the transaction decides when to save.

Reasoning and example
A user opens an order, changes several fields and then presses Save. Classic dialog steps can cause database transaction boundaries before that final business decision. The application cannot simply keep ordinary database locks open while the user thinks. It uses the appropriate SAP enqueue lock and save mechanism to protect the business operation.

This is why a helper method must not commit just because its own work is finished. The larger operation may still fail. In RAP, the framework controls the transaction and save sequence, so classic COMMIT WORK patterns cannot simply be inserted into behavior methods. I first identify who owns the complete save.

Avoid
A database commit caused by a work-process boundary is not permission to split a business operation into independently committed fragments.

column1: ABAP-08 | Who should issue COMMIT WORK, and what does AND WAIT guarantee?
column2:
Short answer
The caller responsible for the complete business operation should commit. A helper must not save half the work unexpectedly. In classic update processing, COMMIT WORK AND WAIT waits for high-priority updates: sy-subrc is 0 for success and 4 for failure. Without AND WAIT, sy-subrc is 0 without confirming the asynchronous update result. Neither form waits for every external follow-up.

Reasoning and example
Imagine a process that creates a document and then adds required accounting data. If the document helper commits immediately, a later accounting error can leave an incomplete business result. The helper should follow the agreed transaction rules and let the owner decide when the complete operation is ready to save.

AND WAIT is useful for checking the relevant classic update result, but it does not prove that an email, background job or remote system has finished. In a RAP behavior implementation, I do not add COMMIT WORK or BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT. I check both RAP restrictions and any legacy API, because an internal commit hidden inside that API is also a problem.

Avoid
COMMIT WORK AND WAIT is not a distributed transaction guarantee and does not authorize commits inside RAP handlers.

column1: ABAP-09 | Why do SAP enqueue locks exist in addition to database locks?
column2:
Short answer
A database lock protects database work during a database transaction. An SAP enqueue lock says that a business object is being changed and lets cooperating applications detect conflicts. It can cover a longer business interaction, such as editing a document. Every writer must follow the same locking rules. I also handle errors and cancellation so lock ownership is released or transferred correctly.

Reasoning and example
Two users open the same order. The first obtains the appropriate SAP lock; the second receives a clear conflict instead of silently overwriting the first change. The first user then reads the state, edits it and saves through the agreed transaction process. Cancellation must also end the edit cleanly.

An enqueue lock only works when programs respect it. An unrelated SQL update can ignore that agreement, so the lock is not a physical barrier around every table write. In classic systems I may inspect SM12 for diagnosis. The exact lock scope and update ownership matter; in cloud applications I use the supported APIs and tools for that environment.

For classic generated ENQUEUE/DEQUEUE modules, _SCOPE controls dialog/update ownership; do not assume every lock ends at the same COMMIT. Initial key fields together with initial X_<field> flags can request a generic lock covering multiple records. Check that breadth deliberately. If an operation needs several locks, acquire them in a consistent order across callers and clean up on failure.

Avoid
An enqueue lock does not physically prevent unrelated SQL code from updating a table if that code ignores the locking protocol.

column1: ABAP-10 | How do you choose and propagate class-based exceptions?
column2:
Short answer
I choose an exception type that tells callers how failure must be handled. CX_STATIC_CHECK makes handling or declaration a syntax-check concern. CX_DYNAMIC_CHECK uses runtime rules when exceptions leave a procedure. CX_NO_CHECK can propagate without a RAISING declaration. I catch an exception where I can recover or explain it better, and keep PREVIOUS when wrapping the original cause.

Reasoning and example
A document reader may fail because a dependency is unavailable. The business service can raise a document-read exception with a useful message while keeping the technical exception in PREVIOUS. Support can then inspect the original cause, and the caller can still tell failure from an ordinary missing document.

I avoid an empty CATCH that makes the program continue as if reading succeeded. I also do not replace an established framework error format without checking callers. All three exception categories can be caught. CX_DYNAMIC_CHECK does not mean an exception may cross any undeclared procedure interface without consequences; its propagation rules still have to be respected.

Avoid
NO_CHECK does not mean an exception cannot be caught; DYNAMIC_CHECK does not mean it can cross any procedure interface without declaration.

column1: ABAP-11 | Which modern ABAP expressions are useful, and when should you avoid them?
column2:
Short answer
Modern expressions can make simple work easier to read. VALUE builds values, CORRESPONDING copies matching fields, COND chooses a value, and CONV converts a type. Inline declarations and string templates also reduce clutter. I use the syntax supported by the target release. If one expression becomes difficult to explain or debug, I split it into named steps.

Reasoning and example
Suppose an import creates a result row from several input fields. A short VALUE expression can show the resulting row in one place. CORRESPONDING is useful when fields have matching names, but I check any mapping and what happens to unmatched fields. CONV performs a technical conversion; it does not prove that a price or business identifier is valid.

For a calculation with several decisions, intermediate variables can explain the work better than a deeply nested COND or REDUCE. I choose readability over the fewest lines. These expressions execute ABAP logic; using newer syntax does not automatically move processing to the database or make the program faster.

Avoid
Modern expression syntax is not synonymous with ABAP SQL and does not automatically improve runtime performance.

column1: ABAP-12 | How do you handle amounts, quantities, dates, and timestamps correctly?
column2:
Short answer
An amount needs its currency, and a quantity needs its unit. I use suitable numeric types and explicit conversion and rounding rules. A date identifies a calendar day; a timestamp identifies an instant when its time basis is known. I keep time-zone context when showing it to users. Display formatting must not silently change calculation rules.

Reasoning and example
An order contains 100 EUR and 100 USD. Adding the numbers to show 200 without a currency conversion is wrong. I either show separate totals or convert using the required rate and date. I also test currencies with different decimal rules and quantities that use different units.

For time, a deadline stored as an instant can be Monday for one user and Sunday for another. I convert it with the intended time zone instead of treating a local clock string as universal. Tests should include daylight-saving changes and rounding boundaries, because those cases often reveal errors that ordinary values hide.

Avoid
A numeric field alone does not explain its currency or unit, and a local date-time string is not an unambiguous global instant.

column1: ABAP-13 | When would you use RTTI, RTTC, or dynamic ABAP?
column2:
Short answer
RTTI lets a program inspect a type at runtime. RTTC lets it create type descriptions for data whose structure is decided at runtime. These tools help genuinely generic code, such as configurable exports. For ordinary business code with known fields, static types are usually easier to understand and check. Any dynamic field or SQL choice still needs validation.

Reasoning and example
An export tool lets an administrator choose a supported set of columns. It may inspect the source structure and build an output structure with just those columns. Runtime type tools can help because the final shape is not fixed when the program is written. An invoice calculation with a stable list of fields usually does not need that complexity.

I map choices to known fields and reject unsupported names. If dynamic SQL is involved, escaping a value is not enough to approve a table name or a whole condition. Static types remain my default because the compiler, editor and reviewer can see more errors before the program runs.

Avoid
Dynamic programming is not inherently more reusable, and escaping values alone does not validate arbitrary dynamic SQL identifiers or syntax.

column1: ABAP-14 | How would you investigate an ABAP failure without changing production behavior?
column2:
Short answer
I first collect the failed operation, inputs, time, user and system version. Then I use the relevant logs, dump and call stack to find where it failed. I reproduce the problem safely with controlled data. The fix must address the cause and keep authorization, locks and transaction behavior correct. I add a test for the failing case before declaring it fixed.

Reasoning and example
A job fails while the same operation succeeds in a dialog session. I compare the execution user, authorizations, input data and processing context instead of assuming the code path is identical. In a classic system, ST22 may show the failing statement and call stack. Traces and debugging require suitable permission and a limited scope.

Once I can explain the failure, I test the smallest useful correction and the surrounding success path. Catching every exception or granting broad access may remove the visible error while creating a worse problem. If evidence only suggests a cause, I say it is a hypothesis and identify the next check that can confirm it.

Avoid
Suppressing an exception or granting broad authorization may hide the symptom while leaving the defect and data-integrity risk intact.
