    Check how the language feature behaves. A classic example does not prove that its APIs are allowed in ABAP Cloud.

column1: BASE-01 | What changes when a method receives a CHANGING parameter by value instead of by reference?
column2:
Short answer
By reference, the method works on the caller's data directly. With VALUE on a CHANGING parameter, it works on a local value and copies it back when the method finishes normally. If an exception leaves the method, that normal copy-back does not happen. This can protect the caller's value, but it does not roll back database writes or changes to shared objects.

Reasoning and example
Start with a plain integer containing 10. A method changes its CHANGING parameter to 20 and then raises an exception that leaves the method. With reference passing, the caller can already see 20. With value passing, the caller retains 10 because the local result was not copied back. On normal completion, both forms can return the changed value.

That difference is important when changing an existing method signature. Tests must cover both successful completion and escaping exceptions. If the value contains an object reference, changing the referenced object is a separate effect: the copy still points to that object. VALUE is not a general undo mechanism for everything the method does.

Avoid
Pass-by-value is not a transaction rollback and does not clone objects behind reference parameters.
Parameter values after exceptional exit

Compare the same assignment under two transfer modes. The final caller value is visible evidence of the difference.
Explain it: Which result changes if the method returns normally? What changes if the parameter holds an object reference?
Limit: This assumes a plain integer, value-result passing, and no additional side effects.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How would this change with an object reference parameter?
  • Can an IMPORTING reference variable still expose a mutable object?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates input/output direction from value/reference passing
  • Explains when a local value is copied back
  • Identifies effects on the database and shared objects
Verification evidence
A small method-call test showing caller values after normal return and exception.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Pass by value
    Formal parameters are local copies; parameter direction controls transfer.

column1: BASE-02 | A copied structure contains a string, a nested table, and an object reference. Is it an independent snapshot?
column2:
Short answer
Not completely. The copied string and nested internal table behave as independent values when changed. A copied object reference still points to the same object. Changing that object through either structure can therefore affect what the other sees. For a true snapshot, I decide how to handle every mutable referenced object instead of assuming ordinary assignment clones it.

Reasoning and example
Suppose ls_request contains a note, an item table and a reference to a pricing object. I copy it to keep a before-change version. Editing the copied note or item values does not change the original value components. But calling a setter on the copied pricing reference changes the same pricing object used by the original structure.

If the snapshot must preserve the old price, I store the calculated price as a value, use an immutable object or implement a deliberate copy of the required object state. A full clone needs rules for shared identities and cycles. Runtime memory-sharing optimizations do not change these value-versus-reference rules; a deep ABAP type is not automatically a deep object clone.

Avoid
A deep ABAP type is not a promise that ordinary assignment recursively clones the entire object graph.
Value components versus a shared referent

Two structure values own independent string values but lead to the same pricing object. The arrow targets explain why a getter can expose mutable state.
Explain it: Which change affects only ls_copy, and which change affects an object visible through both?
Limit: Conceptual object identity, not physical memory addresses or a particular sharing optimization.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which components need copying for an audit snapshot?
  • How would you test sharing without inspecting memory addresses?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates copied values from copied references
  • Explains why both references still point to one object
  • Defines what a snapshot must preserve
Verification evidence
Mutation tests for a copied string, nested row, and referenced object's attribute.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Sharing between dynamic data objects
    Distinguishes copying reference values from internal sharing of strings and tables.

column1: BASE-03 | A large temporary internal table is no longer needed. When would you choose CLEAR or FREE?
column2:
Short answer
For an internal table without a header line, CLEAR and FREE both remove the rows. CLEAR keeps the initial memory allocation available; FREE releases that allocation too. I use CLEAR when I expect to refill the table soon, and FREE when it is finished for now. Neither removes the variable declaration or guarantees that the operating system immediately shows lower process memory.

Reasoning and example
A package loop fills a small work table, processes it and starts the next package. CLEAR is often a sensible reset because the table will be used again. Repeatedly freeing and allocating it may add unnecessary work. After a one-off large reconciliation, FREE may be appropriate when the table will no longer be needed.

I distinguish memory used by current rows from memory retained for future use, and measure in the relevant ABAP session. CLEAR does not promise to retain every byte the table ever needed. FREE also does not destroy an object that another reference still reaches. A single process-memory number cannot explain all of those separate lifetimes.

Avoid
Do not claim CLEAR retains every byte ever allocated, or that FREE destroys referenced objects still reachable elsewhere.
Three distinct state and memory lifetimes

Empty row slots and the initial allocation are deliberately drawn separately. A new object does not imply a new internal session or empty class cache.
Explain it: Why can recreating a service leave a test-order failure unchanged?
Limit: Allocation diagram is qualitative; measure actual ABAP memory and cache lifetime in the target context.

Read and verify
  • SAP: CLEAR
    CLEAR releases table rows but retains the initial memory requirement; FREE releases that too.

column1: BASE-04 | A dynamic ASSIGN fails, but IS ASSIGNED is still true. How can the program update the wrong field?
column2:
Short answer
The field symbol may still point to the previous successful target after a failed dynamic ASSIGN. IS ASSIGNED only says it points somewhere; it does not prove the latest lookup worked. I check the ASSIGN result immediately. Where supported, ELSE UNASSIGN makes failure clear. Otherwise I unassign before the lookup and handle failure before writing through the field symbol.

Reasoning and example
A generic mapper first assigns component PRICE and writes an amount. It then tries the misspelled component PRCIE using the same field symbol. If that lookup fails but the old assignment remains, checking only IS ASSIGNED can allow the next write to change PRICE again. The program has updated a real field, but the wrong one.

I test the sequence of one successful lookup followed by one failed lookup. An isolated failure test can miss the stale assignment. The mapper should reject the unknown component or follow a clearly defined skip rule, and it must not write through the old alias. I verify release support before using ELSE UNASSIGN syntax.

Avoid
An assigned field symbol is not evidence that the most recent dynamic ASSIGN succeeded.
Stale aliases and overwritten return codes

The first sequence can write to the previous target. The second takes a success branch for a different operation than the programmer intended.
Explain it: Which test requires a successful operation before the failure to expose the defect?
Limit: Only statements documented to set sy-subrc replace it. Assignment failure behavior depends on the exact form and additions.

Read and verify
  • SAP: ASSIGN, ELSE UNASSIGN
    Failed assignments may preserve an earlier alias unless explicitly unassigned.

column1: BASE-05 | A READ TABLE fails, yet a later IF sy-subrc = 0 takes the success branch. What do you inspect?
column2:
Short answer
sy-subrc holds the result of the most recent statement that set it. It is not permanently attached to READ TABLE. Another statement between the read and the IF may have replaced the value. I check it immediately or save it in a named variable. Table expressions have their own exception or predicate behavior, so I do not assume they work like READ TABLE.

Reasoning and example
A READ TABLE does not find an order. Before checking the result, the program uses FIND to prepare a log message, and FIND succeeds. The later IF sy-subrc = 0 now checks the FIND result, so it enters the success branch even though the order lookup failed.

I move the decision directly after the read or preserve the read result before doing other work. The regression case includes a missing order and successful log preparation, because that is the sequence that caused the bug. Not every statement changes sy-subrc, so I inspect the actual intervening statements rather than guess. A modern table expression must be handled according to its documented missing-row behavior.

Avoid
Not every statement resets sy-subrc, and a table expression is not a drop-in sy-subrc-producing READ TABLE.
Stale aliases and overwritten return codes

The first sequence can write to the previous target. The second takes a success branch for a different operation than the programmer intended.
Explain it: Which test requires a successful operation before the failure to expose the defect?
Limit: Only statements documented to set sy-subrc replace it. Assignment failure behavior depends on the exact form and additions.

Read and verify
  • SAP: SY-SUBRC
    Return values belong to particular statements and can be replaced by later statements.

column1: BASE-06 | An import must reject precision loss rather than silently round or truncate. Where does EXACT help?
column2:
Short answer
EXACT checks that an assignment or calculation can produce its target value without losing information. It raises an appropriate exception when that is impossible. CONV uses normal conversion rules and is not the same check. I catch conversion failures at the input boundary and explain them to the caller. I still validate business rules, because an exact value can still be forbidden.

Reasoning and example
An import receives a text value longer than the fixed-length target field. A normal conversion may discard characters, while a lossless conversion can reject that input. For a packed result with two decimals, a calculation such as one divided by three cannot be represented exactly, so EXACT is useful if rounding is prohibited.

If the business actually requires rounding, I apply the agreed rounding rule explicitly instead of treating every inexact result as invalid. I also check rules such as a positive amount, a known currency or an allowed identifier. EXACT can detect loss of technical information; it cannot decide whether a perfectly representable negative amount is acceptable for this document.

Avoid
EXACT does not prove that a technically representable value is an allowed business value.
Conversion, rounding, and reduction counterexamples

A lost character, a one-cent difference, and a false maximum reveal three unrelated errors that concise syntax can hide.
Explain it: Which expected results change with a different rounding mode, and which are independent of rounding?
Limit: Half-up and two decimals are explicit exercise assumptions, not a universal currency rule. MAX notation is explanatory.

Read and verify
  • SAP: EXACT examples
    Official executable illustrations of lossless assignments and calculations.

column1: BASE-07 | Two invoice totals differ by one cent although both use decimal types. How do you diagnose rounding?
column2:
Short answer
I check where rounding happens, which rounding mode is required and the precision of intermediate values. Rounding each line and then adding can differ from adding first and rounding the total. Decimal types do not decide that business rule for me. I keep the currency context and write tests for values near the rounding boundary.

Reasoning and example
Assume the agreed rule is half-up rounding to two decimals. Two positive line results are each 0.005. If each line is rounded first, each becomes 0.01 and the total is 0.02. If I add the precise values first, the sum is 0.010 and rounds to 0.01. Both calculations follow their chosen order, but only the specified order is correct for the document.

I compare the implementation with that rule, including intermediate assignments that may already round a value. I test multiple small lines, negative amounts where allowed and currency-specific requirements. Changing the display to two decimals or choosing decfloat34 does not by itself settle when or how the business wants rounding.

Avoid
Choosing decfloat34 or formatting two decimals does not settle the business rounding policy.
Conversion, rounding, and reduction counterexamples

A lost character, a one-cent difference, and a false maximum reveal three unrelated errors that concise syntax can hide.
Explain it: Which expected results change with a different rounding mode, and which are independent of rounding?
Limit: Half-up and two decimals are explicit exercise assumptions, not a universal currency rule. MAX notation is explanatory.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How do negative half-way values affect the selected mode?
  • Where is currency conversion applied relative to tax rounding?
Strong answer criteria
  • Checks precision at each calculation step
  • States when and how rounding occurs
  • Keeps the correct currency and conversion rules
Verification evidence
Worked positive/negative boundary examples with independently calculated expected totals.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Rounding function ROUND
    Decimal places, precision, and explicit rounding modes are distinct choices.

column1: BASE-08 | Why can replacing MOVE-CORRESPONDING with CORRESPONDING erase an existing structure field?
column2:
Short answer
Plain CORRESPONDING builds a new result. Fields missing from the source therefore become initial in that result. MOVE-CORRESPONDING between structures keeps unmatched fields already in the target. A CORRESPONDING expression with BASE can start from existing values, but matching source fields still overwrite them, even with initial values. I choose the form based on the intended update behavior.

Reasoning and example
The existing request has status Approved and a note. The incoming structure contains only a new note. MOVE-CORRESPONDING updates the note and leaves the status. Assigning a plain CORRESPONDING result replaces the whole target with a new value, so the unmatched status becomes initial. Supplying the existing structure as BASE preserves that unmatched status.

Now consider a source type that also contains status, but with a blank value. Status matches by name, so it can overwrite the BASE value with blank. BASE is not an automatic ignore-empty or PATCH rule. If an API must distinguish an omitted field from an explicitly cleared field, I define and test field-presence handling separately.

Avoid
BASE preserves unmatched components; it does not mean ignore every initial source value or implement PATCH automatically.
Three mapping cases and two presence cases

The matching initial status overwrites BASE just as a populated status does. A separate parameter table shows why zero cannot encode omission.
Explain it: Which source needs a presence flag when the source type always contains status?
Limit: Structure mapping example; internal-table BASE preserves rows under different construction semantics.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Working with structures
    Compares MOVE-CORRESPONDING with CORRESPONDING and BASE.

column1: BASE-09 | Unsorted orders must be processed once per customer with their member rows. How does GROUP BY change the loop?
column2:
Short answer
LOOP AT with GROUP BY collects rows with equal group keys even when they are not adjacent. The outer loop then runs once per group. LOOP AT GROUP can process that group's members. This avoids relying on the input being sorted for traditional control-level processing. I still define the required group and member order rather than assume grouping provides the business sort order.

Reasoning and example
The input customer sequence is A, B, A. Grouping by customer creates two groups, and both A orders belong together despite being separated in the input. The group loop runs twice. Inside the A group, a member loop can calculate its total or process each of its orders.

I use an explicit group key when it makes the code easier to follow. If I request WITHOUT MEMBERS because only distinct customers are needed, I cannot later loop over the missing group members. This processing happens on an internal table in ABAP memory, not as database aggregation. If the output must be customer-sorted, I express and test that ordering instead of relying on encounter order.

Avoid
Grouping an internal table is not database aggregation, and its default group order is not automatically business sort order.
Unsorted group membership and explicit filter keys

Arrows bring nonadjacent A rows into one group. The grouping total is computed from members, not read from the representative row.
Explain it: What changes with WITHOUT MEMBERS, and why is an arbitrary OR predicate not automatically a basic FILTER condition?
Limit: Source rows and totals are illustrative; no measured performance advantage is asserted.

Read and verify
  • SAP: LOOP AT itab, GROUP BY
    Grouping and group iteration are separate phases; prior sorting is not required.

column1: BASE-10 | A FILTER expression is proposed for a standard table with an empty primary key. Is that enough?
column2:
Short answer
An empty primary key alone is not enough for the basic FILTER form. It needs a suitable sorted or hashed key. A standard table can work if it has a suitable secondary key selected with USING KEY. The condition must also follow the chosen key rules. For an arbitrary condition, a FOR expression or a normal loop may be clearer.

Reasoning and example
A standard table keeps orders in arrival order but also has a sorted secondary key starting with customer. A key-based FILTER can use that secondary key to select a customer according to the supported predicate rules. The table does not need to lose its arrival-order use just to gain another access path.

A condition combining unrelated fields with a complex OR is a different problem. I do not force it into FILTER just because the syntax looks shorter. A straightforward loop or suitable FOR expression can express the intended rule more clearly. I check the actual key definition and target-release syntax, then measure if performance matters; the keyword alone does not prove a faster implementation.

Avoid
FILTER is not a general-purpose synonym for every WHERE expression supported by LOOP or FOR.
Unsorted group membership and explicit filter keys

Arrows bring nonadjacent A rows into one group. The grouping total is computed from members, not read from the representative row.
Explain it: What changes with WITHOUT MEMBERS, and why is an arbitrary OR predicate not automatically a basic FILTER condition?
Limit: Source rows and totals are illustrative; no measured performance advantage is asserted.

Read and verify
  • SAP: FILTER, basic form
    Defines sorted/hash key requirements and supported predicate forms.

column1: BASE-11 | A REDUCE expression calculates a maximum, but all-negative input returns zero. What went wrong?
column2:
Short answer
The initial accumulator value is wrong for this input. Starting a maximum at zero makes zero a candidate, even if every real value is negative. I start from a valid member or represent no result explicitly. I also define what empty input means. REDUCE makes the loop concise, but it does not choose the correct starting value or numeric type for me.

Reasoning and example
For values -8 and -3, the maximum is -3. An accumulator initialized to zero stays at zero because neither input is larger. The result looks like a valid number but does not occur in the input and is not its maximum. Initializing from a valid first member avoids that invented candidate.

An empty table needs a separate decision: perhaps return an optional result, or raise a meaningful exception if at least one value is required. I test empty, all-negative, mixed and single-value inputs. I also check intermediate type limits and rounding. A reviewer should be able to see initialization, comparison and update clearly; if the expression hides them, I use a named step or loop.

Avoid
REDUCE does not supply mathematically correct initial values or empty-set semantics on the developer's behalf.
Conversion, rounding, and reduction counterexamples

A lost character, a one-cent difference, and a false maximum reveal three unrelated errors that concise syntax can hide.
Explain it: Which expected results change with a different rounding mode, and which are independent of rounding?
Limit: Half-up and two decimals are explicit exercise assumptions, not a universal currency rule. MAX notation is explanatory.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Table reductions, structured result
    Shows explicit initialization and iterative accumulator updates.

column1: BASE-12 | A report accepts a filter value and a sort-column name. Is escaping quotes sufficient for safe SQL?
column2:
Short answer
No. A filter value and a column name are different kinds of input. I pass values through host variables in static ABAP SQL where possible. For a configurable column or dynamic clause, I map approved choices to known SQL elements and reject anything else. Escaping quotes in a value does not make arbitrary SQL text safe or authorized.

Reasoning and example
A customer name containing an apostrophe should be treated as a value, not assembled into executable SQL text. A requested sort option is different: I map an accepted choice such as newest to a known timestamp column and direction. I do not accept any string and insert it as ORDER BY syntax.

Mandatory authorization restrictions are built separately from optional user filters. The user must not be able to remove them by changing a filter or sort parameter. I test unknown columns, invalid directions and inputs containing SQL-like text, as well as ordinary names. Safe quoting protects one kind of value; it does not approve table names, operators, whole conditions or access to restricted data.

Avoid
Input that is safely quoted as a literal is not therefore safe as SQL syntax or an authorized data access.
Two input kinds and two safe handling paths

The apostrophe is intentionally harmless data on the left. The sort request on the right selects a predefined identifier rather than supplying executable SQL.
Explain it: Why would quoting the sort option as a literal fail to solve identifier validation?
Limit: Conceptual SQL boundary; available dynamic-programming helpers and API release status depend on the target environment.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How would you test an input that is valid syntax but unauthorized?
  • Which parts of the SQL shape can remain completely static?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates data values from SQL names and syntax
  • Maps choices to explicitly allowed SQL elements
  • Keeps mandatory authorization conditions in place
Verification evidence
Negative tests for quoted values, forbidden columns, injected operators, and unauthorized records.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Prevent SQL injection
    Prefer static SQL; validate and escape dynamic content using supported facilities.

column1: BASE-13 | A resource release is placed only in CLEANUP. Why can it remain unreleased after success?
column2:
Short answer
CLEANUP is not a finally block that runs after every TRY. It is used during the relevant exception propagation to an outer handler. It does not run just because normal processing reaches ENDTRY. I arrange release on success and on the required error paths. I also check who owns the resource so I do not release framework-owned locks too early.

Reasoning and example
A method opens an application-owned temporary handle and processes data successfully. If release exists only in CLEANUP, reaching ENDTRY normally leaves that handle open. An exception caught inside the same TRY also does not make CLEANUP a universal after-CATCH step. I therefore make the successful release and exceptional release paths explicit.

I test normal completion, a locally handled exception and an exception that leaves for an outer handler. Release can fail too, so I handle that without hiding the original error or letting an exception escape CLEANUP. The same reasoning applies to lock ownership: cleanup must respect the intended lifetime, not remove a framework lock while the business transaction still needs it.

Avoid
Do not assume CLEANUP automatically runs after a CATCH in the same TRY, or release framework-owned locks prematurely.
Exceptional exits and preserved causes

The table names three exit paths that require separate reasoning. The exception chain carries the lower-level diagnosis through a meaningful service-level failure.
Explain it: Which path would a test of only propagated exceptions miss?
Limit: Simplified non-resumable scenarios; exact nesting and handlers determine CLEANUP execution. Resource ownership remains application-specific.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What changes when the exception is caught inside the same TRY?
  • Who owns release when a caller supplied the resource?
Strong answer criteria
  • Explains why CLEANUP is not a general finally block
  • Tests successful and failed execution
  • Releases only resources owned by this code
Verification evidence
Instrumented resource tests show one correct release on every intended exit.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Exception system response
    Explains stack unwinding and when CLEANUP blocks run or do not run.

column1: BASE-14 | An optional limit parameter is omitted in one call and explicitly set to zero in another. How can a method distinguish them?
column2:
Short answer
IS SUPPLIED checks whether the caller passed the parameter. IS INITIAL checks its value. Those are different: an omitted parameter and an explicit zero can both contain zero. I use presence only when omission has a defined meaning in the API. A wrapper must preserve that meaning, because forwarding its own initial variable makes the downstream parameter supplied.

Reasoning and example
A helper treats an omitted limit as use the configured default, while a supplied zero means return no rows. Checking IS INITIAL cannot distinguish these calls. IS SUPPLIED can, so the helper first decides which meaning the caller requested and then applies the value rule.

A wrapper introduces another risk. If it always forwards its own optional parameter variable, the next method sees a supplied argument even when the original caller omitted it. I test the direct calls and the wrapper path, and forward conditionally or pass explicit presence information where appropriate. OPTIONAL permits omission; it does not automatically carry that omission through every later method call.

Avoid
OPTIONAL does not automatically preserve absent-versus-present semantics across another method boundary.
Three mapping cases and two presence cases

The matching initial status overwrites BASE just as a populated status does. A separate parameter table shows why zero cannot encode omission.
Explain it: Which source needs a presence flag when the source type always contains status?
Limit: Structure mapping example; internal-table BASE preserves rows under different construction semantics.

Read and verify
  • SAP: IS SUPPLIED
    Presence of an actual argument is independent of its initial value.

column1: BASE-15 | A single-line INSERT INTO TABLE hits an existing unique primary key. Does it update the existing row?
column2:
Short answer
No. In this single-row internal-table INSERT case, a duplicate unique primary key prevents insertion and is reported through sy-subrc. The existing row is not updated. I decide whether duplicates should be rejected, merged or replaced and implement that decision explicitly. Other insertion forms and secondary-key conflicts can behave differently, so I do not generalize this return-code rule.

Reasoning and example
An import contains order 7 twice, first with amount 100 and then with amount 200. Inserting both into a hashed table with a unique order key does not replace 100 with 200 automatically. If the program ignores the failed insertion, it may silently keep the first row and hide conflicting input.

I define the import rule before coding. Identical duplicates might be acceptable, in which case I compare the relevant values. Conflicting duplicates should produce a useful error with the order and input position, unless a deliberate replacement rule exists. I check sy-subrc immediately for this operation and test both cases. Uniqueness prevents duplicate keys; it does not explain which business value should win.

Avoid
Uniqueness enforcement is not a complete deduplication policy, and INSERT is not an automatic upsert.
Duplicate insertion and empty authorization boundaries

A duplicate unique key preserves the original row for the specified insertion form. An initial selection range has a very different meaning from an empty list of permissions.
Explain it: How would you distinguish identical duplicates from conflicting ones, and prove a user with no plants sees nothing?
Limit: Single-line INSERT INTO TABLE with a unique primary key; other insertion and key-conflict forms need their own documented handling.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Populating internal tables
    Single-line insertion with duplicate unique primary key returns sy-subrc 4.

column1: BASE-16 | An authorization helper returns an empty range table. Why is WHERE field IN range unsafe as the only access restriction?
column2:
Short answer
An empty ABAP selection range means no restriction for IN. It does not mean the user is allowed no values. If an authorization lookup returns no allowed plants, I return no data or reject the request before querying. I keep mandatory access restrictions separate from optional user filters. Nonempty ranges also have inclusion and exclusion rules, not just list membership.

Reasoning and example
A user has no permission for any plant. The helper returns an empty range, and a query uses WHERE plant IN that range as its only access check. The initial range does not narrow the selection, so the query can expose records the user should never see. The program must handle the no-permission result explicitly first.

I test a user with no allowed plants, one allowed plant and relevant exclusions. I also test that adding or omitting a user search filter cannot remove the mandatory restriction. An empty optional filter may correctly mean show all permitted data; an empty authorization result means no permitted data. They must not share an ambiguous representation without an explicit check.

Avoid
An empty ABAP selection range is not the same as an SQL list containing zero allowed values.
Duplicate insertion and empty authorization boundaries

A duplicate unique key preserves the original row for the specified insertion form. An initial selection range has a very different meaning from an empty list of permissions.
Explain it: How would you distinguish identical duplicates from conflicting ones, and prove a user with no plants sees nothing?
Limit: Single-line INSERT INTO TABLE with a unique primary key; other insertion and key-conflict forms need their own documented handling.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How do you distinguish an optional filter from mandatory authorization?
  • What result do you expect from a range containing only exclusions?
Strong answer criteria
  • Explains why an empty range does not restrict IN
  • Returns no data when there are no permissions
  • Separates optional search filters from required access checks
Verification evidence
A denied-user test proves zero data and zero aggregate leakage with an empty authorization result.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Comparison with selection tables
    Defines inclusion/exclusion semantics and the initial selection-table case.

column1: OO-01 | Explain abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism with one example.
column2:
Short answer
Abstraction gives callers a simple operation, such as send, without showing every technical step. Encapsulation keeps an object in a valid state by controlling access to its data. Inheritance lets a subclass specialize a base class while keeping its promises. Polymorphism lets the same call use different implementations, such as an email sender or a test sender.

Reasoning and example
An approval coordinator needs to notify a user. It calls send through a notification interface and supplies a message. The production implementation sends email, while a test implementation records the message for an assertion. The coordinator does not need to know which concrete class it received.

The sender protects its own valid setup, such as a required destination, rather than exposing every attribute for arbitrary changes. If inheritance is used, a subclass must still behave as a valid sender. These ideas work together: callers see a small useful operation, implementation details stay inside the sender, and a new delivery method can be added without rewriting the approval decision.

Avoid
Encapsulation means protecting valid behavior and state, not merely generating getters and setters for every attribute.
OO interfaces and dependency injection

The service depends on a repository contract. Production and test implementations fit the same socket; the composition boundary supplies the appropriate collaborator.
Explain it: Which object chooses the implementation, and what does a double-based test fail to prove?
Limit: The plug is a design metaphor, not a SAP connector or code signature. Injection does not itself guarantee a good abstraction or production integration.

Read and verify
  • SAP ABAP object orientation examples
    Compare the language contract with the Clean ABAP design guidance. Project conventions can differ from style recommendations.

column1: OO-02 | What can an ABAP interface contain, and when would you use one?
column2:
Short answer
An ABAP interface describes what an implementing class provides. It can contain methods, types, constants, attributes and events, not just method names. I use a small interface when callers need one clear capability and different implementations can provide it. This also lets a test supply a controlled replacement. Specialized interfaces, such as BAdI interfaces, can have additional rules.

Reasoning and example
A checkout needs a price, so its price-provider interface can define how to request one and what happens when no price is available. One class reads local data; another calls an external service. The checkout uses the same operation, while the implementations keep their technical work private.

The contract must include behavior as well as types. Returning an empty price on network failure is different from reporting that no price exists. I avoid putting unrelated operations into the interface simply because one concrete class already has them. A narrow interface makes both the caller and its test double easier to understand, and it reduces the effect of future changes.

Avoid
An interface is not an abstract class, and a collection of similarly named methods alone does not establish a meaningful common contract.
OO interfaces and dependency injection

The service depends on a repository contract. Production and test implementations fit the same socket; the composition boundary supplies the appropriate collaborator.
Explain it: Which object chooses the implementation, and what does a double-based test fail to prove?
Limit: The plug is a design metaphor, not a SAP connector or code signature. Injection does not itself guarantee a good abstraction or production integration.

    Compare the language contract with the Clean ABAP design guidance. Project conventions can differ from style recommendations.

column1: OO-03 | How do ABSTRACT and FINAL affect classes and methods?
column2:
Short answer
An abstract class cannot be created directly, but it may contain working shared code. It does not have to contain an abstract method. An abstract method leaves implementation to a subclass before that subclass can be concrete. FINAL on a class prevents subclasses. FINAL on a method prevents further redefinition of that method.

Reasoning and example
A document-processing base class could provide common logging while leaving a processing step abstract. A concrete subclass implements that step and can then be instantiated if no abstract methods remain. This is useful only when the shared process and the allowed variation are deliberate parts of the design.

For a service that should not be specialized through inheritance, FINAL makes that limit explicit. It can still implement interfaces and receive other objects as dependencies. I follow ABAP rules rather than copying assumptions from another language: redefining an inherited method preserves its interface, and ABAP does not solve this with same-name methods that have different parameter lists.

Avoid
Do not import another language's virtual keyword or method-overloading rules into ABAP; use ABAP's actual redefinition and signature rules.

column1: OO-04 | How do upcasting and downcasting work in ABAP Objects?
column2:
Short answer
Upcasting uses a general reference type for an object, such as its superclass or interface. Downcasting asks to use a more specific type. Neither creates a new object. A downcast fails if the actual object does not support the requested type, so I check it or handle CX_SY_MOVE_CAST_ERROR. Frequent downcasts can mean the caller needs a better interface.

Reasoning and example
A payment-interface reference can point to a card-payment object. Through that reference, I can use operations declared by the interface. If I really need a card-specific operation, a valid downcast exposes it, but the reference still points to the same object with the same state.

If the reference actually points to a bank-transfer implementation, casting it to the card class cannot turn it into a card. The cast fails. I test that path when a cast is necessary. More often, if ordinary payment processing keeps checking concrete classes, I move the shared capability into a suitable interface so callers can work without knowing every implementation.

Avoid
Casting a reference changes the accessible static view, not the object's dynamic type or stored data.

column1: OO-05 | What is the difference between instance and static methods and constructors?
column2:
Short answer
An instance method works with a particular object and its data. A static method belongs to the class and has no current object of its own. The instance constructor prepares a newly created object. The class constructor prepares class-level state when the runtime first needs the class in that internal session. I keep that hidden initialization small and predictable.

Reasoning and example
Two approval-service objects can each hold a different repository reference. Their instance methods use their own repository. A static helper, by contrast, cannot assume that either object is its current instance. Class-level data can be shared by those instances within the internal session, so changing it may affect both.

I use the instance constructor to receive required dependencies and establish a usable object. I avoid loading large datasets or calling remote systems unexpectedly from a class constructor. Also, declaring CLASS-METHODS does not itself prevent object creation. Creation visibility or an abstract class controls that, and class data is not automatically one shared value across the whole SAP system.

Avoid
ABAP does not make a class uninstantiable simply because it has static methods, and class data is not automatically shared system-wide.

column1: OO-06 | When do you prefer composition over inheritance?
column2:
Short answer
I prefer composition when one object needs help from another: the service has a repository or a formatter. Those helpers can change independently. Inheritance fits a real specialization where the subclass keeps the base class promises. I do not build a class hierarchy just to reuse a few methods. Composition often makes testing and replacing a dependency simpler.

Reasoning and example
A report service reads data, checks access and formats output. It can receive a repository, an authorization policy and a formatter as separate helpers. A test replaces the repository while using the real calculation. A new output format does not require a new version of the entire report hierarchy.

A large base report class may instead force every subclass to inherit database, output and security decisions it does not need. That makes a small change affect unrelated reports. I use inheritance when a shared process and its extension steps are genuinely stable. The practical test is whether a subclass can be used wherever the base type is expected without surprising its caller.

Avoid
Code reuse alone is weak justification for inheritance; a subclass that violates caller expectations is not a sound substitute.

column1: OO-07 | How do dependency injection and dependency inversion differ?
column2:
Short answer
Dependency inversion means business code depends on the capability it needs, usually an interface, rather than one technical implementation. Dependency injection means someone else supplies that implementation, often through the constructor. The first is a design rule; the second is a way to connect objects. Together they make dependencies visible and easier to replace in tests.

Reasoning and example
An approval service needs to read a request. It accepts a repository interface in its constructor instead of creating a database repository inside approve. Production setup supplies the real repository; a unit test supplies a fake that returns a known request. The approval rule itself runs unchanged in both cases.

Passing an object is not enough if the service ignores it and creates another dependency internally. Also, injecting a large concrete database class can still leave business code dependent on database details. I keep the required operations small and meaningful, and test both successful reads and failures through that interface. This reveals what the service really relies on.

Avoid
Injecting a concrete class everywhere may aid construction while still leaving the business layer tightly coupled to infrastructure.

column1: OO-08 | How would you apply SOLID without overengineering?
column2:
Short answer
I use SOLID to keep changes understandable. A class should have a clear job, and new variations should not require editing every caller. Replacements should keep the same promises, interfaces should contain what their callers need, and business rules should depend on useful abstractions. I add structure for a real need. More classes do not automatically mean better design.

Reasoning and example
A tax calculation mixed with database reads and printing is difficult to test. Separating the calculation lets me give it known values and check the result without a printer or live database. A narrow rate-provider interface may help if rates can come from different places or the source can fail.

That does not mean every five-line helper needs its own interface and factory. I ask which change or test becomes easier because of each extra layer. Single responsibility does not mean exactly one method per class. Open/closed also does not forbid fixing existing code; it encourages a design where expected variations can be added without repeatedly disrupting stable business logic.

Avoid
Single responsibility does not mean one method per class, and open/closed does not mean existing code must never be changed.

column1: OO-09 | What is a Factory, when do you use it, and how does it work with Strategy?
column2:
Short answer
A Factory creates the right object for the caller. Strategy is the object that contains one version of a rule. For example, a Factory chooses a domestic or export price calculator; both expose the same calculate method. Use a Factory when choosing or setting up objects is repeated or complicated. For one simple class, NEW at the entry point may be enough.

Reasoning and example
Imagine three reports need prices for domestic and export orders. Without a Factory, every report repeats the same IF and knows both concrete class names. Move that choice into a create_calculator method returning the calculator interface. A report then asks the returned object to calculate; it does not need to know which class was created. An unknown country must give a clear error, not silently choose a price rule.

Strategy separates the calculations. Factory separates object creation. The Factory can return a new object each time; it does not imply Singleton. Inject the resulting interface into the business service so a unit test can supply a fake calculator.

A static method with CASE is commonly called a simple Factory. The formal Factory Method pattern lets subclasses decide which product to create. Abstract Factory creates related families, such as a serializer and sender for the same provider. Choose the simplest variant that solves the actual problem.

Avoid
Do not call every method that returns an object Factory Method without distinguishing a simple factory from the formal pattern.

column1: OO-10 | What is a Facade, when is it useful, and how does it differ from Adapter?
column2:
Short answer
A Facade gives a complicated subsystem a small, easy-to-use interface. Instead of making every caller run prepare, check and submit, expose one submit_request operation. An Adapter solves a different problem: it converts one interface or data format into another. You can use both. Neither pattern changes the transaction rules of the code it calls.

Reasoning and example
Suppose a delivery preview needs three services: read the order, calculate package sizes, and estimate delivery cost. A Facade offers preview_delivery(order_id). It coordinates those services and returns one result. The UI no longer repeats the sequence, and changing the packaging service affects fewer callers. This is useful when several screens or jobs use the same multi-step operation.

If an old carrier API expects technical structures, an Adapter maps your request to those structures. The Facade coordinates the overall task; the Adapter translates one dependency. Keep the dependencies behind interfaces so tests can verify the sequence and stop on a failed check without contacting a carrier.

For a posting Facade, explicitly document who owns COMMIT and what can be rolled back. A Facade is not a new LUW. Do not use it just to rename one trivial method, or hide unreleased SAP dependencies and claim they are now released.

Avoid
Wrapping an unreleased SAP object does not by itself make that underlying dependency released, cloud compliant, or clean-core Level A.

column1: OO-11 | What is Singleton in ABAP, how do you implement it, and when would you use it?
column2:
Short answer
Singleton lets callers reuse one object instead of creating a new one each time. In ABAP, a typical implementation uses CREATE PRIVATE, a static reference, and get_instance. The first call creates the object; later calls return the same reference. That instance belongs to an internal session, not the whole SAP system. Use it only when sharing that lifetime is intentional.

Reasoning and example
Imagine a report repeatedly needs the same read-only configuration. A Singleton can read it once and reuse the same cache during that internal session. Calling get_instance twice returns the same object. A different user or internal session can have another instance, so this is not a system-wide lock or shared cache.

Do not store the current order, current approver, or other request-specific data in a long-lived Singleton. The next operation can see stale values; one test can affect another test. Define refresh and invalidation rules for configuration too. CREATE PRIVATE only prevents arbitrary construction: the class must also retain and reuse its instance.

If shared lifetime is not needed, create an ordinary service and pass it into the caller through an interface. That is easier to replace in tests. Singleton answers how many instances to reuse; Factory answers how to create an object; Facade answers how to simplify a subsystem.

Avoid
A singleton does not synchronize business updates across sessions, work processes, application servers, or users.

column1: OO-12 | How do ABAP OO events differ from durable business events?
column2:
Short answer
An ABAP OO event calls registered handlers in the current runtime context. It is useful for local notifications, such as a UI interaction. A durable business event must survive failures and support delivery after the business change is saved. That needs a supported event or integration mechanism. RAISE EVENT alone does not provide persistence, retry or reliable external delivery.

Reasoning and example
An ALV can raise a local event when the user selects a row. A controller registered with SET HANDLER reacts and updates the display. If that session ends, the local event is not a saved message waiting for another system. This is appropriate for an immediate screen interaction.

Starting an external approval workflow after a document is saved is a different requirement. The design must coordinate save and publication, identify duplicates, monitor failed delivery and support retries. Otherwise the workflow could start for a document that later fails to save, or never start after a temporary outage. Similar event terminology does not make the two delivery mechanisms interchangeable.

Avoid
RAISE EVENT by itself does not persist a message or guarantee workflow creation after a commit.
Duplicate events and stale approvals

The event identity and current business state decide whether to apply, ignore or reject the request.
Explain it: Two consumers process the same event simultaneously: what prevents a double effect?
Limit: Exact transactional deduplication mechanisms depend on the chosen infrastructure.

column1: OO-13 | What would you change first in a difficult legacy ABAP method?
column2:
Short answer
I first find out what the method promises to its callers and who owns its save. Then I make small changes: clearer names, less duplication and separate calculation from database or remote calls. I protect risky behavior with focused tests before larger changes. The goal is easier understanding without changing the business result accidentally.

Reasoning and example
A long posting method calculates a discount, reads configuration and saves a document. I first extract the discount calculation if its inputs and result can be made clear. I leave commit, authorization and locking behavior in place until I understand their callers and tests. That gives reviewers a small change they can verify.

Next I use tests around important amounts, rejection paths and existing edge cases before moving more code. Merely converting every loop into an expression can obscure the actual change. Team naming also helps consistency: this project uses lt_ for tables, ls_ for structures and co_ for constants. Those are project conventions, not special ABAP syntax or universal Clean ABAP requirements.

Avoid
A broad stylistic rewrite without behavior evidence can introduce regressions and make review harder, even if the result looks more modern.

column1: OO-14 | How do you make an OO design testable, and what should ABAP Unit assert?
column2:
Short answer
I keep the business rule real and make outside dependencies replaceable. Tests supply known data, time or service responses and check the result a caller can observe. I cover normal cases, limits and failures. Coverage can reveal untested code, but it cannot prove the assertions are useful. Real database, authorization and service behavior still need integration checks.

Reasoning and example
An approval rule sends amounts above a limit to a manager. I test below, exactly at and above that limit, plus the case where no manager is available. A repository double supplies the request, and the test checks the real decision and reported error. The expected result comes from the rule, not from repeating the implementation in the test.

I also simulate a read failure so it cannot become an accidental approval. Separate tests in the target environment verify the actual repository and security behavior. A unit test with fake persistence is valuable, but it cannot prove a real service call, save or role assignment works correctly.

Avoid
A test that only asserts that a method returned, or mirrors its implementation step by step, provides weak evidence.

column1: OO-15 | How does MVC separate responsibilities?
column2:
Short answer
The Model holds application data and relevant behavior. The View displays information and accepts user input. The Controller handles interactions and coordinates what happens next. MVC separates these jobs so changes are easier to manage. It does not require one fixed call sequence, and it does not move backend business rules into the browser.

Reasoning and example
In a SAPUI5 application, a view binds a list to a model. When a user presses Submit, the controller gathers the intended action and calls the backend. The backend checks the business rules and permissions, then returns success or an error. The model and bindings help the screen reflect the result.

A disabled Submit button is useful feedback, but it cannot be the only enforcement of the rule. Someone can call the service directly. I keep required validation in the backend and use the UI for a clear experience. This division also helps testing: a controller interaction test and a backend business-rule test prove different parts of the application.

Avoid
MVC does not mean copying all backend business logic into the UI controller or assuming the view must always be manually rebuilt.

column1: OO-16 | Singleton, Factory or Facade: how do you choose with a simple example?
column2:
Short answer
Ask what problem you have. Need the right object created? Use a Factory. Need one deliberately shared instance? Consider Singleton. Need one easy entry point to several services? Use a Facade. These patterns can work together, but none is required just because the application uses ABAP Objects.

Reasoning and example
For a delivery preview, a Factory can choose a carrier calculator. A Facade can then read the order, calculate package sizes and ask that calculator for a price. A read-only configuration cache might be shared within the internal session, but that is a separate lifetime decision.

Start with ordinary classes. Add a Factory when creation logic repeats, a Facade when callers repeat a multi-step sequence, and Singleton only when one shared instance has a clear benefit and safe lifetime. In an interview, explain the problem and trade-off before naming the pattern. A report with one fixed calculation may need none of them.

Avoid
A Factory does not require Singleton, and a Facade does not automatically add COMMIT, retries, authorization or transactional safety.

column1: OO-17 | Two NEW calls create two objects. How often do constructor and class_constructor run, and in what order?
column2:
Short answer
constructor prepares each new object, so two successful NEW calls run it twice. class_constructor prepares the class once in an internal session, before its first relevant use. If the first use is creating an object, class initialization happens before instance initialization. Use constructor for each object’s required data and dependencies. Keep class_constructor small: its work happens implicitly.

Reasoning and example
Create an order helper for order 7, then another for order 9. Each CONSTRUCTOR receives its own ID through IMPORTING and stores it in that object. If this is the first class use, the order is CLASS_CONSTRUCTOR → CONSTRUCTOR for 7 → CONSTRUCTOR for 9. The example shows a class counter of 1 and an object counter of 2. CLASS_CONSTRUCTOR has no parameters and does not repeat after COMMIT. Once means one internal session, not the whole SAP system.

Calling a static method or accessing a static attribute can initialize the class before any object is created. Merely referring to a type or a constant does not trigger class_constructor. It has no parameters and is called by the runtime, not explicitly by application code.

With inheritance, static constructors initialize the hierarchy from the superclass down. An explicitly implemented subclass constructor calls super->constructor( ) before using the new object’s instance components, passing any required parent parameters. The subclass constructor is not a redefinition. If it is not declared, the inherited constructor interface and implicit parent initialization rules apply. Do not hide remote calls or a large data load in this automatic startup path.

Avoid
Once per internal session does not mean once per SAP system, once per user forever, or once per SAP LUW. A static constructor is not a substitute for passing request-specific data to an object.

column1: OODEEP-01 | A method named reserve returns a reservation ID. Which promises must be explicit beyond its parameter types?
column2:
Short answer
I explain what inputs are accepted, what success means and what can change before a failure. The caller also needs to know whether the reservation is already saved, whether repeating the call is safe and who commits. Parameter types cannot answer those questions. I document these rules and test them so another implementation cannot quietly change the caller's expectations.

Reasoning and example
A caller needs to reserve two items together. The first implementation returns an ID but leaves saving to the caller. A replacement implementation returns an ID and commits immediately. Both can have the same ABAP signature, yet the second leaves the first reservation saved if reserving the second item fails.

I therefore state whether reserve only prepares the change or makes it permanent. I also define repeated calls, invalid inputs and error results in ABAP Doc or the relevant API documentation. Tests include failure on the second item and inspect the first item afterward. Returning an ID is useful, but it is not proof that a save has happened or that rollback remains possible.

Avoid
RETURNING an identifier does not itself promise committed persistence, and a method name cannot replace a transaction contract.
A concrete counterexample to substitutability

A valid quantity-one call exposes a behavioral violation invisible in matching parameter types. The lower table separates redefinition from a genuinely new capability.
Explain it: Would downcasting every caller to Provider B repair the contract? What else besides accepted inputs must agree?

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What state is allowed after reserve raises an exception?
  • What is the result when the same business request is retried?
Strong answer criteria
  • Defines the state after success and failure
  • States who commits
  • Defines what repeated calls do
Verification evidence

column1: OODEEP-02 | A new price-provider implementation rejects quantities below ten although the interface accepts any positive quantity. Is it a valid substitute?
column2:
Short answer
No, because callers are allowed to request any positive quantity. Refusing quantities below ten adds a new restriction and breaks valid callers. The replacement must keep the original promise, or expose its narrower capability separately. I compare errors and side effects as well as successful results. Implementing the same ABAP interface proves compatible types, not compatible behavior.

Reasoning and example
A checkout calls the price-provider interface for one unit. The existing provider returns a quote, as documented. A new bulk provider rejects that request because its own minimum is ten. The program activates, but the checkout now fails for an input it was always allowed to send.

I can keep the shared behavior, choose the provider only through an explicit bulk-specific capability, or change the shared API through a planned migration. I do not hide the new restriction behind the old interface. A common test suite should run the same accepted-input, result and failure cases against each implementation. That checks the promises a caller relies on, rather than merely whether both classes compile.

Avoid
Implementing an interface or passing a cast check proves type compatibility, not behavioral substitutability.
A concrete counterexample to substitutability

A valid quantity-one call exposes a behavioral violation invisible in matching parameter types. The lower table separates redefinition from a genuinely new capability.
Explain it: Would downcasting every caller to Provider B repair the contract? What else besides accepted inputs must agree?
Limit: Hypothetical contract; a narrower published domain would lead to a different assessment. No executable interface is implied.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Can a substitute silently return a different currency?
  • Which common tests would run against every provider?
Strong answer criteria
  • Identifies the new restriction on valid inputs
  • Checks results, errors and other changes
  • Runs the same behavior tests for each provider
Verification evidence
A contract suite exercises minimum positive quantity, currency, failures, and repeat calls for both providers.

column1: OODEEP-03 | Two unrelated services share a capability and some validation code. Should their callers depend on an abstract superclass?
column2:
Short answer
I would use an interface for the shared capability and a helper object for shared validation. That lets unrelated services reuse what they need without pretending they belong to one class family. An abstract superclass is useful when there is a real shared process and deliberate specialization. Similar code alone is not enough reason, especially because an ABAP class has only one superclass.

Reasoning and example
A document exporter and a notification sender both support cancellation, but their work is otherwise unrelated. A small cancellation interface lets a coordinator call either one. If both need the same cancellation policy, they can each use a policy object without inheriting all of one another's shared setup.

By contrast, a family of parsers may genuinely share a fixed sequence with a few defined steps implemented by subclasses. An abstract base class could fit that situation. I ask what the caller needs and what implementation is actually reusable before choosing. Putting shared code into a base class is convenient initially, but a forced hierarchy can make later independent changes much harder.

Avoid
An abstract superclass is not automatically a better contract because it can carry reusable implementation.
A concrete counterexample to substitutability

A valid quantity-one call exposes a behavioral violation invisible in matching parameter types. The lower table separates redefinition from a genuinely new capability.
Explain it: Would downcasting every caller to Provider B repair the contract? What else besides accepted inputs must agree?
Limit: Hypothetical contract; a narrower published domain would lead to a different assessment. No executable interface is implied.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which invariant would the superclass enforce?
  • How would the design accommodate a class already inheriting from a framework base?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates what callers need from shared implementation code
  • Checks whether a subclass really is a valid kind of its base
  • Allows unrelated behaviors to change separately
Verification evidence

column1: OODEEP-04 | A subclass needs a different implementation and an extra mandatory input for an inherited method. Can REDEFINITION add it?
column2:
Short answer
No. REDEFINITION changes an eligible inherited instance method implementation while keeping its interface. It cannot add a new mandatory parameter. ABAP does not solve this with same-name methods having different signatures. If the new input changes what the operation means, I design a separate operation or a deliberate API change. Existing base-type callers must still work as promised.

Reasoning and example
A base method formats a document using its declared inputs. A specialized formatter now needs an extra profile. I cannot simply add that profile to the redefined method signature. A separately named operation may be clearer, or a required profile can be supplied during valid object setup if that still fits the original method rules.

The important test is a caller holding only the base reference. It must not suddenly need a downcast and a hidden setup call to use an operation that previously worked. I check successful results, errors and initialization together. Even adding an optional parameter elsewhere does not automatically make a changed behavior compatible; the caller's expectations still need review.

Avoid
Redefinition is not method overloading, and optional parameters do not automatically make every behavioral change compatible.

A valid quantity-one call exposes a behavioral violation invisible in matching parameter types. The lower table separates redefinition from a genuinely new capability.
Explain it: Would downcasting every caller to Provider B repair the contract? What else besides accepted inputs must agree?

column1: OODEEP-05 | A local test class needs access to private state. What does granting friendship expose, and what does it not imply?
column2:
Short answer
Friendship allows access to the granting class's private and protected components. It goes one way; the granting class does not automatically gain the same access back. A superclass friend is not automatically a friend of its subclasses, while subclasses of a friend can gain access. I keep the grant narrow and prefer testing public behavior when that is enough.

Reasoning and example
A local test class needs a legacy seam that cannot yet be reached through the public API. Granting friendship to that focused final test class can be narrower than making production attributes public. The test can then access the granting class's internals without opening them to every ordinary caller.

I still inspect who receives the permission. Granting friendship to a broadly implemented interface can give access to its implementing classes, which is much wider than one test class. The inheritance directions matter too: a friend class and a subclass of the class granting friendship are different situations. I do not reduce the rule to friendship is inherited or is never inherited; I check the actual classes involved.

Avoid
Do not summarize friendship as simply inherited or not inherited; the direction and which class is subclassed matter.
Construction invariants and meaningful test boundaries

Invalid dependencies are rejected before use. In the successful test, the input price is controlled but the discount rule itself executes.
Explain it: What defect should make the assertion fail, and which private access is actually necessary?
Limit: The 10-percent discount is an illustrative fixture, not an application rule. Friendship details and real integration require separate checks.
