    Friendship is unilateral; distinguishes friends' subclasses from subclasses of the granting class.

column1: OODEEP-06 | Two references point to one resource-owning object. Does clearing one reference close the resource or destroy the object?
column2:
Short answer
Clearing one reference only clears that variable. If another reference still points to the object, the object remains reachable. Memory cleanup is also different from closing a connection or releasing a business lock. For resources that must be released promptly, I define an explicit owner and close or release operation. I run it on the required success and error paths.

Reasoning and example
A coordinator and a cache both refer to one session object. Clearing the coordinator reference leaves the cache reference usable, so it cannot guarantee that the session resource was closed. Even when an object later becomes unreachable, relying on garbage collection is not a precise business-resource release plan.

If the coordinator owns the resource, an explicit close operation may be appropriate. Other holders then need a defined response if they try to use it after closure. If the coordinator merely borrowed it, closing it may break the real owner. I test both ownership and failure paths instead of assuming CLEAR on a reference provides object destruction or lock release.

Avoid
Reference clearing is not an object-level close operation and must not be used as a lock-release guarantee.
Value components versus a shared referent

Two structure values own independent string values but lead to the same pricing object. The arrow targets explain why a getter can expose mutable state.
Explain it: Which change affects only ls_copy, and which change affects an object visible through both?
Limit: Conceptual object identity, not physical memory addresses or a particular sharing optimization.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Who may close a shared or borrowed object?
  • What should a second close or a call after close do?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates object reachability from timely resource release
  • Identifies who owns or borrows the resource
  • Defines behavior after close
Verification evidence
Tests cover multiple aliases, explicit close, repeated close, and use after closure.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Initializations
    Initializing a reference is distinct from the garbage collector deleting an unreachable object.

column1: OODEEP-07 | An object can be created with a missing repository and fails much later on its first business call. What would you change?
column2:
Short answer
I would require the repository when creating the service and reject an invalid reference immediately. That avoids an object that looks usable but fails later because setup was forgotten. Constructor injection makes required helpers visible. A factory can coordinate more complex creation. I still check the reference explicitly; declaring a constructor parameter does not guarantee the caller passed a bound object.

Reasoning and example
An approval service currently has a public empty constructor and a later set_repository call. One caller forgets that setter, and approve fails far away from the mistake. Requiring the repository and policy during creation makes the missing setup visible at the point where the object is built.

I validate the required references and return a meaningful construction failure where appropriate. I do not need to perform every remote call in the constructor. If opening an external session is a separate step, I define that lifecycle clearly and test calls before and after opening. The goal is a predictable usable state, not heavy hidden initialization that surprises callers.

Avoid
Constructor injection does not validate an initial reference automatically, and heavy I/O is not required for good initialization.
Construction invariants and meaningful test boundaries

Invalid dependencies are rejected before use. In the successful test, the input price is controlled but the discount rule itself executes.
Explain it: What defect should make the assertion fail, and which private access is actually necessary?
Limit: The 10-percent discount is an illustrative fixture, not an application rule. Friendship details and real integration require separate checks.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • When would a factory improve error handling over constructor work?
  • How do you prevent this object escaping before setup succeeds?
Strong answer criteria
  • Defines what a usable new object requires
  • Rejects missing dependencies at creation
  • Separates setup from later business operations
Verification evidence
Creation tests prove invalid dependencies fail immediately and valid instances need no undocumented setup call.

Read and verify
  • SAP Learning: Encapsulation and consistency
    Constructors establish initial state and can report construction failure.

column1: OODEEP-08 | A test passes alone but fails after another test changes CLASS-DATA. Why does NEW not reliably isolate it?
column2:
Short answer
NEW creates a new instance, but it does not reset CLASS-DATA. That class-level state can be shared by instances in the same internal session and can remain after a test finishes. I remove unnecessary shared mutable state or provide a controlled reset. If a cache is required, I define its keys and refresh rules. It is not automatically synchronized across servers.

Reasoning and example
The first test loads a policy into a static cache. The second prepares different policy data and creates a new service, but the service still reads the old class-level cache. The second test fails only when run after the first, which is a sign that test state is leaking.

An injected provider created for each test can remove that unwanted sharing. If production genuinely needs caching, I test cache invalidation and all relevant context in the key, such as the intended user or organizational scope. A reset can help isolate legacy tests, but it does not fix an incorrect production cache lifetime. Changing test order only hides the problem.

Avoid
CLASS-DATA is not per instance, but it is also not a globally synchronized cache across application servers.
Three distinct state and memory lifetimes

Empty row slots and the initial allocation are deliberately drawn separately. A new object does not imply a new internal session or empty class cache.
Explain it: Why can recreating a service leave a test-order failure unchanged?
Limit: Allocation diagram is qualitative; measure actual ABAP memory and cache lifetime in the target context.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Does a class constructor rerun for every NEW?
  • Which context must appear in a security-sensitive cache key?
Strong answer criteria
  • Explains how long class-level data remains
  • Does not assume NEW resets shared test state
  • Defines cache keys, lifetime and refresh rules
Verification evidence
The suite passes individually, together, and with varied order without stale shared state.

Read and verify
  • SAP: CLASS-METHODS
    Static members and initialization have class semantics, separate from instance state.

column1: OODEEP-09 | A repository raises a low-level exception. Should a business service catch CX_ROOT and return an empty result?
column2:
Short answer
Usually no. Returning an empty result can make a technical failure look like a valid not-found result. I catch the failure where I can recover or turn it into a meaningful service error. If I wrap the exception, I keep PREVIOUS so the original cause remains available. Missing data, a rejected business request and an unavailable dependency should remain distinguishable.

Reasoning and example
A pricing repository cannot be reached. If the service catches CX_ROOT and returns an empty price, the caller might assume no price exists and apply a default such as zero. A network problem has now become an apparently valid business result, which is more dangerous than a clear error.

I define separate handling for a confirmed missing price and a failed attempt to read the price. The service can expose a useful unavailable message while preserving the low-level cause for diagnosis. Tests simulate both cases and verify that neither accidentally produces a successful free item. A broad catch can be appropriate at a final error-handling point, but not as permission to invent success data.

Avoid
Broad catch-and-default handling is not resilience when it changes an unknown outcome into valid-looking data.
Exceptional exits and preserved causes

The table names three exit paths that require separate reasoning. The exception chain carries the lower-level diagnosis through a meaningful service-level failure.
Explain it: Which path would a test of only propagated exceptions miss?
Limit: Simplified non-resumable scenarios; exact nesting and handlers determine CLEANUP execution. Resource ownership remains application-specific.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • When is catching CX_ROOT justified at an application boundary?
  • What information belongs in user feedback versus technical diagnostics?
Strong answer criteria
  • Keeps missing data different from a failed read
  • Converts errors into useful service-level meaning
  • Retains the original exception cause
Verification evidence
Tests assert distinct not-found and technical-failure paths, including the previous exception chain.

Read and verify
  • SAP Learning: Working with exception classes
    Exception propagation and previous preserve a technical cause during translation.

column1: OODEEP-10 | A getter returns a reference to a mutable internal collection. Has private visibility protected the object's invariants?
column2:
Short answer
No. Private storage is not protected if a getter returns a reference that lets callers change the same data directly. I decide whether the getter returns an independent value, read access or intentionally shared state. Business changes should normally go through methods that check the rules. Returning a table value removes that table alias, but object references inside its rows can still be shared.

Reasoning and example
A cart add_item method rejects negative quantities. Its get_items method returns a writable reference to the real internal item table. A caller uses that reference to insert a negative quantity, bypassing add_item completely. The attribute is private, but the cart can still enter a state its own rules forbid.

Returning a suitable value copy can prevent direct changes to that table. I still inspect row components: a copied object reference points to the same object, so it may expose another way to change internal state. Alternatively, I offer the specific read operations callers need. Tests should try the exposed access paths, not only check that the attribute declaration says PRIVATE.

Avoid
A copied reference is not a copied referent; changing the static view alone does not create immutable state.
Value components versus a shared referent

Two structure values own independent string values but lead to the same pricing object. The arrow targets explain why a getter can expose mutable state.
Explain it: Which change affects only ls_copy, and which change affects an object visible through both?
Limit: Conceptual object identity, not physical memory addresses or a particular sharing optimization.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Does returning a table value solve reference components inside its rows?
  • Which mutation should remain an operation of the owning object?
Strong answer criteria
  • Finds how a reference can bypass validation
  • Defines who may change the data
  • Checks object references inside copied rows
Verification evidence
Attempted external mutation cannot bypass the owner's quantity rule or alter a promised snapshot.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Assignment rules for reference variables
    Reference assignment preserves the same object; static views do not clone mutable state.

column1: OODEEP-11 | A widely used provider interface needs an optional new capability. How do you avoid forcing unrelated implementations into fake behavior?
column2:
Short answer
I would consider a separate interface for the optional capability. Providers that really support it can implement it, while existing callers keep using the original interface. Adding a method affects implementers even if old callers never use it. If the main interface must change, I plan the meaning and rollout. Returning fake success is not a valid way to pretend support.

Reasoning and example
A price-provider interface is widely used, and a new caller needs simulation. One external provider cannot simulate. Adding simulate to every provider and having that one return an empty successful result hides the limitation and can mislead the caller.

A separate simulation capability lets setup code choose a suitable provider or report that the capability is unavailable. Ordinary pricing callers need not change. I test supported and unsupported selection as well as the simulation itself. A no-op implementation is acceptable only if doing nothing truly meets the documented rule. Interface evolution requires checking both sides: existing callers and every class that must implement the new operation.

Avoid
Adding a method is not automatically harmless merely because existing callers do not invoke it.
A concrete counterexample to substitutability

A valid quantity-one call exposes a behavioral violation invisible in matching parameter types. The lower table separates redefinition from a genuinely new capability.
Explain it: Would downcasting every caller to Provider B repair the contract? What else besides accepted inputs must agree?
Limit: Hypothetical contract; a narrower published domain would lead to a different assessment. No executable interface is implied.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How will existing implementers activate after the interface change?
  • When would a separate version be clearer than optional capability discovery?
Strong answer criteria
  • Checks effects on callers and implementing classes
  • Does not return fake success for unsupported work
  • Plans rollout and explicit unsupported-capability handling
Verification evidence
An implementation inventory and compatibility tests cover old clients and providers without simulation.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Interfaces in ABAP Objects
    Interface components and implementation syntax underpin capability evolution.

column1: OODEEP-12 | An OO unit test mocks calculate_total and then asserts the mocked total. What behavior has it proved?
column2:
Short answer
It mainly proves that the mock returns the value configured by the test. It does not prove the real total calculation. To test calculation, I keep calculate_total real and replace outside inputs such as a price source. A different test may mock the calculator when it is testing checkout coordination. The important question is which real behavior the test claims to verify.

Reasoning and example
For a discount rule, the test supplies known prices and calls the real calculation with quantities below, at and above the threshold. It asserts totals derived from the business rule. If the calculation method itself is mocked to return 90 and the test checks 90, a broken implementation could still pass unchanged.

A checkout test has another purpose: it may verify that a total is requested before posting or that a calculation error prevents posting. There, a calculator double can be appropriate. I name the subject and expected behavior clearly so reviewers can tell these cases apart. High coverage or many mocks alone cannot establish useful test evidence.

Avoid
The same component can be a real subject in one test and a doubled dependency in another; coverage alone does not settle test quality.
Construction invariants and meaningful test boundaries

Invalid dependencies are rejected before use. In the successful test, the input price is controlled but the discount rule itself executes.
Explain it: What defect should make the assertion fail, and which private access is actually necessary?
Limit: The 10-percent discount is an illustrative fixture, not an application rule. Friendship details and real integration require separate checks.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which defect should make this test fail?
  • What real integration evidence remains necessary after a double-based unit test?
Strong answer criteria
  • Names the real behavior being tested
  • Replaces dependencies rather than the tested rule
  • Derives expected results independently from the implementation
Verification evidence
A deliberately changed business rule makes its calculation test fail, while orchestration tests remain separately meaningful.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Adding test doubles
    Doubles isolate dependencies; the application scenario distinguishes a dependency from the behavior being tested.

column1: PAT-01 | Approval rules vary by country, while the application workflow should remain stable. Strategy or Template Method?
column2:
Short answer
I would use Strategy for country-specific approval rules. The coordinator keeps the workflow, and the selected strategy returns the rule decision. Template Method fits a shared sequence where subclasses intentionally fill in a few fixed steps. Here the rule can vary without changing the coordinator class. I would only choose inheritance if the shared sequence and permitted overrides are clear requirements.

Reasoning and example
The application receives an order for 8,000 EUR and supplies the appropriate country rule. In this example, the DE rule requires a manager above 5,000 EUR, while the FR rule uses 10,000 EUR. The same amount therefore requires a manager for DE but not for FR. Each rule receives the required order data and returns a decision, such as the required approver. It should not secretly commit, send email or change global data. The coordinator stays responsible for applying the decision and continuing the workflow.

I test that coordinator with several rules and verify the same success and failure expectations. If countries later need different process sequences, I review the workflow itself instead of adding increasingly powerful subclass hooks. Strategy works best when the changing part is a replaceable rule. Template Method works when a stable base algorithm deliberately controls which steps subclasses may customize.

Avoid
Choosing inheritance solely to share code, or allowing a rule implementation to take over transaction ownership.
Strategy versus Template Method in approval rules

The same 700 EUR request receives different policy decisions through the same Strategy contract. Template Method instead fixes a call skeleton and exposes deliberate subclass steps.
Explain it: Which part varies, who selects it, and which object keeps transaction ownership?
Limit: Conceptual pattern comparison, not executable ABAP or a universal approval rule. Framework-owned construction may require a supported delegation seam.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which variation changes at runtime rather than through subclassing?
  • How would you prevent a new rule from changing the workflow's transaction boundary?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates country rules from workflow coordination
  • Explains why composition or inheritance fits this case
  • Keeps rules replaceable and separately testable
Verification evidence
Run identical coordinator contract tests with two country rules and a test double; assert decision and side-effect boundaries.

column1: PAT-02 | A posting integration needs matching serializer and sender implementations for each provider. Is one static factory sufficient?
column2:
Short answer
A simple factory may be enough for a small fixed set of providers. Abstract Factory helps when several objects must belong to a compatible family, such as a serializer and sender for one provider. Factory Method means a creation operation that subclasses can override. I choose the smallest design that prevents incompatible combinations. Returning an object from a static method does not automatically make it Factory Method.

Reasoning and example
Provider A expects one message format and endpoint behavior; provider B expects another. If the caller independently chooses a serializer and sender, it could combine A format with B sender. A factory that returns a validated pair can prevent that mistake without a large hierarchy when only a few combinations exist.

If each provider supplies several related products that evolve together, a provider-factory interface may make the family clearer. I test that every configured provider returns compatible objects and that unknown configuration fails explicitly. Silently choosing a default can send a business document to the wrong destination. The purpose is safe construction, not using the largest possible pattern.

Avoid
Confusing a static creation helper with inheritance-based Factory Method or introducing an Abstract Factory for one trivial object.
Three factory choices and a concrete family constraint

The family boundary prevents an A serializer from being combined accidentally with a B sender. The table distinguishes a simple choice from subclass creation and related-product creation.
Explain it: What invalid combination does this factory prevent, and when would a simple factory be enough?
Limit: Provider compatibility is a fictional fixture. Pattern names do not grant API release eligibility, security or transaction guarantees.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What concrete invalid combination must construction prevent?
  • When would adding a creator subclass be better than changing a configuration map?
Strong answer criteria
  • Distinguishes simple factory, Factory Method and Abstract Factory
  • Names which related objects must be compatible
  • Checks unknown configuration and future changes
Verification evidence
Test each supported provider family and an unknown provider; verify no serializer/sender cross-pairing can be constructed.

Read and verify
  • SAP ABAP pattern examples: Abstract Factory
    Primary SAP demonstration of the mechanism; the interview scenario and trade-off analysis here are original. Examples require target-release review and are not production templates.
  • SAP Factory Method pattern
    Supports subclass-controlled creation; the simple-factory comparison is explanatory analysis.

column1: PAT-03 | A legacy posting API has awkward parameters and a three-step prepare/check/post sequence. Would you build an Adapter, a Facade, or both?
column2:
Short answer
An Adapter can translate the application request and errors into the legacy API format. A Facade can offer one posting operation over prepare, check and post. Both may be useful, but they must preserve failures, authorization and commit rules. I inspect the actual underlying calls. Neither wrapper makes an unreleased API available to ABAP Cloud or removes an internal commit.

Reasoning and example
The application sends a simple posting request. An adapter maps it into the required function-module structures and converts responses into meaningful results. A facade coordinates prepare, check and post, and stops before posting when the check fails. I test mapping separately from that sequence so errors are easy to locate.

Important cases include an explicit zero amount, a warning that must be handled according to the API rules and a remote timeout with an unknown outcome. A timeout is not always proof that nothing was posted. The caller needs enough information to reconcile rather than repeat the operation blindly. The wrapper must expose those facts instead of making the API look safer than it is.

Avoid
Treating any wrapper as both a supported API and a transaction adapter without inspecting its dependencies.
Adapter, Facade and Decorator with observable outcomes

Mapping, orchestration and added behavior are different responsibilities. The lower example shows why wrapper order changes whether a log records one logical call or two attempts.
Explain it: Where would you translate an explicit clear, stop after a failed check, and record retry attempts?
Limit: The retry example is deliberately an eligible read. Write retries need the actual idempotency and uncertainty contract; no pattern automatically supplies it.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which errors belong to the domain contract and which retain technical detail?
  • What evidence would make the legacy API unsuitable despite a neat interface?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates field/error translation from coordinating several calls
  • Preserves commit rules and API release restrictions
  • Tests important values and error mapping
Verification evidence
Trace all three steps with injected failures and inspect dependency release state; assert no hidden commit or swallowed business rejection.

Read and verify

  • SAP ABAP pattern examples: Facade
    Primary SAP demonstration of the mechanism; the interview scenario and trade-off analysis here are original. Examples require target-release review and are not production templates.

column1: PAT-04 | You want timing, diagnostic logging and retries around an outbound service. Would stacked Decorators be safe?
column2:
Short answer
Decorators can add logging or timing around the same service interface. Their order matters. Retrying needs extra care because repeating a request can repeat a business effect. I only retry when the operation rules make that safe, and I distinguish a rejection from an unknown remote outcome. I also decide whether logs and timing describe each attempt or the complete operation.

Reasoning and example
Put logging outside retry and it can record one logical call with several attempts inside it. Put logging inside retry and it can record every attempt. Either can be useful, but the records should share an identifier so support can understand what happened instead of counting attempts as separate business requests.

I test exceptions and return values through the full decorator chain. Logs must avoid sensitive payloads. A diagnostic logging failure should not silently turn a successful business call into failure unless a required audit rule deliberately demands that. Automatic retries on every POST are unsafe: after a timeout, the remote system may already have applied the first request.

Avoid
Adding automatic retries to every POST or assuming decorator order cannot change observable behavior.
Adapter, Facade and Decorator with observable outcomes

Mapping, orchestration and added behavior are different responsibilities. The lower example shows why wrapper order changes whether a log records one logical call or two attempts.
Explain it: Where would you translate an explicit clear, stop after a failed check, and record retry attempts?
Limit: The retry example is deliberately an eligible read. Write retries need the actual idempotency and uncertainty contract; no pattern automatically supplies it.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which wrapper should count attempts and which should measure total latency?
  • How does a timeout after remote success affect the retry policy?
Strong answer criteria
  • Preserves the service results and errors
  • Explains how wrapper order changes observation
  • Does not assume retry automatically prevents duplicate effects
Verification evidence
Test wrapper orders, a transient read failure, uncertain write completion and logging failure; inspect returned outcome and number of remote effects.

Read and verify
  • SAP ABAP pattern examples: Decorator
    Primary SAP demonstration of the mechanism; the interview scenario and trade-off analysis here are original. Examples require target-release review and are not production templates.
  • SAP Clean ABAP: explicit failure flow
    Supports the stated design or testability principle; concrete scenario decisions are contextual recommendations.

column1: PAT-05 | Three handlers can route a request to an approver. The first matching rule should win. How would you implement and test Chain of Responsibility?
column2:
Short answer
I would use an ordered Chain of Responsibility when the first matching handler should choose the route. Each handler must distinguish handled, not applicable and failed. I define what happens when no rule matches and test the configured order. A technical failure must not quietly fall through to another approver. If all validations must run, I use a different execute-all process.

Reasoning and example
A high-value rule, a regional rule and a fallback can all potentially apply to one request. If the high-value rule must win, it appears before the general fallback. The selected handler returns an approver decision, while the transaction coordinator applies it. The rule should not secretly save data during selection.

Tests include overlapping matches, no match and a failure while a rule reads required information. I record which rule selected the approver so support can explain the route. Treating a failed lookup as not applicable can accidentally send the request to a less restrictive fallback. First-match routing is useful, but it does not mean every validation in the chain has run.

Avoid
Treating an exception as 'not applicable', or confusing first-match routing with execute-all validation.
First-match routing and idempotent command execution

The 700 EUR fixture passes the team-lead rule and stops at the manager rule. The selected operation then needs its own durable identity to handle duplicate delivery safely.
Explain it: What changes if all rules must run, and what must a repeated SUBMIT-42 return?
Limit: Routing thresholds and command identity are fictional. The actual business transition, persistence and compensation contracts must be designed separately.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What happens when two handlers match?
  • How is a configuration error different from a valid request with no applicable route?
Strong answer criteria
  • Defines rule order and each routing outcome
  • Separates first-match routing from running all validations
  • Explains the selected route and controls data changes
Verification evidence
Test overlapping rules, no match, handler failure and reordered configuration; assert exactly which handlers execute and which route is chosen.

Read and verify
  • SAP ABAP pattern examples: Chain of Responsibility
    Primary SAP demonstration of the mechanism; the interview scenario and trade-off analysis here are original. Examples require target-release review and are not production templates.

column1: PAT-06 | A local ABAP event updates an ALV, and the team proposes another handler to start an external workflow. What boundary has changed?
column2:
Short answer
The requirement changed from a local notification to reliable work in another system. An ABAP OO event can notify registered listeners in the current execution context. It does not save a message or guarantee delivery after commit. An external workflow needs a supported publication mechanism plus retry and recovery rules. I separate display updates from the saved business transition that should start the workflow.

Reasoning and example
An ALV listener reacts to a local event and refreshes the screen. It can also be accidentally registered twice or left registered when obsolete, so I manage its lifetime and test error handling. None of that registration creates a durable subscription that survives the runtime context.

For an external workflow, I need to know that the document change was saved and that publication can recover after an outage. The receiving side must identify repeated or delayed messages and avoid creating duplicate workflows. A local handler that directly calls the external system can run before a later save failure or lose delivery on an error. Observer alone does not solve those business guarantees.

Avoid
Assuming SET HANDLER creates a durable subscription or that Observer guarantees exactly-once business effects.
Observer delivery and hidden singleton state

A registered local handler can update an ALV, while an external process needs transactional publication and durable processing evidence. Session-shared mutable state is a separate source of repeated-test failures.
Explain it: Which facts survive a process restart, and which request-specific values must not be cached implicitly?
Limit: The lower path describes required responsibilities, not an automatic feature of ABAP Objects events. Verify the chosen event infrastructure and service lifetime.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which part of the design survives an application-server restart?
  • What if one local listener fails after another already changed its state?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates local notification from messages that survive failures
  • Connects external work to saved business changes
  • Defines handling for listener and delivery failures
Verification evidence
Test local listener registration separately from rejected save, duplicate event and delayed workflow delivery cases.

Read and verify
  • SAP Observer pattern
    Describes ABAP event-based observation; it does not claim durable messaging.
  • SAP RAP business events
    Supports the separate RAP business-event mechanism and its lifecycle.

column1: PAT-07 | A command object represents Submit and can be queued or retried. Does using Command make execution idempotent or undoable?
column2:
Short answer
No. Command packages an action and its inputs; it does not automatically make repeats safe or provide undo. I define a stable operation ID, storage, authorization and repeated-execution rules separately. An undo operation only works when the business has a valid reverse action. A posted document may require a compensating document rather than deletion or a simple rollback.

Reasoning and example
A Submit command stored only as an object in memory disappears when its runtime context ends. For a reliable queue, I store a suitable versioned data record and use it to reconstruct an allowed executor. A saved object reference is not a durable message format. At execution time, I check the required business state and authorization.

I also test a repeated operation ID with the same payload and with a conflicting payload. The first may return the existing result; the second may need rejection, according to the defined rules. If submission already posted a document, local rollback cannot erase that completed effect. Recovery may need a separate, audited reversal operation.

Avoid
Assuming execute can safely run twice or that every business command has an exact inverse.
First-match routing and idempotent command execution

The 700 EUR fixture passes the team-lead rule and stops at the manager rule. The selected operation then needs its own durable identity to handle duplicate delivery safely.
Explain it: What changes if all rules must run, and what must a repeated SUBMIT-42 return?
Limit: Routing thresholds and command identity are fictional. The actual business transition, persistence and compensation contracts must be designed separately.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What result should a retry return after the first response was lost?
  • How would you evolve a persisted command payload across application releases?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates packaging an action from safe execution
  • Defines a saved operation ID and repeat-call behavior
  • Uses a business reversal where simple undo is impossible
Verification evidence
Simulate duplicate execution, conflicting payload reuse, lost response and executor upgrade; assert one effective transition and traceable recovery.

Read and verify
  • SAP ABAP pattern examples: Command
    Primary SAP demonstration of the mechanism; the interview scenario and trade-off analysis here are original. Examples require target-release review and are not production templates.
  • SAP LUWs in ABAP
    Provides the transaction boundary; command replay and compensation are design decisions in this scenario.

column1: PAT-08 | A repository interface improves testability, but its RAP implementation reads managed persistence directly. What can go wrong?
column2:
Short answer
A testable interface can still hide an incorrect implementation. Direct table reads can miss changes waiting in the RAP transaction buffer. I first define whether the repository should read saved data or the current transaction state. For BO logic that needs current changes, I use suitable EML access. I do not write managed tables directly and bypass the RAP behavior checks.

Reasoning and example
An operation changes an item, and a validation then reads it through a repository before save. If the repository selects the database table, it can return the old value even though the current RAP transaction already contains the new one. Newly created or deleted instances make the difference even more obvious.

A reporting read of persisted data may legitimately use a different approach. I give those needs distinct names or responsibilities so callers understand which state they receive. Tests should cover update-then-read, create-then-read and delete-then-read before save using the real BO path. A convenient fake returning expected rows will not reveal a production implementation that reads the wrong state, and a second home-made buffer adds more consistency problems.

Avoid
Equating a mockable interface with correct behavior or recreating RAP's transactional buffer in a second general-purpose cache.
Repository read semantics and proportional abstraction

A direct persistence read returns 100 while the transaction already sees 120. The repository seam is valuable only if its real implementation honors the state contract required by the caller.
Explain it: Which integration test catches a mockable repository that reads the wrong state, and when is no new abstraction needed?
Limit: Conceptual read semantics rather than an SQL isolation guarantee. The specific BO, EML operation, authorization and target release remain authoritative.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which caller actually needs persisted rather than buffered state?
  • What integration test would fail if the repository used SELECT instead of EML?
Strong answer criteria
  • States whether a read returns saved or current buffered data
  • Respects RAP save ownership and pending changes
  • Tests the interface and the real BO integration
Verification evidence
Compare unsaved create/update/delete reads through the adapter with the BO contract, then run rollback and save paths on the target system.

column1: PAT-09 | A singleton caches the current approver and makes tests pass alone but fail as a suite. How do you redesign its lifetime?
column2:
Short answer
I would remove the current approver from long-lived shared mutable state. I would pass the relevant context explicitly and use an operation-scoped service, or a cache with clear keys and refresh rules. An ABAP singleton normally belongs to an internal session, not the whole system. Its lifetime can still span several operations or tests. Forcing test order does not fix that design.

Reasoning and example
One test asks for an approver for company A and populates the singleton. A later test for company B reuses the cached value and gets the wrong approver. Similar trouble can occur when a job processes several contexts. The cache stored current approver without saying current for which request or policy.

I make that context explicit in the operation and, if caching is needed, include every relevant distinction in its key and invalidation rules. Tests get controlled service instances. A reset method may temporarily isolate legacy tests, but production must still have the correct lifetime. Clearing a cache between tests cannot repair an application that mixes request-specific decisions during normal use.

Avoid
Claiming singleton means one system-wide instance or solving hidden state solely by forcing test order.

A registered local handler can update an ALV, while an external process needs transactional publication and durable processing evidence. Session-shared mutable state is a separate source of repeated-test failures.

column1: PAT-10 | A service obtains every dependency from a global factory inside its methods. How would you introduce dependency injection without building a framework?
column2:
Short answer
I would build the service near the application entry point and pass its required interface-typed helpers through the constructor. Business methods then use those supplied helpers instead of finding them globally. A small factory can assemble them if setup is complex. This makes tests predictable without requiring a dependency-injection framework. Framework-created classes may need a supported seam or a delegated service instead.

Reasoning and example
An approval method currently calls a global factory to obtain a repository and posting client every time. A unit test cannot easily control what it receives and may accidentally reach a live dependency. I move that construction into application setup and give the service the two objects explicitly.

The test supplies a known repository and a client that cannot post externally, then exercises the real approval decision. A separate integration check verifies production wiring. If RAP or another framework controls construction, I do not invent unsupported constructor parameters; I use a suitable delegated application service or supported test seam. Replacing the factory with another global lookup would still hide the same dependencies.

Replacing one hidden global singleton with a service locator and calling the result fully decoupled.

column1: PAT-11 | A small report has one stable calculation. A reviewer requests Strategy, Abstract Factory and Repository 'for clean architecture'. How do you respond?
column2:
Short answer
I would ask what concrete problem each pattern solves. One stable calculation may need only a clearly named method and good tests. An external service may deserve an interface because it can fail or needs replacement in tests. I add Strategy or factories when real variations make them useful. The aim is understandable change, not a high count of classes.

A small report calculates a tax base with one supported rule. A method with explicit inputs, an explicit result and boundary tests can be easy to read and maintain. Adding Strategy, Abstract Factory and Repository around that pure calculation may introduce many files without removing any actual difficulty.

If the rate comes from a remote service, that dependency is a real reason for a seam: tests need controlled values and failures. If a second tax rule arrives later, extracting a Strategy can then make sense. I leave a clear reason for that future change. I neither reject patterns automatically nor apply them as decoration; each added layer should make a named responsibility easier to understand or test.

column1: PAT-12 | A factory selects country approval Strategies from configuration. How do you keep that combination safe, explainable and testable?
column2:
Short answer
I map supported configuration values to known approval strategies and pass the selected strategy to the coordinator. Missing or unknown configuration should fail clearly, not default to approval. Each rule returns the same kind of result. I test selection separately from calculation. Configuration selects a country rule and, when needed, a policy version. A factory validates that choice and creates the corresponding strategy. Tests check every supported mapping and an unknown value. Separate tests verify each rule, while common cases check that all strategies keep the same result and failure promises.

For a long-running approval, I decide whether it keeps the policy version from submission or deliberately uses the current policy. Otherwise a configuration change could alter the rule halfway through without an explanation. When audit requires it, I record which policy produced the decision. Arbitrary class names from untrusted input and a fallback that approves after configuration failure are both unsafe shortcuts.

column1: SQL-01 | How do ABAP SQL, Native SQL, CDS, and AMDP differ?
column2:
Short answer
ABAP SQL is the usual way to read and change database data from ABAP. CDS defines reusable data models and queries. Native SQL uses database-specific SQL, so the developer must handle more details. AMDP manages HANA database procedures and functions written in SQLScript through ABAP classes. I start with the simplest supported option and check client, authorization and release rules.

Reasoning and example
A report needs totals for one company and month. ABAP SQL may express the whole selection and sum clearly. CDS becomes useful when the same data model should be reused by several consumers. Neither requirement automatically needs a database procedure.

If a necessary calculation cannot be expressed well in supported ABAP SQL or CDS, I consider AMDP and measure the result. I also check which dependencies are allowed in the target environment. Writing SQLScript inside an ABAP-managed method does not turn it into ABAP SQL. In particular, direct table reads must not be assumed to apply the access control of a CDS entity that would otherwise protect those records.

ADBC is an ABAP API for Native SQL, useful when a permitted database-specific operation cannot be expressed through ABAP SQL. It does not add ABAP SQL client handling: a client-dependent table needs the correct explicit client restriction. Bind data values, allowlist any configurable identifiers, and perform the required authorization checks. Native SQL also does not inherit a CDS entity's DCL just because it reads the same tables. ABAP Cloud requires the language and released APIs allowed in the target environment.

Avoid
ABAP syntax around an AMDP method does not turn its SQLScript body into ABAP SQL or automatically apply CDS access control.

column1: SQL-02 | What is the empty-table trap in FOR ALL ENTRIES?
column2:
Short answer
An empty FOR ALL ENTRIES driver is dangerous: the WHERE condition is ignored, so the query can read all rows in scope. I check that the driver is not empty before selecting. I also decide how duplicates should be handled. FOR ALL ENTRIES removes duplicate result rows, which can matter when selected columns do not uniquely identify records.

Reasoning and example
A report receives a list of customer IDs and should read their orders. If the list is empty, I normally return an empty result without running the selection. Adding another condition in the same WHERE clause is not a replacement for that guard: the empty-driver rule still applies.

I can remove repeated driver keys to reduce unnecessary work, but I separately check the output. Two different orders may have the same selected customer and amount. If I omit the order identity, result duplicate elimination can collapse those rows. I test empty input, repeated IDs and distinct records with equal displayed values before deciding the query is correct.

Avoid
An empty FAE driver does not mean no rows; a separate filter in the same WHERE clause is not a safe replacement for the guard.

column1: SQL-03 | When would you use a join instead of FOR ALL ENTRIES?
column2:
Short answer
A join is useful when related database rows can be selected together with clear matching rules. FOR ALL ENTRIES can fit when the driver data already exists in ABAP. Neither is always faster. They can return different duplicates and row counts, so I check the required result first. Then I compare database work, transferred data and performance with realistic inputs.

Reasoning and example
An order-to-item join produces a row for each matching item. That is useful when the report needs the item details, but it repeats order fields. If the report only needs orders that have an item meeting a condition, an EXISTS selection may describe the requirement more clearly than joining and removing duplicates afterward.

FOR ALL ENTRIES also has its own duplicate elimination and empty-driver behavior. Replacing it with a join requires tests for those differences, not just a runtime comparison. I include large customers, customers with no matching items and repeated driver values. A faster statement is only an improvement if it still produces the business result the caller expects.

Avoid
Replacing FAE with a join can change duplicates and row counts even when the new query runs faster.

column1: SQL-04 | How can a LEFT OUTER JOIN accidentally behave like an inner join?
column2:
Short answer
A LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps left-side rows even when no right-side row matches. The missing right side contains SQL NULL values. A WHERE condition demanding a right-side value can remove those rows again. I put a condition in ON when it defines which right rows may match. I use WHERE when I really want to filter the final result.

Reasoning and example
The report must show every order, with an English description where available. I join the description using the order key and language condition in ON. An order without English text remains in the list, with no matching description. The user can still see that the order exists.

If I put the right-side language condition in WHERE instead, the unmatched row does not meet it and disappears. The report now hides some orders, even though the SQL still says LEFT OUTER JOIN. I test an order with English text, one with only another language and one with no text. That makes the intended behavior visible before tuning the query.

Avoid
Moving conditions between ON and WHERE is not always semantics-preserving for outer joins.

Joining two order headers to three items repeats order 10's total, inflating a naive sum from EUR 180 to EUR 280. For outer joins, matching conditions in ON can preserve unmatched left rows, while right-side conditions in WHERE can remove them.

column1: SQL-05 | What is the difference between SQL NULL and an ABAP initial value?
column2:
Short answer
SQL NULL means a value is missing or unknown. An ABAP initial value is a real value, such as zero or blank. Comparing something with NULL does not behave like comparing it with zero. I use IS NULL to check for NULL and COALESCE when a replacement is intended. Supported null indicators can preserve the distinction when reading into ABAP.

Reasoning and example
A left outer join reads orders and optional payments. One order has a payment of zero; another has no payment row. Those are different facts, but a plain transfer into an ABAP amount field can make both look like zero. I preserve the missing-row information if the report needs to distinguish them.

For example, I can include a suitable existence indicator or use supported null handling rather than guessing from the amount. COALESCE replaces NULL with a chosen value, but that deliberately loses the distinction unless I keep it elsewhere. It does not replace an ordinary stored zero or blank. I test both cases so missing data is not shown as a confirmed amount.

Avoid
COALESCE replaces NULL, not every initial or blank value, and WHERE column = NULL is not a correct null test.

column1: SQL-06 | How do GROUP BY, WHERE, and HAVING work together?
column2:
Short answer
WHERE filters the rows before grouping. GROUP BY collects rows with the same chosen fields, and functions such as SUM calculate a result for each group. HAVING filters the resulting groups. I let the database do this work when it is appropriate. I still check currencies and joins, because a fast sum can be wrong if it adds incompatible or repeated amounts.

Reasoning and example
To show monthly sales totals above a threshold, I first use WHERE to select the month. I group by company and currency so euros and dollars remain separate. SUM calculates each total, and HAVING keeps only groups above the required threshold. The application receives a small result instead of every sales row.

Before trusting it, I check any join added to the query. If one sales item matches three partner rows, its amount may be counted three times. A small fixture with one known item and several partners reveals that error. The right fix is to model the required rows correctly, not simply to accept the database total because aggregation ran successfully.

Avoid
Database aggregation is not automatically correct if different currencies are mixed or joins multiply the rows being aggregated.

column1: SQL-07 | What do cardinality and uniqueness mean for join correctness?
column2:
Short answer
Cardinality describes how many matches a relationship can have: none, one or many. The actual join fields and data decide which rows are returned. Missing key fields can multiply rows or join unrelated records. I check the complete identity and test missing and multiple matches. A CDS key or a to-one declaration does not repair incorrect data or matching logic.

Reasoning and example
A document number may be unique only together with company code and year. Joining by number alone can connect an item to a different document with the same number. Text tables introduce another common issue: one record can have several languages, so omitting language can multiply the result.

I prepare test data with the same number in different years and with several text languages. Then I compare the returned rows with the intended matches. DISTINCT may hide duplicated output rows, but it does not correct a wrong selected description or an inflated sum. I fix the join condition and only declare cardinality that the model and data actually support.

Avoid
DISTINCT can conceal an incomplete join condition while leaving aggregates or selected attributes logically wrong.

column1: SQL-08 | Does SELECT SINGLE return a predictable first row?
column2:
Short answer
SELECT SINGLE does not mean the latest, smallest or first business record. It is suitable when the conditions identify one required row, or when any match is acceptable. If several rows match and their order matters, I use a supported limited query with ORDER BY. I include a unique tie-breaker so equal sort values still give a predictable result.

Reasoning and example
A status table contains several events for one order. Reading one matching row without ordering can return an old event. If I need the latest status, I sort by event time and a unique sequence or ID, then limit the result to one row using supported syntax.

The unique extra sort field matters when two events have the same timestamp. Without it, either tied row may be chosen. I test those equal timestamps and an order with no events. I do not rely on the row that happened to be returned in development: a changed index, execution plan or data distribution can change that result without any change to the ABAP statement.

Avoid
The primary key definition or a convenient current execution plan is not an implicit ORDER BY guarantee.

column1: SQL-09 | What do you optimize first in a slow data selection?
column2:
Short answer
I first confirm the correct result and measure a repeatable slow case. Then I look for too many rows, unnecessary columns, repeated queries and joins that create extra work. Reducing database calls and data transfer often helps more than changing ABAP syntax. I measure each change with realistic data and verify that permissions and business results stay correct.

Reasoning and example
A report loops over thousands of items and issues one SELECT for each item. Even a fast individual query can become expensive when called thousands of times. Reading the required data together can reduce those round trips, provided the new query preserves the intended matching and authorization rules.

I compare total runtime, number of calls and transferred rows before and after the change. I also test missing records and a large customer whose data is much less evenly distributed than the development sample. Selecting every column or returning an unlimited result can still waste memory after the repeated calls are removed. The goal is less necessary work, supported by measurements.

There is no universal sequence such as indexes first, then CDS, then AMDP. Start with the measured bottleneck: ABAP work, database work, transfer, locks or a remote dependency. Choose a change that removes that cost and preserves behavior. Pushdown is useful when appropriate set processing belongs near the data, not merely because the target database is HANA.

Avoid
A query that is fast on ten development rows may be unsuitable for millions of production rows or a different key distribution.

Inspect database work, ABAP computation, transferred volume, and repeated calls as different possible causes. Choose the trace and change based on evidence.
Explain it: Is the largest cost one slow statement, many cheap statements, ABAP processing, or transfer volume?

column1: SQL-10 | Which tools help locate ABAP, database, and memory performance problems?
column2:
Short answer
Start with the slow business request and locate where its time or memory goes. Where available, ST03N/STAD help identify costly workloads or requests, SAT traces ABAP execution, and ST05 traces SQL. ST12 combines relevant traces. SQL Monitor helps prioritize SQL across a wider workload; a database plan explains one statement. Memory analysis needs its own evidence.

Reasoning and example
A report is slow, but the longest individual SQL statement may not dominate total time. Use workload/request statistics to choose a representative case, then trace it. Compare call count, transferred rows and total time: a short statement called thousands of times may be the real problem. SQLM can collect a broader SQL profile; SWLT can combine runtime evidence and static findings where supported. Its low monitoring overhead is not zero or a guarantee for every workload: scope collection and permissions appropriately.

For a memory dump, inspect ST22 and compare Memory Inspector snapshots at comparable phases. Look for growing internal tables, retained copies and objects. A database execution plan instead helps explain scans, joins, sorts and large database intermediates. Change one measured bottleneck, then verify the same result, runtime and peak memory again.

Tool access depends on the deployment. Do not promise classic transactions in every ABAP Cloud environment. Use supported ADT profiling/SQL analysis and the available monitoring apps. In SAP BTP ABAP environment, administrator SQL tracing can be started through Capture Request Statistics; detailed trace evaluation uses the Technical Monitoring Cockpit. The exact role, release and tool entry point must be checked.

Avoid
The slowest individual SQL statement may not be the largest total cost if another cheap statement is executed thousands of times.

column1: SQL-11 | Does SAP HANA remove the need for indexes and performance tuning?
column2:
Short answer
HANA still needs performance analysis. Its storage and processing are fast, but a query can still read too much data or create huge intermediate results. A secondary index may help a particular lookup, while costing memory and extra update work. I decide from the actual table, workload and execution plan. I do not add indexes just because another database used them.

Reasoning and example
A service repeatedly finds a tiny number of records using the same combination of attributes. I inspect how HANA executes that selection and whether a supported secondary index could help. I compare the lookup gain with memory use and the effect on inserts and updates, because the workload includes writes too.

For a query that legitimately reads much of a column, the same index may offer little benefit. I also avoid describing every primary key as a SQL Server-style clustered index that defines physical row order. HANA has its own storage and index structures. Query correctness and explicit ORDER BY remain necessary regardless of which access path the optimizer selects.

Avoid
Do not say HANA needs no indexes or that every primary key is a clustered index with a predictable physical row order.

column1: SQL-12 | When is table buffering appropriate?
column2:
Short answer
The ABAP table buffer can help with small, rarely changing tables that are read often in supported ways. It is a poor default for constantly changing business data or reads that need immediate freshness across servers. I check the table setting and the actual SQL form, because some statements bypass the buffer. This buffer is separate from HANA caches and internal tables.

Reasoning and example
A small customizing table is read for nearly every document, while its values change only occasionally. Buffering may reduce repeated database access if the table and its reads qualify. I inspect both the configuration and the query forms instead of assuming the buffered setting benefits every SELECT.

An order status that changes continuously has different needs. A buffered value on another application server may not immediately reflect a change, so it may be unsuitable for a decision requiring the latest state. I test the expected consistency and workload before choosing buffering. An internal table used by one ABAP session is another mechanism again; it does not provide shared buffer synchronization.

Avoid
Buffering is not universally faster, and reading buffered data does not guarantee immediate visibility of every change across application servers.

column1: SQL-13 | What are normalization and denormalization, and how do they affect ABAP design?
column2:
Short answer
Normalization stores facts where they belong so one change does not require repairing many copies. First normal form avoids repeating groups; second removes dependence on only part of a candidate key; third removes unsuitable indirect dependencies between non-key facts. Denormalization deliberately stores extra copies or calculated results. I use it for a clear need and define how those copies stay correct.

Reasoning and example
If a customer current address is copied onto every order and all copies are meant to stay current, an address change becomes difficult: some rows may be missed. Keeping that current fact with the customer avoids the repeated update. The order can refer to the customer when it needs the latest address.

An issued invoice may instead need the address exactly as it was when issued. Keeping that historical snapshot is an intentional business rule, not automatically a design error. I clarify which meaning is required before removing duplication. Similarly, a stored total may improve a measured read problem, but it needs a clear update rule so the total cannot silently become stale.

Avoid
NoSQL is not automatically faster or better for large data, and normalization is not a rule against all intentionally stored business snapshots.

column1: SQL-14 | When is AMDP justified, and what risks must you address?
column2:
Short answer
I consider AMDP when a required HANA operation is difficult to express with supported ABAP SQL or CDS, or measurements justify keeping a large calculation in the database. I check release support, dependencies, client handling and authorization. The team also needs SQLScript skills and suitable tests. AMDP should solve a real problem, not be a default replacement for a simple SELECT.

Reasoning and example
A complex analytical calculation repeatedly transfers a large dataset to ABAP and back. After trying simpler supported SQL and CDS options, I may compare an AMDP implementation that keeps the calculation on HANA. I measure the full operation and compare the actual result, including empty data and unusual values.

I also inspect access rules. Reading an underlying table inside database logic does not automatically enforce the DCL attached to a CDS entity used elsewhere. Transaction ownership still matters: the procedure must not introduce an independent commit into the application operation. A short filtered selection normally gains little from an extra SQLScript layer and may become harder to maintain.

In ABAP for Cloud Development, AMDP procedures must be read-only and client-safe, with permitted dependencies. Standard ABAP has broader procedure options. CDS table functions remain read-only. Check the exact language version and release before reusing an example; AMDP does not allow its own COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

Avoid
AMDP is not a universal performance upgrade, and an AMDP method should not introduce an independent commit into an application transaction.

Read and verify
  • SAP AMDP use and selection guidance
    Check what the query returns and measure it in the target system before choosing a performance change.
  • SAP: AMDP language versions and restrictions
    Distinguish Standard ABAP from ABAP for Cloud Development.

column1: SQL-15 | AMDP procedure or CDS table function: what is the difference, and when would you use each?
column2:
Short answer
An AMDP procedure runs SQLScript on HANA and is called from ABAP as a method with input and output parameters. A CDS table function exposes a table-shaped result that ABAP SQL and other CDS entities can read. Its implementation is an AMDP database function. Choose a procedure for an operation your ABAP code calls; choose a CDS table function when a calculation must be a reusable query source. Try supported ABAP SQL or CDS first.

Reasoning and example
For example, an ABAP report passes rows to a multi-stage allocation calculation and receives the calculated rows back. A procedure can fit that calling style. If several CDS consumers need the calculated rows in further joins or filters, a CDS table function may fit better. These are design examples, not proof that SQLScript is faster; first check whether the target release already supports the calculation in ordinary SQL or CDS.

The declarations differ. A procedure uses IMPORTING/EXPORTING or CHANGING parameters passed by VALUE; it has no RETURNING parameter. A CDS table function declares its parameters and result columns in DEFINE TABLE FUNCTION. A public static method declared FOR TABLE FUNCTION implements that contract with BY DATABASE FUNCTION and OPTIONS READ-ONLY. Read the CDS entity with SELECT; do not call its implementation as an ordinary ABAP method. An AMDP table function intended only for other AMDP methods is another variant and is not directly callable from ABAP.

A CDS table function cannot write a helper table. ABAP for Cloud Development also restricts AMDP procedures to read-only, client-safe access and permitted dependencies. Standard ABAP allows broader procedure capabilities, but not an independent COMMIT inside AMDP. Check client handling, authorization, numeric types and empty results explicitly. The small code examples show the different contracts using a trivial calculation; that calculation itself does not require AMDP.

READ-ONLY is not a third kind of AMDP; it restricts database changes. In Code, switch between three parts: a procedure with its ABAP call, the CDS table-function definition, and its implementation with a SELECT consumer. The procedure adds 40 and 60 to produce 100; the table function filters rows by an amount threshold.

Avoid
AMDP is the framework, not a synonym for procedure. Not every AMDP function is a CDS table function, and read-only code is not automatically authorized or client-safe.

Read and verify
  • SAP: AMDP procedures, functions and ABAP Cloud restrictions
    Compare procedure parameters, table-function variants and client-safety requirements for the target release.
  • SAP: CDS table functions
    The CDS contract defines the returned columns; the AMDP database function implements the query.

column1: SQL-16 | What do window functions do in ABAP SQL, and when are they useful?
column2:
Short answer
A window function calculates a value across related result rows while keeping each detail row. Use it for a customer total beside each sale, a running total, or a rank. GROUP BY instead combines rows into one result per group. OVER defines the window; PARTITION BY separates groups, window ORDER BY orders calculations, and a frame selects which rows contribute.

Reasoning and example
Customer A has three sales with quantities 100, 100 and 50. SUM( quantity ) OVER( PARTITION BY customer_id ) adds 250 beside each of the three rows. GROUP BY customer_id with SUM returns just one row for A. A running ROWS frame ordered by the unique sale ID instead produces 100, 200, 250. Its final value matches the partition total, but the earlier values answer a different question.

For descending quantity, RANK gives 1, 1, 3 and DENSE_RANK gives 1, 1, 2. ROW_NUMBER gives a separate position to each row; add sale_id as a tie-breaker if that position must be repeatable. Do not add this unique tie-breaker to RANK when equal quantities should share a rank. The final SELECT ORDER BY controls displayed row order separately from the window ORDER BY.

WHERE filters the input before the window calculation. To rank first and then keep only selected ranks, use a supported outer query or CTE instead of expecting a window alias to be available in the same WHERE. Check the ABAP release and permitted data source; ABAP SQL support does not prove that the same syntax is available in an ABAP CDS definition. A window can avoid extra ABAP aggregation loops, but it still needs measured database cost, especially for sorting and large partitions.

Avoid
Do not replace GROUP BY with a window without checking the required row count, and do not leave tie ordering or a running-total frame implicit.

Read and verify
  • SAP ABAP SQL: window expressions and worked examples
    ABAP SQL syntax; check the supported functions and additions in your target release.
  • SAP ABAP Keyword Documentation: window functions
    Use the ABAP SQL documentation, not a HANA SQLScript syntax assumption.

column1: SQL-17 | A large report still runs out of memory with PACKAGE SIZE. What do you check?
column2:
Short answer
PACKAGE SIZE limits rows delivered to the target table per iteration; it does not guarantee bounded total memory. Check whether the program appends every package elsewhere, retains copies or references, or builds a large final result. With FOR ALL ENTRIES, the result can first be materialized in an internal system table, so small packages are not a reliable memory guard.

Reasoning and example
Suppose the report reads 1,000 rows per package but appends each package to lt_all. After a million source rows, lt_all still contains a million rows. Instead, process the current package and keep only the output actually needed: a bounded aggregate, streamed output, or an explicitly designed persisted result. A growing output table, cache, log or deep object graph can defeat an otherwise small package.

Start from the dump or failing phase: use ST22 where available, then compare memory snapshots before and after representative processing steps. Find which internal tables or retained objects grow. Distinguish ABAP session memory from expensive database intermediates; a database plan and an ABAP memory snapshot answer different questions. Select fewer columns and rows, avoid retained duplicates, then measure peak memory and runtime on realistic volumes.

Use INTO TABLE for the current package; APPENDING TABLE keeps adding rows. Do not COMMIT while a SELECT loop still needs its open cursor. If processing needs commits between chunks, design separate restartable reads with a stable continuation key and explicit consistency/transaction rules. Simply adding PACKAGE SIZE is not that design. FOR ALL ENTRIES requires particular care because packaging its target can happen after the full matching result is collected internally.

Avoid
A small package count is not proof of small peak memory. Inspect retained data, database work and the selection variant.

Read and verify
  • SAP ABAP SQL: SELECT INTO and PACKAGE SIZE
    Read the PACKAGE SIZE restrictions, including FOR ALL ENTRIES and INTO versus APPENDING.
  • SAP Memory Inspector: compare memory snapshots
    Inspect retained ABAP memory in comparable program phases; tool availability depends on the environment.
  • SAP ABAP COMMIT WORK and open cursors
    COMMIT WORK closes database cursors; a later fetch from that cursor can fail.

column1: ODATA-01 | OData V2 vs V4: what really changes, and what are the benefits of each?
column2:
Short answer
Both let an app read and change business data over HTTP. V4 gives a clearer API contract: separate actions and functions, a date-only type, and more expressive queries. V2 is valuable when existing SAP apps or partners already depend on it. For a new RAP app, I normally choose V4 when the backend and UI support the required features. V4 is not an automatic speed upgrade, and a V2 client cannot simply switch its URL and become a V4 client.

Reasoning and example
One example: a purchase-request app shows 20 orders and lets the user approve one. In V2, an inline count uses $inlinecount=allpages; its JSON collection is inside d.results with __count. In V4, use $count=true; the rows are in value with @odata.count. The screen can look identical, but the client must understand the different contract. Open the two Code examples to compare the same two orders.

Dates and operations: V4 has Edm.Date for a calendar date such as a delivery day. V2 has no equivalent date-only primitive; SAP services commonly use Edm.DateTime with a date-display annotation. V4 also distinguishes a read/calculation function from a potentially modifying action called with POST; V2 exposes service operations through function imports. These differences make intent clearer, but the exact RAP exposure still depends on the supported binding.

Queries: V4 can place query options inside $expand, for example requesting only selected fields of related items. This can avoid unnecessary transferred data when the service supports it. V2 already has $filter, $select, $expand and $batch, so these are not all new V4 features. Both versions support batch changesets; putting requests in one batch does not by itself make the whole batch atomic.

The practical benefit of V2 is compatibility: keep a working partner integration or older Fiori app without forcing a client rewrite. The benefit of V4 is its richer protocol and the matching modern SAPUI5/Fiori elements capabilities on supported releases. SAPUI5 V2 and V4 models have different programming APIs; changing only the service URL is not a migration.

My decision: use a supported V4 binding for the new purchase-request UI, but keep the existing V2 partner endpoint while that consumer migrates. Test metadata, dates, action calls, errors, paging and concurrency. RAP and draft are available in supported V2 scenarios too. Measure real payload size, round trips and backend processing before claiming a performance benefit.

Avoid
Do not claim that V2 only supports XML, V4 introduced $batch, or only V4 supports RAP/draft. Both can use JSON. Protocol support, SAP provider support and UI5 model capabilities are separate checks.

Read and verify

    Check the format and capabilities against the service version. For SAP, also verify the release, binding and UI5 support.
  • OASIS: OData V4 JSON format
    Check the format and capabilities against the service version. For SAP, also verify the release, binding and UI5 support.
  • OASIS: OData V4 protocol
    Check the format and capabilities against the service version. For SAP, also verify the release, binding and UI5 support.
  • SAP: RAP service binding
    Check the format and capabilities against the service version. For SAP, also verify the release, binding and UI5 support.
  • SAPUI5: changes compared to the V2 model
    Check the format and capabilities against the service version. For SAP, also verify the release, binding and UI5 support.

column1: ODATA-02 | What does $metadata describe?
column2:
Short answer
$metadata tells a client what the service offers. It lists fields, their types, keys, relationships and available operations. It describes the shape of the API, rather than the actual orders or customers. When a field or action is missing in an app, I check this document first.

Reasoning and example
Imagine adding an Approve action to a RAP business object, but no button appears in Fiori. First, I open the metadata of the endpoint the app actually calls. If the action is absent, I check whether the projection and service expose it. Debugging the action handler would not help yet because the client cannot see that action.

If the action is present, I next check the UI annotations, template support and the metadata used by the running app. The same approach works for a missing field. Adding a database column does not automatically add a property to the public service.

Avoid
A database field is not automatically visible in the service just because it exists in persistence.
RAP contract stack

Read from the client down to storage, then explain what each artifact contributes.
Explain it: Where would you restrict the exposed operation set?
Limit: Conceptual layers; the exact artifact set depends on the scenario and release.
HTTP request and response anatomy

Read the method, target, status and headers before interpreting the body. The sample domain is deliberately non-production.
Explain it: Which header describes the returned body, and which requests a response format?
Limit: A teaching example, not a runnable endpoint. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 use different wire framing.

Read and verify

    Check the protocol version and what the SAP service actually supports. A feature in the standard is not automatically available in every service.

column1: ODATA-03 | What are the main query options?
column2:
Short answer
OData query options tell the service which data the client needs. $filter chooses rows, $select chooses fields and $orderby sorts them. $top and $skip request a page, while $expand includes related data. I check which options the service supports and keep the request as small as the use case allows.

Reasoning and example
For a list of open orders, I request only the order number, customer and amount. I filter for open status and use a stable order, such as order number, before requesting the first page. This avoids sending full orders with every item when the screen only needs a short list.

If the user opens one order, I can request its items separately or use a supported $expand. Free-text $search is useful only when that service implements it. Count and search details also differ by protocol version. An option appearing in the OData standard does not mean an individual SAP endpoint accepts it.

Avoid
The existence of an OData option in the standard does not guarantee that every SAP service implements it.
Filtering, paging and total count

Count and paging answer different questions. Stable ordering matters when the client requests successive pages.
Explain it: For this example, what count belongs beside a page of five records?
Limit: Provider-side execution order may be optimized while preserving request semantics.

Read and verify
