    Check the protocol version and what the SAP service actually supports. A feature in the standard is not automatically available in every service.

column1: ODATA-04 | How do paging and total count work in V2 and V4?
column2:
Short answer
The total count tells the client how many rows match the filter, not how many fit on one page. Filter first, then count and page with a stable order. V2 commonly uses $inlinecount=allpages; V4 uses $count=true for an inline count. When the server returns a next link, the client should follow it.

Reasoning and example
A filter finds 500 open orders, but the screen displays 20 at a time. The response can correctly contain 20 orders and a total of 500. Returning 20 as the total would make the screen think there are no more pages. The /$count resource is another way to request a count.

Sorting matters too. Without a stable order, rows may move between pages even when the underlying data has not changed. Concurrent inserts or deletes can still affect offset paging. In a custom provider, I use the actual response API for that framework; I do not assume every Gateway implementation has the same method for setting the count.

Avoid
Use the response API of the actual provider. Do not assume every Gateway implementation has one generic SET_COUNT method.
Filtering, paging and total count

Count and paging answer different questions. Stable ordering matters when the client requests successive pages.
Explain it: For this example, what count belongs beside a page of five records?
Limit: Provider-side execution order may be optimized while preserving request semantics.

Read and verify

    Check the protocol version and what the SAP service actually supports. A feature in the standard is not automatically available in every service.

column1: ODATA-05 | What is the difference between actions and functions?
column2:
Short answer
In OData V4, a function reads or calculates a result without requesting a business change. An action can change business data and is called with POST. An operation can belong to a particular entity, a collection, or neither. V2 uses function imports for its operation patterns, so I check the version before explaining the endpoint.

Reasoning and example
Consider a request with a calculated delivery estimate and a Submit button. A supported function could return the estimate without saving or approving anything. Submit is an action because it moves the request to a new business state. The action must check whether that transition is allowed.

A bound action might operate on request 4711, while an unbound operation is not attached to a specific entity. These choices are part of the service definition and client contract. I do not implement approval behind GET: a read can be repeated by clients or infrastructure, and it should not unexpectedly approve a document.

Avoid
An HTTP GET should not create or approve business documents.

Read and verify
  • OASIS OData V4 protocol
    Check the protocol version and what the SAP service actually supports. A feature in the standard is not automatically available in every service.

column1: ODATA-06 | How do ETags prevent lost updates?
column2:
Short answer
An ETag is a version token for the data a client read. The client sends it back in If-Match when changing that data. If someone else has changed the version, the service normally rejects the request with HTTP 412. The user can then reload and resolve the conflict instead of losing the other person's changes.

Reasoning and example
Alice and Ben both read order 4711 with the same ETag. Alice changes the amount and saves, so the server now has a new version. Ben then sends his old ETag with a change to that same order. The service should reject Ben's stale update instead of silently overwriting Alice's work.

I test this with independent clients and inspect both the response and saved data. In RAP, the configured ETag field must change when the relevant data changes. Sending If-Match with a wildcard removes the specific version comparison. An ETag also does not replace authorization: Ben still needs permission to change the order.

Avoid
An If-Match wildcard can skip the intended version comparison. A timestamp also does not give a user permission to update.
Two editors and one version: an illustrated story

Alice and Ben read version 7. Alice updates successfully, producing version 8. Ben must not overwrite that newer state using the stale version 7 precondition.
Explain it: Why should the client refresh and resolve the conflict instead of blindly retrying its old payload?
Limit: Version numbers are illustrative. Real ETags are opaque validators; a failed If-Match precondition commonly returns HTTP 412. This is optimistic concurrency, not a pessimistic lock.

Read and verify
  • OASIS OData V4 protocol
    Check the protocol version and what the SAP service actually supports. A feature in the standard is not automatically available in every service.

column1: ODATA-07 | Is a batch request one database transaction?
column2:
Short answer
A batch is an envelope containing several requests. It does not automatically make them one transaction. Changesets provide atomic groups in multipart batches; OData 4.01 JSON batch has atomicity groups. I check what the service supports and inspect every inner result. An outer success response does not mean every operation succeeded.

Reasoning and example
Suppose a batch contains an order creation and an unrelated address change. These may belong to different groups and finish differently. If creating an order and its items must succeed together, the requests need the supported atomic grouping, or a supported deep-create operation for that structure. Deep create still needs correct backend transaction handling.

I test an invalid item and verify that the intended group leaves no partly created order. I also test a failure in a separate group and inspect each inner response. A service called V4 does not automatically implement every V4.01 JSON batch feature, so I verify its actual protocol and provider capabilities.

Avoid
HTTP 200 for a batch does not mean every operation inside it succeeded.
OData batch envelope and atomic groups

The outer envelope reduces HTTP packaging overhead; it does not establish one universal database transaction.
Explain it: If a later independent group fails, must an earlier successful group be rolled back?
Limit: Conceptual grouping, not an exact multipart or JSON batch payload.

Read and verify
  • OASIS OData V4 protocol
    Check the protocol version and what the SAP service actually supports. A feature in the standard is not automatically available in every service.
  • OASIS OData 4.01 JSON Format: Batch Requests
    Explains atomicityGroup in JSON batch. Check that the SAP service supports this protocol version and format.

column1: ODATA-08 | What are MPC_EXT and DPC_EXT in classic Gateway?
column2:
Short answer
In classic Gateway, MPC_EXT describes or extends the service model. DPC_EXT handles data requests and their errors. Customer changes belong in these extension classes rather than generated base classes. I keep reusable business rules in separate classes where practical. RAP uses a different model, with behavior implementations instead of this classic provider structure.

Reasoning and example
In a SEGW service, a list request may reach GET_ENTITYSET in DPC_EXT. I use that method to read the requested collection and map the result to the service response. CREATE_ENTITY, or the relevant deep-create implementation, handles an incoming creation request. Model changes and metadata belong on the model-provider side.

For a pricing rule used by several entry points, I put the calculation in a separate class and call it from the provider. This lets tests check the rule without building an HTTP request each time. It also reduces duplicated logic. I still test the provider itself for request mapping and correct business error responses.

Avoid
Putting all business rules in DPC_EXT makes them harder to reuse and test. MPC_EXT still matters when the model needs extending.

Read and verify
  • SAP Learning on OData
    Check the protocol version and what the SAP service actually supports. A feature in the standard is not automatically available in every service.

column1: ODATA-09 | How do authentication authorization and CSRF differ?
column2:
Short answer
Authentication tells the system who is calling. Authorization decides what that caller may do. CSRF protection helps stop unwanted requests that misuse a browser's logged-in session. Gateway writes commonly need a fetched CSRF token and the matching session. I check the endpoint's authentication flow because the exact requirements can differ.

Reasoning and example
An app reads an order successfully but gets 403 when saving. I inspect the error first. A missing CSRF token, missing service permission and a denied business action need different fixes, even if they use the same HTTP status. For a token problem, I check how the client fetched the token and kept the required session context.

If the user lacks approval permission, fetching another token will not help. The backend must still deny that action. CSRF protection is not a universal requirement imposed by the OData standard itself, and a valid token never grants the user access to a business operation.

Avoid
CSRF is not a universal OData-standard requirement and a valid token does not grant business permission.
Identity, authorization and feature control

Treat identity, business permission and contextual availability as separate checks.
Explain it: If Submit is disabled in Fiori, what happens when someone calls the service directly?
Limit: Static operation characteristics differ from dynamic instance/global feature checks.

Read and verify
  • SAP Learning on OData
    Check the protocol version and what the SAP service actually supports. A feature in the standard is not automatically available in every service.

column1: ODATA-10 | How do you design dates media and errors?
column2:
Short answer
I use the service's documented types for dates and timestamps, with a clear time-zone meaning. Files need the supported binary endpoint and correct content type. Errors should tell the client what failed without exposing secrets or internal details. I follow the actual Gateway or RAP error model because their implementation APIs are different.

Reasoning and example
An invoice date such as 12 October is a calendar date; converting it between time zones should not turn it into the previous day. An event timestamp represents a point in time and needs the agreed time-zone handling. V4 has Edm.Date, but V2 does not use the same date representation. I test both against the actual consumer.

For an invoice PDF, I verify the binary content, media type and download behavior. For a rejected update, I use Gateway's supported exception and message facilities, or RAP FAILED and REPORTED as required. The response should identify the problem clearly while keeping credentials and implementation details out.

Avoid
Edm.Date is a V4 type; do not assume identical date serialization in V2.

Read and verify
  • OASIS OData V4 protocol
    Check the protocol version and what the SAP service actually supports. A feature in the standard is not automatically available in every service.

column1: ODATA-11 | How do you troubleshoot a slow or failing Fiori request?
column2:
Short answer
I start with the exact failing or slow request from the browser. Then I check its response, service metadata and backend logs. For performance, I measure network size, backend time and database work before changing code. I also repeat the request with the affected user's permissions, because a developer preview may use a different setup.

Reasoning and example
A Fiori list takes eight seconds to open. The network trace shows that it requests every order together with all items through $expand. Each database statement may be reasonably fast, but the combined result is huge. I compare a small page request with the expanded request and measure row counts, payload size and total time.

If the request fails instead, I keep the timestamp and correlation ID to find the matching server log. I check routing, identity, authorization and metadata before blaming the UI. Traces belong in an authorized test context. A working ADT preview does not prove that the deployed app reaches the same endpoint under the same user.

Avoid
A working ADT preview does not prove a deployed app's routing, identity, metadata cache and backend authorization are correct.
Filtering, paging and total count

Count and paging answer different questions. Stable ordering matters when the client requests successive pages.
Explain it: For this example, what count belongs beside a page of five records?
Limit: Provider-side execution order may be optimized while preserving request semantics.

Read and verify

    Check the protocol version and what the SAP service actually supports. A feature in the standard is not automatically available in every service.

column1: ODATA-12 | How do you evolve an existing API safely?
column2:
Short answer
I treat an API as an agreement with every app that uses it. Changing keys, field names, types or action behavior can break those apps. I prefer additions that existing clients can tolerate and use a new version for breaking changes. Before retiring an old endpoint, I test the old clients and confirm they have moved.

Reasoning and example
Suppose an existing integration reads a field named CustomerNumber. Renaming it to BusinessPartner might make the new model clearer, but the old client still sends and reads the original name. Saved UI state or generated client code can also depend on that field. I identify these consumers before changing the public contract.

A separate RAP service can run alongside a classic Gateway service while consumers migrate. I document the new behavior, test both contracts and track actual use of the old endpoint. Even an added field needs compatibility checks for strict clients. Creating a new RAP service does not automatically update a V2 consumer or preserve every old business rule.

Avoid
A new RAP service does not automatically update an old V2 client or preserve every behavior that client relies on.

Read and verify
  • SAP Learning on UI service bindings
    Check the protocol version and what the SAP service actually supports. A feature in the standard is not automatically available in every service.

column1: BTP-01 | What is BTP and how is ABAP Cloud different?
column2:
Short answer
SAP BTP provides services for building apps, connecting systems and handling data. ABAP Cloud is a way of developing ABAP with allowed language features and released APIs. You can use that model in BTP ABAP environment and supported S/4HANA systems. BTP is therefore a platform; ABAP Cloud describes how you develop.

Reasoning and example
A team wants a supplier portal separate from its ERP system. It might build the ABAP part in BTP ABAP environment and call a released ERP API. Another team needs a field and validation close to an S/4HANA document. It might use ABAP Cloud directly in that supported S/4HANA system instead.

Both teams follow ABAP Cloud rules, but their applications run in different places. That difference matters for latency, identity and transactions. BTP ABAP environment is a managed ABAP system with its own development and delivery tools. It is not a regular Cloud Foundry application that you deploy with cf push.

Avoid
Do not call BTP ABAP simply a normal application container deployed with cf push.
Extension placement decision

Start from the business need and transaction boundary before choosing an extension location.
Explain it: When would local transactional consistency favor an on-stack extension?
Limit: Placement does not establish Clean Core level or availability in a specific edition.
BTP account and runtime map

Read the nesting as an organizational example, then distinguish the application, service instance and credentials.
Explain it: How is a service instance different from a binding or service key?
Limit: Schematic Cloud Foundry route; other BTP environments have different runtime structures.

Read and verify

    Check where the app runs, which user it calls as and how it connects.

column1: BTP-02 | How do global accounts subaccounts entitlements and spaces relate?
column2:
Short answer
A global account is the top-level place for managing your BTP use. Subaccounts separate applications and administration, for example by region or environment. Entitlements say which services and quotas you can use. For Cloud Foundry apps, organizations and spaces organize deployment. These layers have different jobs, so I check them separately when something cannot be created.

Reasoning and example
A developer wants to create a service in a test subaccount but cannot find the required plan. I check whether the global account has that entitlement and whether enough quota was assigned to the subaccount. I also check that the service is available in the selected region and that the developer has the necessary role.

If it is a Cloud Foundry application, I then check its organization and space. I do not apply that same space-based procedure to every BTP service. An entitlement permits consumption; it does not mean a running service instance already exists. The actual creation steps depend on the selected service and account setup.

Avoid
An entitlement is not a runtime container, and every BTP service does not require the same CF-space workflow.
BTP account and runtime map

Explain it: How is a service instance different from a binding or service key?

column1: BTP-03 | What is the difference between IaaS PaaS and SaaS?
column2:
Short answer
The difference is how much you operate yourself. With IaaS, you receive infrastructure and manage more of the software above it. With PaaS, the provider runs an application platform and you build on it. With SaaS, you use an existing application. In each case, I check who manages security, configuration and data.

Reasoning and example
Imagine a business needs an approval solution. With infrastructure services, its team may have to manage the operating system and application runtime before building the solution. A managed application platform removes much of that runtime work, but the team still develops and maintains its own approval code. A ready-made business application supplies the business capability itself.

A managed ABAP environment is a useful platform example: developers work within the available ABAP services and rules. They still own their custom application's behavior and access setup. SAP HANA Cloud is a managed database service, so I would not describe it as a finished business application simply because it is delivered as a service.

Avoid
SAP HANA Cloud is a managed database service, not a generic example of a finished business SaaS application.

Read and verify
  • SAP BTP documentation
    This is a documentation starting point, not proof of every statement. Find the named feature for your target release. The example decision and test plan are original study guidance.

column1: BTP-04 | What are a service instance binding and service key?
column2:
Short answer
A service instance is a service resource you have created. A binding connects an application to that resource and gives it the required connection information. A service key supplies credentials for a supported external-client use case. These are different objects; creating a binding does not always create a separate service key.

Reasoning and example
Suppose a Cloud Foundry app needs a database service. I create the supported service instance and bind the app to it. The app reads the supplied connection settings rather than keeping a password in source code. In Cloud Foundry, this information is commonly available through VCAP_SERVICES, though other delivery methods exist.

An external tool may instead need a service key if that service supports the use case. I protect and rotate those credentials too. When a binding changes, I check whether the app needs a restart or restage to use the new settings. A local default-env.json file is a development convention, not the universal way Cloud Foundry delivers credentials.

column1: BTP-05 | What do containers buildpacks droplets and routes do?
column2:
Short answer
In Cloud Foundry, a buildpack prepares an app with the runtime it needs. Staging produces a runnable package called a droplet. Containers run isolated app instances, and routes send requests to them. One app can have several instances. Reliability still depends on those instances and the services they need, not just on having a container.

Reasoning and example
A Java app is staged with a suitable buildpack, which prepares the runtime and application package. Two app instances then run that package. A route lets users reach the app without knowing which instance handles their request. If one instance fails, the design needs enough healthy capacity and working dependencies to keep serving users.

During blue-green deployment, traffic moves from the old version to the new one. I still check database compatibility and what happens to requests already running on the old version. Changing a route does not repair an incompatible database change. A container is also not the same as a full virtual machine.

column1: BTP-06 | What do destinations and Cloud Connector solve?
column2:
Short answer
A destination stores connection and authentication settings for a service call. Cloud Connector allows configured cloud access to selected on-premise resources. Together they help an app reach the backend without putting passwords in code. I still check the caller's permissions and the API's release status. Connectivity alone does not make an internal SAP API supported.

Reasoning and example
A BTP app needs to read orders from an on-premise system. I check the destination, the configured Cloud Connector connection and the specific resource exposed through it. Then I verify the certificate or token and the user's backend permissions. A connection can be technically available while the business request is still forbidden.

When troubleshooting, I locate the failing step instead of changing all settings at once. Cloud Connector exposes configured resources; it is not an unrestricted opening into the entire company network. I also confirm that the chosen order API is allowed for this extension. A successful request to an internal endpoint is not proof that SAP supports that use.

column1: BTP-07 | How do remote transactions differ from local RAP transactions?
column2:
Short answer
A remote API usually saves data in a separate transaction. If my local RAP transaction rolls back, the remote system may still keep its change. I therefore plan how to find the original result, retry safely and handle partial success. A timeout means the outcome may be unknown; it does not prove the remote operation failed.

Reasoning and example
Our app asks a remote payment service to create a payment. The service creates it, but the response is lost. If we simply send a new creation request, we may pay twice. I use the service's documented idempotency mechanism, meaning the same request identifier reuses the original business effect, or query the payment by a stable reference.

The local app keeps a recoverable pending or uncertain status until it knows the result. If one side succeeds and the other cannot complete, a supported cancellation or other compensating business step may be needed. Calling HTTP inside a RAP action does not make the two systems share one rollback.

column1: BTP-08 | What makes event-driven integration reliable?
column2:
Short answer
Reliable event handling assumes messages can be delayed or delivered again. I publish events in a way that matches committed business data and use durable delivery when needed. The consumer remembers a stable event or business identifier so repeating a message does not repeat the effect. I also define retries and how failed messages reach an operator.

Reasoning and example
An order submission should start one approval workflow. If an event is delivered twice, the consumer checks the request and event identifiers and finds the workflow already started. It must not create another process just because the transport delivered another copy. The publication mechanism must also avoid announcing a submission that later rolls back.

I test a temporary outage, a duplicate delivery and a message that repeatedly fails. After bounded retries, the failed message needs a visible recovery path, such as a dead-letter queue where supported. Ordering and retention depend on the configured broker and protocol. I do not promise global ordering or exactly-once business processing without proving the complete design.

column1: BTP-09 | Which tools matter to an ABAP developer on BTP?
column2:
Short answer
I use ADT in Eclipse for ABAP development. Fiori tools support UI development, while the BTP cockpit and service tools manage accounts, access and connections. The correct tool depends on where the application runs. For ABAP work, I should be able to find a released API, run checks and tests, and investigate a failed service call.

To build an ABAP extension, I first connect ADT to the intended ABAP system. I check available APIs and their release status there, then develop and test the service. If the project includes a Fiori app, I use supported Fiori tooling for that UI rather than assuming the ABAP deployment also deploys every frontend artifact.

For a connection failure, I may need the BTP cockpit or a service-specific monitor to inspect roles, destinations or communication setup. I verify tool versions against the target system. column1: BTP-10 | How would you secure and operate a side-by-side extension?
column2:
Short answer
I secure both the extension and its calls to other systems. Users and technical identities get only the permissions they need, and credentials stay outside source code. I monitor failures and response times, with a clear owner for recovery. Production readiness also includes safe deployment, API compatibility and a tested way to recover data or service availability.

Reasoning and example
A supplier portal works in development, but production needs more than a successful API call. I check which identity reads each supplier's data, how credentials are stored and revoked, and whether logs hide sensitive fields. Test and production use separate configuration so a test request cannot accidentally post a production order.

For an outage, the operator needs a request identifier, a visible status and instructions for safe retry. I also define who owns failures in the ERP API and who owns portal failures. Before changing a dependency, we test compatibility. Backup and recovery procedures must fit the actual services rather than rely on an assumed platform guarantee.

column1: RICEFW-01 | What does RICEFW mean, and how would you scope a deliverable?
column2:
Short answer
RICEFW groups work into Reports, Interfaces, Conversions, Enhancements, Forms and Workflows. I still need a clear business result before estimating any of them. I ask what data is involved, who uses it and what happens on failure. I also check the target system, supported options and who will operate the solution.

Reasoning and example
A request says 'build one supplier conversion.' That sounds small, but it hides several jobs: cleaning source data, mapping fields, checking mandatory values, loading through a supported interface and proving the right suppliers were created. I clarify duplicate rules and expected volume before giving an estimate.

I also define acceptance checks, such as matching supplier counts and recording every rejected row. The cutover plan needs an owner and a safe restart procedure. If standard migration functionality already meets these needs, custom code may be unnecessary. The RICEFW label helps organize delivery; it does not select the technology or tell us the true effort.

column1: RICEFW-02 | How do you choose between a standard API, IDoc, migration tooling, and BDC?
column2:
Short answer
I choose the supported business interface that fits the task and target system. A one-time migration may suit migration tooling; ongoing integration may suit an API or IDoc. BDC can be a classic-system fallback, but screen changes make it fragile. I check required fields, volume and recovery instead of choosing by name alone.

Reasoning and example
For a one-time supplier migration, I first check the delivered migration objects and supported fields. If they cover the requirement, building a permanent custom interface may add needless maintenance. For a continuing partner feed, I compare the available APIs or IDoc scenarios and how they report and recover from individual errors.

BDC drives screens, so its suitability depends on the screen flow and configuration. It is not a general ABAP Cloud option. A BAPI may also lack a required field or be unavailable for direct cloud development. I verify release status and Clean Core classification individually; the word BAPI does not automatically mean Level B or suitability for mass loading.

column1: RICEFW-03 | How do BAdIs, customer exits, and user exits differ?
column2:
Short answer
A BAdI is an object-oriented extension interface. Classic customer exits can add function, screen or menu behavior through enhancement projects. User exit often means an older application-specific routine. I check the actual extension's timing and allowed use. A BAdI is only suitable if it supports the needed change in the target release.

Reasoning and example
Suppose an order must reject an invalid reference before saving. I look for a supported extension that runs early enough and can report that error. An extension that runs only after posting would not solve the requirement, even if its name sounds relevant. For a BAdI, I also inspect whether filters or multiple implementations are supported by its definition.

In classic systems, SMOD describes customer-enhancement components and CMOD manages their projects. Some SD routines named USEREXIT use another older mechanism. These names are not interchangeable. A released BAdI is a good choice when it fits, but being a BAdI alone does not prove ABAP Cloud availability or eliminate upgrade testing.

Avoid
CMOD/SMOD exits and routines named USEREXIT are not the same mechanism. Filters and multiple implementations depend on the BAdI definition.

column1: RICEFW-04 | What is the difference between implicit and explicit enhancement options?
column2:
Short answer
Explicit enhancement options are places deliberately marked for extensions. Implicit options exist at predefined positions without a marker there. An enhancement point adds code; an enhancement section can replace the defined section's implementation. These are extension mechanisms. Explicit enhancement does not automatically mean editing SAP's original source directly.

Reasoning and example
A standard program contains an explicit enhancement point after a calculation. A customer implementation can add permitted logic at that point. An implicit option may instead be available at a predefined location, such as a procedure boundary, without a dedicated enhancement marker in that location. I inspect the actual option and surrounding behavior before using either.

An enhancement spot organizes explicit options; an enhancement implementation contains the customer logic. Replacing an enhancement section deserves extra care because it can remove standard processing the application needs. These classic mechanisms are also different from released ABAP Cloud extension contracts. I check target support instead of assuming every available editor option is an approved extension.

Avoid
Explicit enhancement does not simply mean modifying SAP source. Source modification is a separate technique.

column1: RICEFW-05 | How would you design a reliable interface?
column2:
Short answer
I define what the message means, who may send it and how success or failure is reported. Synchronous calls fit immediate answers; asynchronous processing can let systems work at different times. Both need clear duplicate and recovery rules. I choose the protocol after understanding these needs, including what to do when the outcome is unknown.

Reasoning and example
An interface posts an invoice, but the sender times out before receiving the result. The receiver may already have saved it. I use a stable request reference and a documented way to query or reuse the original result before retrying. Otherwise, a temporary network problem can become a duplicate invoice.

A temporary outage may justify delayed retries. An invalid company code needs correction instead of repeated automatic posting attempts. I record correlation information so support can follow the same request through both systems. Whether the interface uses OData, SOAP or IDoc, a transport acknowledgment or accepted message is not proof that the business document was posted.

column1: RICEFW-06 | How would you troubleshoot a failed IDoc in a classic system?
column2:
Short answer
I find the IDoc for the business request and read its control data, segments and status history. The detailed error usually shows whether the problem is routing, mapping, master data, permissions or posting logic. I fix that cause before retrying. I also check for an existing business document so recovery does not post it twice.

Reasoning and example
A supplier-order IDoc has an application error because a material is unknown. In a classic system, WE02 or WE05 can show the IDoc and its messages. I inspect the incoming material value and its mapping, then correct the master data or mapping through the approved process. Changing a destination would not fix that particular error.

If the IDoc never reached application processing, partner profiles, ports, process codes or communication logs may be the right next check. Where appropriate and authorized, BD87 supports reprocessing. After retry, I inspect the linked business result. Repeated retries or a manual status change can hide the original problem and may create duplicate effects.

Avoid
Changing a status or repeatedly reprocessing without checking business effects can hide the cause or create duplicates.

column1: RICEFW-07 | What makes a data conversion safe and supportable?
column2:
Short answer
I separate cleaning and checking the data from loading it. Every source record needs a stable identity, a visible result and a safe restart rule. I use supported business interfaces and reconcile business totals after loading. Trial runs reveal bad data and realistic runtime. The cutover plan must also say who stops, restarts or repairs the load.

Reasoning and example
A document migration loads 10,000 source records. Matching that count is not enough: some documents may have wrong currencies, values or relationships. I reconcile counts and amounts by company and currency, and keep rejected records separate from accepted records whose follow-up work is still pending. Trial loads help discover these problems before cutover.

If one package fails, the rerun must skip or safely identify documents already posted. Stable source references help link the source to the actual business results. I also plan load order, data freezes and recovery ownership. Direct table updates may bypass application rules, so a technically completed write is not evidence of a correct migration.

column1: RICEFW-08 | How do you choose between SAPscript, Smart Forms, and Adobe output forms?
column2:
Short answer
I start with the output framework supported by the business application. Existing systems may use SAPscript or Smart Forms; other scenarios use Adobe-based forms with the required rendering setup. S/4HANA does not use one universal output solution for everything. I check document needs, languages and delivery channels before choosing or replacing a form technology.

Reasoning and example
An invoice PDF looks correct in one test, but that proves only part of the output process. I separately check how the application decides to generate it, how data reaches the form, how the layout renders and how the result reaches the customer. Email routing or spool processing can fail even when the PDF itself is fine.

My test set includes long item lists, page breaks, totals, several languages, fonts, attachments and reprints. I also verify the application's actual output framework before proposing a BRF+ or Adobe change. An Adobe output form need not be interactive, and not every S/4HANA application follows the same framework or migration path.

column1: RICEFW-09 | How do classic Workflow, Flexible Workflow, and SAP Build Process Automation differ?
column2:
Short answer
Classic SAP Business Workflow models processes in the ABAP system. Flexible Workflow offers configurable approval scenarios using SAP workflow concepts. SAP Build Process Automation runs on BTP and supports automation across systems. I first check the delivered business scenario, then choose the option that fits its approval rules, integrations and operating needs.

Reasoning and example
For purchase approval, I first inspect the supported Flexible Workflow scenario and its available start conditions, steps and extensions. It may already cover the business requirement without a custom process. A cross-system approval involving several applications may instead need a BTP-based solution, depending on available connectors and requirements.

These options are not automatic substitutes for each other. Flexible Workflow builds on SAP workflow concepts, and its features vary by business scenario. A custom RAP Submit action also does not create a complete approval process by itself. We still need process creation, approver selection, decisions, callbacks, permissions and a way to handle failures.

Flexible Workflow uses SAP workflow concepts, and available features depend on the business scenario.

column1: RICEFW-10 | What are a workflow container, task, work item, and agent?
column2:
Short answer
A workflow container holds the process data. Bindings pass that data between workflow components. A task defines work; a work item is one running instance of that task. Agent determination finds the person who should do it. The process also needs a clear response when nobody can act or a decision cannot be completed.

Reasoning and example
A request for 5,000 EUR starts an approval workflow. The container might carry the request ID and the information needed to choose an approver. Bindings pass the relevant values to the approval task. The created work item is the actual item the selected approver handles; the task is its reusable definition.

I avoid copying every field if that would leave the workflow using stale business data. I also test the case where no valid approver is found and define an error or fallback route. An email notification is only a notification, not the work item itself. Being selected as an agent does not remove the need for business authorization.

column1: RICEFW-11 | How should a RAP submit action start an approval process reliably?
column2:
Short answer
Submit should check the request and change its state through RAP's transaction rules. The external approval process should start in a way coordinated with a successful save. I use the supported event or integration mechanism for that release. Stable identifiers and duplicate handling stop retries from starting several workflows for the same submission.

Reasoning and example
A request moves from Created to Submitted. Only after that change is successfully committed should the integration create its external approval process using the supported mechanism. If save fails, we must not leave an approval waiting for a request that never became submitted. If delivery is repeated, the receiver should find the existing process rather than create another.

I link the request version and workflow instance so an authorized callback can later update the correct state. Draft activation is a separate RAP operation unless the application explicitly coordinates it with submission. I verify the target's event capabilities instead of assuming one universal implementation. Calling a workflow endpoint before save completes is not a reliable substitute.

Calling an external workflow endpoint before save succeeds can start approval for a document that never committed.

column1: RICEFW-12 | How do you handle duplicate events, stale approvals, and callback retries?
column2:
Short answer
I assume events and callbacks can arrive more than once. The receiver checks a stable event or process identifier before repeating work. An approval also checks the current request version, state and caller permissions. An old decision must not approve a changed or withdrawn request. Repeated successful callbacks should have a stable, safe result.

A manager receives approval for version one of a request. Before the manager answers, the requester withdraws it or changes a material detail. When the old approval arrives, the callback compares the stored workflow link and request version with the current record. It rejects or handles the stale decision according to the business rule instead of approving the new data.

A retry of a decision already applied should return a safe result without applying the effect twice. I retain an audit trail and test deadline escalation racing with the original approver. A queue or HTTP success response alone does not provide exactly-once business behavior; the application must enforce the intended transitions.

column1: RICEFW-13 | How would you diagnose a workflow that did not start or is stuck?
column2:

A request is submitted but nobody sees an approval. First, I confirm that submission actually committed. Then I check whether an event was sent and whether the start conditions selected the intended workflow. If a workflow exists, I inspect its context and agent determination. An existing work item with no recipient needs a different fix from a missing start event.

In classic systems, SWEL can show recorded events when tracing is enabled, and SWI1 can help inspect work items and logs. Cloud scenarios use their supported monitors. No SWEL entry proves little if tracing was off. A session breakpoint may also miss background processing that runs under another user.

column1: RICEFW-14 | How would you test a workflow or enhancement end to end?
column2:

A request is submitted, then changed before the manager answers. My test sends the old approval and checks that it cannot silently approve the new request version. For an enhancement, I test a normal save and a rejected save to check its timing and transaction effects. A mock endpoint is useful for checking request contents and simulated errors. It does not prove the real system's identity setup, event delivery or callback behavior. I record which checks used real integration and which used doubles.

column1: RICEFW-15 | Which S/4HANA changes can affect existing ABAP developments?
column2:
Short answer
I check the simplification information and custom-code findings for the target S/4HANA release. Important areas can include MATDOC, ACDOCA, Business Partner and changed output or transactions. I trace how the existing application uses the affected objects. Replacing a table name mechanically is not enough; the business meaning and supported access may have changed.

A report reads inventory data directly from old tables. Before changing it, I list its reads, writes and called transactions and check the target release's recommended access. I compare the old report's intended result with the new data model, then test totals, filters and runtime using representative business cases.

The same care applies to finance and Business Partner changes. Business Partner integration does not mean every customer and supplier table simply disappeared. Compatibility mechanisms and migration prerequisites vary. I use release-specific findings and functional tests to decide the change, rather than assume that replacing a reference with MATDOC or ACDOCA preserves the original behavior.

column1: TEST-01 | What makes a useful ABAP Unit test?
column2:
Short answer
A useful test checks a real rule with known inputs and a clear expected result. It should behave the same each time and not depend on another test or shared production data. I cover errors and limits as well as success. A test that only creates an object or reaches a line of code says little about whether the business behavior is correct.

Reasoning and example
For a date-range validator, I prepare a valid range, equal start and end dates, and an end date before the start. The expected result follows the actual business rule: equal dates might be allowed or rejected, so I make that decision explicit. The test name describes the rule that would be broken.

I keep the validator real and control any outside dependency, such as the current date. A failing assertion should explain which result was wrong. High coverage is useful for finding untested areas, but a test can execute every line without checking the right outcome. I therefore review the cases and assertions, not only the percentage. Fresh mutable fixtures belong in setup; do not rely on another test having run first.

Avoid
High statement coverage alone does not prove that assertions or business cases are meaningful.
Testing scope and evidence

The widening base suggests many focused checks, but there is no mandatory numerical ratio.
Explain it: Which risk remains after an ABAP Unit test with doubles passes?
Limit: Conceptual coverage map, not a count of tests actually run in SAP.

column1: TEST-02 | How does dependency injection help?
column2:
Short answer
Dependency injection means giving an object the helpers it needs instead of letting it create all of them internally. A test can supply a fake repository, clock or service client. Production supplies the real one through the same interface. This makes failures and timing predictable in tests. I keep the behavior I am testing real, rather than mocking it away.

Reasoning and example
A retry policy may retry an idempotent remote lookup once. In a unit test, I supply a client that returns a timeout on its first call and customer C20 on its second. A controlled clock or delay seam avoids waiting real minutes. The test checks the actual policy: which failures it retries, how many attempts it allows and what result it returns.

Another case returns a business rejection that should not be retried. A third returns two timeouts: the policy must stop after two calls, request only one delay and return the final failure. If I replaced the retry policy itself with a mock, I would only prove my mock setup. The interface should describe the few operations the policy needs; copying a huge client interface makes both the design and test unnecessarily complicated.

Avoid
Mocking everything, including the object being tested, removes the behavior the test should verify.
Testing scope and evidence

The widening base suggests many focused checks, but there is no mandatory numerical ratio.

column1: TEST-03 | How would you test a RAP business object?
column2:
Short answer
I test the real RAP business object with controlled data, using suitable EML tests where supported. I check successful changes, rejected changes, messages and what is saved. I also cover authorization and conflicting edits at the appropriate test level. Service and UI tests cover different behavior. Available RAP test frameworks depend on the target release.

Reasoning and example
For a Submit action, I create a request in the required initial state and call the real behavior. I check the resulting state and the FAILED and REPORTED responses. I verify persistence only after the intended save, because a change in the transaction buffer is not yet a committed database record.

A second test submits an invalid request and checks that it is rejected without an unintended saved change. Separate tests cover the service protocol and real user permissions. A mocked Fiori success screen or a double replacing the BO cannot prove the implementation works. I state which dependencies were controlled and which real integration paths were actually executed.

Avoid
A mock Fiori success or a doubled BO does not establish that the real RAP implementation works.
Testing scope and evidence

The widening base suggests many focused checks, but there is no mandatory numerical ratio.

column1: TEST-04 | How do SQL and CDS test doubles help?
column2:
Short answer
SQL and CDS test doubles replace supported database dependencies with test-controlled data. That lets a test run with known rows instead of changing production-like tables. I use the framework suited to the component and configure its dependencies carefully. I also clean up the test environment. These tests do not prove real database performance, network behavior or the complete authorization setup.

Reasoning and example
For a CDS total, I load a small fixture with two currencies, an order without a matching text and one record that could match several joined rows. Then I check the expected totals and ensure no extra rows appear. This exposes model errors more clearly than testing against whatever data happens to be in a shared system.

The setup must cover the dependencies the tested component actually reads. An incorrect double configuration can test a different situation from production. After each test, the environment must be reset or destroyed appropriately. I still use real-system checks for the execution plan, deployed access control and integration behavior; a passing double-based test is not a HANA benchmark. A common lifecycle is to create the double environment once in class_setup, clear and load fixture data in setup, and destroy it in class_teardown. Use the actual framework contract; RISK LEVEL HARMLESS does not create the isolation.

Avoid
Passing a double-based test is not a HANA execution-plan benchmark.
Testing scope and evidence

The widening base suggests many focused checks, but there is no mandatory numerical ratio.

column1: TEST-05 | What does ATC cover and what remains outside it?
column2:
Short answer
ATC runs the static checks configured for the system and check variant. It can find code problems and check supported API or enhancement usage. A pass means those checks found no blocking issue; it does not prove every business case works. Unit tests, security tests and deployment checks are still needed. I record exemptions and the target release used for the checks.

Reasoning and example
A new RAP service may pass syntax and activation but still return the wrong total. It may also pass unit tests while using an API forbidden by the target rules. ATC and runtime tests answer different questions, so I keep their results separate in the handoff instead of summarizing everything as tested.

I record the ATC variant and review any exemptions, including their reason and owner. If the target release changes, I recheck which rules and API classifications apply. An empty finding list is useful evidence, but it is not proof of complete Clean Core compliance, correct authorization for every user or a successful end-to-end business process.

Avoid
Do not say that an ATC pass proves an application is error-free or fully Clean Core compliant.
Testing scope and evidence

column1: TEST-06 | What security tests would you include?
column2:
Short answer
I test what a user may do and what they must be prevented from doing. That includes direct API reads and actions, not only visible buttons. I check realistic roles, company or organizational limits, bulk requests and sensitive fields. Login, CDS access control and operation authorization are separate checks. Error messages must also avoid revealing data the user may not see.

Reasoning and example
A user assigned to company A should see A records and be unable to read B records by editing a URL. I also try an action using a known B record key, because hiding B in a list does not prove that the action is protected. A mixed bulk request should behave according to the documented authorization rules.

I test with restricted users as well as an administrator. The UI may hide fields or disable buttons for convenience, but a client can still call the backend directly. I inspect error details too: a rejection must not return another company's sensitive data. These checks make the actual security boundary visible.

Avoid
Feature control, UI.hidden and disabled buttons are not sufficient security boundaries.
CDS security boundaries

Review security where consumers enter the model, rather than assuming that lower layers protect every upper view.
Explain it: Which two tests prove that an exposed service rejects unauthorized access?
Limit: Authorization behavior depends on the access path and supported DCL inheritance mechanisms.
Identity, authorization and feature control

Treat identity, business permission and contextual availability as separate checks.
Explain it: If Submit is disabled in Fiori, what happens when someone calls the service directly?
Limit: Static operation characteristics differ from dynamic instance/global feature checks.

column1: TEST-07 | How do you test concurrency and rollback?
column2:
Short answer
I use separate consumers to reproduce conflicting changes. One saves first, then the other tries to save an older version. I check the expected ETag and lock behavior. I also trigger a failure and inspect whether unintended partial data remains. Remote calls need separate retry and recovery tests, because rolling back the local database cannot undo every external effect.

Reasoning and example
Two clients read the same document version. Client A changes and saves it. Client B then sends a change with its older ETag, and the service should reject it where that concurrency check applies. I inspect both the response and stored document, rather than assume an error message guarantees the state stayed correct.

For rollback, I fail a child operation inside the intended atomic group and check the related records. A separate scenario makes a remote call time out after the remote system may have acted. That case needs reconciliation or safe retry logic; a local rollback alone cannot tell me whether the remote work happened.

Avoid
Sequential happy-path tests cannot establish concurrency safety.
OData batch envelope and atomic groups

The outer envelope reduces HTTP packaging overhead; it does not establish one universal database transaction.
Explain it: If a later independent group fails, must an earlier successful group be rolled back?
Limit: Conceptual grouping, not an exact multipart or JSON batch payload.
Testing scope and evidence

The widening base suggests many focused checks, but there is no mandatory numerical ratio.
Explain it: Which risk remains after an ABAP Unit test with doubles passes?
Limit: Conceptual coverage map, not a count of tests actually run in SAP.
Two editors and one version: an illustrated story

Alice and Ben read version 7. Alice updates successfully, producing version 8. Ben must not overwrite that newer state using the stale version 7 precondition.
Explain it: Why should the client refresh and resolve the conflict instead of blindly retrying its old payload?
Limit: Version numbers are illustrative. Real ETags are opaque validators; a failed If-Match precondition commonly returns HTTP 412. This is optimistic concurrency, not a pessimistic lock.

column1: TEST-08 | What would you include in a transport and deployment handoff?
column2:
Short answer
A useful handoff says what must be moved, configured and checked in the target system. I include object dependencies, roles, service setup and required communication settings. I record the source revision, target version, checks actually run and checks still pending. I also explain recovery if deployment fails. A successful transport import is only one part of making the application usable.

Reasoning and example
For a RAP service, I check that the data model, behavior, DCL, metadata and service dependencies arrive together. If a UI is involved, its deployment and roles must also be ready. A missing authorization or endpoint setup can leave a technically imported application unusable. I list these steps with an owner and expected result.

After import, the team should open the real endpoint with a representative user and run the agreed business flow. Local publication in the development system does not prove publication or configuration elsewhere. The handoff identifies the tested revision and a recovery approach, so support can tell what changed and what to do if the rollout is incomplete.

Avoid
Local binding publication or a successful source copy is not proof of cross-system deployment.

column1: TEST-09 | How would you investigate a production defect?
column2:
Short answer
I collect the exact symptom, affected users, time, inputs and deployed revision. Then I use authorized logs, dumps and traces to narrow down the cause. I reproduce safely and test a focused fix against the failing case. I separate code problems from configuration and data problems. Until evidence confirms the cause, I describe my explanation as a hypothesis.

Reasoning and example
A user reports occasional duplicate documents. I compare request identifiers, retries, timeouts and commit points to see whether the same operation was executed twice. A UI delay might hide the symptom without fixing a retry after a network failure. I avoid exposing sensitive payloads while collecting enough evidence to follow the request.

Once the sequence is understood, I add a regression case that reproduces it and verify the expected outcome after the change. I also check the ordinary success path and any duplicate-recovery behavior. The rollout record should distinguish confirmed findings from open questions, so the next person does not treat an attractive but untested explanation as the root cause.

Avoid
A plausible explanation without evidence should not be presented as a confirmed root cause.

column1: TEST-10 | How should you describe tests you have not run?
column2:
Short answer
I say exactly what I checked and what I did not run. Prepared test cases are not passing test results. I name the source revision, environment and observed outcome for actual runs. If I only reviewed local files, I say that clearly and list the SAP checks still needed. This makes the handoff useful and avoids giving false confidence.

Reasoning and example
An honest handoff might say: I reviewed revision [revision] and prepared EML cases for valid submission, missing data and rejected authorization. I have not run them in SAP yet. Activation, ABAP Unit and ATC must still be executed in [target system]. The placeholders must be replaced with the real revision and environment.

If local JSON or frontend checks passed, I list those as their own results. They can prove file structure or browser behavior, but they cannot prove SAP activation or a real RAP save. I include the exact next action and expected result so another developer can finish validation without guessing which evidence is still missing.

Avoid
Never claim a passing SAP syntax check, measured coverage or successful activation without an actual run.
Testing scope and evidence

The widening base suggests many focused checks, but there is no mandatory numerical ratio.

column1: STORY-01 | How would you introduce yourself for an ABAP role?
column2:
Short answer
I would give a short, truthful summary of my ABAP work and connect it to this role. I would name my main responsibilities, two relevant strengths and one real example. I would clearly separate production work from courses or personal projects. The aim is to give the interviewer useful starting points, rather than list every technology I have heard of.

Reasoning and example
Use this outline with your own facts: My current focus is [real area]. I mainly work on [actual responsibilities]. My strongest relevant skills are [skill one] and [skill two]. In [real project or clearly labeled lab], I handled [your contribution], and the result was [supported outcome]. This role interests me because [honest reason].

Keep the first version short enough to say naturally. Prepare a deeper explanation for each claim, including the system context and what you personally did. If RAP experience comes from a lab, say so and explain what you built and tested there. Do not fill missing experience with invented clients, years or metrics.

Avoid
Do not invent years, clients, performance metrics or RAP production experience.
Explain decisions with evidence

Practice a 60-second version first, then expand the mechanism and evidence when prompted.
Explain it: Can you name the decision, trade-off and evidence without inventing metrics?

column1: STORY-02 | How do you explain a project you owned?
column2:
Short answer
I start with the problem and who needed it solved. Then I explain my own responsibility, the important constraint and the design I chose. I describe how I tested the work and what actually happened after delivery. Finally, I mention one thing I would improve. I keep the background short so there is time for technical follow-up questions.

Reasoning and example
Prepare a real example using these prompts: [users] needed [business outcome]. I owned [specific part], while [other team] owned [their part]. The main constraint was [actual constraint]. I chose [design] because [reason], and checked it with [tests actually run]. The observed result was [truthful outcome].

Be ready to draw the request and save flow, explain one rejected option and discuss a failure case. If you have a classic ABAP example and a modern service example, prepare both. A learning project is still useful when labeled accurately. Listing transaction codes alone does not explain ownership; your decisions and evidence show what you contributed.

Avoid
Listing transactions and technologies without explaining the result does not show ownership.
Explain decisions with evidence

Practice a 60-second version first, then expand the mechanism and evidence when prompted.
Explain it: Can you name the decision, trade-off and evidence without inventing metrics?

column1: STORY-03 | How do you answer a question when the SAP release is unknown?
column2:
Short answer
I explain the part of the answer that is generally true, then identify what depends on the SAP edition or release. I ask for that missing context and say how I would verify support. I can also describe a supported alternative if the feature is unavailable. This is more useful than guessing syntax or just saying it depends.

Reasoning and example
For a RAP question, I can first explain the business need: for example, reject an invalid change before saving. Then I identify the exact feature or BDL syntax whose availability needs checking in the target release. For an API, I check whether the required operation is released for the intended use, not just whether an object with that name exists.

A spoken answer can use placeholders honestly: On [known environment] I used [actual feature]. For your release, I would check [specific documentation or repository release information] before choosing it. If unavailable, I would evaluate [real alternative]. This shows a verification method without pretending all SAP systems support the same implementation.

Avoid
Saying it depends without explaining what it depends on is not a useful answer.
Explain decisions with evidence

Practice a 60-second version first, then expand the mechanism and evidence when prompted.
Explain it: Can you name the decision, trade-off and evidence without inventing metrics?
Limit: A rehearsal structure, not a scripted personal history or a substitute for technical depth.

column1: STORY-04 | How do you discuss a performance improvement?
column2:
Short answer
I explain what was slow, how I measured it and what data volume the measurement used. Then I describe the bottleneck, the change and the measured result. I also explain how I checked that the result stayed correct. I use only figures from my actual work. If no reliable numbers were recorded, I say that instead of inventing a speedup.

Reasoning and example
Prepare a real sequence: [operation] was slow with [representative workload]. I used [tool actually used] and found [observed cause]. I changed [specific access or processing step]. Under [comparable test conditions], the result changed from [measured baseline] to [measured outcome]. I checked correctness using [actual comparison or tests].

Be ready to explain why the change helped. Fewer database round trips, fewer transferred rows or an appropriate internal-table key are clearer than saying the code was optimized. Include a limitation, such as a workload not yet measured, if it is real. If your example is a lab benchmark, identify it as one and do not present its results as production evidence.

Avoid
Do not claim a speedup from code appearance alone or memorize an invented percentage.
Explain decisions with evidence

Practice a 60-second version first, then expand the mechanism and evidence when prompted.
Explain it: Can you name the decision, trade-off and evidence without inventing metrics?
Limit: A rehearsal structure, not a scripted personal history or a substitute for technical depth.

column1: STORY-05 | How would you defend an architecture trade-off?
column2:
Short answer
I compare options using the actual requirement: what must save together, which APIs exist, who uses the result and how failures are handled. I state my choice and its main cost. I also explain what would make me choose differently. A good answer shows why the decision fits this situation, not loyalty to a particular SAP product.

Reasoning and example
For a real extension decision, describe [business need] and the change that must happen reliably. If validation must reject a local save, explain which supported extension point can run at the right time. If a separate portal is involved, explain its remote calls, login needs and recovery when one system is unavailable.

Then state the evidence you would check: API availability in [target product], transaction behavior and a realistic failure test. Use your actual experience or label the example as a proposed design. Saying always use BTP or always use RAP skips the reason for the choice. A convincing answer includes the downside of the selected option and when it stops being suitable.

Avoid
Always use RAP or always use BTP is not an architecture argument.
Explain decisions with evidence

Practice a 60-second version first, then expand the mechanism and evidence when prompted.
Explain it: Can you name the decision, trade-off and evidence without inventing metrics?
Limit: A rehearsal structure, not a scripted personal history or a substitute for technical depth.

column1: STORY-06 | What should you ask the interviewer?
column2:
Short answer
I would ask about the SAP systems, the work I would own and how the team delivers changes. I want to know the mix of classic ABAP and RAP, the Clean Core rules, and the testing and release process. I would also ask who handles UI, integration and production incidents. Three focused questions are usually better than a long technology checklist.

Reasoning and example
Choose questions that affect your daily work: Which editions and releases do you support? What would I build or maintain in the first few months? How does a change move from development to production? These invite concrete answers about the role, rather than only a list of products.

Then follow one answer with a practical example: Can you describe a recent Clean Core decision or a difficult production issue and how the team handled it? Listen for ownership, review and testing responsibilities. The title ABAP Developer can cover maintenance, new services or migration work. Use the discussion to understand the actual job and compare it with your real experience and learning goals.

Avoid
Do not assume the role title tells you whether the work is maintenance, migration or new development.
Explain decisions with evidence

Practice a 60-second version first, then expand the mechanism and evidence when prompted.
Explain it: Can you name the decision, trade-off and evidence without inventing metrics?

column1: STORY-07 | How do you estimate an ABAP or RAP task when some requirements are still unclear?
column2:
Short answer
First agree what finished means, then split the work into small parts. Compare familiar parts with similar completed work and estimate them from the bottom up. Use a range for uncertain parts and a short investigation for the biggest unknown. Include testing, review and delivery. Effort in person-days is not the same as a calendar deadline.

Reasoning and example
Suppose the task is a RAP Submit action. A teaching example for the most likely effort is: clarify the API and rules, 0.5 day; implement the action, 1 day; authorization and validation, 1 day; automated and integration tests, 1 day; review and handoff, 0.5 day. That is 4 person-days under the stated assumptions. These are illustrative numbers, not standard durations for RAP work. Waiting for an API owner or a test system affects the delivery date separately.

Choose the technique for the information available. Analogy compares a genuinely similar completed task and adjusts for differences. Bottom-up estimation adds the work packages. Three-point estimation records optimistic, most likely and pessimistic cases, for example 2, 4 and 8 person-days. Explain what causes each case; these values are not guaranteed bounds or a promised probability. Planning Poker helps a team compare relative size and discuss different assumptions. Story points are not a fixed number of hours and should not be used to compare developer productivity.

If the key uncertainty is whether an API supports the required save behavior, time-box a small spike before committing to a delivery forecast. Agree its question, owner and time limit. Record assumptions, exclusions, dependencies and acceptance checks, then update the estimate when evidence changes. Include the spike effort explicitly; do not hide it in an unexplained buffer. A date forecast also needs team availability, dependencies and the planned release window.

Avoid
Do not estimate only coding time, convert story points into fixed hours, or present an uncertain forecast as a guaranteed deadline.

Read and verify
  • SAP Activate: release planning and Planning Poker
    Supports acceptance criteria, backlog sizing and team discussion; the RAP work breakdown is an original teaching example.
  • PMI: Practice Standard for Scheduling, three-point estimates
    Section 3.4.4 describes optimistic, most likely and pessimistic durations. A range is not automatically a calibrated confidence interval.
  • Scrum.org: story-point estimation pitfalls
    Explains why fixed hour conversion and individual productivity comparisons misuse relative estimates.

column1: HTTP-01 | What is the difference between HTTP, REST, OData and a payload format?
column2:
Short answer
HTTP defines how requests and responses work. REST is a set of design rules for an API. OData adds rules for data services, such as querying related records. JSON and XML are formats for the data you send. Using JSON over HTTP does not, by itself, make an API RESTful.

Reasoning and example
An order app sends an HTTP GET request and receives a response with a status code. The response body might use JSON to describe order 4711. If the service uses OData, the client can use its supported query rules to request selected fields or related items. These choices describe different parts of the same call.

REST adds architectural rules, including stateless requests. Here, stateless means the request carries the context the server needs to understand it. It does not mean the server cannot store orders in a database. Keeping these ideas separate makes it easier to explain why a payload problem differs from a protocol or API-design problem.

Avoid
Do not use REST, HTTP and JSON as interchangeable names.
HTTP request and response anatomy

Read the method, target, status and headers before interpreting the body. The sample domain is deliberately non-production.
Explain it: Which header describes the returned body, and which requests a response format?
Limit: A teaching example, not a runnable endpoint. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 use different wire framing.

Read and verify

    Check the protocol or format rules here, separately from how the ABAP code implements them.
  • REST constraints: Fielding dissertation
    Check the protocol or format rules here, separately from how the ABAP code implements them.

column1: HTTP-02 | What is inside an HTTP request and response?
column2:
Short answer
An HTTP request contains a method, a target address, headers and sometimes a body. The response contains a status, headers and sometimes content. Headers carry information such as authentication or content type. HTTPS protects the connection, but the response still needs checking: a secure connection does not mean the business operation succeeded.

Reasoning and example
For an order update, I inspect the target order URL, the method and the fields in the body. I also check credentials, Content-Type and any If-Match version token. In the response, I examine both the status code and the returned data or error message. This shows whether the server accepted the requested business change.

For example, TLS can connect successfully while the server returns 403 because the user cannot change that order. I would then investigate permissions rather than the certificate. HTTP/1.1 is often shown as readable text for teaching; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry the same broad message concepts using different framing.

Avoid
A successful TCP/TLS connection does not prove that the business request succeeded.
HTTP request and response anatomy

Read the method, target, status and headers before interpreting the body. The sample domain is deliberately non-production.
Explain it: Which header describes the returned body, and which requests a response format?
Limit: A teaching example, not a runnable endpoint. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 use different wire framing.

column1: HTTP-03 | How do GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE differ?
column2:
Short answer
GET reads data. POST asks the target to process submitted content. PUT creates or replaces the identified resource's state, while PATCH applies a described change. DELETE asks to remove the target resource association. I follow the endpoint's documented meaning; these methods are not interchangeable labels for the same operation.

Reasoning and example
To change only an order's delivery note, I check whether the service supports PATCH and which patch format it accepts. Leaving a field out may mean keep its value, while sending null or an empty string may mean something different. The API contract decides those details. PUT should not be assumed to mean an arbitrary partial update.

POST might create an order or invoke a business action; it does not always insert one row. DELETE also does not promise physical erasure of every database record. Repeating PATCH is not inherently safe: setting a value can be repeatable, while an instruction to increment a value may change it again.

Avoid
PUT is not an arbitrary partial update, and POST does not always mean creating exactly one row.
JSON and XML: values and mapping

These are two explicitly designed representations of the same sample values, not a universal automatic JSON/XML conversion.
Explain it: What could go wrong if an ABAP mapper converts the identifier to an integer?
Limit: XML namespace/schema rules and JSON API types must be defined by the actual interface contract.

Read and verify
  • HTTP semantics: IETF RFC 9110
    Check the protocol or format rules here, separately from how the ABAP code implements them.
  • PATCH method: IETF RFC 5789
    Explains PATCH, how it differs from PUT and when repeating a particular patch can have the same intended effect.

column1: HTTP-04 | What do safe and idempotent mean, and how do they affect retries?
column2:
Short answer
Safe means the requested operation is read-oriented. Idempotent means repeating the same request has the same intended effect as doing it once. PUT and DELETE are idempotent by HTTP semantics, although their responses may differ. POST and PATCH need a specific guarantee before I repeat a business change after a timeout.

Reasoning and example
A client sends CreateOrder and times out before receiving a response. The server may already have saved the order. Sending a new request without checking could create a duplicate. I use a documented idempotency key, which identifies repeated attempts at the same request, or query the result using a stable business reference.

For DELETE, the first request might report success and the second might report that the resource is absent. That does not contradict idempotency: the intended final state is still that the resource is removed. Safe methods can also cause incidental logging; the key point is that the client did not request a business change.

For retryable failures, use a maximum attempt count, a total time limit and increasing delays with jitter: a small random spread prevents many clients from retrying at once. Respect Retry-After when supplied. Set connection and response time limits using the APIs available on the target platform. A timeout limits waiting; it does not prove that the receiver cancelled its work.

Do not blindly retry a potentially committed business creation because the response was lost.

column1: HTTP-05 | Which HTTP statuses should an ABAP API developer explain?
column2:
Short answer
I distinguish successful completion from acceptance for later processing: 200 is success, 201 creation, 202 accepted and 204 success without content. Common errors are 400 invalid request, 401 missing or invalid authentication, 403 refusal and 404 not found. I also know 409 conflict, 412 failed precondition and 415 unsupported content type.

Reasoning and example
A payment API returns 202. I cannot tell the user that payment has finished; I need the documented status check or callback to learn the final result. If an update returns 412, I investigate the stale version condition instead of treating it as a server outage. The error body often explains more than the status alone.

For 429 or 503, the contract may allow a delayed, bounded retry, sometimes using Retry-After. I still consider whether the original operation might have succeeded. A 500 needs diagnosis too. I keep a correlation ID for support without logging credentials, and inspect inner results when a batch envelope returns HTTP 200.

A 413 Content Too Large response means the request content exceeds what the server is willing or able to process. Reduce or split the payload only if the API supports it; sending the same oversized request repeatedly is not a useful default. Distinguish this from 429 Too Many Requests, where the issue is request rate rather than the size of one payload.

Avoid
HTTP 200 on a batch envelope does not prove every contained operation succeeded.
