column1: HTTP-06 | How do Accept and Content-Type differ?
column2:
Short answer
Content-Type says what format a message actually contains. Accept says which response formats the client can understand. A client can send JSON and ask for JSON back, but those are two separate settings. I check the actual response type before parsing it, especially when the call fails.

Reasoning and example
An app sends a JSON order with Content-Type: application/json and Accept: application/json. If the endpoint only accepts a different request format, it can return 415. If it cannot provide an acceptable response format, it can return 406. These are format problems, not automatically password or authorization problems.

An intermediary might return an HTML error page instead of the expected JSON. Trying to parse that page as an order produces a confusing second error. I therefore inspect the status and response Content-Type first. Merely changing the header from XML to JSON does not convert the body; the serialized data must actually match the declared format.

column1: HTTP-07 | What must you preserve when mapping JSON to ABAP?
column2:
Short answer
I preserve field names, data types and the meaning of missing values. JSON distinguishes an absent property, null and an empty string; an ABAP update may need to distinguish them too. Arrays keep their order, but object-property order is not a reliable contract. I also protect number precision and identifiers with leading zeros.

Reasoning and example
An external customer ID is "0004711". If I read it as a number, the leading zeros disappear, so the contract should treat it as a string. For an amount, I preserve the agreed decimal precision and currency. Whether that amount is sent as a JSON number or string depends on the API.

A PATCH request with no Phone property might leave the phone unchanged, while Phone set to null might clear it. Mapping both to the same initial ABAP value can destroy that distinction. JSON itself has no native date type, comments, NaN or Infinity. I also avoid relying on duplicate object-property names because parsers may handle them differently.

Avoid
Treating missing and null fields as the same initial ABAP value can accidentally change or clear data.

column1: HTTP-08 | What XML concepts matter in an integration interview?
column2:
Short answer
XML represents data with elements, attributes and nested content. Well-formed XML follows syntax rules; schema validation checks further rules about its structure and values. Namespace prefixes are aliases, so I identify names using the namespace URI and local name. I use a real XML parser rather than splitting the text by hand.

Reasoning and example
One partner sends a:Order and another sends b:Order. If both prefixes refer to the same namespace URI, they can identify the same element name. A parser that only looks for the literal text a:Order would wrongly reject the second message. The namespace URI plus the local name Order identifies what the element means.

A default namespace applies to unprefixed elements, not unprefixed attributes. I also check how the contract distinguishes a missing element, an empty element and an explicit schema-defined nil value. Encoding, escaping and secure parser settings matter. Valid XML syntax alone does not prove that the order contains a valid customer or amount.

column1: HTTP-09 | How do you choose ABAP JSON and XML processing tools?
column2:
Short answer
I choose a parser, serializer or transformation allowed in the target ABAP environment. The tool must produce the partner's actual format and handle bad input clearly. CALL TRANSFORMATION, sXML and JSON libraries serve different needs. I test real sample payloads and check release status; a familiar classic helper may not be allowed in ABAP Cloud.

Reasoning and example
A partner expects a small JSON object with its own property names. The identity transformation can produce canonical ABAP formats such as asJSON or asXML, but that is not automatically the partner's format. I check the output and choose a supported mapping approach that matches the contract, including numbers, missing values and errors.

For a very large XML file, a streaming parser can process sections without loading the whole document into a DOM tree. I compare that with the navigation needs of the task. I never build XML or JSON by simply joining unescaped user values into strings, because quotes and special characters can corrupt the message.

column1: HTTP-10 | How would you implement and troubleshoot an outbound HTTP call in ABAP?
column2:
Short answer
I use an allowed destination and HTTP client, with credentials stored in configuration. I send the documented request, set a timeout and handle connection failures separately from HTTP error responses. Then I parse and validate the response. Retries need an explicit rule, because the remote system may have saved a change before the connection failed.

Reasoning and example
An outbound supplier call fails. I first locate the failing step: name resolution, TLS trust, destination configuration, authentication or the application request. If I receive HTTP 400 with a useful error body, repeatedly changing the certificate is unlikely to help. I compare the headers and payload with the API contract instead.

In ABAP Cloud, I use the released client and destination APIs and the communication setup supported by that environment. Classic systems may use different APIs. Logs should help find the request without exposing passwords, tokens or sensitive business data. I also verify the retry policy: rolling back the local transaction does not undo a remote commit.

If users can configure the target URL, also consider SSRF: the server could be tricked into calling an unintended internal or privileged endpoint. Prefer approved destinations and allowlisted targets. Revalidate redirects or disable them as the client permits; validating only the original hostname is insufficient. Keep network restrictions and credential scope aligned with the destination.

Avoid
Do not hard-code a password, suppress all exceptions, or assume a remote call shares the local rollback.

column1: HTTP-11 | How do authentication, authorization, CORS and CSRF differ?
column2:
Short answer
Authentication answers who is calling; authorization answers what they may do. CORS controls which cross-origin responses browser scripts can access. CSRF defenses help stop forged requests that misuse browser credentials in relevant flows. These protections solve different problems. Allowing an origin does not give its users permission to approve an order.

Reasoning and example
The same API call works from an ABAP backend but fails from a browser app hosted on another origin. I inspect the browser's CORS error and any preflight request. The backend call is not subject to the browser's CORS enforcement in the same way, so its success does not prove that the browser configuration is correct.

After fixing CORS, a user may still receive an authorization error when approving an order. That check must remain. In a session-based browser flow, the endpoint may also require CSRF protection for writes. CORS is neither a general server-to-server firewall nor a replacement for authentication, authorization or the applicable CSRF defenses.

Avoid
CORS is not a general server-to-server firewall or a replacement for authentication.

column1: HTTP-12 | How would you test an HTTP integration contract?
column2:
Short answer
I test what the integration does, not just whether it can send JSON. Cases include bad input, missing values, business errors, expired credentials and timeouts. I also test repeated requests and conflicting updates. Controlled doubles help reproduce failures, but a real integration test must check the actual destination, identity and partner behavior.

Reasoning and example
For an order creation API, I test a normal order, an invalid customer and a price that needs exact decimal handling. I also simulate a lost response after creation. Recovery should find or safely reuse the first result rather than create a second order. A wrong Content-Type or malformed body should produce a clear error.

I use a test double to make these failures repeatable, then run authorized tests against the real endpoint for TLS, authentication, serialization and permissions. The evidence includes a redacted request, correlation ID and final business outcome. Serializing an object and reading it back locally does not prove the partner accepts that representation.

Avoid

column1: HTTP-13 | How do you send a GET request with released ABAP HTTP APIs?
column2:
Short answer
First configure an approved connection. Resolve an IF_HTTP_DESTINATION, create a client with CL_WEB_HTTP_CLIENT_MANAGER, set the path and headers, then execute GET. Check the status before using the response body. Close the client after success or failure, and keep connection errors separate from HTTP error responses.

Reasoning and example
For example, read order 4711 from a partner API. A custom communication scenario contains the HTTP outbound service. An administrator configures the communication system and arrangement with the host and authentication. CL_HTTP_DESTINATION_PROVIDER=>CREATE_BY_COMM_ARRANGEMENT resolves that setup; passwords stay out of the program. This method is for your developed scenario, not an arbitrary SAP-delivered scenario. Newer supported systems also offer communication targets, which SAP now recommends.

The code cards separate connection setup from the GET operation. This example expects HTTP 200 and JSON. A received 404 means the resource was not found; a client exception means the call itself failed. After a 200, verify the content type and required fields rather than assuming every body is valid order data. Close the client in either case and report any cleanup failure separately. Adapt the path, timeout and success contract to the real endpoint.

Avoid
A configured destination does not prove that the remote business user has permission. A returned HTTP response does not prove that the request succeeded.

column1: HTTP-14 | How do you change remote data safely with PATCH or POST from ABAP?
column2:
Short answer
Follow the API contract: choose the method and body format, use its authentication, and fetch a CSRF token if required. For a versioned update, send the ETag you actually read in If-Match. Inspect the response, close the client on every path, and treat a timeout as an unknown outcome. Do not automatically repeat a business change.

Reasoning and example
Suppose order 4711 has an ETag from a successful GET. The PATCH example changes only its note. This fictional endpoint accepts JSON Merge Patch, fetches a CSRF token with HEAD, and uses cookies. Keep the same HTTP client for the token and the modifying request. SET_CSRF_TOKEN fetches and sets the token; If-Match separately prevents changing an obsolete version. A 412 response requires a fresh read and conflict handling, not replacing the ETag with *.

For this API, 200 or 204 confirms the completed update; 204 has no body to parse. A 202 response, if the real API supports it, means work was accepted and still needs tracking. A POST to create an order instead needs its documented create payload and success result, often a 201 with Location. A lost response does not prove that either operation failed: reconcile by a stable business reference or use the API's documented duplicate protection. Local ROLLBACK cannot undo a completed remote save.

CSRF is not required by every API, and HEAD-based token fetching is not universal. Follow the service's documented flow. Raw JSON Merge Patch rules are not automatically OData PATCH rules; use the real media type, entity metadata and ETag contract.

Avoid
CSRF token, ETag and an idempotency key are not interchangeable: they address request-session protection, concurrent updates and duplicate attempts respectively.

column1: RFC-01 | How does a function module differ from an ABAP method?
column2:
Short answer
A function module is a procedure in a function group; modules in that group can share state. A method belongs to a class or interface and fits object-oriented design. I usually put new business rules in testable classes. Existing function modules can remain as required API or framework entry points and call those classes.

Reasoning and example
An integration already calls a function module to calculate an order charge. I can keep that public interface and move the calculation into a class with clear inputs and outputs. The function module then passes the request to the class and returns the result. Existing callers keep working, while unit tests can exercise the calculation directly.

I still check the function module's actual attributes. A normal function module is not automatically remote-enabled or an update module; those are different execution models. Moving code into a method also does not make it stateless, remotely callable or released for ABAP Cloud. Those properties need their own design and checks.

Avoid
A method is not automatically stateless, remotely callable or released for ABAP Cloud.

column1: RFC-02 | How do synchronous, asynchronous, transactional, queued, and background RFC differ?
column2:
Short answer
sRFC waits for a reply; aRFC lets the caller continue and collect results later. tRFC records a unit for processing after commit, with durable retry. qRFC adds ordering through queues, while bgRFC supports transactional and queued units with newer infrastructure. I choose by response, retry and ordering needs, within the target system's supported options.

Reasoning and example
A tRFC call is first registered in the current SAP LUW. COMMIT WORK triggers processing of that registered unit; ROLLBACK WORK removes the current registrations. The registration itself is not proof that the receiver has finished. sRFC and aRFC do not provide that same durable retry model.

The documented unit guarantees are Exactly Once for tRFC and bgRFC type T, with ordering in the configured scope for qRFC and bgRFC type Q. That does not guarantee one business effect across an entire distributed process: two separate submissions may still create two orders. bgRFC is the successor technology. I let the runtime manage the unit's transaction and do not assume unrelated queues share one global order.

STARTING NEW TASK does not provide durable message retry. Separate queues do not automatically have one shared processing order.

column1: RFC-03 | What is the difference between a BAPI and an RFC-enabled function module?
column2:
Short answer
RFC is a mechanism for calling remote-enabled function modules. A BAPI is a business API, traditionally implemented by such a module for a business object or interface. A remote-enabled module is not automatically a BAPI. I check the particular API's business rules, return messages, transaction handling and release status before using it.

Reasoning and example
A classic integration may call a BAPI to create a sales order. The BAPI defines the business input, supported behavior and returned messages; RFC provides the remote call mechanism. A custom remote-enabled utility function has the mechanism too, but that alone does not give it a BAPI business contract.

Release status is another separate question. A BAPI supported in a classic integration may not be released for direct ABAP Cloud use. A modern released business API may use HTTP or OData instead of a classic BAPI. I therefore check the target development model and Clean Core classification rather than infer them from the name or remote-enabled flag.

column1: RFC-04 | When should BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT or BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK be called, and what does WAIT mean?
column2:
Short answer
The code that owns the BAPI transaction decides when to commit or roll back after checking the business results. For a remote BAPI, transaction control must reach the correct remote context. WAIT requests completion of high-priority updates; it does not wait for every later workflow or interface. I also check the specific BAPI's documented exceptions.

Reasoning and example
A client calls two BAPIs that are meant to form one transaction. It checks their relevant return messages and exceptions before asking the correct transaction context to commit. If the operation fails, it follows the documented rollback path. A local COMMIT WORK is not a way to commit an unrelated remote session.

After BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT with WAIT, I check the commit result as well. Downstream messages, lower-priority work or workflows may still be pending. Some documented legacy BAPIs commit internally, so I verify the actual API behavior before combining calls. Inside RAP behavior code, inserting this commit function is not a permitted shortcut around framework transaction ownership.

column1: RFC-05 | Does a remote call participate in the caller's local SAP LUW?
column2:
Short answer
I do not assume that the caller and remote system share one rollback. Remote execution has its own context, and each side's transaction owner must be clear. Calls that must share a remote transaction need the correct session handling. If the remote side has already committed, local rollback cannot undo it; recovery needs an explicit business step.

Reasoning and example
A program remotely creates a document, then fails while recording its local reference. If the remote document was committed, rolling back the caller leaves that document in place. The program must find it using a stable reference and either complete the local record or use a supported cancellation process. Sending another creation request may duplicate it.

For two remote BAPI calls intended to commit together, I use the connector's supported transaction context and send transaction control to that context. Reusing a destination name alone is not a complete session design. An aRFC worker also cannot simply inherit the caller's uncommitted transaction buffer or memory.

column1: RFC-06 | How would you collect results from CALL FUNCTION STARTING NEW TASK?
column2:
Short answer
I start each aRFC call with a task ID and an end-of-task callback. In the callback, RECEIVE RESULTS FROM FUNCTION collects the result and handles communication or system errors. I track which tasks started, completed, failed or timed out. Starting a task successfully only proves dispatch, not that its business work succeeded.

Reasoning and example
A coordinator splits six invoices into three packages of two and launches remote-enabled function calls with STARTING NEW TASK within its concurrency limit. Each task ID points back to its package. CALLING or PERFORMING ON END OF TASK registers the callback, which uses RECEIVE RESULTS FROM FUNCTION to collect the output and record the outcome.

Package three may finish before package one, so I never match results by arrival order. The caller must stay alive and allow callbacks to run, using an appropriate bounded wait where needed. I also handle tasks that never return in time. The usual synchronous IMPORTING pattern is not how an aRFC caller receives its eventual results.

column1: RFC-07 | How do you prevent parallel RFC processing from exhausting resources?
column2:
Short answer
I limit how many tasks can run at once and give each task a useful-sized package. In classic ABAP, DESTINATION IN GROUP can use a configured RFC server group. Resource availability can change, so I handle RESOURCE_FAILURE and reduce or delay dispatch. I measure the result: more parallel tasks can increase waiting and make the job slower.

Reasoning and example
A report needs to process 100,000 independent records. Starting one task per record wastes resources. I choose packages large enough to justify call overhead, use the agreed RFC group and cap outstanding tasks. RZ12 defines the relevant groups in classic systems, and SPBT_INITIALIZE can help inspect currently available resources.

That resource count is only a snapshot, not a reservation. If dispatch fails because capacity disappeared, the coordinator must throttle or retry within a limit. I also measure locks and database load. A background coordinator may start aRFC workers in dialog work processes, so its own job type does not mean every worker uses a background process.

column1: RFC-08 | Why are WAIT and implicit database commits important in parallel processing?
column2:
Short answer
WAIT is not always a harmless pause. Classic WAIT can cause a database commit, so I avoid placing it around unfinished writes or an open database cursor without checking the exact rules. RFC boundaries can matter too. A database commit does not mean every update task or remote business operation has completed successfully.

Reasoning and example
A coordinator writes some rows and then waits for parallel workers. If that wait causes an unexpected database boundary, the program may save part of its work earlier than intended. An open database cursor can also be affected. I therefore design the commit boundaries before dispatch and waiting instead of relying on timing to make the program work.

Workers should receive self-contained input rather than depend on the caller's pending writes or transaction buffer. COMMIT WORK AND WAIT, WAIT UNTIL and collecting an aRFC callback solve different problems. I check the exact statement and framework context; neither 'RFC never commits' nor 'every RFC commits the whole business transaction' is a safe general rule.

column1: RFC-09 | How would you design parallel workers that can be restarted safely?
column2:
Short answer
Each worker needs a clear package, transaction boundary and restart rule. I use stable business keys so a retry can find work already completed. Different workers should avoid changing the same locked object at the same time. After a timeout, I check the actual business result rather than assume the package failed and run everything again.

Reasoning and example
Six workers process six packages. Five report success and the sixth times out. Restarting all six could repeat work that already committed. I record completed, pending and uncertain outcomes and use stable references to locate each package's business documents. Independent worker commits mean the overall job can be partly complete.

There is a harder case: the sixth worker saved its document but failed before recording completion. A package status alone cannot prove that nothing happened. Recovery must check the business effect or use a documented idempotent operation. I also test two packages that accidentally contain the same object, because lock contention can remove the benefit of parallel processing.

For a custom work queue, define how two workers claim one item atomically. One design is to lock the item, re-read its pending state, record the owner and claim, then release the lock under a documented transaction boundary. Every worker must follow that protocol. Recovery of an abandoned claim must check whether the original worker is still active and whether its business effect already exists; an expired timer alone must not authorize duplicate processing.

Avoid
Separately committed workers are not one all-or-nothing transaction. Extra workers can also make lock contention worse.

column1: RFC-10 | How do you schedule and troubleshoot a classic background job?
column2:
Short answer
In a classic system, I schedule job steps, variants, user and start conditions, commonly in SM36. In SM37, I inspect status, job log, steps and spool. I then follow application errors or dumps. A nightly posting job is canceled halfway through its input. I inspect the job log and application records to find the last confirmed business results. The rerun must use a stable selection and avoid posting the completed records again. If the job is periodic, I also check whether the next run could overlap with recovery.

Job states such as scheduled, released, ready, active, finished and canceled describe execution progress. Finished only means the job completed technically; the report may still have rejected individual business records. I reconcile accepted and failed records and define who handles missed runs, authorization errors and unavailable external systems.

Short answer

I test both temporary technical failures and permanent business errors using realistic volumes. column1: INTF-01 | What does an IDoc contain, and how do message type, basic type, and extension differ?
column2:
Short answer
An IDoc has control data, business data in segments and a processing-status history. The message type says what business message it represents. The basic type defines the standard structure, and an extension adds supported customer segments. Sender and receiver must agree on these parts; adding a segment definition does not automatically fill or process its values.

Reasoning and example
An order message needs an extra customer reference. I check whether a supported IDoc extension is appropriate, then arrange for the sender to fill the new segment and the receiver to understand it. Middleware mappings may need an update too. Declaring the extension in configuration alone does not transfer the business value into the target order.

When diagnosing the message, the control record helps identify routing and structure, data records hold the actual values, and status records show processing progress. The technical IDoc number identifies that message. It is not automatically the number of the order created by the receiver, so I keep the business reference for correlation.

Avoid
Message type and basic type have different jobs. An IDoc number is also not automatically the target business document number.

column1: INTF-02 | What do ALE distribution models, partner profiles, ports, and process codes do?
column2:
Short answer
The ALE distribution model describes configured distribution relationships. A partner profile says how a partner's messages are handled. A port defines the technical communication mechanism, and an inbound process code selects processing logic. I check these settings together. An inbound order IDoc arrives, but the receiver cannot select the expected processing. I inspect the partner and message settings, then the assigned process code and application implementation. In a classic landscape, WE20 shows partner profiles and WE21 shows ports; BD64 is relevant where an ALE distribution model controls the scenario.

Not every interface uses the same model-driven routing. A logical or business partner identifies a participant, while a port and an RFC destination serve different technical roles. A successful connection test only proves part of the path. It does not prove that the right partner-profile entry matches or that the inbound processor can post this business data.

column1: INTF-03 | Walk through outbound and inbound IDoc processing.
column2:
Short answer
Outbound processing creates an IDoc from a business trigger, chooses a receiver and sends it through the configured channel. Inbound processing receives it and passes it to the appropriate application logic. Each stage records progress. Receiving the message is not the same as posting its business document, especially when processing waits for a background run.

Reasoning and example
A sales process produces an outbound order message. Depending on the scenario, the trigger may be application output, change pointers or an application API. The sender creates the IDoc and dispatches it. The receiver can store the incoming IDoc immediately but postpone application processing until a scheduled job runs.

I therefore track creation, dispatch, receipt and posting as separate milestones. If the sender says it dispatched the message, I still inspect the receiver's status and linked document. Immediate, collected and background settings affect timing. Sender and receiver may also use different technical IDs, so I correlate them using message context and business references rather than assume the numbers match.

column1: INTF-04 | How do you interpret common IDoc statuses without overstating success?
column2:
Short answer

Common inbound statuses are 51 for a posting error, 53 for a posted application document and 64 for pending application processing. Outbound 03 means the data reached the port. An outbound IDoc shows 03, while the customer says no order exists. That is possible: the sender has handed data to the port, but later transport or receiver processing may have failed. I follow the message into the receiver and inspect its status and application messages. Outbound 30 commonly means it is still ready for dispatch.

For an inbound 51, I read the error instead of guessing from the number alone. For 53, I verify the linked application document and any later business steps the requirement includes. Even a successful posting status does not prove that every downstream approval or delivery process has completed.

The sender shows dispatch, but no matching IDoc appears on the receiver. I first verify the search criteria, including partner and time range. column1: INTF-06 | How do you reprocess an IDoc without creating duplicate business documents?
column2:
Short answer
I correct the cause and check whether the business document already exists before reprocessing. Then I use the supported restart path for that message and status. After retry, I verify both the IDoc and the business result. Duplicate prevention needs a stable business reference or documented application rule, not blind trust in a technical message number.

Reasoning and example
An IDoc failed during order processing, but the outcome is unclear after a timeout. I search for the expected order using the external business reference before trying again. If it already exists, recovery must follow the documented process rather than create another order. Where appropriate and authorized, BD87 can reprocess the original IDoc.

Creating a test copy or sending a new message gives it a new technical identity. That can bypass duplicate checks that only remember the old IDoc number. I preserve the original history and correlation, then inspect the final status and linked document. Manually making a status look successful does not fix the failed business step.

column2:

A partner sends company code EXT01, but SAP expects 1000. Value mapping translates the code, while structure mapping puts it into the field expected by the target. I verify the configured engine and processing order rather than assume every AIF interface follows the same steps. I separately test users with different purchasing permissions through the real supported read path. SQLScript does not automatically reproduce ABAP SQL or CDS access checks. I also review return types, intended rows and USING dependencies. If supported CDS or ABAP SQL already solves the task, it may be simpler. column1: SQLX-02 | A report transfers one million item rows to ABAP to calculate totals. A rewrite uses AMDP but doubles amounts after a text join. Which implementation would you recommend?

Only after proving the totals do I compare alternatives using realistic data. I test missing texts, duplicate texts, different currencies and null values. column2:
Short answer
Git stores source history, and abapGit transfers supported development objects. Neither proves that the feature is deployed and usable. I choose the delivery route supported by the actual ABAP product, then verify the target version, activation, tests and configuration. A real service check must show that the intended user can work and a denied user cannot.

Reasoning and example
A pull request passes local lint, but the target system may still reject an object during activation or lack a required dependency. I link the source revision to the component versions, delivery identifiers and target import evidence. For BTP ABAP environment, supported transport/gCTS or add-on scenarios may apply; other ABAP Cloud products have their own delivery routes.

The target checks include syntax, activation, ATC, meaningful ABAP Unit tests and relevant integration tests. I also verify service access, communication setup and recovery ownership. Local lint is not SAP activation, and mocks do not prove real permissions. Technical identities and secrets stay out of Git. A source export alone is not a complete application deployment.

Avoid
An abapGit push is not a transport release, and gCTS is not another name for abapGit. Delivery routes differ across ABAP Cloud products.
Source transfer, delivery and verified runtime evidence

Four evidence layers answer different questions. A release links the reviewed and tested revision to an actual imported state, then verifies the target consumer and configuration.
Explain it: Which artifact proves what was imported, and what can fail after a successful import?
Limit: REV-42, D-17 and TST are fictional identifiers. The table is an evidence checklist, not a mandatory sequence requiring abapGit in every transport landscape.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How do you prove the target received the same source revision that was tested?
  • Which missing configuration can break an active service after a successful import?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates Git history, source transfer and deployment
  • Chooses the delivery route for the actual product
  • Requires target-system results and working configuration
Verification evidence
Record the commit, component and dependency versions, and delivery IDs. Keep target activation, ATC, test and import logs plus real allowed-user and denied-user service checks.

Read and verify

    Explains source transfer, supported object types and activation after import. Transferring source alone does not prove deployment.
  • SAP BTP ABAP environment: delivery via add-on or gCTS
    Explains these BTP ABAP environment delivery options and checks. Other ABAP Cloud products may use different routes.

column1: DEVCORE-01 | How do roles, authorization objects and AUTHORITY-CHECK work together?
column2:
Short answer
An administrator assigns roles that give a user the required authorizations. An authorization object groups the fields to check, such as activity and company. AUTHORITY-CHECK compares the requested values with the current user's authorizations. Check sy-subrc immediately: zero means success; any other result must stop the protected operation. The statement reports the result; your code must enforce it.

Reasoning and example
A user may display orders in company 1000 but cannot change them. Checking ACTVT 02 and BUKRS 1000 against the application authorization object fails for that user. The application must then reject the change before it writes anything. Checking display activity 03 would answer the wrong question.

The object and its fields must already exist and match the application security design. Read the organizational value from trusted data, not an unchecked client claim. Do not run another statement that changes sy-subrc before evaluating it. Test an allowed user and a denied user; a hidden button is not the check.

In classic AS ABAP, an administrator maintains authorizations in PFCG roles and generates authorization profiles for assigned users. SAP BTP ABAP environment uses IAM apps, business catalogs and business roles with appropriate restrictions. Administration depends on the product; PFCG is not a universal Cloud setup screen. A role named Approver does not by itself prove that the required field values are present.

In RAP, separately check service access, read restrictions through CDS DCL and operation permissions through global/instance authorization. These layers complement one another. An accessible Fiori tile does not automatically grant every order, and an allowed read does not permit Submit. ADV-02 and TEST-06 explain those boundaries further.

Avoid
AUTHORITY-CHECK only reports its result. Ignoring a nonzero sy-subrc leaves the protected operation open.

Read and verify
  • SAP Learning: AUTHORITY-CHECK
    Explains the object fields, immediate sy-subrc evaluation and the application responsibility to deny access. The custom object in the example is an explicit prerequisite.
  • SAP Learning: roles and authorization profiles
    Classic AS ABAP role administration; not a universal cloud procedure.
  • SAP BTP ABAP environment: authorization basics
    Business-user IAM apps, catalogs, roles and restrictions; read and operation checks remain distinct.

column1: DEVCORE-02 | When are ABAP Shared Objects useful, and how do you access them safely?
column2:
Short answer
In classic ABAP, Shared Objects can hold reusable objects in shared memory on an application server. They are useful for a read-heavy cache, not as a durable work queue. Define the area in SHMA, attach with the required access mode, and detach correctly. Plan rebuilding and invalidation so readers do not rely on stale data.

Reasoning and example
Suppose many sessions read the same tax configuration on server A. ATTACH_FOR_READ accesses an available area version. ATTACH_FOR_WRITE creates a new version; ATTACH_FOR_UPDATE copies the active version when versioning is enabled, or attaches to the active version without versioning. Release read handles with DETACH; finish changes using DETACH_COMMIT or discard them with DETACH_ROLLBACK. Handle missing versions and lock conflicts.

If configuration changes from version 4 to 5, readers need an invalidation and rebuild policy. Server B does not automatically share server A's memory contents. Restart or invalidation must not lose the only record of pending business work. DETACH_COMMIT concerns the area handle; it is not a general database COMMIT substitute, and transactional areas have additional rules. This is classic Standard ABAP guidance, not a promise of ABAP Cloud API availability.

Avoid
A cache is replaceable. Do not use application-server shared memory as the only durable record of messages or unfinished transactions.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Access to shared object area instances
    Describes read, write and update attachment and detachment. Versioning and transactional-area settings affect the lifecycle.
  • SAP: Shared Objects example
    Shows SHMA, the area root and a minimal create/read lifecycle in classic ABAP. Verify the target release and server scope.
  • SAP: Shared Objects introduction
    Defines shared memory on one application server and shared-memory-enabled classes.

column1: DEVCORE-03 | How do you page through changed records without skipping equal timestamps?
column2:
Short answer
Use a stable order with a tie-breaker, such as changed_at plus a unique ID. Continue after the last complete pair, not after the timestamp alone. Limit each page and keep a fixed upper boundary for the run. This avoids one common paging gap, but timestamps alone do not guarantee a complete or consistent delta feed.

Reasoning and example
Orders 7 and 9 both changed at 09:00; order 10 changed at 09:01. If a page ends at (09:00, 7), the next page must include (09:00, 9), then (09:01, 10). A condition changed_at > 09:00 would lose order 9. Use the same pair in the continuation condition and ORDER BY, and advance the extraction checkpoint after the page and continuation are durably staged atomically, or after downstream confirmation when no durable stage exists. Track staged delivery separately.

A transaction can receive a timestamp before it commits and become visible after the reader has passed that position. Rows may also change between pages. A fixed upper time does not create a database snapshot or capture deletions. For reliable extraction, prefer a supported delta or change-log contract; otherwise define overlap, deduplication, deletion handling and reconciliation from the source guarantees. The accompanying example illustrates ordering on fixed in-memory data only.

Avoid
A timestamp plus ID fixes ties, not late commits. Do not describe keyset paging alone as exactly-once delivery or a consistent snapshot.

Read and verify
  • SAP: ABAP SQL selection and ordering
    Documents ordered selection and row limits. The continuation example and late-commit analysis are a design exercise, not a documented universal SAP delta API.

column1: DEVCORE-04 | When do setup, class_setup and teardown run in ABAP Unit?
column2:
Short answer
setup runs before each test method; teardown runs afterwards. class_setup runs once before the class tests, and class_teardown once after them. Use setup for fresh mutable test data. Keep tests independent of execution order. RISK LEVEL HARMLESS describes the intended risk; it does not turn unsafe code into a sandbox.

Reasoning and example
Two tests check a total calculator. setup creates a new input table containing 40 and 60 before each test. One test expects 100. The other clears its input and expects 0. Because each gets fresh data, running the empty-input test first must not break the total test.

Use class_setup for an expensive shared test environment when appropriate, then reset its mutable data in setup. Destroy that environment in class_teardown and release per-test resources in teardown. The example needs no external cleanup because it only uses local memory. A real database write or remote call still needs deliberate isolation; the HARMLESS label does not intercept it.

Avoid
Do not make one test prepare data for another. Shared mutable fixtures and unsafe dependencies remain problems even with RISK LEVEL HARMLESS.

Read and verify
  • SAP: ABAP Unit fixtures and examples
    Describes the lifecycle methods and test isolation. The small total calculator is an original teaching fixture.
  • SAP: Test attributes
    Risk declarations control which tests may run; they are not an automatic isolation mechanism.

column1: DEVCORE-05 | How do logs, metrics and traces help explain a failing request?
column2:
Short answer
Logs describe individual events. Metrics summarize measurements, such as request counts and duration. Traces connect the stages of one request across components. Use them together: a metric reveals a pattern, a trace locates a slow stage, and a log explains a specific failure. Correlation IDs connect evidence without recording entire business payloads.

Reasoning and example
Request Q7 reads the database quickly, then its HTTP call times out and retries once. A log records the timeout and correlation ID. A retry counter increases by one. A trace with database and HTTP spans shows where the time went. Together they distinguish a slow remote dependency from slow SQL.

Keep metric dimensions bounded, such as operation and outcome; avoid a new series for every request ID. Put suitable IDs in logs or traces instead, with access controls and redaction. Distinguish event time from the time telemetry was observed or collected: delayed delivery must not make yesterday's failure look like today's new event.

Avoid
Logging every payload creates noise and can expose secrets. A request ID is useful for correlation but usually a poor metric dimension.

Read and verify
  • OpenTelemetry: Signals
    Defines the roles of logs, metrics and traces. The ABAP request scenario is an original example, independent of a particular monitoring product.
  • OpenTelemetry: Metrics
    Explains aggregated measurements and attributes; choose bounded dimensions for application metrics.
  • OpenTelemetry: Traces
    Explains spans and the request path; actual tracing support depends on the system instrumentation.
  • OpenTelemetry: Log timestamps
    Distinguishes the event Timestamp from ObservedTimestamp.
